ECON-SP-EASY-52.q: A tax cut usually shifts aggregate demand:
ECON-SP-EASY-52.commonError: Confusing tax cuts and tax increases.
ECON-SP-EASY-52.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption, shifting AD right.

options: higher government spending or lower taxes
lower government spending or higher taxes
a decrease in the money supply
LG-Q-49.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy

options: lower government spending or higher taxes
higher government spending or lower taxes
a decrease in interest on reserves only
LG-Q-50.commonError: confusing fiscal tightening with monetary tightening
LG-Q-50.feedback: Contractionary fiscal policy means lower government spending or higher taxes, which reduces aggregate demand.

LG-Q-51.q: An increase in government spending shifts aggregate demand
options: only downward along the same curve
not at all because G is not part of AD
LG-Q-51.commonError: forgetting that G is a component of aggregate demand
LG-Q-51.feedback: Government spending is part of aggregate demand, so an increase in G shifts AD right.

LG-Q-52.q: A decrease in taxes usually shifts aggregate demand
options: nowhere because taxes are not related to spending
LG-Q-52.feedback: Lower taxes raise disposable income, which can raise consumption and shift AD right.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-151.q: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Moving from AD1 to AD2 changes output from:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-151.feedback: At the same price level, output rises from Y1 to Y2 when AD shifts from AD1 to AD2.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-152.q: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Which curve shows the largest aggregate demand level?
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-152.commonError: Confusing curve position with label order.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-152.feedback: AD3 is farthest to the right, so it shows the largest AD at price level P.

LG-Q-164.q: Which policy is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: Selling government bonds by the Fed
LG-Q-164.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with Fed policy
LG-Q-164.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy uses higher government spending or lower taxes to raise aggregate demand.

LG-Q-165.q: Which policy is contractionary fiscal policy?
options: Buying government bonds by the Fed
LG-Q-165.commonError: confusing fiscal and monetary policy tools
LG-Q-165.feedback: Higher taxes are contractionary fiscal policy because they reduce disposable income and aggregate demand.

LG-Q-166.q: A tax cut shifts aggregate demand right mainly because it
options: forces banks to hold more reserves
LG-Q-166.commonError: thinking tax cuts work through bank reserves
LG-Q-166.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.

LG-Q-167.q: A cut in government purchases shifts aggregate demand left because
options: government spending is a component of aggregate demand
LG-Q-167.commonError: forgetting that G is directly part of AD
LG-Q-167.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD, so reducing G shifts AD left.

LG-Q-168.q: If Congress increases infrastructure spending during a recession, the direct effect is to
LG-Q-168.commonError: treating fiscal stimulus like contractionary policy
LG-Q-168.feedback: Higher infrastructure spending raises G and shifts AD right.

LG-Q-169.q: If the government raises taxes during an expansion, the likely AD effect is
LG-Q-169.feedback: Higher taxes reduce disposable income and consumption, shifting AD left.

P52A-FISCAD-H-001.q: Congress increases government purchases by $80 billion while households cut consumption by $50 billion for unrelated reasons. Before multiplier effects, the net direct change in aggregate demand is:
P52A-FISCAD-H-001.commonError: Adding changes without respecting their directions.
P52A-FISCAD-H-001.feedback: Government purchases add $80 billion while consumption subtracts $50 billion.

P52A-FISCAD-H-002.q: A $120 billion tax rebate is issued and households spend 65 percent of the added disposable income initially. What is the first-round consumption increase?
P52A-FISCAD-H-002.commonError: Using the MPS or the full tax cut as first-round consumption.

P52A-FISCAD-H-003.q: A government raises taxes and increases purchases by the same dollar amount. Which statement is most precise about the immediate AD effects?
options: The two actions must cancel exactly before behavior is considered.
Both actions shift AD right by the same amount.
Taxes enter AD directly as a negative component.
Purchases enter AD directly, while higher taxes reduce consumption indirectly.
P52A-FISCAD-H-003.commonError: Treating taxes as a direct component of aggregate demand.
P52A-FISCAD-H-003.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD; taxes work through disposable income and consumption.

P52A-FISCAD-H-004.q: A temporary tax cut is mostly saved because households expect it to be reversed next year. Compared with a tax cut that is mostly spent, the AD shift is:
P52A-FISCAD-H-004.feedback: A smaller consumption response weakens the tax cut’s effect on aggregate demand.

P52A-FISCAD-H-005.q: The government cuts purchases during a recession but also cuts taxes. Which conclusion is valid without knowing the magnitudes and household response?
options: The two policies always cancel exactly.
The net direction of aggregate demand is ambiguous.
P52A-FISCAD-H-005.commonError: Assuming one policy label determines the combined outcome.
P52A-FISCAD-H-005.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left, while a tax cut tends to shift it right; magnitudes matter.

P52A-FISCAD-H-006.q: A tax increase of $60 billion reduces consumption by $42 billion in the first round. The implied MPC is:
P52A-FISCAD-H-006.commonError: Dividing in the wrong direction or using the MPS.

ECON-SP-ELITE-345.q: A tax cut occurs while households expect future taxes to rise and save much of the extra income. What happens to the tax multiplier?
options: It is weaker than simple models predict
It shifts SRAS instead of AD
ECON-SP-ELITE-345.commonError: Assuming every tax cut creates the same consumption response.
ECON-SP-ELITE-345.feedback: If households save much of the tax cut, the increase in consumption and AD is weaker.

LG-Q-379.q: An economy faces a positive AD shock of $240 billion. If policymakers use a tax increase that reduces disposable income by $100 billion and MPC is 0.8, what is the first-round consumption reduction?
LG-Q-379.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
LG-Q-379.feedback: The first-round consumption reduction is MPC times the disposable income change: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

P52A-FISCAD-EL-001.q: A fiscal package raises government purchases by $120 billion and taxes by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, the package’s first-round effect on AD is:
P52A-FISCAD-EL-001.commonError: Ignoring that the tax increase reduces consumption by MPC times the tax change.
P52A-FISCAD-EL-001.feedback: Purchases add $120 billion; the tax increase reduces consumption by $80 billion.

P52A-FISCAD-EL-002.q: A tax cut is announced, but credit-constrained households spend 90 percent while high-income households spend 30 percent. Which feature matters most for the AD effect?
options: The long-run natural rate of output
Whether government purchases are counted in GDP
Only the statutory size of the tax cut
How the tax cut is distributed across groups with different marginal propensities to consume.
P52A-FISCAD-EL-002.commonError: Assuming every dollar of tax reduction produces the same consumption response.
P52A-FISCAD-EL-002.feedback: The aggregate consumption response depends on who receives the tax cut and how much they spend.

P52A-FISCAD-L-001.q: A government increases purchases by $50 billion and raises taxes by $50 billion. MPC is 0.75. Before subsequent multiplier rounds, the net first-round AD change is:
P52A-FISCAD-L-001.commonError: Assuming equal spending and tax changes have equal direct AD effects.
P52A-FISCAD-L-001.feedback: Purchases add $50 billion; the tax increase cuts consumption by $37.5 billion.

P52A-FISCAD-L-002.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $160 billion. Households spend 60 percent of the increase initially. If later rounds follow a simple spending multiplier of 2.5, the total AD increase before other offsets is:
P52A-FISCAD-L-002.commonError: Applying the multiplier to the full tax cut instead of the first-round consumption change.
P52A-FISCAD-L-002.feedback: First-round consumption rises $96 billion; multiplying by 2.5 gives $240 billion.

P52A-FISCAD-L-003.q: The government increases infrastructure purchases, but imports rise sharply because much of the equipment is purchased abroad. Relative to a package using domestic inputs, the increase in domestic aggregate demand is likely:
options: Leftward because any import increase reduces government purchases.
Identical because all government spending counts equally.
Smaller because part of the spending leaks into imports.
Larger because imports are part of domestic production.
P52A-FISCAD-L-003.commonError: Ignoring import leakage from domestic demand.
P52A-FISCAD-L-003.feedback: Spending on imports does not directly purchase domestically produced output.

P52A-FISCAD-L-004.q: A tax cut and transfer increase have the same budget cost. The transfer is targeted to households with a higher MPC. Which package is likely to shift AD more in the short run?
options: The broad tax cut regardless of spending behavior.
P52A-FISCAD-L-004.commonError: Ignoring differences in marginal propensity to consume.
P52A-FISCAD-L-004.feedback: More of the targeted transfer is likely to be spent, producing a larger initial consumption increase.

P52A-FISCAD-L-005.q: A government plans contractionary fiscal policy. Which combination most clearly supports that goal?
options: Higher government purchases and lower taxes.
Lower government purchases and higher taxes.
P52A-FISCAD-L-005.feedback: Lower purchases and higher taxes both push aggregate demand left.

P52A-FISCAD-L-006.q: A recessionary economy receives a temporary tax rebate. Households use half to repay debt, save one quarter, and spend one quarter. The immediate consumption channel equals:
P52A-FISCAD-L-006.commonError: Treating saving or debt repayment as immediate consumption.
P52A-FISCAD-L-006.feedback: Only the portion spent on current consumption directly raises the consumption component of AD.

PM2D2-FISCAD-L-001.q: A temporary $120 billion tax credit is split equally between two household groups. One group has MPC 0.90 and the other MPC 0.40. Before multiplier rounds or crowding out, what is the first-round change in aggregate demand from consumption?
PM2D2-FISCAD-L-001.commonError: Applies one MPC to the entire tax change even when recipient groups have different spending responses.
PM2D2-FISCAD-L-001.feedback: Compute each group’s first-round consumption response separately, then add them before considering later multiplier rounds.

PM2D2-FISCAD-L-002.q: Congress replaces $100 billion of government purchases with a $100 billion tax cut. Households have MPC 0.80. Holding other AD determinants fixed and looking only at the first round, what happens to aggregate demand?
options: AD is unchanged because the two fiscal changes are equal.
PM2D2-FISCAD-L-002.commonError: Treats equal-dollar spending and tax changes as having identical direct effects on aggregate demand.
PM2D2-FISCAD-L-002.feedback: Government purchases enter AD directly, while tax changes affect AD through the share of disposable income households spend.

LG-Q-277.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
LG-Q-277.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
LG-Q-277.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is MPC times disposable income: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

LG-Q-4006.q: Which policy combination is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: higher government spending or lower taxes
lower government spending or higher taxes
LG-Q-4006.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy
LG-Q-4006.feedback: Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxes. Expansionary fiscal policy raises G or lowers T.

LG-Q-4007.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $120 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
LG-Q-4007.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
LG-Q-4007.feedback: First-round consumption rises by MPC times the tax cut: 0.8 x $120 billion = $96 billion.

LG-Q-4008.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $120 billion. MPC = 0.8. If the first-round consumption increase enters the multiplier process, what is the total AD increase before crowding out?
LG-Q-4008.commonError: multiplying the full tax cut by the multiplier before applying MPC
LG-Q-4008.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is $96 billion. With MPC 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so AD rises $480 billion.

P52A-FISCAD-B1-001.q: Expansionary fiscal policy most directly includes:
options: Higher government purchases or lower taxes.
Lower government purchases or higher taxes.
P52A-FISCAD-B1-001.commonError: Confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy or private behavior.
P52A-FISCAD-B1-001.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government demand or supports private spending.

P52A-FISCAD-B1-002.q: Which fiscal action shifts aggregate demand left through lower disposable income?
P52A-FISCAD-B1-002.commonError: Reversing the effect of taxes on disposable income and consumption.
P52A-FISCAD-B1-002.feedback: A tax increase reduces disposable income and tends to reduce consumption.

options: A direct component of aggregate demand.
A direct component of short-run aggregate supply.
P52A-FISCAD-B1-003.commonError: Misplacing government purchases in the macro model.
P52A-FISCAD-B1-003.feedback: Government purchases are included directly in C + I + G + NX.

P52A-FISCAD-B2-001.q: A $100 billion tax cut with MPC 0.8 raises first-round consumption by:
P52A-FISCAD-B2-001.commonError: Using the MPS or multiplier too early.
P52A-FISCAD-B2-001.feedback: MPC times the tax cut gives the first-round consumption increase.

P52A-FISCAD-B2-002.q: A cut in government purchases shifts AD left because it directly reduces:
P52A-FISCAD-B2-002.commonError: Confusing an AD shift with an AS or banking change.
P52A-FISCAD-B2-002.feedback: Government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.

P52A-FISCAD-B2-003.q: A tax cut has a weak AD effect when households:
options: Save most of the increase in disposable income.
Face a high marginal propensity to consume.
Increase consumption by more than the tax cut.
P52A-FISCAD-B2-003.feedback: More saving means less immediate consumption and a smaller rightward AD shift.

LG-Q-9142.q: Refer to the multiplier graph. A $60 billion tax cut raises disposable income, and MPC = 0.75. What is the correct order of AD effects before crowding out?
options: Consumption first rises $45 billion, then the multiplier expands the AD shift to $180 billion.
AD first rises $60 billion, then the multiplier expands it to $240 billion.
Consumption first rises $15 billion, then AD rises $60 billion.
AD falls $45 billion, then the multiplier reduces it by $180 billion.
LG-Q-9142.commonError: multiplying the full tax cut by the spending multiplier without first applying MPC
LG-Q-9142.feedback: First-round consumption rises 0.75 x $60 billion = $45 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $180 billion.

P52A-FISCAD-LB-001.q: Government purchases rise $90 billion and taxes rise $60 billion. MPC is 0.75. What is the net first-round change in AD?
P52A-FISCAD-LB-001.commonError: Failing to distinguish the direct spending effect from the tax-induced consumption effect.
P52A-FISCAD-LB-001.feedback: Purchases add $90 billion; taxes reduce consumption by $45 billion.

P52A-FISCAD-LB-002.q: A $200 billion tax cut reaches two equal groups. One group spends 80 percent and the other spends 40 percent. What is the combined first-round consumption increase?
P52A-FISCAD-LB-002.commonError: Applying one group’s MPC to the entire tax cut.
P52A-FISCAD-LB-002.feedback: Each group receives $100 billion; spending rises $80 billion plus $40 billion.

ECON-SP-FISCAL-POLICY-AD-SHIFT-5041.q: Congress increases government purchases while taxes and other aggregate-demand determinants are unchanged. Which change should a student predict in the AD-AS model?
ECON-SP-FISCAL-POLICY-AD-SHIFT-5041.feedback: Government purchases and tax-induced consumption changes work primarily through aggregate demand in this Principles model.
ECON-SP-FISCAL-POLICY-AD-SHIFT-5041.commonError: Confuses a fiscal-policy change with an aggregate-supply shift.

ECON-SP-TAX-CUT-AD-5042.q: A $40 billion tax cut raises disposable income and MPC is 0.75. Before later multiplier rounds, how much does consumption increase?
ECON-SP-TAX-CUT-AD-5042.feedback: The first-round consumption effect equals the change in disposable income times MPC.
ECON-SP-TAX-CUT-AD-5042.commonError: Treats the full tax cut as immediate consumption.

LG-R-5048.commonError: Classifies fiscal policy from the state of the economy rather than from what government purchases and taxes actually do.
LG-R-5048.q: Congress lowers government purchases and raises taxes in the same bill to reduce excessive aggregate demand. How should the package be classified?
LG-R-5048.feedback: Classify the package from its fiscal actions: higher purchases/lower taxes are expansionary; lower purchases/higher taxes are contractionary.

LG-R-5049.commonError: Thinking fiscal expansion shifts AD left.
LG-R-5049.q: Higher government spending usually shifts AD:
LG-R-5049.feedback: Government spending is part of AD, so higher G shifts AD right.

LG-R-5050.commonError: Forgetting taxes work through disposable income and consumption.
LG-R-5050.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income.

LG-R-5051.commonError: Jumps from a tax change directly to total output without identifying the first spending channel.
LG-R-5051.q: Why can a tax cut shift aggregate demand to the right in the short run?
options: It raises disposable income, which can raise consumption spending.
It directly increases the money supply.
It directly lowers firms’ production costs and shifts SRAS right.
LG-R-5051.feedback: A tax change first changes disposable income, then consumption according to MPC, which shifts aggregate demand.

ECON-SP-FISCAL-POLICY-AD-SHIFT-6032.q: The government cuts spending during a recession. What happens to AD?
ECON-SP-FISCAL-POLICY-AD-SHIFT-6032.feedback: Lower government spending reduces aggregate demand.

ECON-SP-TAX-CUT-AD-6033.q: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption. What happens to AD?
ECON-SP-TAX-CUT-AD-6033.feedback: Higher consumption shifts aggregate demand right.

LG-B-6021.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
LG-B-6021.q: A tax cut produces an $80 billion first-round increase in consumption. Which next idea is needed to move from that first-round fiscal impulse to the larger total aggregate-demand effect?
options: The multiplier process traces additional income-and-spending rounds.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts by the same $80 billion.
The inflation tax converts the consumption increase into government revenue.
The natural rate of unemployment determines the tax cut directly.
LG-B-6021.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

ECON-SP-EASY-53.q: The multiplier effect means that government spending can shift AD by:
options: Less than the initial spending only
ECON-SP-EASY-53.feedback: The multiplier effect occurs when initial spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

ECON-SP-EASY-54.q: Crowding out occurs when fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces:
ECON-SP-EASY-54.feedback: Crowding out reduces private investment when fiscal expansion raises interest rates.

LG-Q-53.q: The multiplier effect occurs because an initial increase in spending
options: raises income and causes additional consumption spending
always raises interest rates enough to cancel itself completely
LG-Q-53.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the first round of spending
LG-Q-53.feedback: The multiplier effect happens because one person's spending becomes another person's income, causing additional consumption.

LG-Q-54.q: The marginal propensity to consume is the fraction of extra income that households
LG-Q-54.commonError: confusing MPC with the fraction saved
LG-Q-54.feedback: MPC is the fraction of extra income that households consume rather than save.

LG-Q-56.q: The simple spending multiplier is calculated as
LG-Q-56.commonError: using MPC itself as the multiplier
LG-Q-56.feedback: The simple spending multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

LG-Q-58.q: Crowding out occurs when expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates and reduces
LG-Q-58.commonError: thinking crowding out makes government spending disappear
LG-Q-58.feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment spending.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-147.q: If fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces investment, the final AD shift is likely:
options: Larger because crowding out amplifies it
Smaller because crowding out offsets it
Zero because fiscal policy cannot affect AD
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-147.commonError: Thinking the multiplier is never offset.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-147.feedback: Crowding out weakens the final effect of fiscal expansion on AD.

LG-Q-170.q: The multiplier effect exists because one person's spending becomes
options: a fall in money demand every time
LG-Q-170.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the initial spending increase
LG-Q-170.feedback: The multiplier works because spending becomes income, and some of that income gets spent again.

LG-Q-174.q: The movement from the first AD shift to the larger final AD shift represents
LG-Q-174.commonError: confusing the multiplier effect with monetary policy
LG-Q-174.feedback: The multiplier effect is the extra AD shift caused by income leading to additional consumption spending.

LG-Q-175.q: The initial shift in aggregate demand from higher government spending is followed by a larger shift because
options: higher income leads to additional consumption spending
interest rates always fall to zero
LG-Q-175.commonError: thinking only the first round of government spending matters
LG-Q-175.feedback: The first increase in spending raises income, which causes more consumption and a further AD shift.

LG-Q-176.q: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion because higher government spending can raise interest rates and reduce
LG-Q-176.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens fiscal stimulus
LG-Q-176.feedback: Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise.

LG-Q-177.q: Which situation would make the multiplier effect larger?
LG-Q-177.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
LG-Q-177.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, which makes the multiplier larger.

LG-Q-178.q: Which situation would make fiscal stimulus less powerful?
options: A high MPC with no interest-rate effect
A large initial increase in government spending
A high willingness to consume extra income
LG-Q-178.commonError: ignoring offsetting effects from interest rates
LG-Q-178.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal stimulus by reducing private investment.

ECON-SP-HARD-228.q: Refer to the AD multiplier graph. If government spending first shifts AD from AD1 to AD2, the multiplier effect is best shown by:
ECON-SP-HARD-228.commonError: Confusing the initial shift with the multiplied shift.
ECON-SP-HARD-228.feedback: The multiplier effect expands the initial AD shift farther right, from AD2 to AD3.

ECON-SP-HARD-229.q: Refer to the AD multiplier graph. If crowding out occurs after AD reaches AD3, the final AD position may move back toward:
ECON-SP-HARD-229.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of fiscal expansion, pulling the final effect back from AD3 toward AD2.

LG-Q-272.q: If the initial government spending increase shifts AD by $20 billion, why might the final shift be larger?
options: The spending raises income, which triggers additional consumption spending.
The spending lowers income, which reduces consumption.
The spending automatically reduces money supply.
The spending makes MPC equal zero.
LG-Q-272.commonError: thinking only the first spending round matters
LG-Q-272.feedback: The multiplier effect comes from income causing additional consumption, which pushes AD farther.

LG-Q-273.q: If MPC is higher, the distance between the initial AD shift and the final AD shift should
LG-Q-273.commonError: thinking a higher MPC weakens the multiplier
LG-Q-273.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, so the final AD shift is larger.

LG-Q-274.q: If expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates, which effect offsets part of the multiplier?
LG-Q-274.commonError: confusing crowding out with the multiplier effect itself
LG-Q-274.feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment, offsetting fiscal stimulus.

LG-Q-276.q: Which fiscal policy has the strongest predicted multiplier effect before crowding out?
options: MPC = 0.9 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.5 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.25 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.1 and government spending rises by $50 billion
LG-Q-276.commonError: thinking lower MPC creates a stronger multiplier
LG-Q-276.feedback: Higher MPC means a larger multiplier. MPC = 0.9 gives the strongest multiplier here.

ECON-SP-ELITE-319.q: Fiscal expansion raises AD through the multiplier, but interest rates rise and investment falls. Which description best fits the final result?
options: Initial AD shift partly offset by crowding out
SRAS shift fully offset by lower taxes
LRPC shift partly offset by higher inflation
Money demand shift fully offset by M1
ECON-SP-ELITE-319.commonError: Treating the multiplier as the final effect every time.
ECON-SP-ELITE-319.feedback: Fiscal expansion can be amplified by the multiplier but weakened by crowding out.

ECON-SP-ELITE-320.q: Refer to the multiplier graph. Government spending initially moves AD1 to AD2, the multiplier moves AD2 to AD3, and crowding out offsets part of it. The final effect is likely:
ECON-SP-ELITE-320.commonError: Ignoring crowding out after multiplier expansion.
ECON-SP-ELITE-320.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the multiplied AD increase, so the final shift may land between AD2 and AD3.

ECON-SP-ELITE-346.q: If government spending rises, MPC is high, and interest rates do not rise, which effect dominates?
ECON-SP-ELITE-346.commonError: Assuming crowding out always dominates fiscal policy.
ECON-SP-ELITE-346.feedback: A high MPC strengthens the multiplier, and little interest-rate increase means crowding out is weak.

ECON-SP-ELITE-347.q: If government spending rises, MPC is low, and interest rates rise sharply, which concern dominates?
options: Weak multiplier with strong crowding out
Strong multiplier with no crowding out
Money neutrality with no AD change
ECON-SP-ELITE-347.commonError: Ignoring both MPC size and interest-rate effects.
ECON-SP-ELITE-347.feedback: A low MPC weakens the multiplier, while higher rates crowd out private investment.

LG-Q-370.q: If government spending initially shifts AD right by $40 billion and MPC is 0.75, what is the total shift before crowding out?
LG-Q-370.commonError: using MPC as the multiplier instead of 1 divided by 1 minus MPC
LG-Q-370.feedback: With MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is 4. A $40 billion initial shift becomes $160 billion before crowding out.

LG-Q-371.q: If the initial AD shift is $30 billion and the final shift is $150 billion, what MPC is implied by the simple multiplier?
LG-Q-371.commonError: using final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
LG-Q-371.feedback: The multiplier is 150/30 = 5. If 1/(1-MPC)=5, then MPC = 0.8.

LG-Q-372.q: If the initial shift is $50 billion and MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.5, what happens to the final AD shift before crowding out?
options: It falls from $250 billion to $100 billion.
It rises from $100 billion to $250 billion.
It falls from $250 billion to $50 billion.
LG-Q-372.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
LG-Q-372.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so $250 billion. MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so $100 billion.

LG-Q-373.q: Suppose the multiplier would shift AD right by $200 billion, but crowding out reduces investment by $60 billion. What is the net shift?
LG-Q-373.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
LG-Q-373.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the multiplier effect. Net shift is $200 billion - $60 billion = $140 billion.

LG-Q-374.q: If policymakers expect the multiplier shift to close a recessionary gap exactly, but crowding out is stronger than expected, what is the likely result?
options: AD does not shift far enough right to fully close the gap.
AD shifts too far right because crowding out magnifies fiscal policy.
AD shifts left because government spending is not part of AD.
LG-Q-374.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens the fiscal multiplier
LG-Q-374.feedback: Stronger crowding out reduces the net AD shift, so stimulus may fall short.

LG-Q-376.q: If government spending rises by $60 billion, MPC is 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $50 billion, what is the net AD shift?
LG-Q-376.commonError: forgetting to apply the multiplier before subtracting crowding out
LG-Q-376.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so the gross shift is $240 billion. Subtract $50 billion crowding out for a net $190 billion.

LG-Q-377.q: A government spending increase raises income, consumption, and AD, but also raises interest rates and lowers investment. Which answer correctly names both effects?
LG-Q-377.commonError: treating all fiscal policy effects as multiplier effects only
LG-Q-377.feedback: The multiplier amplifies the AD increase; crowding out offsets part of it by reducing investment.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9023.q: A student says fiscal expansion raises AD and therefore can never crowd out investment. What is the best correction?
options: Fiscal expansion can raise AD while higher rates reduce private investment.
Fiscal expansion lowers rates because government borrowing reduces money demand.
Fiscal expansion shifts SRAS right because firms face lower costs.
Fiscal expansion eliminates the multiplier because taxes disappear.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9023.commonError: Thinking multiplier effects rule out crowding out.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9023.feedback: Fiscal expansion can increase AD, but rising interest rates can reduce investment and offset part of the effect.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9024.q: Refer to the aggregate-demand multiplier graph. AD moves from AD1 to AD2, then from AD2 to AD3, followed by a partial move back. Which interpretation fits?
options: Initial fiscal shift, multiplier expansion, then crowding out offset.
Initial monetary contraction, SRAS expansion, then LRPC adjustment.
Initial supply shock, expected price decline, then AD collapse.
Initial inflation tax, M1 expansion, then velocity collapse.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9024.feedback: Fiscal policy can shift AD right, the multiplier can push it farther, and crowding out can pull the final effect back.

LG-Q-9066.q: Government spending rises by $70 billion and MPC = 0.8. What is the correct order of AD shifts before crowding out?
options: AD first shifts right by $70 billion, then shifts farther right to a total of $350 billion.
AD first shifts right by $350 billion, then shifts back to $70 billion.
AD shifts left by $70 billion, then left by $350 billion.
AD does not shift because the multiplier only affects money demand.
LG-Q-9066.commonError: confusing the initial AD shift with the final multiplier shift
LG-Q-9066.feedback: The first AD shift is the direct $70 billion increase in G. With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so the final AD shift is $350 billion.

LG-Q-9067.q: Government spending rises by $60 billion and the final AD shift is $300 billion. What order of AD shifts and implied MPC fit these data?
options: AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts right first by $300 billion, then back to $60 billion; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts left first by $60 billion, then left by $300 billion; MPC = 0.2.
AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.6.
LG-Q-9067.commonError: treating final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of the multiplier
LG-Q-9067.feedback: The multiplier is $300/$60 = 5. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 5, then MPC = 0.8.

LG-Q-9068.q: Government spending rises by $40 billion. If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, how does the order of AD shifts change?
options: The initial AD shift stays $40 billion, but the final shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion.
The initial AD shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion, but the final shift stays $40 billion.
Both the initial and final AD shifts stay $40 billion.
The initial AD shift becomes $200 billion and the final shift becomes $80 billion.
LG-Q-9068.commonError: thinking same initial government spending creates same final AD shift regardless of MPC
LG-Q-9068.feedback: The initial shift is still $40 billion. With MPC = 0.5, multiplier is 2 and final shift is $80 billion. With MPC = 0.8, multiplier is 5 and final shift is $200 billion.

LG-Q-9073.q: Government spending rises by $100 billion and MPC = 0.6. Crowding out reduces investment by $75 billion. What is the correct order of AD effects?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $175 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out increases it to $325 billion.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $250 billion, then crowding out leaves $175 billion.
AD shifts right $100 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
LG-Q-9073.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it from the gross multiplier shift
LG-Q-9073.feedback: MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. The $100 billion initial shift becomes $250 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $175 billion.

PM2D2-MULT-L-001.q: Two governments each increase purchases by $60 billion. Economy A has MPC 0.80 and $100 billion of crowding out; Economy B has MPC 0.60 and $20 billion of crowding out. Using the simple multiplier and the stated offsets, which comparison is correct?
options: Economy A has a $200 billion net AD increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy B.
Economy A has a $300 billion net increase and Economy B has a $150 billion net increase because crowding out does not affect AD.
Economy B has a $200 billion net increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy A.
Both economies have the same $180 billion net AD increase because the initial spending changes are equal.
PM2D2-MULT-L-001.commonError: Compares gross multiplier effects without subtracting the private spending displaced by higher interest rates.
PM2D2-MULT-L-001.feedback: For the simplified model used here, compare each policy’s gross multiplier effect and then subtract its stated crowding-out offset.

PM2D2-MULT-L-002.q: Government purchases rise by $80 billion and MPC is 0.75. The observed net increase in aggregate demand is $230 billion after crowding out. Under the simple model used in this bank, how much of the gross multiplier effect was crowded out?
PM2D2-MULT-L-002.commonError: Uses the net AD shift as if it were the gross multiplier effect.
PM2D2-MULT-L-002.feedback: First compute the gross multiplier effect, then infer the crowding-out offset from the difference between gross and observed net AD.

ECON-SP-EASY-55.q: If the MPC is 0.75, the simple government purchases multiplier is:

ECON-SP-HARD-230.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion, MPC is 0.75, and crowding out offsets $100 billion, final AD rises by:
ECON-SP-HARD-230.commonError: Ignoring crowding out after applying the multiplier.
ECON-SP-HARD-230.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so $80 billion x 4 = $320 billion; minus $100 billion gives $220 billion.

ECON-SP-HARD-231.q: If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, the government purchases multiplier changes from:
ECON-SP-HARD-231.commonError: Using MPC itself as the multiplier.
ECON-SP-HARD-231.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so it rises from 2 to 5.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-146.q: If the government raises spending by $50 billion and the multiplier is 3, the first-pass AD increase before crowding out is:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-146.commonError: Using the spending change instead of multiplying it.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-146.feedback: The initial multiplier effect is $50 billion x 3 = $150 billion.

LG-Q-171.q: If MPC = 0.6 and income rises by $1,000, consumption rises by
LG-Q-171.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
LG-Q-171.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the change in income: 0.6 x $1,000 = $600.

LG-Q-172.q: If MPC = 0.6, the simple spending multiplier is
LG-Q-172.commonError: using MPC itself as the multiplier

LG-Q-173.q: If MPC = 0.8 and government spending increases by $50 billion, the simple multiplier predicts a total AD increase of
LG-Q-173.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
LG-Q-173.feedback: With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5. Total increase is 5 x $50 billion = $250 billion.

LG-Q-270.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the simple multiplier and total AD increase before crowding out?
LG-Q-270.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
LG-Q-270.feedback: Multiplier = 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4. Total AD increase = 4 x $80 billion = $320 billion.

LG-Q-271.q: If MPC = 0.9 and government spending increases by $25 billion, what is the simple multiplier effect on AD before crowding out?
LG-Q-271.commonError: using 0.9 as the multiplier instead of 10
LG-Q-271.feedback: With MPC = 0.9, the multiplier is 10. AD increases by 10 x $25 billion = $250 billion.

LG-Q-275.q: Suppose fiscal stimulus initially raises AD by $300 billion through the multiplier, but crowding out reduces investment by $80 billion. What is the net AD increase?
LG-Q-275.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
LG-Q-275.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the stimulus, so net AD rises by $300 billion - $80 billion = $220 billion.

LG-Q-55.q: If MPC = 0.8, then a $100 increase in income raises consumption by
LG-Q-55.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
LG-Q-55.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the income increase: 0.8 x $100 = $80.

LG-Q-57.q: If MPC = 0.75, the simple spending multiplier equals
LG-Q-57.commonError: dividing MPC by 1 instead of using 1 divided by 1 minus MPC

LG-Q-4009.q: Why can an initial increase in spending generate a larger total increase in aggregate demand?
options: raises income and causes additional consumption spending
LG-Q-4009.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the first spending round
LG-Q-4009.feedback: The multiplier happens because spending becomes income, and part of that income is spent again.

LG-Q-4010.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the gross AD shift before crowding out?
LG-Q-4010.commonError: using MPC instead of the multiplier
LG-Q-4010.feedback: MPC 0.75 gives multiplier 4. Gross AD shift is $80 billion x 4 = $320 billion.

LG-Q-4011.q: Government spending rises by $80 billion, MPC = 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $70 billion. What is the net AD shift?
LG-Q-4011.commonError: forgetting to subtract crowding out after applying the multiplier
LG-Q-4011.feedback: Gross AD shift is $320 billion. Subtract $70 billion of crowding out, leaving $250 billion.

P52B-S4-FMCO-B1-001.q: Households spend 75 cents of each additional dollar of disposable income. What does that imply?
options: The marginal propensity to save is 0.75, so the multiplier equals one.
The MPC is 0.75, so repeated spending creates a multiplier greater than one.
Crowding out must eliminate every later spending round.
P52B-S4-FMCO-B1-001.commonError: Confusing the marginal propensity to consume with the multiplier itself.
P52B-S4-FMCO-B1-001.feedback: An MPC of 0.75 means each spending round passes along 75 percent of added income, generating further rounds of expenditure.

P52B-S4-FMCO-B1-002.q: What is the central mechanism of crowding out?
options: Fiscal expansion lowers interest rates and increases private investment.
Higher government spending directly reduces the money supply.
A larger multiplier forces households to stop consuming.
Fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces some private investment spending.
P52B-S4-FMCO-B1-002.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate and investment effects of fiscal expansion.
P52B-S4-FMCO-B1-002.feedback: Government borrowing and stronger money demand can raise interest rates, discouraging private investment.

P52B-S4-FMCO-B1-003.q: Holding other factors constant, which change makes the simple spending multiplier larger?
options: A lower marginal propensity to save.
A higher marginal propensity to save.
A larger amount of crowding out.
A smaller initial change in government purchases.
P52B-S4-FMCO-B1-003.commonError: Treating more saving as a force that strengthens repeated spending rounds.
P52B-S4-FMCO-B1-003.feedback: A lower marginal propensity to save means a larger MPC, so more income is respent in each round.

P52B-S4-FMCO-B2-001.q: Government purchases rise by $20 billion and the MPC is 0.50. Ignoring crowding out, what is the predicted total increase in aggregate demand?
P52B-S4-FMCO-B2-001.commonError: Using the MPC itself as the multiplier or ignoring the repeated-spending process.
P52B-S4-FMCO-B2-001.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1 - 0.50) = 2, so a $20 billion increase produces a $40 billion gross shift.

P52B-S4-FMCO-B2-002.q: A fiscal package creates a gross $120 billion increase in aggregate demand, but higher interest rates reduce investment by $25 billion. What is the net shift?
P52B-S4-FMCO-B2-002.commonError: Adding the crowded-out investment to the gross effect rather than subtracting it.
P52B-S4-FMCO-B2-002.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the expansion: $120 billion minus $25 billion equals a $95 billion net increase.

P52B-S4-FMCO-B2-003.q: Why can an equal-dollar tax cut create a smaller initial aggregate-demand shift than an equal increase in government purchases?
options: Tax cuts always raise interest rates before households receive them.
Government purchases do not pass through the multiplier process.
Tax cuts reduce disposable income before they affect consumption.
Tax cuts are partly saved; government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.
P52B-S4-FMCO-B2-003.commonError: Assuming every dollar of a tax cut is spent immediately.
P52B-S4-FMCO-B2-003.feedback: Only the consumed portion of a tax cut enters the first spending round, whereas government purchases are direct expenditure.

LG-Q-9133.q: Government spending rises by $90 billion and MPC = 0.8. Crowding out reduces investment by $180 billion. What is the correct order of AD effects?
options: AD first shifts right $90 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $450 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $270 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $450 billion, then crowding out increases the shift to $630 billion.
AD first shifts left $90 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $450 billion, then crowding out leaves $270 billion.
AD shifts right only $90 billion because crowding out eliminates the multiplier.
LG-Q-9133.commonError: not following initial shift, multiplier shift, then crowding-out offset
LG-Q-9133.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5. The $90 billion initial shift becomes $450 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $270 billion.

LG-Q-9134.q: The initial government-spending shift is $100 billion and the final AD shift is $400 billion. What MPC is implied, and what is the correct shift order?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then to $400 billion; MPC = 0.75.
AD first shifts right $400 billion, then back to $100 billion; MPC = 0.75.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then left $400 billion; MPC = 0.25.
AD first shifts right $100 billion, then to $400 billion; MPC = 0.8.
LG-Q-9134.commonError: treating final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
LG-Q-9134.feedback: The multiplier is 400/100 = 4. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 4, MPC = 0.75.

LG-Q-9141.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. Expansionary fiscal policy also raises interest rates through crowding out. What happens to investment if both effects occur?
options: Investment falls from both interest-rate channels.
Investment rises from both interest-rate channels.
Investment rises from the money-demand channel but falls from crowding out.
Investment is unaffected because r is not connected to investment.
LG-Q-9141.feedback: Higher money demand raises r. Crowding out also raises r. Higher r reduces investment.

ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SPENDING-MULTIPLIER-50.q: If MPC = 0.5, the government purchases multiplier is:

ECON-SP-CROWDING-OUT-EFFECT-5045.q: Crowding out happens when fiscal expansion raises rates and reduces:
ECON-SP-CROWDING-OUT-EFFECT-5045.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion by reducing private investment.

ECON-SP-FISCAL-POLICY-MAGNITUDE-5071.q: Why might a tax cut have a smaller immediate effect than an equal increase in government purchases?
options: Households may save part of the tax cut
Government purchases are not part of GDP
ECON-SP-FISCAL-POLICY-MAGNITUDE-5071.feedback: Some of a tax cut is saved, so its initial spending effect can be smaller than direct government purchases.

ECON-SP-MULTIPLIER-EFFECT-5043.q: The multiplier effect means an initial spending increase can raise AD by:
options: Only less than the initial spending
ECON-SP-MULTIPLIER-EFFECT-5043.feedback: The multiplier occurs when spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

ECON-SP-READ-MULTIPLIER-GRAPH-5090.q: The multiplier effect means an initial increase in government spending can:
options: Create a larger total increase in aggregate demand and output
Affect only the first recipient of spending
Reduce GDP by the same amount
ECON-SP-READ-MULTIPLIER-GRAPH-5090.feedback: Initial spending becomes income for others, whose further spending magnifies the total effect.

LG-R-5052.feedback: The multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

LG-R-5053.commonError: Using MPC directly as the multiplier.

LG-R-5054.commonError: Adding crowding out instead of subtracting it.
LG-R-5054.q: Crowding out reduces the effect of fiscal expansion by reducing:
LG-R-5054.feedback: Crowding out happens when higher interest rates reduce private investment.

LG-R-5055.commonError: Adding the crowding-out amount to the multiplier effect.
LG-R-5055.q: If gross AD rises $200 billion and crowding out is $50 billion, net AD rises:
LG-R-5055.feedback: Crowding out subtracts from the gross effect: $200 - $50 = $150 billion.

ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SPENDING-MULTIPLIER-60.q: If MPC = 0.8, the government purchases multiplier is:

ECON-SP-CROWDING-OUT-EFFECT-6036.q: Fiscal expansion raises interest rates. Which part of spending is most likely crowded out?
ECON-SP-CROWDING-OUT-EFFECT-6036.feedback: Higher interest rates reduce private investment.

ECON-SP-MULTIPLIER-EFFECT-6034.q: Government spending rises by $20 billion and the multiplier is 3. Before crowding out, AD rises by:
ECON-SP-MULTIPLIER-EFFECT-6034.feedback: The multiplier effect is $20 billion x 3 = $60 billion.

LG-B-6022.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
LG-B-6022.q: Government purchases rise $50 billion and MPC is 0.75. Which statement correctly connects the fiscal action to the multiplier concept?
options: The $50 billion first-round AD impulse is magnified to $200 billion before any crowding-out offset.
The $50 billion first-round impulse remains $50 billion because later spending rounds do not affect AD.
The multiplier reduces the initial AD impulse to $37.5 billion.
The fiscal action shifts LRAS rather than aggregate demand.
LG-B-6022.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

LG-B-6023.commonError: Carries the gross fiscal impulse into stabilization analysis even after an offset has been specified.
LG-B-6023.q: A fiscal package generates a $300 billion gross AD increase, but crowding out reduces private investment by $80 billion in the simplified model. What AD impulse should stabilization analysis carry forward?
options: $300 billion because stabilization uses only the gross multiplier effect.
$80 billion because crowding out replaces the fiscal impulse.
LG-B-6023.feedback: Stabilization analysis should use the net aggregate-demand impulse after the multiplier and stated crowding-out offset.

ECON-SP-EASY-56.q: A liquidity trap occurs when monetary policy has trouble stimulating AD because:
ECON-SP-EASY-56.commonError: Thinking monetary policy is always equally powerful.
ECON-SP-EASY-56.feedback: In a liquidity trap, nominal interest rates are near zero, making traditional monetary stimulus weaker.

ECON-SP-EASY-57.q: An automatic stabilizer is best described as:
options: A built-in response to the economy
ECON-SP-EASY-57.commonError: Confusing automatic stabilizers with discretionary policy.
ECON-SP-EASY-57.feedback: Automatic stabilizers, such as taxes and transfer payments, respond automatically as conditions change.

ECON-SP-EASY-58.q: Policy lags matter because stabilization policy may:
options: Arrive after conditions have already changed
Make money neutral in the short run
ECON-SP-EASY-58.commonError: Ignoring timing problems in stabilization policy.
ECON-SP-EASY-58.feedback: Policy can become destabilizing if it takes effect after the economy has already moved.

LG-Q-60.q: A policy lag is a reason stabilization policy can be risky because policy actions may
options: take effect after conditions have already changed
remove the need for aggregate demand
make money supply impossible to change
LG-Q-60.feedback: Policy lags matter because by the time policy takes effect, the economy may have already changed.

LG-Q-81.q: If a recession lowers aggregate demand, a stabilization policy response could be
options: lower government spending and lower money supply
higher taxes and higher interest rates
doing anything that shifts AD left
LG-Q-81.commonError: choosing contractionary policy during weak demand
LG-Q-81.feedback: If aggregate demand is too low, expansionary policy can help shift AD right.

LG-Q-82.q: If aggregate demand is pushing output above its natural level and raising inflation pressure, policymakers might use
options: higher government spending and lower interest rates
only policies that shift AD right
LG-Q-82.commonError: using expansionary policy when AD is already too strong
LG-Q-82.feedback: When AD is too high and inflation pressure builds, contractionary policy can shift AD left.

LG-Q-83.q: One argument in favor of stabilization policy is that it can help offset
LG-Q-83.commonError: thinking stabilization policy is meant to eliminate scarcity
LG-Q-83.feedback: Supporters argue stabilization policy can reduce the damage caused by short-run aggregate demand shocks.

LG-Q-84.q: One argument against aggressive stabilization policy is that
options: policy lags can cause actions to hit the economy too late
monetary and fiscal policy always work instantly
LG-Q-84.commonError: thinking policy timing is never a problem
LG-Q-84.feedback: Critics warn that policy lags can make stabilization efforts arrive after the economy has already changed.

LG-Q-85.q: If policymakers respond too late to a recession that has already recovered, expansionary policy may
LG-Q-85.commonError: thinking late expansionary policy is harmless
LG-Q-85.feedback: If expansionary policy arrives after recovery is underway, it can push aggregate demand too far and create inflation pressure.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-148.q: Which policy pair is expansionary for aggregate demand?
options: Higher taxes and lower money supply
Lower taxes and higher money supply
Higher reserve requirements and lower spending
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-148.feedback: Lower taxes and higher money supply both tend to shift AD right.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-149.q: A recession begins, but Congress passes stimulus after the economy has already recovered. This illustrates:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-149.feedback: Policy lags can make stabilization arrive after conditions have changed.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-150.q: If the economy is in a liquidity trap, a traditional money-supply increase may fail because:
options: Interest rates cannot fall much further
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-150.commonError: Thinking monetary policy works the same at zero rates.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-150.feedback: When rates are near zero, traditional monetary policy may not lower rates enough to boost spending.

LG-Q-179.q: If a negative demand shock pushes output below its natural level, stabilization policy would most likely try to
LG-Q-179.commonError: choosing contractionary policy during a demand slump
LG-Q-179.feedback: A negative demand shock reduces output, so stabilization policy would typically try to shift AD right.

LG-Q-180.q: If aggregate demand is too high and inflation pressure is building, stabilization policy would most likely try to
LG-Q-180.commonError: stimulating AD when inflation pressure is already high
LG-Q-180.feedback: If AD is too strong, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

LG-Q-181.q: A key argument for active stabilization policy is that policymakers can
LG-Q-181.commonError: thinking stabilization policy is meant to solve every economic problem
LG-Q-181.feedback: Supporters argue that active policy can reduce the damage caused by short-run AD shocks.

LG-Q-182.q: A key argument against aggressive stabilization policy is that
options: policy lags can cause poorly timed interventions
the Fed cannot affect interest rates
government spending is not part of aggregate demand
LG-Q-182.commonError: thinking stabilization policy works instantly and perfectly
LG-Q-182.feedback: Policy lags can cause interventions to arrive after conditions have already changed.

LG-Q-183.q: If policymakers misread a temporary shock as a lasting recession, they risk
options: turning fiat money into commodity money
LG-Q-183.commonError: thinking wrong policy timing has no cost
LG-Q-183.feedback: If policymakers stimulate after the economy is already recovering, they may push AD too far.

LG-Q-184.q: A pandemic reduces production and also weakens spending. Why is stabilization policy harder here than with a simple demand shock?
options: Because both supply and demand may be affected.
Because monetary policy cannot affect interest rates in any economy.
Because fiscal policy cannot affect aggregate demand.
Because money demand must be zero during pandemics.
LG-Q-184.commonError: treating every downturn as only an aggregate demand problem
LG-Q-184.feedback: A mixed shock is harder because policy may support demand, but it cannot instantly fix lost production capacity.

ECON-SP-HARD-233.q: Congress cuts spending to reduce deficits during a recession. What policy concern is most direct?
options: AD may fall further before recovery
ECON-SP-HARD-233.commonError: Ignoring demand effects of spending cuts.
ECON-SP-HARD-233.feedback: Cutting spending during a recession can reduce AD further and deepen the downturn.

ECON-SP-HARD-234.q: If interest rates are near zero and output is below potential, why may monetary policy struggle?
options: Rates have little room to fall
ECON-SP-HARD-234.commonError: Treating monetary policy as equally strong at all rates.
ECON-SP-HARD-234.feedback: At near-zero nominal rates, standard rate-cut channels have little room to stimulate spending.

ECON-SP-HARD-235.q: A policy takes six months to pass and another year to affect spending. The main risk is:
options: The shock may reverse before policy hits
The money multiplier must equal zero
ECON-SP-HARD-235.feedback: Inside and outside lags can make policy arrive after conditions have changed.

LG-Q-268.q: Congress cuts government spending to reduce the deficit. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, what should it do?
options: Increase money supply to lower interest rates and support AD.
Decrease money supply to raise interest rates and reduce AD further.
Raise taxes to lower consumption further.
Do nothing because fiscal policy cannot affect AD.
LG-Q-268.commonError: doubling down on contraction after AD falls
LG-Q-268.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left. Expansionary monetary policy can partly offset that.

LG-Q-269.q: A stock market boom increases household wealth and pushes output above its natural level. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, it should
options: reduce money supply and raise interest rates
increase money supply and lower interest rates
LG-Q-269.commonError: using expansionary policy after a positive demand shock
LG-Q-269.feedback: A positive AD shock can push output too high, so contractionary monetary policy can stabilize output.

LG-Q-278.q: Which policy mix is most expansionary for aggregate demand?
options: Fed buys bonds and Congress increases government spending.
Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
Fed sells bonds and Congress cuts spending.
Fed raises interest rates and Congress raises taxes.
LG-Q-278.feedback: Fed bond purchases are expansionary monetary policy, and higher government spending is expansionary fiscal policy.

LG-Q-279.q: Which policy mix is most contractionary for aggregate demand?
options: Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
Fed buys bonds and Congress cuts taxes.
Fed buys bonds and Congress increases spending.
Fed lowers interest rates and Congress increases transfers.
LG-Q-279.feedback: Fed bond sales reduce money supply, and tax increases reduce consumption. Both push AD left.

LG-Q-280.q: Why can stabilization policy accidentally destabilize the economy?
options: Policy lags can make action arrive after conditions change.
Aggregate demand never responds to policy.
The Fed cannot change the money supply.
LG-Q-280.feedback: Policy lags can make a policy hit after the original problem has faded, creating a new problem.

LG-Q-281.q: A recession is already ending, but expansionary fiscal policy passed months earlier now takes effect. What is the risk?
options: AD may be pushed too far right, creating inflation pressure.
Interest rates must fall to zero forever.
LG-Q-281.commonError: thinking late stimulus is always harmless
LG-Q-281.feedback: Late stimulus can overstimulate demand after recovery is already underway.

LG-Q-282.q: A supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why is the policy response harder than for a pure demand shock?
options: Stimulating AD may raise output somewhat but can worsen inflation.
Stimulating AD always lowers prices and raises output with no tradeoff.
Supply shocks only affect money demand.
LG-Q-282.commonError: treating every downturn like a demand shock
LG-Q-282.feedback: A supply shock creates a tradeoff: boosting aggregate demand may support output but can add inflation pressure.

LG-Q-283.q: A negative AD shock reduces output and the price level. Which policy response best targets the shock without relying on supply-side repair?
options: Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy to shift AD right
Contractionary policy to shift AD left
Higher taxes and lower government spending
A policy that reduces investment spending
LG-Q-283.commonError: using contractionary policy against weak demand
LG-Q-283.feedback: A negative AD shock calls for policies that shift AD right if the goal is stabilizing output.

LG-Q-284.q: An economy is above potential output because AD is too high. Which response best reduces the boom without increasing AD further?
options: Contractionary monetary policy or contractionary fiscal policy
Expansionary monetary policy and tax cuts
Higher government spending and lower interest rates
LG-Q-284.commonError: stimulating an economy that is already overheating
LG-Q-284.feedback: When AD is too high, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

ECON-SP-ELITE-321.q: A recessionary demand shock hits, but the Fed is at the zero lower bound. Which option best describes the policy problem?
options: AD needs support, but rate cuts have limited room
AD is too high, and rate cuts work too strongly
SRAS needs support, but wages rise instantly
LRPC must shift, but M2 is too small
ECON-SP-ELITE-321.commonError: Ignoring why zero rates weaken monetary stimulus.
ECON-SP-ELITE-321.feedback: When rates are near zero, traditional monetary policy may struggle to shift AD right enough.

ECON-SP-ELITE-322.q: A government passes stimulus after a recession has ended, and the economy is already above potential. What is the risk?
options: The stimulus may worsen inflation pressure
The stimulus must lower output below potential
The stimulus shifts SRAS right automatically
The stimulus lowers expected prices instantly
ECON-SP-ELITE-322.feedback: Because of lags, stimulus can hit after recovery and add excess demand.

ECON-SP-ELITE-344.q: Fiscal stimulus raises AD, but the central bank offsets it with tighter money. Which final outcome is most plausible?
options: AD rises less than fiscal policy alone suggests
AD rises more than fiscal policy alone suggests
SRAS shifts right because interest rates rise
LRPC shifts left because taxes fall
ECON-SP-ELITE-344.feedback: Tighter monetary policy can offset fiscal stimulus by raising interest rates and weakening AD.

LG-Q-362.q: Suppose output is below its natural level because AD is weak. Which Fed action through the money market would move AD in the stabilizing direction?
options: Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
Shift money demand right to raise r and lower investment.
Keep money supply fixed and raise taxes.
LG-Q-362.commonError: choosing tighter money during a demand slump
LG-Q-362.feedback: When AD is weak, expansionary monetary policy shifts MS right, lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

LG-Q-363.q: Suppose output is above its natural level because AD is too strong. Which Fed action through the money market would move AD in the stabilizing direction?
options: Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
Shift money demand left to lower r and raise investment.
LG-Q-363.commonError: stimulating AD when output is already above natural level
LG-Q-363.feedback: When AD is too strong, tighter money shifts MS left, raises rates, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

LG-Q-375.q: If the economy is already near full employment and fiscal policy shifts AD right through the multiplier, what risk becomes more important?
options: A lower price level from higher government spending
A smaller price level because MPC is positive
LG-Q-375.commonError: thinking all rightward AD shifts are good regardless of starting point
LG-Q-375.feedback: If the economy is already near capacity, more AD can create inflation pressure instead of useful output gains.

LG-Q-378.q: A recession lowers AD by $300 billion. The government increases spending by $100 billion and MPC is 0.5. Ignoring crowding out, what remains of the AD shortfall?
LG-Q-378.commonError: not comparing stimulus size to the original AD shortfall
LG-Q-378.feedback: MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2. A $100 billion spending increase shifts AD by $200 billion, leaving a $100 billion shortfall.

LG-Q-380.q: Congress cuts spending during a recession while the Fed also sells bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
options: Both policies shift AD left or reduce support for AD, worsening the demand problem.
Both policies shift AD right, stabilizing output.
Fiscal policy shifts AD right while monetary policy shifts AD right.
LG-Q-380.commonError: missing that Fed bond sales are contractionary
LG-Q-380.feedback: Cutting spending reduces AD, and Fed bond sales raise rates and reduce investment. That is contraction on top of contraction.

LG-Q-381.q: Congress raises spending during an inflationary boom while the Fed buys bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
options: Both policies shift AD right, risking more inflation pressure.
Both policies shift AD left, reducing inflation pressure.
Fiscal policy shifts AD left while monetary policy shifts AD left.
Neither affects AD because output is already high.
LG-Q-381.commonError: thinking expansionary policy is always appropriate
LG-Q-381.feedback: Spending increases and bond purchases both shift AD right. During an inflationary boom, that pours gasoline on the fire.

LG-Q-382.q: A negative supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why can expansionary AD policy be a blunt tool here?
options: It may raise output somewhat but can worsen the price-level increase.
It directly restores lost productive capacity with no inflation risk.
It lowers prices and lowers output at the same time.
LG-Q-382.commonError: treating supply shocks like pure demand shocks
LG-Q-382.feedback: AD stimulus can support spending, but it does not fix the supply loss and may worsen inflation.

LG-Q-383.q: A negative demand shock reduces output and prices. Why is expansionary monetary policy more directly suited to this case than to a pure supply shock?
options: It targets weak spending by lowering r and raising investment.
It directly increases labor, capital, and natural resources.
It shifts SRAS right by changing the reserve ratio.
It lowers AD to reduce output further.
LG-Q-383.commonError: not distinguishing AD shocks from AS shocks
LG-Q-383.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy works through spending, so it is more directly suited to weak AD than to lost productive capacity.

LG-Q-384.q: A policy is passed to fight a recession, but because of recognition, implementation, and impact lags, it takes effect after output has already recovered. What is the likely stabilization problem?
options: The delayed policy can push AD too far right and create inflation pressure.
The delayed policy must shift AD left automatically.
The delayed policy cannot affect AD after recovery.
The delayed policy eliminates crowding out.
LG-Q-384.commonError: thinking late stimulus is harmless because it was originally well-intended
LG-Q-384.feedback: Good timing matters. Late expansion can overstimulate AD after the recession has already passed.

LG-Q-9057.q: If the economy initially needed AD to fall by $300 billion and the MS1 to MS2 movement reduces AD by $200 billion, what remains?
options: Output rises from Y2 to Y1.
LG-Q-9057.commonError: not comparing the graph's AD shift with the size of the gap
LG-Q-9057.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. If AD needed to fall $300 billion but falls $200 billion, $100 billion of excess AD remains.

LG-Q-9058.q: A contractionary monetary-policy move must reduce AD by $240 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what investment decrease is needed to produce that AD movement?
LG-Q-9058.commonError: not dividing the AD target by the multiplier
LG-Q-9058.feedback: The graph shows a leftward AD movement. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so investment must fall by $240 billion / 4 = $60 billion.

LG-Q-9063.q: The MS1 to MS2 movement causes AD to shift left by $180 billion. A separate fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $60 billion. What is the net AD change?
LG-Q-9063.commonError: adding both policies in the same direction without checking graph direction
LG-Q-9063.feedback: The graph's monetary policy lowers AD by $180 billion. Fiscal policy raises AD by $60 billion. Net AD falls by $120 billion.

LG-Q-9065.q: The Fed pushes r high enough to reduce investment by $90 billion, but AD only needed to move left by $240 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what happens?
options: AD falls $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.
AD falls $240 billion, closing the gap exactly.
LG-Q-9065.commonError: failing to compare the multiplied AD effect to the needed AD change
LG-Q-9065.feedback: The graph shows AD moving left. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so a $90 billion investment fall lowers AD by $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.

LG-Q-9069.q: A $50 billion government spending increase is intended to close a $250 billion AD gap. MPC = 0.75, but crowding out reduces investment by $40 billion. What is the correct sequence?
options: AD first shifts right $50 billion, then the multiplier pushes it to $200 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $160 billion shift and a $90 billion gap.
AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a $210 billion surplus.
AD first shifts left $50 billion, then the multiplier shifts it left $200 billion, leaving a $90 billion gap.
AD shifts right $50 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
LG-Q-9069.commonError: calculating the multiplier but ignoring the order: initial shift, multiplied shift, crowding-out offset
LG-Q-9069.feedback: MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4. The $50 billion initial shift becomes $200 billion, then crowding out lowers the net shift to $160 billion, leaving a $90 billion gap.

LG-Q-9070.q: The economy is already above potential output by $180 billion. Congress raises spending by $30 billion and MPC = 0.8. What is the correct AD-shift interpretation?
options: AD first shifts right $30 billion, then the multiplier expands the shift to $150 billion, worsening the overheating gap to $330 billion.
AD first shifts left $30 billion, then left $150 billion, reducing the overheating gap to $30 billion.
AD shifts right $30 billion only, closing part of the overheating gap.
AD does not shift because the economy is already above potential.
LG-Q-9070.commonError: thinking any rightward AD shift is good regardless of the starting gap
LG-Q-9070.feedback: MPC = 0.8 gives multiplier 5. The $30 billion spending increase becomes a $150 billion AD increase, making the $180 billion overheating gap worse.

LG-Q-9071.q: The monetary-policy movement shifts AD left by $160 billion. Fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $160 billion. What is the net AD effect?
LG-Q-9071.commonError: not matching the leftward AD shift in the graph before adding the fiscal offset
LG-Q-9071.feedback: The graph shows monetary policy shifting AD left. A fiscal expansion of the same size shifts AD right by the same amount, so the net AD effect is zero.

LG-Q-9074.q: A recessionary gap is $400 billion. Government spending rises by $100 billion and MPC = 0.75. What is the order of AD shifts and the final gap, ignoring crowding out?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier expands the shift to $400 billion, closing the gap.
AD first shifts right $400 billion, then falls back to $100 billion, leaving a $300 billion gap.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then left $400 billion, worsening the gap.
AD shifts right $100 billion only, leaving a $300 billion gap.
LG-Q-9074.commonError: confusing the first AD shift with the final multiplied AD shift
LG-Q-9074.feedback: MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4. The $100 billion initial spending increase becomes a $400 billion final AD shift, closing the gap.

PM2D2-STAB-L-001.q: A recessionary gap begins closing without new policy as wage growth slows and SRAS shifts right. A large discretionary stimulus designed for the original gap is still scheduled to take effect several quarters later. What is the strongest stabilization concern?
options: The delayed stimulus may arrive after much of the gap has self-corrected, pushing AD too far right and creating overheating pressure.
The stimulus becomes contractionary once SRAS begins shifting right.
Self-correction guarantees the stimulus has no effect on aggregate demand.
The delayed stimulus automatically shifts LRAS right by the amount of the original gap.
PM2D2-STAB-L-001.commonError: Assumes a policy designed for an old output gap remains correctly sized after self-correction has already reduced the gap.
PM2D2-STAB-L-001.feedback: Policy lags matter because wages, costs, expectations, and private spending can change before discretionary policy takes effect, creating overshoot risk.

PM2D2-STAB-L-002.q: Policymakers initially estimate a $300 billion recessionary gap and enact a $75 billion spending increase with a simple multiplier of 4. By the time the policy takes effect, revised data show the gap is only $100 billion. Ignoring crowding out, what is the implication?
options: The policy closes the revised gap exactly because it was calibrated to the original estimate.
The $75 billion initial spending increase leaves a $25 billion gap because only the first round matters.
The policy raises AD by $100 billion because stabilization automatically adjusts to revised data.
The $300 billion AD increase overshoots the revised gap by $200 billion.
PM2D2-STAB-L-002.commonError: Uses the original output-gap estimate even after newer data show a much smaller gap.
PM2D2-STAB-L-002.feedback: Compare the policy’s expected AD shift with the output gap that exists when the policy actually takes effect, not only the initial estimate.

PM2D2-STAB-L-003.q: Inflation pressure is being driven by excessive aggregate demand. Policymakers use contractionary stabilization policy and the policy succeeds in lowering aggregate demand. Before inflation expectations fully adjust, which short-run combination is most consistent with the policy mechanism?
options: Higher inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
No change in unemployment because stabilization policy affects only the price level.
Lower inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
Lower inflation pressure together with stronger output and lower unemployment.
PM2D2-STAB-L-003.commonError: Treats lower inflation pressure from contractionary demand policy as costless in the short run.
PM2D2-STAB-L-003.feedback: A contractionary AD policy can reduce inflation pressure while also lowering output and raising unemployment before expectations fully adjust.

PM2D2-STAB-L-004.q: A short recession causes tax receipts to fall and unemployment-benefit payments to rise automatically. Congress also approves an infrastructure stimulus, but construction begins after the economy has already recovered. Which comparison is strongest?
options: The infrastructure program cannot affect aggregate demand once the recession has ended.
The automatic stabilizers cushion the downturn and recede with conditions, while the delayed discretionary program can add demand after the original gap has faded.
Both responses have the same implementation timing because each changes the government budget.
The automatic stabilizers become contractionary during the recession, while delayed infrastructure is always stabilizing.
PM2D2-STAB-L-004.commonError: Assumes automatic stabilizers and discretionary fiscal programs have the same activation and phase-out timing.
PM2D2-STAB-L-004.feedback: Automatic stabilizers respond as income and employment change without new legislation; discretionary programs can arrive later and may outlast the original gap.

LG-Q-4012.q: If output is below its natural level because aggregate demand is weak, stabilization policy would usually try to
LG-Q-4012.commonError: using contractionary policy during weak demand
LG-Q-4012.feedback: If AD is too weak, expansionary policy can shift AD right.

LG-Q-4013.q: The economy has a recessionary AD gap of $500 billion. Monetary policy raises investment by $50 billion and fiscal policy raises government spending by $60 billion. If MPC = 0.75 and there is no crowding out, what happens?
options: AD rises $440 billion, leaving a $60 billion gap.
AD rises $110 billion, leaving a $390 billion gap.
AD rises $500 billion, closing the gap exactly.
LG-Q-4013.commonError: not applying the multiplier to the combined spending impulse
LG-Q-4013.feedback: Initial impulse is $50 billion + $60 billion = $110 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $440 billion, leaving a $60 billion gap.

LG-Q-4014.q: A recessionary AD gap is $500 billion. Monetary policy raises investment by $50 billion, fiscal policy raises government spending by $60 billion, MPC = 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $40 billion. What gap remains?
LG-Q-4014.commonError: not subtracting crowding out after applying the multiplier
LG-Q-4014.feedback: Initial impulse is $110 billion. Multiplier is 4, so gross AD rise is $440 billion. Subtract $40 billion crowding out, net AD rise is $400 billion. A $100 billion gap remains.

P52B-S4-STAB-B1-001.q: Which example is an automatic stabilizer during a recession?
options: The central bank announces a new bond-purchase program.
Congress passes a one-time infrastructure bill.
A state raises sales taxes to balance its budget.
Unemployment-benefit payments rise without a new legislative vote.
P52B-S4-STAB-B1-001.commonError: Confusing automatic fiscal responses with newly enacted discretionary policy.
P52B-S4-STAB-B1-001.feedback: Unemployment benefits expand automatically as more workers qualify, supporting income without new legislation.

P52B-S4-STAB-B1-002.q: Real output is below potential and inflation pressure is weak. Which demand-management direction is appropriate?
options: Expansionary policy that shifts aggregate demand to the right.
Contractionary policy that shifts aggregate demand left.
A policy that shifts short-run aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect output in the short run.
P52B-S4-STAB-B1-002.commonError: Applying contractionary policy to a recessionary gap.
P52B-S4-STAB-B1-002.feedback: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can raise aggregate demand and reduce a recessionary gap.

P52B-S4-STAB-B1-003.q: Why can a long implementation lag make discretionary stabilization policy harmful?
options: The policy always reduces aggregate demand before it begins.
It may arrive after conditions change and destabilize the economy.
The lag permanently prevents prices from adjusting.
The lag converts fiscal policy into monetary policy.
P52B-S4-STAB-B1-003.commonError: Treating delayed policy as harmless regardless of the business-cycle phase.
P52B-S4-STAB-B1-003.feedback: A delayed response can arrive after recovery or after inflation has eased, creating a procyclical rather than stabilizing effect.

P52B-S4-STAB-B2-001.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises inflation and lowers real output. Why is stabilization difficult?
options: Both inflation and output automatically improve with any expansionary policy.
The shock shifts aggregate demand, so only tax policy can respond.
Supporting output may worsen inflation; fighting inflation may deepen the output loss.
Monetary and fiscal policy have identical effects on short-run aggregate supply.
P52B-S4-STAB-B2-001.commonError: Treating a negative supply shock like a pure demand recession.
P52B-S4-STAB-B2-001.feedback: A negative supply shock creates stagflation, forcing policymakers to weigh competing inflation and output objectives.

P52B-S4-STAB-B2-002.q: The economy is near potential output, yet fiscal and monetary policy both become strongly expansionary. What is the main risk?
options: Aggregate demand must fall because the policies cancel each other.
Long-run aggregate supply immediately shifts left.
Crowding out guarantees that output and prices do not change.
Aggregate demand may overshoot capacity and increase inflation.
