An AD increase raises both output and the price level here.
An AD increase lowers output while the price level rises here.
The graph cannot distinguish a demand change from a supply change.
PG3-MEQ-L-003.feedback: In a standard AD-AS model, a rightward AD shift raises both output and prices in the short run, unlike a rightward AS shift.

PG3-MEQ-L-004.q: A student says the graph proves output must rise whenever aggregate demand increases. Which graph-based rebuttal is strongest?
options: The AD increase dominates both output and the price-level effects.
The AS decrease dominates both output and the price-level effects.
The two shifts offset the price level but reinforce the output effect.
The AS decrease offsets the AD increase in output, not prices.
PG3-MEQ-L-004.feedback: Point B isolates the AD increase and point D isolates the AS decrease. Point C shows their combination, where the output effect is offset but inflation is amplified.

P52B-S3-MEQS-B1-001.q: A sharp fall in household spending is primarily what kind of macroeconomic disturbance?
P52B-S3-MEQS-B1-001.commonError: Confusing a spending disturbance with a production-cost disturbance.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B1-001.feedback: Household spending is a component of aggregate demand, so a sharp decline shifts aggregate demand left.

P52B-S3-MEQS-B1-002.q: An unexpected increase in energy costs usually shifts which curve first?
options: Long-run aggregate supply shifts right immediately.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B1-002.commonError: Treating a production-cost shock as a demand shock.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B1-002.feedback: Higher energy costs raise firms’ costs and reduce output supplied at each price level, shifting short-run aggregate supply left.

P52B-S3-MEQS-B1-003.q: A negative aggregate-demand shock normally causes what short-run combination?
options: Lower real output and a higher price level.
Higher real output and a lower price level.
Lower real output and a lower price level.
Higher real output and a higher price level.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B1-003.commonError: Reversing the price-level effect of a demand contraction.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B1-003.feedback: A leftward aggregate-demand shift reduces both equilibrium output and the price level in the short run.

P52B-S3-MEQS-B2-001.q: A surge in business investment shifts aggregate demand right. In the short run, what happens other things equal?
options: Real output rises and the price level falls.
Real output falls and the price level rises.
Real output and the price level both fall.
Real output and the price level both rise.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B2-001.commonError: Using supply-shock outcomes for a demand expansion.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B2-001.feedback: A rightward aggregate-demand shift moves the economy to higher short-run output and a higher price level.

P52B-S3-MEQS-B2-002.q: A widespread crop failure raises food-production costs. Which short-run outcome is most likely?
options: Real output falls while the price level rises.
Real output rises while the price level falls.
Real output and the price level both rise.
Real output and the price level both fall.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B2-002.commonError: Forgetting that an adverse supply shock creates stagflation pressure.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B2-002.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts short-run aggregate supply left, lowering output and raising the price level.

P52B-S3-MEQS-B2-003.q: Aggregate demand falls while short-run aggregate supply is unchanged. Which policy direction would most directly offset the output loss?
options: A policy that shifts aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect aggregate demand.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B2-003.commonError: Choosing contractionary policy during a demand-driven recession.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B2-003.feedback: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can shift aggregate demand right and counter a negative demand shock.

P52B-S3-MEQS-B3-001.q: Aggregate demand rises while short-run aggregate supply falls. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Real output rises, while the price level is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output rises.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
Both the price level and real output fall.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B3-001.commonError: Claiming certainty about output when the two shocks move output in opposite directions.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B3-001.feedback: Both shifts raise the price level, but aggregate demand raises output while adverse supply lowers it.

P52B-S3-MEQS-B3-002.q: Aggregate demand falls while short-run aggregate supply rises. Which outcome is certain?
options: Real output falls, while the price level is uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output is uncertain.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B3-002.commonError: Missing the shared price-level direction of the two shifts.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B3-002.feedback: A demand contraction and favorable supply shock both lower the price level, but they push output in opposite directions.

P52B-S3-MEQS-B3-003.q: After an adverse supply shock, policymakers use expansionary demand policy to restore output. Which risk remains?
options: The price level may rise even more than it did from the original shock.
Unemployment must rise because aggregate demand increased.
Short-run aggregate supply automatically returns to its old position.
The economy must move below potential output.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B3-003.commonError: Assuming output stabilization eliminates the inflation tradeoff.
P52B-S3-MEQS-B3-003.feedback: Demand expansion can support output after a supply shock, but it adds inflation pressure rather than repairing supply.

P52B-S3-MEQS-LB-001.q: Government purchases rise while a technology breakthrough lowers unit costs. If output rises but the price level is unchanged, what does the evidence imply?
options: Neither curve shifted because the price level did not change.
The opposing price effects approximately offset while both shifts raise output.
Aggregate demand fell while short-run aggregate supply rose.
Aggregate demand rose while short-run aggregate supply fell.
P52B-S3-MEQS-LB-001.commonError: Assuming an unchanged price level means no macroeconomic shifts occurred.
P52B-S3-MEQS-LB-001.feedback: Higher government purchases shift aggregate demand right and better technology shifts short-run aggregate supply right. Both raise output, while their price effects can offset.

P52B-S3-MEQS-LB-002.q: Oil prices rise sharply and the central bank expands aggregate demand enough to keep real output unchanged. Compared with the initial equilibrium, what is most likely?
options: The price level is unchanged because real output is unchanged.
The price level is lower because monetary expansion reduces costs.
The price level is higher because both the supply shock and policy raise it.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because interest rates fall.
P52B-S3-MEQS-LB-002.commonError: Equating stable output with a stable price level.
P52B-S3-MEQS-LB-002.feedback: The adverse supply shock raises the price level, and the demand expansion used to stabilize output adds additional price pressure.

P52B-S3-MEQS-LB-003.q: Consumer spending collapses at the same time firms adopt a major cost-saving technology. Prices fall sharply, but output changes little. Which interpretation fits best?
options: A positive demand shock and adverse supply shock offset in the price level.
Only aggregate demand shifted because prices fell.
Only short-run aggregate supply shifted because output was stable.
A negative demand shock and positive supply shock had offsetting output effects.
P52B-S3-MEQS-LB-003.commonError: Using one observed variable to infer only one curve shifted.
P52B-S3-MEQS-LB-003.feedback: Both shocks lower the price level, while one lowers output and the other raises it. Similar magnitudes can leave output nearly unchanged.

ECON-SP-CLASSIFY-DEMAND-SHOCK-5065.q: A sharp fall in consumer confidence is primarily which kind of shock?
ECON-SP-CLASSIFY-DEMAND-SHOCK-5065.feedback: Lower consumer confidence reduces consumption and shifts aggregate demand left.

ECON-SP-CLASSIFY-SUPPLY-SHOCK-5066.q: A sudden rise in oil prices is primarily which kind of shock?
options: A change in the money multiplier
ECON-SP-CLASSIFY-SUPPLY-SHOCK-5066.feedback: Higher input costs shift SRAS left, making this a negative supply shock.

options: Balanced budgets and low interest rates
ECON-SP-DEFINE-STAGFLATION-5069.feedback: Stagflation is the difficult combination of rising prices and weak employment/output conditions.

ECON-SP-EVALUATE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-POLICY-506.q: An adverse supply shock creates a policy problem because inflation and unemployment can:
ECON-SP-EVALUATE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-POLICY-506.feedback: Adverse supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment together.

ECON-SP-TRACE-COMBINED-SHOCKS-5093.q: If AD falls while SRAS also falls, what outcome is certain?
ECON-SP-TRACE-COMBINED-SHOCKS-5093.feedback: Both a leftward AD shift and a leftward SRAS shift reduce equilibrium output; their price-level effects conflict.

ECON-SP-TRACE-DEMAND-SHOCK-5032.q: A negative AD shock usually causes output and the price level to:
ECON-SP-TRACE-DEMAND-SHOCK-5032.feedback: A negative AD shock lowers output and the price level.

ECON-SP-TRACE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-5033.q: An adverse supply shock usually causes output to fall and prices to:
ECON-SP-TRACE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-5033.feedback: An adverse supply shock lowers output and raises prices.

ECON-SP-EVALUATE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-POLICY-605.q: An oil shock raises inflation while unemployment rises. Why is policy difficult?
options: Stimulus risks more inflation, while tightening risks more unemployment
Stimulus always lowers inflation, while tightening always raises output
Both stimulus and tightening shift SRAS right
Neither inflation nor unemployment can respond
ECON-SP-EVALUATE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-POLICY-605.feedback: A supply shock creates a tradeoff: supporting output can worsen inflation, while fighting inflation can worsen unemployment.

ECON-SP-TRACE-DEMAND-SHOCK-6025.q: Consumer confidence collapses, shifting AD left and leaving real output below potential. With no new policy response, which process becomes relevant next?
options: Weak wage and price pressures can shift SRAS right over time, moving output back toward potential.
Aggregate demand must automatically shift right to its original position.
LRAS must shift left until it reaches the depressed output level.
A permanent adverse supply shock must occur before output can recover.
ECON-SP-TRACE-DEMAND-SHOCK-6025.feedback: A negative AD shock can create a recessionary gap; with no policy response, wage and expectation adjustment can shift SRAS right over time.
ECON-SP-TRACE-DEMAND-SHOCK-6025.commonError: Stops at the short-run demand-shock outcome and does not connect the recessionary gap to long-run self-correction.

ECON-SP-TRACE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-6026.q: A major oil-price spike hits the economy. In the short run, output and the price level likely:
ECON-SP-TRACE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-6026.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts SRAS left, lowering output and raising prices.

ECON-SP-EASY-44.q: In the long run, an economy returns to natural output because:
ECON-SP-EASY-44.feedback: Over time, wages, prices, and expectations adjust, moving output back toward natural output.

PM2D1-LRADJ-E-001.q: Real GDP is below potential and labor-market slack is putting downward pressure on nominal wage growth. If aggregate demand does not change again, which adjustment helps the economy self-correct?
options: SRAS shifts right as wage and production-cost pressures ease.
AD shifts right automatically because unemployment is high.
LRAS shifts left until it reaches the depressed output level.
SRAS shifts left because firms are producing below potential.
PM2D1-LRADJ-E-001.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-E-001.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-135.q: A boom in foreign economies raises net exports and pushes output above potential. In the long run, expected prices likely:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-135.commonError: Thinking output stays above potential forever.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-135.feedback: When output is above potential, pressures raise expected prices and shift SRAS left over time.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-136.q: A negative demand shock pushes output below potential. If policymakers do nothing, long-run adjustment likely involves:
options: Falling expected prices and SRAS shifting right
Rising expected prices and SRAS shifting left
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-136.feedback: Below-potential output puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, shifting SRAS right.

PM2D1-LRADJ-M-001.q: A temporary demand boom pushes production above potential. Policymakers do nothing, and wage contracts are gradually renegotiated as workers and firms revise price expectations upward. Which change is most consistent with self-correction?
options: Higher wages and input costs shift SRAS left while aggregate demand stays at its post-boom position.
Aggregate demand shifts left automatically as soon as wages rise.
LRAS shifts right because the economy briefly produced above potential.
SRAS shifts right because firms respond to the higher price level by cutting costs.
PM2D1-LRADJ-M-001.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-M-001.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

ECON-SP-HARD-216.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, long-run self-correction most likely shifts:
ECON-SP-HARD-216.commonError: Missing expected price adjustment after an expansionary gap.
ECON-SP-HARD-216.feedback: At Y2 output is above potential, so rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left.

ECON-SP-HARD-217.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, long-run self-correction most likely shifts:
ECON-SP-HARD-217.commonError: Missing expected price adjustment after a recessionary gap.
ECON-SP-HARD-217.feedback: At Y3 output is below potential, so wages and expected prices tend to fall, shifting SRAS right.

ECON-SP-HARD-221.q: A negative AD shock lowers output and prices. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
ECON-SP-HARD-221.feedback: Lower wages and expected prices shift SRAS right and help output return to natural.

ECON-SP-HARD-222.q: A positive AD shock pushes output above potential. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
ECON-SP-HARD-222.commonError: Thinking booms above potential persist forever.
ECON-SP-HARD-222.feedback: Higher wages and expected prices shift SRAS left and return output to potential.

PG3-MEQ-EL-002.q: Which statement best describes the macro outcome shown by the move from A to B?
options: Demand-pull inflation with no long-run growth.
Long-run growth with lower price pressure.
No change in either output or the price level.
PG3-MEQ-EL-002.feedback: Higher LRAS and SRAS support more output alongside a lower price level.

ECON-SP-ELITE-310.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, which long-run adjustment is most consistent with self-correction?
options: SRAS shifts left until output returns to Y1
SRAS shifts right until output reaches Y3
AD shifts right until output reaches Y2
LRAS shifts right until it reaches Y2
ECON-SP-ELITE-310.commonError: Moving LRAS instead of SRAS during short-run self-correction.
ECON-SP-ELITE-310.feedback: At Y2, output is above natural output, so rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left toward long-run equilibrium.

ECON-SP-ELITE-311.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, which long-run adjustment is most consistent with self-correction?
options: SRAS shifts right until output returns to Y1
SRAS shifts left until output returns to Y3
AD shifts left until output returns to Y3
LRAS shifts left until it reaches Y3
ECON-SP-ELITE-311.commonError: Moving AD or LRAS instead of SRAS during self-correction.
ECON-SP-ELITE-311.feedback: At Y3, output is below natural output, so falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right toward long-run equilibrium.

ECON-SP-ELITE-314.q: An economy is above potential because of a demand boom. Which policy and long-run force push in the same direction?
options: Contractionary policy and rising expected prices
Expansionary policy and falling expected prices
Contractionary policy and falling expected prices
Expansionary policy and rising expected prices
ECON-SP-ELITE-314.commonError: Pairing the wrong policy with the wrong output gap.
ECON-SP-ELITE-314.feedback: Contractionary policy shifts AD left, while rising expected prices shift SRAS left; both reduce output toward potential.

ECON-SP-ELITE-315.q: An economy is below potential because AD collapsed. Which policy and long-run force push in the same direction?
options: Expansionary policy and falling expected prices
Contractionary policy and rising expected prices
Expansionary policy and rising expected prices
Contractionary policy and falling expected prices
ECON-SP-ELITE-315.commonError: Pairing recessionary gaps with contractionary policy.
ECON-SP-ELITE-315.feedback: Expansionary policy shifts AD right, while falling expected prices shift SRAS right; both raise output toward potential.

ECON-SP-ELITE-337.q: An economy begins at natural output. AD rises unexpectedly, then expected prices rise. Which sequence is most likely?
options: Output rises first, then SRAS shifts left
Output falls first, then SRAS shifts right
Prices fall first, then AD shifts left
LRAS shifts right, then output falls
ECON-SP-ELITE-337.commonError: Skipping the short-run expansion before long-run adjustment.
ECON-SP-ELITE-337.feedback: An unexpected AD increase raises output in the short run, but higher expected prices later shift SRAS left.

ECON-SP-ELITE-338.q: An economy begins at natural output. AD falls unexpectedly, then expected prices fall. Which sequence is most likely?
options: Output falls first, then SRAS shifts right
Output rises first, then SRAS shifts left
Prices rise first, then LRAS shifts left
AD rises first, then unemployment rises
ECON-SP-ELITE-338.commonError: Skipping the short-run recession before self-correction.
ECON-SP-ELITE-338.feedback: An unexpected AD decrease lowers output first, then lower expected prices shift SRAS right over time.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9003.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, expected prices adjust upward with no policy response. Which movement fits the model?
options: SRAS shifts left toward AS1 and output returns toward Y1.
SRAS shifts right toward AS2 and output rises toward Y2.
AD shifts right toward AD2 and output remains above potential.
LRAS shifts right toward Y2 because actual output was high.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9003.commonError: Confusing short-run output with long-run potential output.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9003.feedback: When output is above potential, rising expected prices shift SRAS left and return output toward LRAS.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9004.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, expected prices adjust downward with no policy response. Which movement fits the model?
options: SRAS shifts right toward AS2 and output returns toward Y1.
SRAS shifts left toward AS1 and output falls toward Y3.
AD shifts left toward AD1 and prices rise toward P3.
LRAS shifts left toward Y3 because unemployment is high.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9004.commonError: Moving LRAS instead of SRAS during self-correction.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9004.feedback: When output is below potential, falling expected prices shift SRAS right and restore output toward natural output.

P52B-S1-LRADJ-L-001.q: A temporary negative aggregate-demand shock lowers output below potential. With no policy response and flexible wages and expected prices over time, what is the long-run outcome?
options: SRAS shifts right and output returns to potential at a lower price level.
Output remains permanently below potential with the original price level.
LRAS shifts left until productive capacity matches the recession output.
Aggregate demand automatically shifts right because unemployment increased.
P52B-S1-LRADJ-L-001.commonError: Treating a temporary demand shock as a permanent change in productive capacity.
P52B-S1-LRADJ-L-001.feedback: Falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right, restoring natural output while leaving the price level lower.

PM2D1-LRADJ-L-001.q: Refer to the graph. A demand increase has moved the economy to the intersection of AD2 and AS2 at Y2 and P2. If no policy reverses AD2 and long-run adjustment is completed, which comparison between the short-run and long-run effects is supported by the graph?
options: The temporary output gain disappears as output returns to Y1, while the price level rises further toward P3.
Output remains at Y2 because long-run adjustment changes only the price level, which falls all the way back toward P1.
Output falls to Y3 as SRAS shifts left past AS1, while the price level stays fixed at the short-run level P2.
Both real output and the price level return to their original Y1 and P1 values once wage contracts and expectations adjust.
PM2D1-LRADJ-L-001.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-L-001.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

PM2D1-LRADJ-L-002.q: Two economies have identical recessionary gaps. In Economy A, most wages can be reset monthly; in Economy B, most wages are fixed by three-year contracts. With no policy response, which prediction best follows from the long-run adjustment model?
options: Economy B should self-correct faster because longer wage contracts make SRAS respond more quickly to the recessionary gap.
Both economies must return to potential at exactly the same speed because a vertical LRAS fixes the timing as well as the destination.
Neither economy can self-correct without an aggregate-demand policy change because wage and cost adjustment cannot move SRAS.
Economy A should tend to self-correct faster because wages and production costs can adjust sooner.
PM2D1-LRADJ-L-002.commonError: Assumes self-correction is instantaneous even when wages and expectations are sticky.
PM2D1-LRADJ-L-002.feedback: Long-run adjustment can take time because wage contracts, input costs, and price expectations may change gradually.

PM2D1-LRADJ-L-003.q: After a negative aggregate-demand shock, real output begins recovering toward potential even though policymakers make no fiscal or monetary change. Nominal wage growth has slowed and firms report easing unit labor costs. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: The evidence requires LRAS to have shifted left until it met current output, converting the recessionary gap into long-run equilibrium.
The recovery shows wage adjustment is irrelevant because only changes in aggregate demand can move real output back toward potential.
The evidence is consistent with self-correction through a rightward SRAS shift, not necessarily an active stabilization policy.
The recovery proves aggregate demand was shifted right by discretionary policy even though no fiscal or monetary action is observed.
PM2D1-LRADJ-L-003.commonError: Attributes any recovery toward potential to active policy even when wages and expectations are adjusting with no policy change.
PM2D1-LRADJ-L-003.feedback: Self-correction is the endogenous SRAS response to an output gap; stabilization policy is a separate deliberate intervention.

P52B-S1-LRADJ-B2-001.q: An economy has a recessionary gap and policymakers do nothing. Which self-correcting sequence is most consistent with the model?
options: Higher wages shift SRAS left and deepen the recessionary gap.
LRAS shifts left until potential output equals the depressed output level.
Lower wage and price expectations shift SRAS right toward potential.
Aggregate demand rises automatically because the current price level is fixed.
P52B-S1-LRADJ-B2-001.commonError: Reversing the wage and SRAS adjustment in a recessionary gap.
P52B-S1-LRADJ-B2-001.feedback: Below-potential output puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, allowing SRAS to shift right.

P52B-S1-LRADJ-B3-001.q: Demand growth pushes output above potential. If no stabilization policy is used, which long-run adjustment is most likely?
options: Falling wages shift SRAS right and push output farther above potential.
LRAS shifts right solely because the current price level has increased.
Output stays permanently above potential without creating inflation pressure.
Rising costs shift SRAS left, returning output to potential at a higher price level.
P52B-S1-LRADJ-B3-001.commonError: Using recessionary-gap adjustment for an inflationary gap.
P52B-S1-LRADJ-B3-001.feedback: An overheated labor market raises costs and expected prices, shifting SRAS left and closing the inflationary gap.

PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-001.q: Output is below potential and unemployment is unusually high. If policymakers do nothing, which pressure is part of the opening self-correction mechanism?
options: Weak labor demand restrains wage and cost growth, creating pressure for SRAS to shift right.
High unemployment automatically shifts aggregate demand right.
Weak labor demand shifts LRAS left by definition.
High unemployment causes SRAS to shift left through higher wage growth.
PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-001.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-001.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

PM2D1-LRADJ-FB-006.q: Refer to the graph. The economy begins at AD1-AS2 at Y1 and then a demand boom shifts AD to AD2, moving output to Y2. With no policy response, which pair of changes completes long-run adjustment?
options: AD shifts back to AD1 automatically; output returns to Y1 at P1.
LRAS shifts right to Y2; output remains above its original potential.
SRAS shifts right beyond AS2; output rises further while the price level falls.
SRAS shifts left toward AS1; output returns to Y1 while the price level rises toward P3.
PM2D1-LRADJ-FB-006.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-FB-006.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-003.q: An economy is above potential because of a temporary surge in household spending. Which observation would be the strongest evidence that long-run self-correction has begun?
options: Aggregate demand is automatically shifting left with no change in spending.
Nominal wage growth is falling, pushing SRAS farther to the right.
Nominal wage and unit-cost growth are rising, putting leftward pressure on SRAS.
Potential output is falling simply because current output is high.
PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-003.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-003.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.q: Refer to the graph. At AD1 and AS1 the economy is at Y3, below Y1. If AD1 remains fixed, which change must occur for self-correction toward Y1?
options: SRAS shifts farther left from AS1, reducing output below Y3.
Falling wage and price expectations shift SRAS right from AS1 toward AS2.
Aggregate demand shifts from AD1 to AD2 while SRAS remains at AS1.
LRAS shifts left from Y1 to Y3 because output is currently low.
PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-001.q: A negative demand shock leaves the economy below potential, and no policy response occurs. Which statement best identifies the long-run adjustment mechanism before tracing the details?
options: Slack puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, allowing SRAS to shift right.
Aggregate demand must automatically shift right enough to restore potential output without any change in wages or expectations.
LRAS must move left until it passes through current output, eliminating the gap without any cost adjustment.
High unemployment raises wage growth and shifts SRAS left, moving output even farther below potential.
PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-001.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-001.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS1 at Y3, expected prices and nominal cost pressures fall gradually while AD1 stays fixed. Which sequence is consistent with the model?
options: SRAS moves farther left from AS1, pushing output below Y3 while the price level rises above its starting point.
AD shifts to AD2 and output jumps to Y2 even though the prompt holds aggregate demand fixed throughout the adjustment.
LRAS shifts left from Y1 to Y3, redefining the depressed output level as potential without any wage or expectation adjustment.
SRAS moves toward AS2, output rises toward Y1, and the price level falls toward P1.
PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-5036.q: If output is below natural output, falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS:
ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-5036.feedback: A recessionary gap tends to push wages and expected prices down, shifting SRAS right.

ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-5037.q: If output is above natural output, rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS:
ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-5037.feedback: An expansionary gap tends to push wages and expected prices up, shifting SRAS left.

ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-6028.q: Output is above potential and self-correction through rising wages and costs is expected to be slow. Which stabilization-policy question becomes relevant?
options: Stabilization policy—whether and how to use an active policy response instead of waiting for self-correction.
Money measurement—whether currency should be counted in M1 or M2.
Growth accounting—how much of productivity comes from capital deepening.
CPI measurement—whether the market basket overstates cost-of-living changes.
ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-6028.feedback: Long-run adjustment describes self-correction; stabilization policy asks whether policymakers should actively shift aggregate demand rather than wait.
ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-6028.commonError: Treats passive long-run adjustment and deliberate stabilization as the same mechanism.

ECON-SP-EASY-59.q: The Phillips curve shows a short-run trade-off between:
ECON-SP-EASY-59.commonError: Confusing the Phillips curve with the money market.
ECON-SP-EASY-59.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

ECON-SP-EASY-60.q: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the vertical axis measures:
ECON-SP-EASY-60.feedback: The vertical axis measures the inflation rate.

ECON-SP-EASY-61.q: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the horizontal axis measures:
ECON-SP-EASY-61.feedback: The horizontal axis measures the unemployment rate.

ECON-SP-EASY-62.q: In the short run, expansionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
ECON-SP-EASY-62.feedback: Expansionary policy raises inflation pressure and lowers unemployment in the short run.

ECON-SP-EASY-63.q: In the short run, contractionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
ECON-SP-EASY-63.feedback: Contractionary policy lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run.

ECON-SP-EASY-66.q: Refer to the graph. Point a has:
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation than point c
Higher unemployment and lower inflation than point c
The same unemployment and lower inflation than point c
ECON-SP-EASY-66.commonError: Reading the Phillips curve axes backward.
ECON-SP-EASY-66.feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, while point c is at U2 and I1.

ECON-SP-EASY-67.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from point c to point a shows:
ECON-SP-EASY-67.feedback: Moving from c to a raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run.

ECON-SP-EASY-76.q: In the long run, unemployment returns to:
ECON-SP-EASY-76.commonError: Thinking policymakers can permanently hold unemployment below natural.
ECON-SP-EASY-76.feedback: The natural-rate hypothesis says unemployment returns to its natural rate in the long run.

PG5-PC-E-007.q: At point A, what is the unemployment rate?
PG5-PC-E-007.feedback: Point A lies directly above 5 on the unemployment axis.

PG5-PC-E-013.q: Relative to point A, what does point B show on SRPC0?
PG5-PC-E-013.feedback: Point B is left of A on the unemployment axis and above A on the inflation axis.

PG5-PC-E-019.q: How does point B compare with the natural-rate point A in the displayed Phillips-curve graph?
PG5-PC-E-019.feedback: Point B is to the right of A on the unemployment axis and below A on the inflation axis.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-153.q: The short-run Phillips curve slopes downward because higher AD tends to:
options: Raise output, lower unemployment, and raise inflation
Lower output, lower unemployment, and lower inflation
Raise unemployment while lowering inflation forever
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-153.feedback: Higher AD raises output and prices, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-154.q: Why is there no permanent Phillips-curve tradeoff?
options: Expectations adjust; unemployment returns to normal
AD stops affecting the short run
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-154.commonError: Treating the short-run tradeoff as permanent.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-154.feedback: Once expectations adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-155.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point c, expansionary policy that raises inflation above expectations moves the economy to:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-155.commonError: Moving to the long-run point immediately.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-155.feedback: Expansionary policy moves the economy along SRPC1 from c to a: higher inflation and lower unemployment.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-160.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A move along SRPC1 from c toward b means:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-160.commonError: Reading movement along the curve backward.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-160.feedback: Moving up-left along SRPC1 raises inflation and lowers unemployment.

PG5-PC-M-008.q: At point A, what is the inflation rate?
PG5-PC-M-008.feedback: The horizontal guide through point A hits the inflation axis at 2.5 percent.

PG5-PC-M-014.q: How far below the natural rate is unemployment at point B?
PG5-PC-M-014.feedback: The natural rate is 5 percent at point A on the LRPC, while point B has 3 percent unemployment.

PG5-PC-M-015.q: What type of change is the move from A to B?
options: An upward shift from SRPC0 to another SRPC
A leftward shift of the LRPC
A movement along the same SRPC0
A movement along the vertical LRPC
PG5-PC-M-015.feedback: Both A and B lie on the same SRPC0, so the graph shows a movement along the curve, not a curve shift.

PG5-PC-M-020.q: Point B is to the right of the LRPC. By how many percentage points does its unemployment rate exceed the natural rate?
PG5-PC-M-020.feedback: The natural rate is 5 percent at A, and point B is at 7 percent unemployment.

PG5-PC-M-021.q: Points A and B lie on the same short-run Phillips curve. How should the change from A to B be classified?
options: A movement along the same SRPC0
A downward shift from SRPC0 to another SRPC
A rightward shift of the LRPC
A movement along the vertical LRPC
PG5-PC-M-021.feedback: A and B lie on the same SRPC0, so the graph shows a movement along the short-run curve.

PM2A-SRPC-M-001.q: Aggregate demand rises unexpectedly while expected inflation is fixed. Which Phillips-curve change best represents the immediate effect?
options: A move up and left along the current SRPC
An upward shift of the SRPC at every unemployment rate
A rightward shift of the vertical LRPC
A move down and right along the current SRPC
PM2A-SRPC-M-001.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
PM2A-SRPC-M-001.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

PM2A-SRPC-M-002.q: Inflation and unemployment both rise after a sharp increase in energy costs. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Aggregate demand causes movement up one unchanged SRPC
Lower expected inflation shifts the SRPC downward
The natural rate necessarily falls and shifts LRPC left
The adverse supply shock shifts the SRPC upward
PM2A-SRPC-M-002.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-M-002.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

ECON-SP-HARD-238.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which point reflects unemployment below the natural rate with inflation above I1?
ECON-SP-HARD-238.feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, so unemployment is below the natural rate U2 and inflation is above I1.

ECON-SP-HARD-241.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Moving from b to c along SRPC1 means:
ECON-SP-HARD-241.feedback: Moving down-right along SRPC1 lowers inflation and raises unemployment.

ECON-SP-HARD-255.q: A policymaker claims higher inflation can permanently hold unemployment below natural. What is the flaw?
ECON-SP-HARD-255.commonError: Believing in a permanent Phillips curve menu.
ECON-SP-HARD-255.feedback: Once expected inflation adjusts, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

ECON-SP-HARD-258.q: Which event moves along SRPC rather than shifting SRPC?
ECON-SP-HARD-258.commonError: Confusing movement along SRPC with shifts of SRPC.
ECON-SP-HARD-258.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion moves the economy along the existing SRPC in the short run.

ECON-SP-HARD-268.q: Which answer best separates short-run and long-run Phillips curve logic?
options: Policy can move unemployment temporarily, but expectations restore the natural rate
Policy cannot affect unemployment even briefly, because money is neutral in every period
Policy permanently lowers unemployment whenever inflation rises above zero
Policy shifts LRPC whenever actual inflation changes
ECON-SP-HARD-268.commonError: Confusing short-run effects with long-run neutrality.
ECON-SP-HARD-268.feedback: Demand policy can move unemployment in the short run, but expectations adjust and unemployment returns to natural.

PG5-PC-H-010.q: Moving leftward along SRPC0 from point A implies which short-run relationship?
options: No change in unemployment as inflation changes
PG5-PC-H-010.feedback: A downward-sloping SRPC shows an inverse short-run relationship: less unemployment comes with more inflation.

PG5-PC-H-016.q: At point B, how do unemployment and inflation compare with the natural-rate point A?
options: Unemployment is higher; inflation is lower
Unemployment is lower; inflation is lower
Unemployment is higher; inflation is higher
Unemployment is lower; inflation is higher
PG5-PC-H-016.feedback: Point B combines a higher inflation rate with unemployment below the 5-percent natural rate.

PG5-PC-H-022.q: At the right-hand point B, which inflation-unemployment comparison with A is correct?
options: Unemployment is lower; inflation is higher
Unemployment is higher; inflation is lower
Unemployment is higher; inflation is higher
Unemployment is lower; inflation is lower
PG5-PC-H-022.feedback: Point B has 1.5 percent inflation instead of 2.5 percent, and unemployment is above the 5-percent natural rate.

PM2A-SRPC-H-003.q: Two years have the same unemployment rate, but inflation is higher in the second after wage setters revise expected inflation upward. What changed?
options: Aggregate demand alone fixed both outcomes
The economy is on a higher SRPC
The economy moved up one unchanged SRPC
PM2A-SRPC-H-003.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-H-003.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

ECON-SP-ELITE-323.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, which sequence best shows an attempted permanent unemployment reduction through expansionary policy?
ECON-SP-ELITE-323.commonError: Thinking point a can be held permanently.
ECON-SP-ELITE-323.feedback: Expansion lowers unemployment at a temporarily, but expectations adjust and unemployment returns to natural at b.

ECON-SP-ELITE-348.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which policy mistake is shown by treating point a as permanent?
ECON-SP-ELITE-348.commonError: Believing unemployment can stay below natural without expectations changing.
ECON-SP-ELITE-348.feedback: Point a is temporary because expected inflation eventually rises and moves the economy toward point b.

ECON-SP-ELITE-351.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. If policy moves the economy from c to b on SRPC1, what must be true?
options: Actual inflation rises while unemployment falls
Expected inflation rises while unemployment stays fixed
Natural unemployment rises while inflation falls
ECON-SP-ELITE-351.commonError: Confusing movement along SRPC with a shift of SRPC.
ECON-SP-ELITE-351.feedback: Movement up-left along the same SRPC means higher inflation and lower unemployment.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9007.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, policymakers try to keep unemployment at U1 through repeated demand expansion. What eventually breaks the plan?
options: Expected inflation rises and shifts the SRPC upward.
Actual inflation falls and shifts the SRPC downward.
The LRPC shifts left because inflation is higher.
The natural rate disappears because output rose once.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9007.commonError: Believing policymakers can permanently buy lower unemployment with inflation.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9007.feedback: Expansion can move unemployment below natural temporarily, but expected inflation adjusts and SRPC shifts upward.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9046.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. The economy moves from c to a, then policymakers mistake a as sustainable. What is the likely correction?
options: Expected inflation rises, SRPC shifts up, and the economy moves toward b.
Expected inflation falls, SRPC shifts down, and the economy moves toward d.
The natural rate falls, LRPC shifts left, and the economy stays at a.
The price level falls, AD shifts left, and unemployment stays at U1.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9046.commonError: Treating a short-run Phillips curve point as permanent.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9046.feedback: Point a is temporary. Expected inflation adjusts upward and the economy returns to the natural rate at higher inflation.

P52B-S2-SRPC-L-001.q: Two episodes produce the same increase in inflation. In one, unemployment falls after aggregate demand expands; in the other, unemployment rises after an adverse supply shock. What explains the difference?
options: Both episodes are movements along one SRPC, but they begin from different unemployment rates.
Both episodes shift the LRPC because inflation changes the natural rate in opposite directions.
The supply shock lowers expected inflation and moves the economy down an unchanged SRPC.
The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.
P52B-S2-SRPC-L-001.commonError: Assuming every inflation change is a movement along one fixed Phillips curve.
P52B-S2-SRPC-L-001.feedback: Demand changes can move the economy along a given SRPC; supply shocks alter the inflation-unemployment relationship and shift the SRPC.

PG5-PC-L-012.q: Which pair of descriptions matches the two curves shown?
options: SRPC0: no short-run tradeoff; LRPC: permanent tradeoff
SRPC0: long-run neutrality; LRPC: short-run tradeoff
SRPC0: fixed unemployment; LRPC: fixed inflation
SRPC0: short-run tradeoff; LRPC: no long-run tradeoff
PG5-PC-L-012.feedback: That is the whole point of showing both curves together: a short-run tradeoff and a vertical long-run benchmark.

PM2A-SRPC-L-004.q: A demand expansion moves the economy to lower unemployment and higher inflation. A year later unemployment returns to its original rate while inflation remains higher. Which sequence fits?
options: A supply improvement followed by movement down the SRPC
Movement along an SRPC followed by an upward SRPC shift
Two movements along one permanently fixed SRPC
An LRPC shift left followed by falling expectations
PM2A-SRPC-L-004.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
PM2A-SRPC-L-004.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

PM2A-SRPC-L-005.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation while output falls. How should the AD-AS result transfer to the Phillips model?
options: Higher inflation and unemployment indicate an upward SRPC shift
Higher inflation and lower unemployment indicate movement along SRPC
Lower inflation and unemployment indicate a downward SRPC shift
Unchanged inflation with lower unemployment indicates an LRPC shift
PM2A-SRPC-L-005.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-L-005.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

PM2A-SRPC-L-006.q: A policymaker cites the downward-sloping SRPC as proof that permanently higher inflation will secure permanently lower unemployment. What is the decisive flaw?
options: The SRPC actually slopes upward for every demand change
Inflation cannot respond to aggregate demand in the short run
The natural rate is always zero after an expansion
Expected inflation adjusts, so the short-run unemployment gain is not permanent
PM2A-SRPC-L-006.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
PM2A-SRPC-L-006.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3000.commonError: Confusing the Phillips curve with the AD-AS model.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3000.q: What does the short-run Phillips curve show?
options: A short-run tradeoff between inflation and unemployment
A long-run tradeoff between inflation and output
A fixed relationship between money supply and GDP
A direct measure of government spending
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3000.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3001.q: Expansionary policy raises aggregate demand. In the short run, what Phillips curve movement should follow?
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3001.feedback: Expansionary policy raises AD, which can lower unemployment but raises inflation in the short run.

P52B-S2-SRPC-B2-001.q: Aggregate demand contracts unexpectedly while expected inflation is initially fixed. What short-run Phillips-curve movement is most likely?
options: Toward lower inflation and higher unemployment.
Toward higher inflation and lower unemployment.
The entire SRPC shifts up-right immediately.
Unemployment stays fixed at the natural rate in the short run.
P52B-S2-SRPC-B2-001.commonError: Confusing a demand-driven movement along the SRPC with a shift of the curve.
P52B-S2-SRPC-B2-001.feedback: An unexpected demand contraction moves the economy down and right along the current SRPC.

PM2A-SRPC-EB-007.q: On a given SRPC, which combination lies farther up and left?
PM2A-SRPC-EB-007.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-007.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

PM2A-SRPC-EB-008.q: Expected inflation is unchanged and aggregate demand falls. What happens first?
options: The economy moves up and left along its SRPC
The economy moves down and right along its SRPC
The SRPC shifts upward at every unemployment rate
The LRPC shifts left of the natural rate
PM2A-SRPC-EB-008.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-008.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

PM2A-SRPC-EB-009.q: Which event most directly shifts rather than moves along the SRPC?
options: An unexpected change in aggregate demand
A temporary change in real spending
A movement between two points on one curve
PM2A-SRPC-EB-009.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-009.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

PM2A-SRPC-FB-010.q: A demand boom first lowers unemployment, then wage expectations catch up. Which complete Phillips sequence is most defensible?
