Cyclical unemployment at every inflation rate
PM2A-LRPC-BR-021.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
PM2A-LRPC-BR-021.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

PM2A-LRPC-BR-022.q: A central bank begins disinflation from the natural rate. Which next family concept measures the possible output cost of the temporary adjustment?
PM2A-LRPC-BR-022.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
PM2A-LRPC-BR-022.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

ECON-SP-EASY-68.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from point a to point b most likely shows:
ECON-SP-EASY-68.commonError: Thinking unemployment stays below natural permanently.
ECON-SP-EASY-68.feedback: After inflation expectations adjust upward, the SRPC shifts and unemployment returns to the natural rate at point b.

ECON-SP-EASY-69.q: If expected inflation rises, the short-run Phillips curve shifts:
ECON-SP-EASY-69.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up and right.

ECON-SP-EASY-70.q: Refer to the graph. SRPC2 compared with SRPC1 represents:
options: A fall in money supply only
ECON-SP-EASY-70.commonError: Missing that the higher SRPC reflects worse inflation expectations.
ECON-SP-EASY-70.feedback: SRPC2 is above SRPC1, meaning higher expected inflation or a worse tradeoff.

ECON-SP-EASY-73.q: An adverse supply shock shifts the short-run Phillips curve:
ECON-SP-EASY-73.commonError: Treating supply shocks as movement along the same SRPC.
ECON-SP-EASY-73.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the tradeoff by shifting the SRPC up and right.

ECON-SP-EASY-74.q: A surge in oil prices can cause inflation and unemployment to:
ECON-SP-EASY-74.commonError: Thinking inflation and unemployment always move opposite ways.
ECON-SP-EASY-74.feedback: A negative supply shock can raise inflation and unemployment together.

PG5-PC-E-001.q: Compared with point A, what combination is shown at point B?
PG5-PC-E-001.feedback: Point A is at 5 percent unemployment and 3 percent inflation, while point B is at 6 percent unemployment and 6 percent inflation.

PM2A-EXP-E-001.q: Workers and firms begin expecting higher inflation next year. Holding unemployment fixed, what happens to the short-run Phillips curve?
options: The economy moves down one unchanged curve
PM2A-EXP-E-001.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
PM2A-EXP-E-001.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-156.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point a, expected inflation adjusts upward. The long-run movement is to:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-156.feedback: Expectations adjust upward, SRPC shifts up, and unemployment returns to U2 at point b.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-158.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Moving from d to c most likely reflects:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-158.feedback: As expected inflation falls, the SRPC shifts downward and unemployment returns to U2 at point c.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-161.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Moving from SRPC1 to SRPC2 at the same unemployment rate means:
options: Inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate
Inflation is lower at the same unemployment rate
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-161.feedback: SRPC2 is above SRPC1, so inflation is higher for a given unemployment rate.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-162.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. If the economy moves from c on SRPC1 to the upper point at the same unemployment rate, the likely cause is:
options: A fall in actual inflation only
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-162.commonError: Confusing a curve shift with movement along one curve.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-162.feedback: At the same unemployment rate, a higher SRPC reflects higher expected inflation or a worse tradeoff.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-163.q: An adverse supply shock affects the Phillips curve by:
options: Moving down along the same SRPC
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-163.commonError: Treating supply shocks as normal AD movements.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-163.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-164.q: If policymakers expand AD to reduce unemployment below the natural rate, what happens after expectations adjust?
options: Unemployment returns to natural and inflation stays higher
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-164.commonError: Believing in a permanent policy tradeoff.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-164.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up, returning unemployment to natural at higher inflation.

PG5-PC-M-002.q: Suppose expected inflation rises while the natural rate is unchanged. Which curve change shown is consistent with that assumption?
options: SRPC0 shifts downward away from SRPC1
LRPC shifts left to a lower natural rate
The economy only moves along unchanged SRPC0
PG5-PC-M-002.feedback: An upward shift of the short-run Phillips curve is the standard way to show higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock with the natural rate unchanged.

ECON-SP-HARD-236.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, which sequence matches expansionary policy and expectations adjustment?
ECON-SP-HARD-236.commonError: Skipping the short-run movement along SRPC.
ECON-SP-HARD-236.feedback: Expansion moves from c to a in the short run; expected inflation rises and moves the economy to b.

ECON-SP-HARD-240.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which movement shows expectations falling after contractionary policy?
ECON-SP-HARD-240.feedback: Moving from d to c reflects lower expected inflation and return to the natural unemployment rate.

ECON-SP-HARD-242.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At U3, moving from SRPC1 to SRPC2 changes inflation from:
ECON-SP-HARD-242.commonError: Reading the wrong inflation level at U3.
ECON-SP-HARD-242.feedback: At U3, the lower curve is at I2 and the upper curve is at I4.

ECON-SP-HARD-243.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, the move from SRPC1 to SRPC2 implies unemployment is:
ECON-SP-HARD-243.commonError: Missing worse tradeoff at the same inflation rate.
ECON-SP-HARD-243.feedback: At a given inflation rate, the higher SRPC implies a higher unemployment rate.

ECON-SP-HARD-244.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A shift from SRPC1 to SRPC2 is most consistent with:
options: Higher expected inflation or adverse supply shock
Lower expected inflation or favorable supply shock
Higher money supply with expectations fixed
Lower unemployment at every inflation rate
ECON-SP-HARD-244.commonError: Treating SRPC shifts as ordinary movement along a curve.
ECON-SP-HARD-244.feedback: The upward SRPC shift reflects higher expected inflation or a worsened supply-side tradeoff.

ECON-SP-HARD-245.q: If the Fed unexpectedly increases inflation while expected inflation is fixed, unemployment moves:
ECON-SP-HARD-245.commonError: Ignoring the gap between actual and expected inflation.
ECON-SP-HARD-245.feedback: When actual inflation exceeds expected inflation, unemployment can temporarily fall below the natural rate.

ECON-SP-HARD-257.q: Which event shifts both SRAS left and SRPC up-right?
ECON-SP-HARD-257.commonError: Confusing supply shocks with AD shocks.
ECON-SP-HARD-257.feedback: An oil price surge raises production costs and worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

ECON-SP-HARD-263.q: If expected inflation rises but actual inflation does not rise with it, unemployment tends to:
ECON-SP-HARD-263.commonError: Ignoring expected inflation in the Phillips curve equation.
ECON-SP-HARD-263.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts SRPC up, so unchanged actual inflation corresponds to higher unemployment.

ECON-SP-HARD-264.q: If expected inflation falls while actual inflation is held steady, unemployment tends to:
ECON-SP-HARD-264.commonError: Reversing the effect of lower expected inflation.
ECON-SP-HARD-264.feedback: Lower expected inflation shifts SRPC down, so the same actual inflation can mean lower unemployment.

ECON-SP-HARD-265.q: A student says an oil shock causes only movement along the SRPC. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC because costs and prices change directly
It shifts only AD because spending changes directly
It shifts only LRPC because inflation changes
It moves only along LRAS because output changes
ECON-SP-HARD-265.commonError: Treating supply shocks as AD movements.
ECON-SP-HARD-265.feedback: A supply shock shifts the SRPC because it directly changes firms' costs and inflation pressure.

ECON-SP-HARD-267.q: A student says higher expected inflation lowers unemployment permanently. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC upward and worsens the short-run tradeoff
It shifts LRPC left and improves the long-run tradeoff
It shifts AD right and lowers prices
It raises money demand and lowers rates
ECON-SP-HARD-267.commonError: Treating expected inflation as beneficial stimulus.
ECON-SP-HARD-267.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward, giving higher inflation at each unemployment rate.

PG5-PC-H-004.q: At a given unemployment rate, how does SRPC1 compare with SRPC0?
options: SRPC1 shows a lower inflation rate
SRPC1 shows the same inflation rate
SRPC1 shows a lower natural rate
SRPC1 shows a higher inflation rate
PG5-PC-H-004.feedback: Point B lies on a different short-run Phillips curve, SRPC1, so the graph is showing a curve shift rather than a movement along SRPC0.

ECON-SP-ELITE-326.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A move from c on SRPC1 to the upper point at U3 on SRPC2 means:
ECON-SP-ELITE-326.commonError: Reading the curve shift as movement along SRPC1.
ECON-SP-ELITE-326.feedback: At U3, SRPC2 shows a higher inflation rate than SRPC1.

ECON-SP-ELITE-327.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, comparing SRPC1 and SRPC2 shows:
ECON-SP-ELITE-327.commonError: Missing the worse tradeoff after SRPC shifts upward.
ECON-SP-ELITE-327.feedback: At the same inflation rate, the higher SRPC shows higher unemployment.

ECON-SP-ELITE-328.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands AD. Later, workers build the higher inflation into wage demands. Which sequence is most accurate?
options: Move along SRPC, then SRPC shifts up
SRPC shifts down, then move along LRPC
LRPC shifts left, then AD falls
Move along LRAS, then M1 falls
ECON-SP-ELITE-328.commonError: Confusing immediate inflation surprise with later expectation adjustment.
ECON-SP-ELITE-328.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion first moves along the SRPC; later expected inflation rises and shifts SRPC upward.

ECON-SP-ELITE-350.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Which labeled move isolates an upward SRPC shift at unemployment U3?
options: The move from point c to point f
The move from point a to point f
The move from point b to point e
The move from point c to point a
ECON-SP-ELITE-350.commonError: Compares points with different unemployment rates, so movement and shift effects are mixed.
ECON-SP-ELITE-350.feedback: Points c and f share unemployment U3; moving from c on SRPC1 to f on SRPC2 isolates higher inflation at the same unemployment rate.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9009.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy moves from SRPC1 to SRPC2. Which statement should be rejected?
options: The tradeoff improved because higher inflation now buys lower unemployment at every point.
The tradeoff worsened because inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate.
Expected inflation may have increased and shifted the curve upward.
An adverse supply shock may have raised both inflation pressure and unemployment risk.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9009.commonError: Calling an upward SRPC shift an improvement.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9009.feedback: An upward SRPC shift worsens the tradeoff because inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9018.q: A policymaker says, 'Inflation is high, so unemployment must be low.' What is the best correction?
options: That only fits demand pressure; supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment together.
That is always true because the Phillips curve never shifts.
That is false only when M1 is larger than M2.
That is true in the long run because LRPC slopes downward.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9018.commonError: Treating the Phillips curve as fixed under every shock.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9018.feedback: The short-run tradeoff can worsen when SRPC shifts up, so inflation and unemployment can rise together.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9048.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy is on SRPC2 rather than SRPC1. Which conclusion is most careful?
options: The tradeoff worsened, but the cause could be expected inflation or a supply shock.
The tradeoff improved, and policymakers can now lower unemployment without cost.
The LRPC shifted left, so natural unemployment must have fallen.
AD must have shifted right, so SRPC cannot have moved.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9048.commonError: Assuming every SRPC shift has only one cause.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9048.feedback: An upward SRPC shift can come from higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock, and both worsen the tradeoff.

PG5-PC-L-006.q: At the unemployment rate marked by the LRPC, how does inflation on SRPC1 compare with inflation at point A on SRPC0?
options: Inflation is lower on SRPC1 while unemployment stays at 5 percent
Inflation is higher on SRPC1 while unemployment stays at 5 percent
Inflation is unchanged because SRPC0 and SRPC1 overlap there
Unemployment falls below 5 percent while inflation stays unchanged
PG5-PC-L-006.feedback: Because the SRPC shifts up while the LRPC stays fixed, maintaining unemployment at the natural rate would involve a higher inflation rate than at point A.

PG5-PC-L-018.q: If policymakers keep unemployment at point B, what expectations adjustment tends to follow?
options: Expected inflation falls and SRPC shifts downward
Expected inflation rises and SRPC shifts upward
Expected inflation stays fixed and LRPC shifts left
Expected inflation rises and LRPC shifts right
PG5-PC-L-018.feedback: Below-natural-rate unemployment tends to raise inflation expectations, shifting the SRPC upward and moving unemployment back toward the natural rate.

PG5-PC-L-024.q: If unemployment remains at the right-hand point B, how should inflation expectations and the SRPC adjust over time?
options: Expected inflation rises and SRPC shifts upward
Expected inflation stays fixed and LRPC shifts right
Expected inflation falls and LRPC shifts left
Expected inflation falls and SRPC shifts downward
PG5-PC-L-024.feedback: Above-natural-rate unemployment tends to reduce inflation expectations, shifting the SRPC downward and returning unemployment toward the natural rate.

PM2A-EXP-L-002.q: A surprise demand expansion initially lowers unemployment. Contracts renew after actual inflation repeatedly exceeds prior forecasts. Which response is most likely?
options: Expected inflation falls and the SRPC shifts downward
The LRPC shifts left because contracts renew
Expected inflation rises and the SRPC shifts upward
PM2A-EXP-L-002.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-L-002.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

PM2A-EXP-L-003.q: Two central banks announce the same lower inflation target. One has a stronger record of meeting targets. Under otherwise similar conditions, what can differ?
options: Actual inflation must reach zero with no output cost
The less credible bank must cause immediate deflation
Expected inflation may fall faster where the announcement is more credible
The natural rate must immediately fall only in the credible economy
PM2A-EXP-L-003.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-EXP-L-003.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

PM2A-EXP-L-004.q: Actual inflation is 5% while wage setters expected 3%, temporarily pushing unemployment below natural. What erodes that effect?
options: The price level returns to its initial value automatically
Forecasts adjust upward, shifting the SRPC until unemployment returns toward natural
The LRPC shifts left because actual inflation is above expected
Forecasts adjust downward, moving unemployment farther below natural
PM2A-EXP-L-004.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-L-004.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.commonError: Treating expected inflation as movement along the same SRPC.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.q: What happens to the short-run Phillips curve when expected inflation rises?
options: It becomes the money demand curve
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the short-run Phillips curve upward.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.commonError: Keeping unemployment below natural forever after an inflation surprise.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at c, expansionary policy moves the economy to a. After expected inflation rises, where does the economy move?
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.feedback: After expected inflation rises, the SRPC shifts up and the economy moves to b at the natural rate of unemployment.

P52B-S2-PCEXP-B2-001.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises firms’ costs. What happens to the short-run Phillips curve, other things equal?
options: It shifts down and to the left.
The economy only moves along an unchanged curve.
It shifts up and to the right.
It becomes vertical at zero unemployment.
P52B-S2-PCEXP-B2-001.commonError: Treating an adverse supply shock as a movement along a fixed SRPC.
P52B-S2-PCEXP-B2-001.feedback: An adverse supply shock can raise both inflation and unemployment, shifting the SRPC up-right.

PM2A-EXP-EB-005.q: If expected inflation increases, which SRPC change follows?
options: Only movement down the same curve
PM2A-EXP-EB-005.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
PM2A-EXP-EB-005.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

PM2A-EXP-EB-006.q: If expected inflation decreases, which SRPC change follows?
options: Only movement up the same curve
PM2A-EXP-EB-006.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
PM2A-EXP-EB-006.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

PM2A-EXP-EB-007.q: Why can actual inflation above expected inflation temporarily reduce unemployment?
options: Higher inflation permanently raises labor productivity
Some wages and prices were set using the lower forecast
The natural rate immediately becomes lower
PM2A-EXP-EB-007.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-EB-007.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

PM2A-EXP-FB-008.q: A credible disinflation announcement lowers expected inflation before much demand contraction occurs. Which graph change is most consistent?
options: The economy can only move up-left along the old SRPC
The SRPC shifts downward, potentially reducing the short-run cost
The LRPC shifts right and permanently raises unemployment
The SRPC shifts upward because actual inflation may fall
PM2A-EXP-FB-008.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-EXP-FB-008.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

PM2A-EXP-FB-009.q: Actual inflation remains above expected inflation for several contract cycles. Which sequence best fits adaptive expectations?
options: Expected inflation rises, shifting SRPC upward and undoing the temporary unemployment gain
Expected inflation falls, shifting SRPC downward and preserving the unemployment gain indefinitely
LRPC shifts left, locking in unemployment below natural after contracts renew
SRPC stays fixed because only actual inflation matters for wage setting
PM2A-EXP-FB-009.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-FB-009.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

PM2A-EXP-FB-010.q: A supply shock raises inflation without a demand boom. Why might a simple expectations-only diagnosis be incomplete?
options: Expected inflation is the only possible SRPC shifter in the introductory model
Every inflation increase is movement along a fixed SRPC regardless of its cause
Supply shocks shift only the vertical LRPC while leaving SRPC unchanged
The shock can shift the SRPC even before expectations adapt
PM2A-EXP-FB-010.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
PM2A-EXP-FB-010.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

PM2A-EXP-LB-011.q: A surprise expansion lifts inflation from 2% to 5% while expected inflation remains 2%. What makes the unemployment effect temporary?
options: Expected inflation falls below 2% and shifts SRPC downward after workers observe prices
The LRPC becomes flatter as actual inflation rises above expected inflation
Expected inflation eventually rises toward actual inflation and shifts the SRPC upward
The natural rate permanently falls three points once actual inflation exceeds its forecast
PM2A-EXP-LB-011.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-LB-011.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

PM2A-EXP-LB-012.q: A disinflation announcement is only partly credible and wage contracts reset slowly. Which conclusion is appropriately bounded?
options: The announcement necessarily causes the price level to fall for several years
Expectations may fall gradually, so some short-run output cost can remain
Partial credibility must eliminate every unemployment cost as soon as policy is announced
Expected inflation cannot change until actual inflation reaches the announced target
PM2A-EXP-LB-012.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-EXP-LB-012.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

PM2A-EXP-LB-013.q: An adverse supply shock raises actual inflation, then wage setters incorporate it into next year’s contracts. What are the two stages?
options: An initial SRPC shift followed by reinforcement through higher expected inflation
Two movements along one fixed SRPC with no change in the inflation-unemployment relation
An LRPC shift followed by lower expected inflation when contracts renew
A demand contraction followed by an SRPC shift downward at each unemployment rate
PM2A-EXP-LB-013.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
PM2A-EXP-LB-013.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-5053.q: Expected inflation rises from 2% to 4%. At a given unemployment rate, how does the SRPC move?
options: The economy moves down the same SRPC
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-5053.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-5053.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.

ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-5055.q: Actual inflation repeatedly exceeds the rate workers expected. Which forecast adjustment is likely?
ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-5055.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-5055.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-50.q: Does a credible announcement guarantee costless disinflation?
options: No; credibility can never affect expectations
No; it can reduce costs without always eliminating them
Yes; credibility removes all nominal rigidities
ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-50.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-50.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-6044.q: The economy moves up-left along SRPC after a demand surprise. Wage setters then revise forecasts upward. What connection is required?
options: A movement along SRPC becomes an upward shift as expectations adjust
The LRPC shifts left as aggregate demand rises and nominal wages renew
The same fixed SRPC supports permanently lower unemployment after forecasts update
A downward expectations shift reinforces the initial unemployment gain
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-6044.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-INFLATION-SHIFT-6044.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-6046.q: Expected inflation falls during a credible disinflation. Which applied family slice uses that change to assess policy costs?
ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-6046.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
ECON-SP-SUPPLY-SHOCK-PC-SHIFT-6046.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-60.q: Expectations fully catch up after repeated inflation surprises. Which curve summarizes the long-run unemployment result?
options: The LRPC at the natural rate
The SRPC as a permanent menu
ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-60.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
ECON-SP-TRACE-EXPECTATIONS-ADJUSTMENT-60.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

ECON-SP-EASY-75.q: If the Fed reduces money growth to fight inflation, unemployment usually:
ECON-SP-EASY-75.commonError: Ignoring the short-run cost of disinflation.
ECON-SP-EASY-75.feedback: Disinflation usually raises unemployment temporarily as the economy moves along the SRPC.

options: The overall price level is falling because average prices are declining.
Unemployment is falling even though output remains below potential.
Inflation is slowing, although the price level may still be rising.
Nominal wages are fixed while real wages rise automatically.
P52B-S1-DIS-E-001.feedback: Disinflation is slower price growth; deflation is a falling price level.

P52B-S1-DIS-E-002.q: Why can a credible anti-inflation announcement reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
options: It permanently eliminates the natural rate of unemployment.
It guarantees that the price level falls immediately.
Expected inflation may adjust downward more quickly.
P52B-S1-DIS-E-002.commonError: Ignoring the role of expected inflation in the transition.
P52B-S1-DIS-E-002.feedback: When expectations fall sooner, wage and price setting can adjust with less output and unemployment loss.

options: Cumulative output lost per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
The permanent unemployment rate created by a recession.
The price-level increase caused by one point of money growth.
The share of public spending financed by current taxes.
P52B-S1-DIS-E-003.commonError: Treating the sacrifice ratio as a permanent unemployment rate.
P52B-S1-DIS-E-003.feedback: The sacrifice ratio summarizes the output cost of lowering inflation.

PM2A-DIS-E-001.q: Inflation slows from 6% to 3%, so the price level still rises more slowly. What is this?
options: A falling real interest rate by definition
PM2A-DIS-E-001.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
PM2A-DIS-E-001.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

PM2A-DIS-E-002.q: Which short-run effect commonly accompanies contractionary disinflation policy?
options: A permanently lower natural unemployment rate
An immediate rise in aggregate demand
PM2A-DIS-E-002.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
PM2A-DIS-E-002.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-157.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point b, contractionary policy that lowers inflation below expectations moves the economy in the short run to:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-157.commonError: Moving directly to lower expected inflation.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-157.feedback: Contractionary policy moves along SRPC2 from b to d: lower inflation and higher unemployment.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-165.q: If the Fed reduces money growth to lower inflation, the short-run Phillips curve predicts:
options: Lower inflation and temporarily higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment immediately
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-165.feedback: Disinflation usually moves the economy toward lower inflation and higher unemployment in the short run.

PM2A-DIS-M-003.q: A central bank reduces aggregate demand to lower inflation. What Phillips movement is expected before expectations adjust?
options: An upward SRPC shift from lower expected inflation
Down and right along the current SRPC
Up and left along the current SRPC
PM2A-DIS-M-003.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
PM2A-DIS-M-003.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

PM2A-DIS-M-004.q: Why can a credible lower-inflation target reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
options: It causes aggregate demand to expand during contraction
It may lower expected inflation and shift the SRPC downward sooner
It permanently lowers the natural rate by announcement
It guarantees wages and prices adjust instantly
PM2A-DIS-M-004.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
PM2A-DIS-M-004.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

PM2A-DIS-M-005.q: Inflation falls from 4% to 1%, but prices continue rising. Which statement is correct?
options: The economy has disinflation, not deflation
The economy has deflation because inflation fell
The price level must be below its initial level

ECON-SP-EASY-78.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 4 and inflation falls by 2 percentage points, the output cost is:
ECON-SP-EASY-78.feedback: The output cost is 4 x 2 = 8 percent of one year's output.

ECON-SP-HARD-249.q: Potential GDP is $400 billion. Cumulative output loss is $24 billion while inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 2% of one year’s output per inflation point
ECON-SP-HARD-249.commonError: Divides the dollar loss directly by the inflation change without converting loss to a share of potential output.
ECON-SP-HARD-249.feedback: The $24 billion loss is 6% of $400 billion. Inflation falls 3 percentage points, so the ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

ECON-SP-HARD-250.q: If inflation falls by 3 points and the output loss is 12 percent of one year’s GDP, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 12% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
3% of one year’s output per inflation point
9% of one year’s output per inflation point
ECON-SP-HARD-250.commonError: Uses the inflation reduction or cumulative output loss alone rather than dividing loss by points reduced.
ECON-SP-HARD-250.feedback: Divide cumulative output loss by the inflation reduction: 12 ÷ 3 = 4% of one year’s output per inflation point.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-167.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 3 and inflation falls from 8 percent to 5 percent, the output cost is:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-167.feedback: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points, so output loss is 3 x 3 = 9 percent of one year's output.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3012.commonError: Confusing the sacrifice ratio with the inflation rate itself.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3012.q: What does the sacrifice ratio measure?
options: The output cost of reducing inflation
The unemployment rate at zero inflation
The tax increase needed to raise AD
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3012.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing inflation.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3013.q: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points. If the sacrifice ratio is 4, what output loss should be expected?
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3013.feedback: Output loss equals sacrifice ratio times inflation reduction, so 4 x 3 = 12 percent of one year's output.

PM2A-SAC-EB-016.q: Which formula states the sacrifice ratio?
options: Price-level decline over the episode ÷ nominal GDP growth
Cumulative output loss ÷ inflation reduction in percentage points
Inflation reduction in points ÷ cumulative output loss relative to potential
Permanent unemployment increase ÷ the final positive inflation rate
PM2A-SAC-EB-016.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
PM2A-SAC-EB-016.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

PM2A-SAC-EB-017.q: Inflation falls from 6% to 4%. What is the denominator?
PM2A-SAC-EB-017.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
PM2A-SAC-EB-017.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

PM2A-SAC-EB-018.q: A ratio of 2 is best read as what?
options: Inflation falls two percent for every percentage point of unemployment added
Unemployment stays two points above natural after expectations completely adjust
The price level declines two percent in each year of disinflation
Two percent of one year’s output lost per inflation point reduced
PM2A-SAC-EB-018.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
PM2A-SAC-EB-018.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

PM2A-SAC-FB-020.q: Annual output gaps are −1%, −2%, and −1%; inflation falls from 7% to 5%. What is the ratio?
options: 2% of one year’s output per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-FB-020.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-FB-020.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-FB-021.q: A report divides cumulative output loss by the final inflation rate. What correction is required?
options: Divide by the percentage-point reduction in inflation
Divide by the initial inflation rate before the policy began
Multiply by the final inflation rate
PM2A-SAC-FB-021.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
PM2A-SAC-FB-021.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

PM2A-SAC-FB-022.q: Path X loses 7.2% of annual GDP to reduce inflation 3 points. Path Y loses 5% to reduce inflation 2 points. Which is more output-efficient?
options: Path Y, with a ratio of 2 versus 2.4
Path X, with a ratio of 3 versus 2
They are equal because both lower inflation
Path X, with a ratio of 2.4 versus 2.5
PM2A-SAC-FB-022.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-FB-022.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-MB-019.q: Loss is 10% of annual GDP and inflation falls 4 points. What is the ratio?
options: 2.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-MB-019.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-MB-019.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-LB-023.q: A two-year policy creates output gaps of −2.4% and −1.8%, lowering inflation from 7.0% to 5.2%. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.33% of one year’s output per inflation point
PM2A-SAC-LB-023.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-LB-023.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-LB-024.q: A credible plan lowers expected inflation and produces a 3% cumulative output loss for a 2-point inflation reduction. A less credible plan loses 7.5% for a 3-point reduction. Which comparison is correct?
options: The plans are equal because both reduce inflation
The credible plan ratio is 1.5; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 2; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 0.67; the other is 0.4
PM2A-SAC-LB-024.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-LB-024.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

PM2A-SAC-LB-025.q: Potential output is $800 billion. A policy creates gaps of 1.5% for two years and 0.5% for one year while inflation falls 2.8 points. What is cumulative loss per inflation point?
PM2A-SAC-LB-025.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
PM2A-SAC-LB-025.feedback: The cumulative loss is 3.5% of $800 billion = $28 billion. Dividing by 2.8 inflation points gives $10 billion per point.
PM2A-SAC-LB-025.roundingRule: Report the exact dollar amount per inflation point.

ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5059.q: Inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What number belongs in the sacrifice-ratio denominator?
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5059.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5059.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.

ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5058.q: Should annual output gaps be added before calculating a multi-year sacrifice ratio?
options: No, only the worst year counts
No, only the final year counts
Yes, but add inflation rates too
Yes, to obtain cumulative output loss
ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5058.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5058.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5060.q: Does the sacrifice ratio normally measure an unemployment increase per inflation point?
options: Yes, but only when inflation stays positive
No, it measures the fall in the price level
No, it measures cumulative output loss per inflation point
Yes, unemployment is always the numerator
ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5060.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-5060.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.

ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6050.q: The economy temporarily moves above natural unemployment during disinflation. How is this cost measured?
options: Sum the output losses and divide by the inflation-point reduction
Divide the unemployment increase by the final positive inflation rate
Treat the change in the price level as the cumulative output numerator
Shift LRPC right by the cumulative inflation reduction during policy
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6050.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6050.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6049.q: Expected inflation falls faster after a credible announcement. How can that connect to the sacrifice ratio?
options: A lower final inflation rate automatically raises the ratio even with unchanged loss
Credibility changes the denominator from inflation reduction to unemployment
The ratio must become zero in every credible disinflation plan
A smaller cumulative output loss can lower the measured ratio
ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6049.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
ECON-SP-DEFINE-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6049.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6051.q: Two disinflation paths reach the same inflation target. Which family destination uses their sacrifice ratios to compare costs?
ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6051.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.
ECON-SP-INTERPRET-SACRIFICE-RATIO-6051.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.

fiscal-policy-and-aggregate-demand.title: Fiscal Policy and Aggregate Demand
fiscal-policy-and-aggregate-demand.description: Trace government purchases and taxes into aggregate demand.

easy.q: Higher government spending usually shifts aggregate demand:
easy.commonError: Reversing expansionary fiscal policy.
easy.feedback: Higher government spending raises aggregate demand.

easy.q: A tax cut usually shifts aggregate demand:
easy.commonError: Confusing tax cuts and tax increases.
easy.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption, shifting AD right.

easy.q: Expansionary fiscal policy includes
options: higher government spending or lower taxes
lower government spending or higher taxes
a decrease in the money supply
easy.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy
easy.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy uses higher government spending or lower taxes to increase aggregate demand.

easy.q: Contractionary fiscal policy includes
options: lower government spending or higher taxes
higher government spending or lower taxes
a decrease in interest on reserves only
easy.commonError: confusing fiscal tightening with monetary tightening
easy.feedback: Contractionary fiscal policy means lower government spending or higher taxes, which reduces aggregate demand.

easy.q: An increase in government spending shifts aggregate demand
options: only downward along the same curve
not at all because G is not part of AD
easy.commonError: forgetting that G is a component of aggregate demand
easy.feedback: Government spending is part of aggregate demand, so an increase in G shifts AD right.

easy.q: A decrease in taxes usually shifts aggregate demand
options: nowhere because taxes are not related to spending
easy.commonError: thinking tax cuts reduce consumption
easy.feedback: Lower taxes raise disposable income, which can raise consumption and shift AD right.

medium.q: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Moving from AD1 to AD2 changes output from:
medium.commonError: Reading the graph backward.
medium.feedback: At the same price level, output rises from Y1 to Y2 when AD shifts from AD1 to AD2.

medium.q: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Which curve shows the largest aggregate demand level?
medium.commonError: Confusing curve position with label order.
medium.feedback: AD3 is farthest to the right, so it shows the largest AD at price level P.

medium.q: Which policy is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: Selling government bonds by the Fed
medium.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with Fed policy
medium.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy uses higher government spending or lower taxes to raise aggregate demand.

medium.q: Which policy is contractionary fiscal policy?
options: Buying government bonds by the Fed
medium.commonError: confusing fiscal and monetary policy tools
medium.feedback: Higher taxes are contractionary fiscal policy because they reduce disposable income and aggregate demand.

medium.q: A tax cut shifts aggregate demand right mainly because it
options: forces banks to hold more reserves
medium.commonError: thinking tax cuts work through bank reserves
medium.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.

medium.q: A cut in government purchases shifts aggregate demand left because
options: government spending is a component of aggregate demand
medium.commonError: forgetting that G is directly part of AD
medium.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD, so reducing G shifts AD left.

medium.q: If Congress increases infrastructure spending during a recession, the direct effect is to
medium.commonError: treating fiscal stimulus like contractionary policy
medium.feedback: Higher infrastructure spending raises G and shifts AD right.

medium.q: If the government raises taxes during an expansion, the likely AD effect is
medium.commonError: thinking tax increases raise consumption
medium.feedback: Higher taxes reduce disposable income and consumption, shifting AD left.

hard.q: Congress increases government purchases by $80 billion while households cut consumption by $50 billion for unrelated reasons. Before multiplier effects, the net direct change in aggregate demand is:
hard.commonError: Adding changes without respecting their directions.
hard.feedback: Government purchases add $80 billion while consumption subtracts $50 billion.

hard.q: A $120 billion tax rebate is issued and households spend 65 percent of the added disposable income initially. What is the first-round consumption increase?
hard.commonError: Using the MPS or the full tax cut as first-round consumption.
hard.feedback: First-round consumption is 0.65 × $120 billion = $78 billion.

hard.q: A government raises taxes and increases purchases by the same dollar amount. Which statement is most precise about the immediate AD effects?
options: The two actions must cancel exactly before behavior is considered.
Both actions shift AD right by the same amount.
Taxes enter AD directly as a negative component.
Purchases enter AD directly, while higher taxes reduce consumption indirectly.
hard.commonError: Treating taxes as a direct component of aggregate demand.
hard.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD; taxes work through disposable income and consumption.

hard.q: A temporary tax cut is mostly saved because households expect it to be reversed next year. Compared with a tax cut that is mostly spent, the AD shift is:
hard.commonError: Ignoring household spending behavior.
hard.feedback: A smaller consumption response weakens the tax cut’s effect on aggregate demand.

hard.q: The government cuts purchases during a recession but also cuts taxes. Which conclusion is valid without knowing the magnitudes and household response?
options: The two policies always cancel exactly.
The net direction of aggregate demand is ambiguous.
hard.commonError: Assuming one policy label determines the combined outcome.
hard.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left, while a tax cut tends to shift it right; magnitudes matter.

hard.q: A tax increase of $60 billion reduces consumption by $42 billion in the first round. The implied MPC is:
hard.commonError: Dividing in the wrong direction or using the MPS.
hard.feedback: MPC = $42 billion / $60 billion = 0.70.

elite.q: A tax cut occurs while households expect future taxes to rise and save much of the extra income. What happens to the tax multiplier?
options: It is weaker than simple models predict
It shifts SRAS instead of AD
elite.commonError: Assuming every tax cut creates the same consumption response.
elite.feedback: If households save much of the tax cut, the increase in consumption and AD is weaker.

elite.q: An economy faces a positive AD shock of $240 billion. If policymakers use a tax increase that reduces disposable income by $100 billion and MPC is 0.8, what is the first-round consumption reduction?
elite.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
elite.feedback: The first-round consumption reduction is MPC times the disposable income change: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

elite.q: A fiscal package raises government purchases by $120 billion and taxes by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, the package’s first-round effect on AD is:
elite.commonError: Ignoring that the tax increase reduces consumption by MPC times the tax change.
elite.feedback: Purchases add $120 billion; the tax increase reduces consumption by $80 billion.

elite.q: A tax cut is announced, but credit-constrained households spend 90 percent while high-income households spend 30 percent. Which feature matters most for the AD effect?
options: The long-run natural rate of output
Whether government purchases are counted in GDP
Only the statutory size of the tax cut
How the tax cut is distributed across groups with different marginal propensities to consume.
elite.commonError: Assuming every dollar of tax reduction produces the same consumption response.
elite.feedback: The aggregate consumption response depends on who receives the tax cut and how much they spend.

legendary.q: A government increases purchases by $50 billion and raises taxes by $50 billion. MPC is 0.75. Before subsequent multiplier rounds, the net first-round AD change is:
legendary.commonError: Assuming equal spending and tax changes have equal direct AD effects.
legendary.feedback: Purchases add $50 billion; the tax increase cuts consumption by $37.5 billion.

legendary.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $160 billion. Households spend 60 percent of the increase initially. If later rounds follow a simple spending multiplier of 2.5, the total AD increase before other offsets is:
legendary.commonError: Applying the multiplier to the full tax cut instead of the first-round consumption change.
legendary.feedback: First-round consumption rises $96 billion; multiplying by 2.5 gives $240 billion.

legendary.q: The government increases infrastructure purchases, but imports rise sharply because much of the equipment is purchased abroad. Relative to a package using domestic inputs, the increase in domestic aggregate demand is likely:
options: Leftward because any import increase reduces government purchases.
Identical because all government spending counts equally.
Smaller because part of the spending leaks into imports.
Larger because imports are part of domestic production.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring import leakage from domestic demand.
legendary.feedback: Spending on imports does not directly purchase domestically produced output.

legendary.q: A tax cut and transfer increase have the same budget cost. The transfer is targeted to households with a higher MPC. Which package is likely to shift AD more in the short run?
options: The broad tax cut regardless of spending behavior.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring differences in marginal propensity to consume.
legendary.feedback: More of the targeted transfer is likely to be spent, producing a larger initial consumption increase.

legendary.q: A government plans contractionary fiscal policy. Which combination most clearly supports that goal?
options: Higher government purchases and lower taxes.
Lower government purchases and higher taxes.
legendary.commonError: Mixing expansionary and contractionary tools.
legendary.feedback: Lower purchases and higher taxes both push aggregate demand left.

legendary.q: A recessionary economy receives a temporary tax rebate. Households use half to repay debt, save one quarter, and spend one quarter. The immediate consumption channel equals:
legendary.commonError: Treating saving or debt repayment as immediate consumption.
legendary.feedback: Only the portion spent on current consumption directly raises the consumption component of AD.

legendary.q: A temporary $120 billion tax credit is split equally between two household groups. One group has MPC 0.90 and the other MPC 0.40. Before multiplier rounds or crowding out, what is the first-round change in aggregate demand from consumption?
legendary.commonError: Applies one MPC to the entire tax change even when recipient groups have different spending responses.
legendary.feedback: Compute each group’s first-round consumption response separately, then add them before considering later multiplier rounds.

legendary.q: Congress replaces $100 billion of government purchases with a $100 billion tax cut. Households have MPC 0.80. Holding other AD determinants fixed and looking only at the first round, what happens to aggregate demand?
options: AD is unchanged because the two fiscal changes are equal.
legendary.commonError: Treats equal-dollar spending and tax changes as having identical direct effects on aggregate demand.
legendary.feedback: Government purchases enter AD directly, while tax changes affect AD through the share of disposable income households spend.

calculation.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
calculation.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
calculation.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is MPC times disposable income: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

calculation.q: Congress increases government purchases by $80 billion while households cut consumption by $50 billion for unrelated reasons. Before multiplier effects, the net direct change in aggregate demand is:
calculation.commonError: Adding changes without respecting their directions.
calculation.feedback: Government purchases add $80 billion while consumption subtracts $50 billion.

calculation.q: A $120 billion tax rebate is issued and households spend 65 percent of the added disposable income initially. What is the first-round consumption increase?
calculation.commonError: Using the MPS or the full tax cut as first-round consumption.
calculation.feedback: First-round consumption is 0.65 × $120 billion = $78 billion.

calculation.q: A tax increase of $60 billion reduces consumption by $42 billion in the first round. The implied MPC is:
calculation.commonError: Dividing in the wrong direction or using the MPS.
calculation.feedback: MPC = $42 billion / $60 billion = 0.70.

boss.q: Which policy combination is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: higher government spending or lower taxes
lower government spending or higher taxes
boss.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy
boss.feedback: Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxes. Expansionary fiscal policy raises G or lowers T.

boss.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $120 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
boss.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
boss.feedback: First-round consumption rises by MPC times the tax cut: 0.8 x $120 billion = $96 billion.

boss.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $120 billion. MPC = 0.8. If the first-round consumption increase enters the multiplier process, what is the total AD increase before crowding out?
boss.commonError: multiplying the full tax cut by the multiplier before applying MPC
boss.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is $96 billion. With MPC 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so AD rises $480 billion.

boss.q: Expansionary fiscal policy most directly includes:
options: Higher government purchases or lower taxes.
Lower government purchases or higher taxes.
boss.commonError: Confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy or private behavior.
boss.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government demand or supports private spending.

boss.q: Which fiscal action shifts aggregate demand left through lower disposable income?
boss.commonError: Reversing the effect of taxes on disposable income and consumption.
boss.feedback: A tax increase reduces disposable income and tends to reduce consumption.

boss.q: Government purchases are:
options: A direct component of aggregate demand.
A direct component of short-run aggregate supply.
boss.commonError: Misplacing government purchases in the macro model.
boss.feedback: Government purchases are included directly in C + I + G + NX.

boss.q: A $100 billion tax cut with MPC 0.8 raises first-round consumption by:
boss.commonError: Using the MPS or multiplier too early.
boss.feedback: MPC times the tax cut gives the first-round consumption increase.

boss.q: A cut in government purchases shifts AD left because it directly reduces:
boss.commonError: Confusing an AD shift with an AS or banking change.
boss.feedback: Government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.

boss.q: A tax cut has a weak AD effect when households:
options: Save most of the increase in disposable income.
Face a high marginal propensity to consume.
Increase consumption by more than the tax cut.
boss.commonError: Ignoring the consumption response.
boss.feedback: More saving means less immediate consumption and a smaller rightward AD shift.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the multiplier graph. A $60 billion tax cut raises disposable income, and MPC = 0.75. What is the correct order of AD effects before crowding out?
options: Consumption first rises $45 billion, then the multiplier expands the AD shift to $180 billion.
AD first rises $60 billion, then the multiplier expands it to $240 billion.
Consumption first rises $15 billion, then AD rises $60 billion.
AD falls $45 billion, then the multiplier reduces it by $180 billion.
legendaryBoss.commonError: multiplying the full tax cut by the spending multiplier without first applying MPC
legendaryBoss.feedback: First-round consumption rises 0.75 x $60 billion = $45 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $180 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: Government purchases rise $90 billion and taxes rise $60 billion. MPC is 0.75. What is the net first-round change in AD?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Failing to distinguish the direct spending effect from the tax-induced consumption effect.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Purchases add $90 billion; taxes reduce consumption by $45 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: A $200 billion tax cut reaches two equal groups. One group spends 80 percent and the other spends 40 percent. What is the combined first-round consumption increase?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Applying one group’s MPC to the entire tax cut.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Each group receives $100 billion; spending rises $80 billion plus $40 billion.

repairQuestions.q: Congress increases government purchases while taxes and other aggregate-demand determinants are unchanged. Which change should a student predict in the AD-AS model?
repairQuestions.feedback: Government purchases and tax-induced consumption changes work primarily through aggregate demand in this Principles model.
repairQuestions.commonError: Confuses a fiscal-policy change with an aggregate-supply shift.

repairQuestions.q: A $40 billion tax cut raises disposable income and MPC is 0.75. Before later multiplier rounds, how much does consumption increase?
repairQuestions.feedback: The first-round consumption effect equals the change in disposable income times MPC.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the full tax cut as immediate consumption.
Classifies fiscal policy from the state of the economy rather than from what government purchases and taxes actually do.
repairQuestions.q: Congress lowers government purchases and raises taxes in the same bill to reduce excessive aggregate demand. How should the package be classified?
repairQuestions.feedback: Classify the package from its fiscal actions: higher purchases/lower taxes are expansionary; lower purchases/higher taxes are contractionary.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking fiscal expansion shifts AD left.
repairQuestions.q: Higher government spending usually shifts AD:
repairQuestions.feedback: Government spending is part of AD, so higher G shifts AD right.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting taxes work through disposable income and consumption.
repairQuestions.q: A tax cut usually increases:
repairQuestions.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income.

repairQuestions.commonError: Jumps from a tax change directly to total output without identifying the first spending channel.
repairQuestions.q: Why can a tax cut shift aggregate demand to the right in the short run?
options: It raises disposable income, which can raise consumption spending.
It directly increases the money supply.
It directly lowers firms’ production costs and shifts SRAS right.
repairQuestions.feedback: A tax change first changes disposable income, then consumption according to MPC, which shifts aggregate demand.

bridgeQuestions.q: The government cuts spending during a recession. What happens to AD?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Lower government spending reduces aggregate demand.

bridgeQuestions.q: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption. What happens to AD?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher consumption shifts aggregate demand right.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
bridgeQuestions.q: A tax cut produces an $80 billion first-round increase in consumption. Which next idea is needed to move from that first-round fiscal impulse to the larger total aggregate-demand effect?
options: The multiplier process traces additional income-and-spending rounds.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts by the same $80 billion.
The inflation tax converts the consumption increase into government revenue.
The natural rate of unemployment determines the tax cut directly.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Aggregate-demand multiplier graph with AD1, AD2, and AD3 shifting progressively right at a fixed price level P, corresponding to output levels Y1, Y2, and Y3.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level P. A horizontal line at price level P crosses three downward-sloping aggregate-demand curves. AD1 intersects at output Y1, AD2 lies to the right and intersects at Y2, and AD3 lies farther right and intersects at Y3, so Y1 is less than Y2, which is less than Y3.

fiscal-multipliers-and-crowding-out.title: Fiscal Multipliers and Crowding Out
fiscal-multipliers-and-crowding-out.description: Calculate multiplier effects and evaluate crowding out.

easy.q: The multiplier effect means that government spending can shift AD by:
options: Less than the initial spending only
easy.commonError: Ignoring induced consumption.
easy.feedback: The multiplier effect occurs when initial spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

easy.q: Crowding out occurs when fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces:
easy.commonError: Missing the interest-rate channel.
easy.feedback: Crowding out reduces private investment when fiscal expansion raises interest rates.

easy.q: The multiplier effect occurs because an initial increase in spending
options: raises income and causes additional consumption spending
always raises interest rates enough to cancel itself completely
easy.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the first round of spending
easy.feedback: The multiplier effect happens because one person's spending becomes another person's income, causing additional consumption.

easy.q: The marginal propensity to consume is the fraction of extra income that households
easy.commonError: confusing MPC with the fraction saved
easy.feedback: MPC is the fraction of extra income that households consume rather than save.

easy.q: The simple spending multiplier is calculated as
easy.commonError: using MPC itself as the multiplier
easy.feedback: The simple spending multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

easy.q: Crowding out occurs when expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates and reduces
easy.commonError: thinking crowding out makes government spending disappear
easy.feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment spending.

medium.q: If fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces investment, the final AD shift is likely:
options: Larger because crowding out amplifies it
Smaller because crowding out offsets it
Zero because fiscal policy cannot affect AD
medium.commonError: Thinking the multiplier is never offset.
medium.feedback: Crowding out weakens the final effect of fiscal expansion on AD.

medium.q: The multiplier effect exists because one person's spending becomes
options: a fall in money demand every time
medium.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the initial spending increase
medium.feedback: The multiplier works because spending becomes income, and some of that income gets spent again.

medium.q: The movement from the first AD shift to the larger final AD shift represents
medium.commonError: confusing the multiplier effect with monetary policy
medium.feedback: The multiplier effect is the extra AD shift caused by income leading to additional consumption spending.

medium.q: The initial shift in aggregate demand from higher government spending is followed by a larger shift because
options: higher income leads to additional consumption spending
interest rates always fall to zero
medium.commonError: thinking only the first round of government spending matters
medium.feedback: The first increase in spending raises income, which causes more consumption and a further AD shift.

medium.q: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion because higher government spending can raise interest rates and reduce
medium.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens fiscal stimulus
medium.feedback: Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise.

medium.q: Which situation would make the multiplier effect larger?
medium.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
medium.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, which makes the multiplier larger.

medium.q: Which situation would make fiscal stimulus less powerful?
options: A high MPC with no interest-rate effect
A large initial increase in government spending
A high willingness to consume extra income
medium.commonError: ignoring offsetting effects from interest rates
medium.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal stimulus by reducing private investment.

hard.q: Refer to the AD multiplier graph. If government spending first shifts AD from AD1 to AD2, the multiplier effect is best shown by:
hard.commonError: Confusing the initial shift with the multiplied shift.
hard.feedback: The multiplier effect expands the initial AD shift farther right, from AD2 to AD3.

hard.q: Refer to the AD multiplier graph. If crowding out occurs after AD reaches AD3, the final AD position may move back toward:
hard.commonError: Thinking crowding out amplifies AD.
hard.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of fiscal expansion, pulling the final effect back from AD3 toward AD2.

hard.q: If the initial government spending increase shifts AD by $20 billion, why might the final shift be larger?
options: The spending raises income, which triggers additional consumption spending.
The spending lowers income, which reduces consumption.
The spending automatically reduces money supply.
The spending makes MPC equal zero.
hard.commonError: thinking only the first spending round matters
hard.feedback: The multiplier effect comes from income causing additional consumption, which pushes AD farther.

hard.q: If MPC is higher, the distance between the initial AD shift and the final AD shift should
hard.commonError: thinking a higher MPC weakens the multiplier
hard.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, so the final AD shift is larger.

hard.q: If expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates, which effect offsets part of the multiplier?
hard.commonError: confusing crowding out with the multiplier effect itself
hard.feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment, offsetting fiscal stimulus.

hard.q: Which fiscal policy has the strongest predicted multiplier effect before crowding out?
options: MPC = 0.9 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.5 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.25 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.1 and government spending rises by $50 billion
hard.commonError: thinking lower MPC creates a stronger multiplier
hard.feedback: Higher MPC means a larger multiplier. MPC = 0.9 gives the strongest multiplier here.

elite.q: Fiscal expansion raises AD through the multiplier, but interest rates rise and investment falls. Which description best fits the final result?
options: Initial AD shift partly offset by crowding out
SRAS shift fully offset by lower taxes
LRPC shift partly offset by higher inflation
Money demand shift fully offset by M1
elite.commonError: Treating the multiplier as the final effect every time.
elite.feedback: Fiscal expansion can be amplified by the multiplier but weakened by crowding out.

elite.q: Refer to the multiplier graph. Government spending initially moves AD1 to AD2, the multiplier moves AD2 to AD3, and crowding out offsets part of it. The final effect is likely:
elite.commonError: Ignoring crowding out after multiplier expansion.
elite.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the multiplied AD increase, so the final shift may land between AD2 and AD3.

elite.q: If government spending rises, MPC is high, and interest rates do not rise, which effect dominates?
elite.commonError: Assuming crowding out always dominates fiscal policy.
elite.feedback: A high MPC strengthens the multiplier, and little interest-rate increase means crowding out is weak.

elite.q: If government spending rises, MPC is low, and interest rates rise sharply, which concern dominates?
options: Weak multiplier with strong crowding out
Strong multiplier with no crowding out
Money neutrality with no AD change
elite.commonError: Ignoring both MPC size and interest-rate effects.
elite.feedback: A low MPC weakens the multiplier, while higher rates crowd out private investment.

elite.q: If government spending initially shifts AD right by $40 billion and MPC is 0.75, what is the total shift before crowding out?
elite.commonError: using MPC as the multiplier instead of 1 divided by 1 minus MPC
elite.feedback: With MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is 4. A $40 billion initial shift becomes $160 billion before crowding out.

elite.q: If the initial AD shift is $30 billion and the final shift is $150 billion, what MPC is implied by the simple multiplier?
elite.commonError: using final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
elite.feedback: The multiplier is 150/30 = 5. If 1/(1-MPC)=5, then MPC = 0.8.

elite.q: If the initial shift is $50 billion and MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.5, what happens to the final AD shift before crowding out?
options: It falls from $250 billion to $100 billion.
It rises from $100 billion to $250 billion.
It falls from $250 billion to $50 billion.
elite.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
elite.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so $250 billion. MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so $100 billion.

elite.q: Suppose the multiplier would shift AD right by $200 billion, but crowding out reduces investment by $60 billion. What is the net shift?
elite.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
elite.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the multiplier effect. Net shift is $200 billion - $60 billion = $140 billion.

elite.q: If policymakers expect the multiplier shift to close a recessionary gap exactly, but crowding out is stronger than expected, what is the likely result?
options: AD does not shift far enough right to fully close the gap.
AD shifts too far right because crowding out magnifies fiscal policy.
AD shifts left because government spending is not part of AD.
elite.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens the fiscal multiplier
elite.feedback: Stronger crowding out reduces the net AD shift, so stimulus may fall short.

elite.q: If government spending rises by $60 billion, MPC is 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $50 billion, what is the net AD shift?
elite.commonError: forgetting to apply the multiplier before subtracting crowding out
elite.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so the gross shift is $240 billion. Subtract $50 billion crowding out for a net $190 billion.

elite.q: A government spending increase raises income, consumption, and AD, but also raises interest rates and lowers investment. Which answer correctly names both effects?
elite.commonError: treating all fiscal policy effects as multiplier effects only
elite.feedback: The multiplier amplifies the AD increase; crowding out offsets part of it by reducing investment.

legendary.q: A student says fiscal expansion raises AD and therefore can never crowd out investment. What is the best correction?
options: Fiscal expansion can raise AD while higher rates reduce private investment.
Fiscal expansion lowers rates because government borrowing reduces money demand.
Fiscal expansion shifts SRAS right because firms face lower costs.
Fiscal expansion eliminates the multiplier because taxes disappear.
legendary.commonError: Thinking multiplier effects rule out crowding out.
legendary.feedback: Fiscal expansion can increase AD, but rising interest rates can reduce investment and offset part of the effect.

legendary.q: Refer to the aggregate-demand multiplier graph. AD moves from AD1 to AD2, then from AD2 to AD3, followed by a partial move back. Which interpretation fits?
options: Initial fiscal shift, multiplier expansion, then crowding out offset.
Initial monetary contraction, SRAS expansion, then LRPC adjustment.
Initial supply shock, expected price decline, then AD collapse.
Initial inflation tax, M1 expansion, then velocity collapse.
legendary.commonError: Confusing multiplier and crowding-out stages.
legendary.feedback: Fiscal policy can shift AD right, the multiplier can push it farther, and crowding out can pull the final effect back.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $70 billion and MPC = 0.8. What is the correct order of AD shifts before crowding out?
options: AD first shifts right by $70 billion, then shifts farther right to a total of $350 billion.
AD first shifts right by $350 billion, then shifts back to $70 billion.
AD shifts left by $70 billion, then left by $350 billion.
AD does not shift because the multiplier only affects money demand.
legendary.commonError: confusing the initial AD shift with the final multiplier shift
legendary.feedback: The first AD shift is the direct $70 billion increase in G. With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so the final AD shift is $350 billion.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $60 billion and the final AD shift is $300 billion. What order of AD shifts and implied MPC fit these data?
options: AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts right first by $300 billion, then back to $60 billion; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts left first by $60 billion, then left by $300 billion; MPC = 0.2.
AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.6.
legendary.commonError: treating final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of the multiplier
legendary.feedback: The multiplier is $300/$60 = 5. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 5, then MPC = 0.8.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $40 billion. If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, how does the order of AD shifts change?
options: The initial AD shift stays $40 billion, but the final shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion.
The initial AD shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion, but the final shift stays $40 billion.
Both the initial and final AD shifts stay $40 billion.
The initial AD shift becomes $200 billion and the final shift becomes $80 billion.
legendary.commonError: thinking same initial government spending creates same final AD shift regardless of MPC
legendary.feedback: The initial shift is still $40 billion. With MPC = 0.5, multiplier is 2 and final shift is $80 billion. With MPC = 0.8, multiplier is 5 and final shift is $200 billion.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $100 billion and MPC = 0.6. Crowding out reduces investment by $75 billion. What is the correct order of AD effects?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $175 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out increases it to $325 billion.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $250 billion, then crowding out leaves $175 billion.
AD shifts right $100 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
legendary.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it from the gross multiplier shift
legendary.feedback: MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. The $100 billion initial shift becomes $250 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $175 billion.

legendary.q: Two governments each increase purchases by $60 billion. Economy A has MPC 0.80 and $100 billion of crowding out; Economy B has MPC 0.60 and $20 billion of crowding out. Using the simple multiplier and the stated offsets, which comparison is correct?
options: Economy A has a $200 billion net AD increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy B.
Economy A has a $300 billion net increase and Economy B has a $150 billion net increase because crowding out does not affect AD.
Economy B has a $200 billion net increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy A.
Both economies have the same $180 billion net AD increase because the initial spending changes are equal.
legendary.commonError: Compares gross multiplier effects without subtracting the private spending displaced by higher interest rates.
legendary.feedback: For the simplified model used here, compare each policy’s gross multiplier effect and then subtract its stated crowding-out offset.

legendary.q: Government purchases rise by $80 billion and MPC is 0.75. The observed net increase in aggregate demand is $230 billion after crowding out. Under the simple model used in this bank, how much of the gross multiplier effect was crowded out?
legendary.commonError: Uses the net AD shift as if it were the gross multiplier effect.
legendary.feedback: First compute the gross multiplier effect, then infer the crowding-out offset from the difference between gross and observed net AD.

calculation.q: If the MPC is 0.75, the simple government purchases multiplier is:
calculation.commonError: Using MPC as the multiplier.
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so 1/(1-0.75)=4.

calculation.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion, MPC is 0.75, and crowding out offsets $100 billion, final AD rises by:
calculation.commonError: Ignoring crowding out after applying the multiplier.
calculation.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so $80 billion x 4 = $320 billion; minus $100 billion gives $220 billion.

calculation.q: If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, the government purchases multiplier changes from:
calculation.commonError: Using MPC itself as the multiplier.
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so it rises from 2 to 5.

calculation.q: If the government raises spending by $50 billion and the multiplier is 3, the first-pass AD increase before crowding out is:
calculation.commonError: Using the spending change instead of multiplying it.
calculation.feedback: The initial multiplier effect is $50 billion x 3 = $150 billion.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.6 and income rises by $1,000, consumption rises by
calculation.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
