calculation.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the change in income: 0.6 x $1,000 = $600.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.6, the simple spending multiplier is
calculation.commonError: using MPC itself as the multiplier
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.6) = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.8 and government spending increases by $50 billion, the simple multiplier predicts a total AD increase of
calculation.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
calculation.feedback: With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5. Total increase is 5 x $50 billion = $250 billion.

calculation.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the simple multiplier and total AD increase before crowding out?
calculation.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
calculation.feedback: Multiplier = 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4. Total AD increase = 4 x $80 billion = $320 billion.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.9 and government spending increases by $25 billion, what is the simple multiplier effect on AD before crowding out?
calculation.commonError: using 0.9 as the multiplier instead of 10
calculation.feedback: With MPC = 0.9, the multiplier is 10. AD increases by 10 x $25 billion = $250 billion.

calculation.q: Suppose fiscal stimulus initially raises AD by $300 billion through the multiplier, but crowding out reduces investment by $80 billion. What is the net AD increase?
calculation.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
calculation.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the stimulus, so net AD rises by $300 billion - $80 billion = $220 billion.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.8, then a $100 increase in income raises consumption by
calculation.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
calculation.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the income increase: 0.8 x $100 = $80.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.75, the simple spending multiplier equals
calculation.commonError: dividing MPC by 1 instead of using 1 divided by 1 minus MPC
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.

boss.q: Why can an initial increase in spending generate a larger total increase in aggregate demand?
options: raises income and causes additional consumption spending
boss.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the first spending round
boss.feedback: The multiplier happens because spending becomes income, and part of that income is spent again.

boss.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the gross AD shift before crowding out?
boss.commonError: using MPC instead of the multiplier
boss.feedback: MPC 0.75 gives multiplier 4. Gross AD shift is $80 billion x 4 = $320 billion.

boss.q: Government spending rises by $80 billion, MPC = 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $70 billion. What is the net AD shift?
boss.commonError: forgetting to subtract crowding out after applying the multiplier
boss.feedback: Gross AD shift is $320 billion. Subtract $70 billion of crowding out, leaving $250 billion.

boss.q: Households spend 75 cents of each additional dollar of disposable income. What does that imply?
options: The marginal propensity to save is 0.75, so the multiplier equals one.
The MPC is 0.75, so repeated spending creates a multiplier greater than one.
Crowding out must eliminate every later spending round.
boss.commonError: Confusing the marginal propensity to consume with the multiplier itself.
boss.feedback: An MPC of 0.75 means each spending round passes along 75 percent of added income, generating further rounds of expenditure.

boss.q: What is the central mechanism of crowding out?
options: Fiscal expansion lowers interest rates and increases private investment.
Higher government spending directly reduces the money supply.
A larger multiplier forces households to stop consuming.
Fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces some private investment spending.
boss.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate and investment effects of fiscal expansion.
boss.feedback: Government borrowing and stronger money demand can raise interest rates, discouraging private investment.

boss.q: Holding other factors constant, which change makes the simple spending multiplier larger?
options: A lower marginal propensity to save.
A higher marginal propensity to save.
A larger amount of crowding out.
A smaller initial change in government purchases.
boss.commonError: Treating more saving as a force that strengthens repeated spending rounds.
boss.feedback: A lower marginal propensity to save means a larger MPC, so more income is respent in each round.

boss.q: Government purchases rise by $20 billion and the MPC is 0.50. Ignoring crowding out, what is the predicted total increase in aggregate demand?
boss.commonError: Using the MPC itself as the multiplier or ignoring the repeated-spending process.
boss.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1 - 0.50) = 2, so a $20 billion increase produces a $40 billion gross shift.

boss.q: A fiscal package creates a gross $120 billion increase in aggregate demand, but higher interest rates reduce investment by $25 billion. What is the net shift?
boss.commonError: Adding the crowded-out investment to the gross effect rather than subtracting it.
boss.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the expansion: $120 billion minus $25 billion equals a $95 billion net increase.

boss.q: Why can an equal-dollar tax cut create a smaller initial aggregate-demand shift than an equal increase in government purchases?
options: Tax cuts always raise interest rates before households receive them.
Government purchases do not pass through the multiplier process.
Tax cuts reduce disposable income before they affect consumption.
Tax cuts are partly saved; government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.
boss.commonError: Assuming every dollar of a tax cut is spent immediately.
boss.feedback: Only the consumed portion of a tax cut enters the first spending round, whereas government purchases are direct expenditure.

legendaryBoss.q: Government spending rises by $90 billion and MPC = 0.8. Crowding out reduces investment by $180 billion. What is the correct order of AD effects?
options: AD first shifts right $90 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $450 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $270 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $450 billion, then crowding out increases the shift to $630 billion.
AD first shifts left $90 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $450 billion, then crowding out leaves $270 billion.
AD shifts right only $90 billion because crowding out eliminates the multiplier.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not following initial shift, multiplier shift, then crowding-out offset
legendaryBoss.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5. The $90 billion initial shift becomes $450 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $270 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: The initial government-spending shift is $100 billion and the final AD shift is $400 billion. What MPC is implied, and what is the correct shift order?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then to $400 billion; MPC = 0.75.
AD first shifts right $400 billion, then back to $100 billion; MPC = 0.75.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then left $400 billion; MPC = 0.25.
AD first shifts right $100 billion, then to $400 billion; MPC = 0.8.
legendaryBoss.commonError: treating final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: The multiplier is 400/100 = 4. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 4, MPC = 0.75.

legendaryBoss.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. Expansionary fiscal policy also raises interest rates through crowding out. What happens to investment if both effects occur?
options: Investment falls from both interest-rate channels.
Investment rises from both interest-rate channels.
Investment rises from the money-demand channel but falls from crowding out.
Investment is unaffected because r is not connected to investment.
legendaryBoss.commonError: tracking only one interest-rate channel
legendaryBoss.feedback: Higher money demand raises r. Crowding out also raises r. Higher r reduces investment.

repairQuestions.q: If MPC = 0.5, the government purchases multiplier is:
repairQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so 1/(1-0.5)=2.

repairQuestions.q: Crowding out happens when fiscal expansion raises rates and reduces:
repairQuestions.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion by reducing private investment.

repairQuestions.q: Why might a tax cut have a smaller immediate effect than an equal increase in government purchases?
options: Households may save part of the tax cut
Government purchases are not part of GDP
repairQuestions.feedback: Some of a tax cut is saved, so its initial spending effect can be smaller than direct government purchases.

repairQuestions.q: The multiplier effect means an initial spending increase can raise AD by:
options: Only less than the initial spending
repairQuestions.feedback: The multiplier occurs when spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

repairQuestions.q: The multiplier effect means an initial increase in government spending can:
options: Create a larger total increase in aggregate demand and output
Affect only the first recipient of spending
Reduce GDP by the same amount
repairQuestions.feedback: Initial spending becomes income for others, whose further spending magnifies the total effect.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using MPC as the multiplier.
repairQuestions.q: The simple spending multiplier equals:
repairQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using MPC directly as the multiplier.
repairQuestions.q: If MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is:

repairQuestions.commonError: Adding crowding out instead of subtracting it.
repairQuestions.q: Crowding out reduces the effect of fiscal expansion by reducing:
repairQuestions.feedback: Crowding out happens when higher interest rates reduce private investment.

repairQuestions.commonError: Adding the crowding-out amount to the multiplier effect.
repairQuestions.q: If gross AD rises $200 billion and crowding out is $50 billion, net AD rises:
repairQuestions.feedback: Crowding out subtracts from the gross effect: $200 - $50 = $150 billion.

bridgeQuestions.q: If MPC = 0.8, the government purchases multiplier is:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-0.8)=5.

bridgeQuestions.q: Fiscal expansion raises interest rates. Which part of spending is most likely crowded out?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher interest rates reduce private investment.

bridgeQuestions.q: Government spending rises by $20 billion and the multiplier is 3. Before crowding out, AD rises by:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The multiplier effect is $20 billion x 3 = $60 billion.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
bridgeQuestions.q: Government purchases rise $50 billion and MPC is 0.75. Which statement correctly connects the fiscal action to the multiplier concept?
options: The $50 billion first-round AD impulse is magnified to $200 billion before any crowding-out offset.
The $50 billion first-round impulse remains $50 billion because later spending rounds do not affect AD.
The multiplier reduces the initial AD impulse to $37.5 billion.
The fiscal action shifts LRAS rather than aggregate demand.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Carries the gross fiscal impulse into stabilization analysis even after an offset has been specified.
bridgeQuestions.q: A fiscal package generates a $300 billion gross AD increase, but crowding out reduces private investment by $80 billion in the simplified model. What AD impulse should stabilization analysis carry forward?
options: $300 billion because stabilization uses only the gross multiplier effect.
$80 billion because crowding out replaces the fiscal impulse.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Stabilization analysis should use the net aggregate-demand impulse after the multiplier and stated crowding-out offset.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with LRAS at Y1, two aggregate-demand curves, two short-run aggregate-supply curves, and labeled output gaps.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. LRAS is vertical at Y1. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above and left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3 left of LRAS, Y1 on LRAS, Y2 right of LRAS, and price levels P1, P2, and P3. AD1-AS2 is at Y1/P1; AD1-AS1 is at Y3/P2; AD2-AS2 is at Y2/P2; AD2-AS1 is at Y1/P3.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves, two downward-sloping money-demand curves, and labeled interest-rate and money-quantity points.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right and upward and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Aggregate-demand multiplier graph with AD1, AD2, and AD3 shifting progressively right at a fixed price level P, corresponding to output levels Y1, Y2, and Y3.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level P. A horizontal line at price level P crosses three downward-sloping aggregate-demand curves. AD1 intersects at output Y1, AD2 lies to the right and intersects at Y2, and AD3 lies farther right and intersects at Y3, so Y1 is less than Y2, which is less than Y3.

stabilization-policy.title: Stabilization Policy
stabilization-policy.description: Evaluate active policy, lags, coordination, automatic stabilizers, and shock response.

easy.q: A liquidity trap occurs when monetary policy has trouble stimulating AD because:
easy.commonError: Thinking monetary policy is always equally powerful.
easy.feedback: In a liquidity trap, nominal interest rates are near zero, making traditional monetary stimulus weaker.

easy.q: An automatic stabilizer is best described as:
options: A built-in response to the economy
easy.commonError: Confusing automatic stabilizers with discretionary policy.
easy.feedback: Automatic stabilizers, such as taxes and transfer payments, respond automatically as conditions change.

easy.q: Policy lags matter because stabilization policy may:
options: Arrive after conditions have already changed
Make money neutral in the short run
easy.commonError: Ignoring timing problems in stabilization policy.
easy.feedback: Policy can become destabilizing if it takes effect after the economy has already moved.

easy.q: A policy lag is a reason stabilization policy can be risky because policy actions may
options: take effect after conditions have already changed
remove the need for aggregate demand
make money supply impossible to change
easy.commonError: thinking stabilization policy works instantly
easy.feedback: Policy lags matter because by the time policy takes effect, the economy may have already changed.

easy.q: If a recession lowers aggregate demand, a stabilization policy response could be
options: lower government spending and lower money supply
higher taxes and higher interest rates
doing anything that shifts AD left
easy.commonError: choosing contractionary policy during weak demand
easy.feedback: If aggregate demand is too low, expansionary policy can help shift AD right.

easy.q: If aggregate demand is pushing output above its natural level and raising inflation pressure, policymakers might use
options: higher government spending and lower interest rates
only policies that shift AD right
easy.commonError: using expansionary policy when AD is already too strong
easy.feedback: When AD is too high and inflation pressure builds, contractionary policy can shift AD left.

easy.q: One argument in favor of stabilization policy is that it can help offset
easy.commonError: thinking stabilization policy is meant to eliminate scarcity
easy.feedback: Supporters argue stabilization policy can reduce the damage caused by short-run aggregate demand shocks.

easy.q: One argument against aggressive stabilization policy is that
options: policy lags can cause actions to hit the economy too late
monetary and fiscal policy always work instantly
easy.commonError: thinking policy timing is never a problem
easy.feedback: Critics warn that policy lags can make stabilization efforts arrive after the economy has already changed.

easy.q: If policymakers respond too late to a recession that has already recovered, expansionary policy may
easy.commonError: thinking late expansionary policy is harmless
easy.feedback: If expansionary policy arrives after recovery is underway, it can push aggregate demand too far and create inflation pressure.

medium.q: Which policy pair is expansionary for aggregate demand?
options: Higher taxes and lower money supply
Lower taxes and higher money supply
Higher reserve requirements and lower spending
medium.commonError: Mixing expansionary and contractionary tools.
medium.feedback: Lower taxes and higher money supply both tend to shift AD right.

medium.q: A recession begins, but Congress passes stimulus after the economy has already recovered. This illustrates:
medium.commonError: Ignoring timing problems.
medium.feedback: Policy lags can make stabilization arrive after conditions have changed.

medium.q: If the economy is in a liquidity trap, a traditional money-supply increase may fail because:
options: Interest rates cannot fall much further
medium.commonError: Thinking monetary policy works the same at zero rates.
medium.feedback: When rates are near zero, traditional monetary policy may not lower rates enough to boost spending.

medium.q: If a negative demand shock pushes output below its natural level, stabilization policy would most likely try to
medium.commonError: choosing contractionary policy during a demand slump
medium.feedback: A negative demand shock reduces output, so stabilization policy would typically try to shift AD right.

medium.q: If aggregate demand is too high and inflation pressure is building, stabilization policy would most likely try to
medium.commonError: stimulating AD when inflation pressure is already high
medium.feedback: If AD is too strong, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

medium.q: A key argument for active stabilization policy is that policymakers can
medium.commonError: thinking stabilization policy is meant to solve every economic problem
medium.feedback: Supporters argue that active policy can reduce the damage caused by short-run AD shocks.

medium.q: A key argument against aggressive stabilization policy is that
options: policy lags can cause poorly timed interventions
the Fed cannot affect interest rates
government spending is not part of aggregate demand
medium.commonError: thinking stabilization policy works instantly and perfectly
medium.feedback: Policy lags can cause interventions to arrive after conditions have already changed.

medium.q: If policymakers misread a temporary shock as a lasting recession, they risk
options: turning fiat money into commodity money
medium.commonError: thinking wrong policy timing has no cost
medium.feedback: If policymakers stimulate after the economy is already recovering, they may push AD too far.

medium.q: A pandemic reduces production and also weakens spending. Why is stabilization policy harder here than with a simple demand shock?
options: Because both supply and demand may be affected.
Because monetary policy cannot affect interest rates in any economy.
Because fiscal policy cannot affect aggregate demand.
Because money demand must be zero during pandemics.
medium.commonError: treating every downturn as only an aggregate demand problem
medium.feedback: A mixed shock is harder because policy may support demand, but it cannot instantly fix lost production capacity.

hard.q: Congress cuts spending to reduce deficits during a recession. What policy concern is most direct?
options: AD may fall further before recovery
hard.commonError: Ignoring demand effects of spending cuts.
hard.feedback: Cutting spending during a recession can reduce AD further and deepen the downturn.

hard.q: If interest rates are near zero and output is below potential, why may monetary policy struggle?
options: Rates have little room to fall
hard.commonError: Treating monetary policy as equally strong at all rates.
hard.feedback: At near-zero nominal rates, standard rate-cut channels have little room to stimulate spending.

hard.q: A policy takes six months to pass and another year to affect spending. The main risk is:
options: The shock may reverse before policy hits
The money multiplier must equal zero
hard.commonError: Ignoring timing in stabilization policy.
hard.feedback: Inside and outside lags can make policy arrive after conditions have changed.

hard.q: Congress cuts government spending to reduce the deficit. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, what should it do?
options: Increase money supply to lower interest rates and support AD.
Decrease money supply to raise interest rates and reduce AD further.
Raise taxes to lower consumption further.
Do nothing because fiscal policy cannot affect AD.
hard.commonError: doubling down on contraction after AD falls
hard.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left. Expansionary monetary policy can partly offset that.

hard.q: A stock market boom increases household wealth and pushes output above its natural level. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, it should
options: reduce money supply and raise interest rates
increase money supply and lower interest rates
hard.commonError: using expansionary policy after a positive demand shock
hard.feedback: A positive AD shock can push output too high, so contractionary monetary policy can stabilize output.

hard.q: Which policy mix is most expansionary for aggregate demand?
options: Fed buys bonds and Congress increases government spending.
Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
Fed sells bonds and Congress cuts spending.
Fed raises interest rates and Congress raises taxes.
hard.commonError: mixing expansionary and contractionary tools
hard.feedback: Fed bond purchases are expansionary monetary policy, and higher government spending is expansionary fiscal policy.

hard.q: Which policy mix is most contractionary for aggregate demand?
options: Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
Fed buys bonds and Congress cuts taxes.
Fed buys bonds and Congress increases spending.
Fed lowers interest rates and Congress increases transfers.
hard.commonError: thinking bond sales are expansionary
hard.feedback: Fed bond sales reduce money supply, and tax increases reduce consumption. Both push AD left.

hard.q: Why can stabilization policy accidentally destabilize the economy?
options: Policy lags can make action arrive after conditions change.
Aggregate demand never responds to policy.
The Fed cannot change the money supply.
hard.commonError: thinking timing never matters
hard.feedback: Policy lags can make a policy hit after the original problem has faded, creating a new problem.

hard.q: A recession is already ending, but expansionary fiscal policy passed months earlier now takes effect. What is the risk?
options: AD may be pushed too far right, creating inflation pressure.
Interest rates must fall to zero forever.
hard.commonError: thinking late stimulus is always harmless
hard.feedback: Late stimulus can overstimulate demand after recovery is already underway.

hard.q: A supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why is the policy response harder than for a pure demand shock?
options: Stimulating AD may raise output somewhat but can worsen inflation.
Stimulating AD always lowers prices and raises output with no tradeoff.
Supply shocks only affect money demand.
hard.commonError: treating every downturn like a demand shock
hard.feedback: A supply shock creates a tradeoff: boosting aggregate demand may support output but can add inflation pressure.

hard.q: A negative AD shock reduces output and the price level. Which policy response best targets the shock without relying on supply-side repair?
options: Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy to shift AD right
Contractionary policy to shift AD left
Higher taxes and lower government spending
A policy that reduces investment spending
hard.commonError: using contractionary policy against weak demand
hard.feedback: A negative AD shock calls for policies that shift AD right if the goal is stabilizing output.

hard.q: An economy is above potential output because AD is too high. Which response best reduces the boom without increasing AD further?
options: Contractionary monetary policy or contractionary fiscal policy
Expansionary monetary policy and tax cuts
Higher government spending and lower interest rates
hard.commonError: stimulating an economy that is already overheating
hard.feedback: When AD is too high, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

elite.q: A recessionary demand shock hits, but the Fed is at the zero lower bound. Which option best describes the policy problem?
options: AD needs support, but rate cuts have limited room
AD is too high, and rate cuts work too strongly
SRAS needs support, but wages rise instantly
LRPC must shift, but M2 is too small
elite.commonError: Ignoring why zero rates weaken monetary stimulus.
elite.feedback: When rates are near zero, traditional monetary policy may struggle to shift AD right enough.

elite.q: A government passes stimulus after a recession has ended, and the economy is already above potential. What is the risk?
options: The stimulus may worsen inflation pressure
The stimulus must lower output below potential
The stimulus shifts SRAS right automatically
The stimulus lowers expected prices instantly
elite.commonError: Ignoring policy timing after recovery.
elite.feedback: Because of lags, stimulus can hit after recovery and add excess demand.

elite.q: Fiscal stimulus raises AD, but the central bank offsets it with tighter money. Which final outcome is most plausible?
options: AD rises less than fiscal policy alone suggests
AD rises more than fiscal policy alone suggests
SRAS shifts right because interest rates rise
LRPC shifts left because taxes fall
elite.commonError: Ignoring policy interactions.
elite.feedback: Tighter monetary policy can offset fiscal stimulus by raising interest rates and weakening AD.

elite.q: Suppose output is below its natural level because AD is weak. Which Fed action through the money market would move AD in the stabilizing direction?
options: Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
Shift money demand right to raise r and lower investment.
Keep money supply fixed and raise taxes.
elite.commonError: choosing tighter money during a demand slump
elite.feedback: When AD is weak, expansionary monetary policy shifts MS right, lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

elite.q: Suppose output is above its natural level because AD is too strong. Which Fed action through the money market would move AD in the stabilizing direction?
options: Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
Shift money demand left to lower r and raise investment.
elite.commonError: stimulating AD when output is already above natural level
elite.feedback: When AD is too strong, tighter money shifts MS left, raises rates, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

elite.q: If the economy is already near full employment and fiscal policy shifts AD right through the multiplier, what risk becomes more important?
options: A lower price level from higher government spending
A smaller price level because MPC is positive
elite.commonError: thinking all rightward AD shifts are good regardless of starting point
elite.feedback: If the economy is already near capacity, more AD can create inflation pressure instead of useful output gains.

elite.q: A recession lowers AD by $300 billion. The government increases spending by $100 billion and MPC is 0.5. Ignoring crowding out, what remains of the AD shortfall?
elite.commonError: not comparing stimulus size to the original AD shortfall
elite.feedback: MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2. A $100 billion spending increase shifts AD by $200 billion, leaving a $100 billion shortfall.

elite.q: Congress cuts spending during a recession while the Fed also sells bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
options: Both policies shift AD left or reduce support for AD, worsening the demand problem.
Both policies shift AD right, stabilizing output.
Fiscal policy shifts AD right while monetary policy shifts AD right.
elite.commonError: missing that Fed bond sales are contractionary
elite.feedback: Cutting spending reduces AD, and Fed bond sales raise rates and reduce investment. That is contraction on top of contraction.

elite.q: Congress raises spending during an inflationary boom while the Fed buys bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
options: Both policies shift AD right, risking more inflation pressure.
Both policies shift AD left, reducing inflation pressure.
Fiscal policy shifts AD left while monetary policy shifts AD left.
Neither affects AD because output is already high.
elite.commonError: thinking expansionary policy is always appropriate
elite.feedback: Spending increases and bond purchases both shift AD right. During an inflationary boom, that pours gasoline on the fire.

elite.q: A negative supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why can expansionary AD policy be a blunt tool here?
options: It may raise output somewhat but can worsen the price-level increase.
It directly restores lost productive capacity with no inflation risk.
It lowers prices and lowers output at the same time.
elite.commonError: treating supply shocks like pure demand shocks
elite.feedback: AD stimulus can support spending, but it does not fix the supply loss and may worsen inflation.

elite.q: A negative demand shock reduces output and prices. Why is expansionary monetary policy more directly suited to this case than to a pure supply shock?
options: It targets weak spending by lowering r and raising investment.
It directly increases labor, capital, and natural resources.
It shifts SRAS right by changing the reserve ratio.
It lowers AD to reduce output further.
elite.commonError: not distinguishing AD shocks from AS shocks
elite.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy works through spending, so it is more directly suited to weak AD than to lost productive capacity.

elite.q: A policy is passed to fight a recession, but because of recognition, implementation, and impact lags, it takes effect after output has already recovered. What is the likely stabilization problem?
options: The delayed policy can push AD too far right and create inflation pressure.
The delayed policy must shift AD left automatically.
The delayed policy cannot affect AD after recovery.
The delayed policy eliminates crowding out.
elite.commonError: thinking late stimulus is harmless because it was originally well-intended
elite.feedback: Good timing matters. Late expansion can overstimulate AD after the recession has already passed.

legendary.q: If the economy initially needed AD to fall by $300 billion and the MS1 to MS2 movement reduces AD by $200 billion, what remains?
options: Output rises from Y2 to Y1.
legendary.commonError: not comparing the graph's AD shift with the size of the gap
legendary.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. If AD needed to fall $300 billion but falls $200 billion, $100 billion of excess AD remains.

legendary.q: A contractionary monetary-policy move must reduce AD by $240 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what investment decrease is needed to produce that AD movement?
legendary.commonError: not dividing the AD target by the multiplier
legendary.feedback: The graph shows a leftward AD movement. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so investment must fall by $240 billion / 4 = $60 billion.

legendary.q: The MS1 to MS2 movement causes AD to shift left by $180 billion. A separate fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $60 billion. What is the net AD change?
legendary.commonError: adding both policies in the same direction without checking graph direction
legendary.feedback: The graph's monetary policy lowers AD by $180 billion. Fiscal policy raises AD by $60 billion. Net AD falls by $120 billion.

legendary.q: The Fed pushes r high enough to reduce investment by $90 billion, but AD only needed to move left by $240 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what happens?
options: AD falls $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.
AD falls $240 billion, closing the gap exactly.
legendary.commonError: failing to compare the multiplied AD effect to the needed AD change
legendary.feedback: The graph shows AD moving left. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so a $90 billion investment fall lowers AD by $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.

legendary.q: A $50 billion government spending increase is intended to close a $250 billion AD gap. MPC = 0.75, but crowding out reduces investment by $40 billion. What is the correct sequence?
options: AD first shifts right $50 billion, then the multiplier pushes it to $200 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $160 billion shift and a $90 billion gap.
AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a $210 billion surplus.
AD first shifts left $50 billion, then the multiplier shifts it left $200 billion, leaving a $90 billion gap.
AD shifts right $50 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
legendary.commonError: calculating the multiplier but ignoring the order: initial shift, multiplied shift, crowding-out offset
legendary.feedback: MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4. The $50 billion initial shift becomes $200 billion, then crowding out lowers the net shift to $160 billion, leaving a $90 billion gap.

legendary.q: The economy is already above potential output by $180 billion. Congress raises spending by $30 billion and MPC = 0.8. What is the correct AD-shift interpretation?
options: AD first shifts right $30 billion, then the multiplier expands the shift to $150 billion, worsening the overheating gap to $330 billion.
AD first shifts left $30 billion, then left $150 billion, reducing the overheating gap to $30 billion.
AD shifts right $30 billion only, closing part of the overheating gap.
AD does not shift because the economy is already above potential.
legendary.commonError: thinking any rightward AD shift is good regardless of the starting gap
legendary.feedback: MPC = 0.8 gives multiplier 5. The $30 billion spending increase becomes a $150 billion AD increase, making the $180 billion overheating gap worse.

legendary.q: The monetary-policy movement shifts AD left by $160 billion. Fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $160 billion. What is the net AD effect?
legendary.commonError: not matching the leftward AD shift in the graph before adding the fiscal offset
legendary.feedback: The graph shows monetary policy shifting AD left. A fiscal expansion of the same size shifts AD right by the same amount, so the net AD effect is zero.

legendary.q: A recessionary gap is $400 billion. Government spending rises by $100 billion and MPC = 0.75. What is the order of AD shifts and the final gap, ignoring crowding out?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier expands the shift to $400 billion, closing the gap.
AD first shifts right $400 billion, then falls back to $100 billion, leaving a $300 billion gap.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then left $400 billion, worsening the gap.
AD shifts right $100 billion only, leaving a $300 billion gap.
legendary.commonError: confusing the first AD shift with the final multiplied AD shift
legendary.feedback: MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4. The $100 billion initial spending increase becomes a $400 billion final AD shift, closing the gap.

legendary.q: A recessionary gap begins closing without new policy as wage growth slows and SRAS shifts right. A large discretionary stimulus designed for the original gap is still scheduled to take effect several quarters later. What is the strongest stabilization concern?
options: The delayed stimulus may arrive after much of the gap has self-corrected, pushing AD too far right and creating overheating pressure.
The stimulus becomes contractionary once SRAS begins shifting right.
Self-correction guarantees the stimulus has no effect on aggregate demand.
The delayed stimulus automatically shifts LRAS right by the amount of the original gap.
legendary.commonError: Assumes a policy designed for an old output gap remains correctly sized after self-correction has already reduced the gap.
legendary.feedback: Policy lags matter because wages, costs, expectations, and private spending can change before discretionary policy takes effect, creating overshoot risk.

legendary.q: Policymakers initially estimate a $300 billion recessionary gap and enact a $75 billion spending increase with a simple multiplier of 4. By the time the policy takes effect, revised data show the gap is only $100 billion. Ignoring crowding out, what is the implication?
options: The policy closes the revised gap exactly because it was calibrated to the original estimate.
The $75 billion initial spending increase leaves a $25 billion gap because only the first round matters.
The policy raises AD by $100 billion because stabilization automatically adjusts to revised data.
The $300 billion AD increase overshoots the revised gap by $200 billion.
legendary.commonError: Uses the original output-gap estimate even after newer data show a much smaller gap.
legendary.feedback: Compare the policy’s expected AD shift with the output gap that exists when the policy actually takes effect, not only the initial estimate.

legendary.q: Inflation pressure is being driven by excessive aggregate demand. Policymakers use contractionary stabilization policy and the policy succeeds in lowering aggregate demand. Before inflation expectations fully adjust, which short-run combination is most consistent with the policy mechanism?
options: Higher inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
No change in unemployment because stabilization policy affects only the price level.
Lower inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
Lower inflation pressure together with stronger output and lower unemployment.
legendary.commonError: Treats lower inflation pressure from contractionary demand policy as costless in the short run.
legendary.feedback: A contractionary AD policy can reduce inflation pressure while also lowering output and raising unemployment before expectations fully adjust.

legendary.q: A short recession causes tax receipts to fall and unemployment-benefit payments to rise automatically. Congress also approves an infrastructure stimulus, but construction begins after the economy has already recovered. Which comparison is strongest?
options: The infrastructure program cannot affect aggregate demand once the recession has ended.
The automatic stabilizers cushion the downturn and recede with conditions, while the delayed discretionary program can add demand after the original gap has faded.
Both responses have the same implementation timing because each changes the government budget.
The automatic stabilizers become contractionary during the recession, while delayed infrastructure is always stabilizing.
legendary.commonError: Assumes automatic stabilizers and discretionary fiscal programs have the same activation and phase-out timing.
legendary.feedback: Automatic stabilizers respond as income and employment change without new legislation; discretionary programs can arrive later and may outlast the original gap.

boss.q: If output is below its natural level because aggregate demand is weak, stabilization policy would usually try to
boss.commonError: using contractionary policy during weak demand
boss.feedback: If AD is too weak, expansionary policy can shift AD right.

boss.q: The economy has a recessionary AD gap of $500 billion. Monetary policy raises investment by $50 billion and fiscal policy raises government spending by $60 billion. If MPC = 0.75 and there is no crowding out, what happens?
options: AD rises $440 billion, leaving a $60 billion gap.
AD rises $110 billion, leaving a $390 billion gap.
AD rises $500 billion, closing the gap exactly.
boss.commonError: not applying the multiplier to the combined spending impulse
boss.feedback: Initial impulse is $50 billion + $60 billion = $110 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $440 billion, leaving a $60 billion gap.

boss.q: A recessionary AD gap is $500 billion. Monetary policy raises investment by $50 billion, fiscal policy raises government spending by $60 billion, MPC = 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $40 billion. What gap remains?
boss.commonError: not subtracting crowding out after applying the multiplier
boss.feedback: Initial impulse is $110 billion. Multiplier is 4, so gross AD rise is $440 billion. Subtract $40 billion crowding out, net AD rise is $400 billion. A $100 billion gap remains.

boss.q: Which example is an automatic stabilizer during a recession?
options: The central bank announces a new bond-purchase program.
Congress passes a one-time infrastructure bill.
A state raises sales taxes to balance its budget.
Unemployment-benefit payments rise without a new legislative vote.
boss.commonError: Confusing automatic fiscal responses with newly enacted discretionary policy.
boss.feedback: Unemployment benefits expand automatically as more workers qualify, supporting income without new legislation.

boss.q: Real output is below potential and inflation pressure is weak. Which demand-management direction is appropriate?
options: Expansionary policy that shifts aggregate demand to the right.
Contractionary policy that shifts aggregate demand left.
A policy that shifts short-run aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect output in the short run.
boss.commonError: Applying contractionary policy to a recessionary gap.
boss.feedback: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can raise aggregate demand and reduce a recessionary gap.

boss.q: Why can a long implementation lag make discretionary stabilization policy harmful?
options: The policy always reduces aggregate demand before it begins.
It may arrive after conditions change and destabilize the economy.
The lag permanently prevents prices from adjusting.
The lag converts fiscal policy into monetary policy.
boss.commonError: Treating delayed policy as harmless regardless of the business-cycle phase.
boss.feedback: A delayed response can arrive after recovery or after inflation has eased, creating a procyclical rather than stabilizing effect.

boss.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises inflation and lowers real output. Why is stabilization difficult?
options: Both inflation and output automatically improve with any expansionary policy.
The shock shifts aggregate demand, so only tax policy can respond.
Supporting output may worsen inflation; fighting inflation may deepen the output loss.
Monetary and fiscal policy have identical effects on short-run aggregate supply.
boss.commonError: Treating a negative supply shock like a pure demand recession.
boss.feedback: A negative supply shock creates stagflation, forcing policymakers to weigh competing inflation and output objectives.

boss.q: The economy is near potential output, yet fiscal and monetary policy both become strongly expansionary. What is the main risk?
options: Aggregate demand must fall because the policies cancel each other.
Long-run aggregate supply immediately shifts left.
Crowding out guarantees that output and prices do not change.
Aggregate demand may overshoot capacity and increase inflation.
boss.commonError: Assuming two expansionary policies cannot create excessive aggregate demand.
boss.feedback: When both policies push spending upward near capacity, the combined demand increase can create an inflationary gap.

boss.q: The central bank tightens monetary policy while the government enacts fiscal expansion. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
options: The net effect is uncertain because the policies work in opposite directions.
Aggregate demand must rise because fiscal policy always dominates.
Aggregate demand must fall because monetary policy always dominates.
Both policies shift aggregate demand to the right.
boss.commonError: Declaring a definite outcome without comparing the strength of opposing policy impulses.
boss.feedback: Fiscal expansion pushes aggregate demand right, while monetary contraction pushes it left; the net change depends on magnitudes.

legendaryBoss.q: AD is weak by $500 billion. Government spending rises by $80 billion, investment rises by $40 billion, and MPC = 0.75. Ignoring crowding out, what happens to the gap?
options: AD rises $480 billion, leaving a $20 billion gap.
AD rises $120 billion, leaving a $380 billion gap.
AD rises $500 billion, closing the gap exactly.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not adding investment and government spending before applying the multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial spending impulse is $80 billion + $40 billion = $120 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $480 billion, leaving a $20 billion gap.

legendaryBoss.q: Output is above potential by $360 billion. The Fed uses contractionary monetary policy, and the investment response is $50 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what overheating gap remains?
options: No gap remains; policy overshoots by $110 billion.
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the investment decrease without applying the multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph shows contractionary policy. MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so AD falls $250 billion. The remaining overheating gap is $110 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: A recessionary AD gap is $600 billion. Government spending rises $100 billion, MPC = 0.8, and crowding out is $150 billion. What is the correct order and remaining gap?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then gross shift reaches $500 billion, then crowding out leaves $350 billion net and a $250 billion gap.
AD first shifts right $600 billion, then crowding out leaves $450 billion net and a $150 billion gap.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then gross shift reaches $500 billion, worsening the gap.
AD shifts right only $100 billion because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
legendaryBoss.commonError: forgetting that crowding out reduces the gross multiplier effect
legendaryBoss.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so gross shift is $500 billion. Net after $150 billion crowding out is $350 billion, leaving a $250 billion gap.

legendaryBoss.q: Contractionary monetary policy is used when the economy is already above potential output. What is the likely effect?
options: It may reduce inflation pressure because it shifts AD left when AD is too high.
It worsens inflation pressure because it shifts AD right.
It cannot affect AD because output is above potential.
It directly shifts SRAS right and fixes supply constraints.
legendaryBoss.commonError: reading the contractionary graph as expansionary policy
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. If AD is too high, that can reduce inflation pressure.

legendaryBoss.q: A contractionary monetary-policy move reduces investment by $60 billion. A separate fiscal expansion raises AD by $400 billion after the multiplier. If MPC = 0.75, what is the final net AD effect?
legendaryBoss.commonError: subtracting only the initial investment drop instead of its multiplied AD effect
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy. A $60 billion investment fall times multiplier 4 reduces AD by $240 billion. Net effect is $400 billion - $240 billion = +$160 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: If policymakers use contractionary monetary policy during a negative supply shock, what is the strongest critique?
options: It may reduce inflation pressure but can worsen the output loss because AD shifts left.
It directly restores lost supply while keeping output unchanged.
It shifts AD right and raises output without inflation risk.
It eliminates the need to consider SRAS.
legendaryBoss.commonError: treating every supply shock as if AD policy has no tradeoff
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. That can cool inflation pressure, but during a negative supply shock it may deepen the output loss.

repairQuestions.q: Which policy acts automatically to cushion a recession without a new vote by Congress?
options: Unemployment benefits that rise as workers lose jobs
repairQuestions.feedback: Automatic stabilizers change with economic conditions; unemployment benefits rise as unemployment rises.

repairQuestions.q: If output is below potential because AD is weak, policy that shifts AD right is:
repairQuestions.feedback: Expansionary policy shifts AD right and can help close a recessionary gap.

repairQuestions.q: In a liquidity trap, interest rates are often near:
repairQuestions.feedback: A liquidity trap occurs when interest rates are near zero and monetary policy has less room to work.

repairQuestions.q: Policy lags matter because policy may arrive:
repairQuestions.feedback: Policy can become poorly timed if it takes effect after the economy has changed.

repairQuestions.commonError: Assumes a delayed policy has the same stabilizing effect regardless of how the economy changes before implementation.
repairQuestions.q: A stimulus is approved during a recession but takes effect only after output has returned close to potential. What problem should the student diagnose?
options: The delayed stimulus can push aggregate demand too far right after the original gap has faded.
The delay automatically turns the stimulus into contractionary policy.
The policy can no longer affect aggregate demand once recovery begins.
The delay directly shifts LRAS left.
repairQuestions.feedback: A policy can destabilize the economy if it arrives after the original gap has already narrowed or reversed.

repairQuestions.commonError: Choosing tighter policy in a recessionary gap.
repairQuestions.q: A recessionary AD gap can be addressed with:
repairQuestions.feedback: Expansionary policy can shift AD right.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treats a negative supply shock as if policymakers can simultaneously eliminate its inflation and output effects by shifting AD.
repairQuestions.q: A negative supply shock lowers real output and raises the price level. If policymakers use expansionary demand policy to support output, what tradeoff should the student remember?
options: It can support output while worsening inflation pressure.
It lowers the price level and raises output with no tradeoff.
It directly shifts SRAS right and restores productive capacity.
It must reduce both output and the price level.
repairQuestions.feedback: Demand stabilization during a negative supply shock involves a tradeoff: supporting output can worsen price pressure, while reducing inflation can deepen the output loss.

repairQuestions.commonError: Choosing expansionary policy during overheating.
repairQuestions.q: During an inflationary boom caused by excessive AD, policymakers may use:
repairQuestions.feedback: Contractionary policy shifts AD left and reduces inflation pressure.

bridgeQuestions.q: After a negative AD shock, output is below potential, but wages and input costs are already adjusting downward and SRAS is shifting right. What additional question belongs to stabilization-policy analysis?
options: Whether policymakers should deliberately shift AD right rather than wait for the self-correcting SRAS adjustment.
Whether LRAS should be moved left to meet the current level of output.
Whether the multiplier should be redefined as zero during every recession.
Whether unemployment should be excluded from the labor force until recovery is complete.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Long-run adjustment describes endogenous SRAS movement; stabilization policy asks whether policymakers should deliberately change AD instead of waiting.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treats self-correction and active stabilization as the same mechanism.

bridgeQuestions.q: The Fed increases money supply, but rates are already near zero and investment barely responds. What is this problem?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A liquidity trap weakens the usual interest-rate channel of monetary policy.

bridgeQuestions.q: A stimulus bill takes effect after the recession has already ended. What problem is this?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Policy lags can cause stimulus to arrive after economic conditions have changed.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Not comparing stimulus size to the recessionary gap.
bridgeQuestions.q: A recessionary AD gap is $300 billion. Policy raises spending by $75 billion and the multiplier is 4. What happens?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: $75 billion x 4 = $300 billion, so the gap closes exactly.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops with an AD shift and does not connect the short-run output response to unemployment and inflation pressure.
bridgeQuestions.q: Contractionary stabilization policy shifts AD left to cool an overheating economy. Which short-run labor-market effect connects this policy choice to Phillips-curve analysis?
options: Unemployment tends to rise as output weakens while inflation pressure falls.
Unemployment must fall because lower AD always increases hiring.
Unemployment is unchanged because only the price level responds to AD.
The natural rate permanently falls by the size of the AD shift.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A contractionary stabilization policy that lowers AD can reduce inflation pressure while raising unemployment in the short run, creating the bridge to Phillips-curve analysis.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Two-panel monetary-transmission graph showing a leftward money-supply shift with a higher interest rate and a leftward aggregate-demand shift with lower output.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The left panel has interest rate r on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. The right panel has price level P on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Aggregate-demand multiplier graph with AD1, AD2, and AD3 shifting progressively right at a fixed price level P, corresponding to output levels Y1, Y2, and Y3.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level P. A horizontal line at price level P crosses three downward-sloping aggregate-demand curves. AD1 intersects at output Y1, AD2 lies to the right and intersects at Y2, and AD3 lies farther right and intersects at Y3, so Y1 is less than Y2, which is less than Y3.

aggregate-demand.title: Aggregate Demand
aggregate-demand.description: Explain the slope and shifters of aggregate demand.

easy.q: In the standard AD–AS convention, the vertical axis measures:
easy.commonError: Confusing output with the price level.
easy.feedback: The vertical axis in the AD-AS model measures the price level.

easy.q: In the standard AD–AS convention, the horizontal axis measures:
easy.commonError: Confusing the AD-AS axes.
easy.feedback: The horizontal axis in the AD-AS model measures real GDP or output.

easy.q: Which change shifts aggregate demand to the right?
easy.commonError: Confusing AD shifters with SRAS shifters.
easy.feedback: Higher consumer confidence increases consumption and shifts AD to the right.

easy.q: Which change shifts aggregate demand to the left?
easy.commonError: Thinking every policy shifts AD right.
easy.feedback: A tax increase reduces spending and shifts aggregate demand left.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from AD1 to AD2 represents:
easy.commonError: Reversing left and right shifts of AD.
easy.feedback: AD2 lies to the right of AD1, so the graph shows an increase in aggregate demand.

easy.q: A decrease in household wealth, holding other factors constant, shifts aggregate demand:
options: Not at all because wealth is not part of spending.
Up along the same AD curve.
easy.commonError: Confusing a spending shifter with a movement along AD.
easy.feedback: Lower wealth tends to reduce consumption, shifting aggregate demand left.

easy.q: What change from AD0 to AD1 is shown?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: A rightward shift of AD means aggregate demand has increased.

easy.q: How should AD1 be classified relative to AD0 in the second aggregate-demand diagram?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: A leftward shift of AD means aggregate demand has decreased.

medium.q: A rise in the price level reduces consumption because money holdings buy less. This is the:
medium.commonError: Confusing the three reasons AD slopes downward.
medium.feedback: The wealth effect works through reduced real purchasing power of money holdings.

medium.q: A rise in the price level raises money demand and interest rates, reducing investment. This is the:
medium.commonError: Confusing AD slope effects with SRAS theories.
medium.feedback: The interest-rate effect explains how a higher price level reduces investment spending.

medium.q: If foreign incomes rise and foreigners buy more U.S. exports, U.S. aggregate demand should:
medium.commonError: Forgetting net exports are part of AD.
medium.feedback: Higher exports raise net exports and shift aggregate demand right.

medium.q: If firms become pessimistic and reduce investment spending, aggregate demand should:
medium.commonError: Treating investment changes as supply changes.
medium.feedback: Lower investment reduces total spending and shifts AD left.

medium.q: If a price-level increase raises money demand, the interest rate rises, and investment falls. This explains:
medium.commonError: Mixing the AD slope with policy shifts.
medium.feedback: This is the interest-rate effect behind the downward-sloping AD curve.

medium.q: A lower domestic price level makes domestic goods relatively cheaper to foreign buyers. This supports the downward slope of AD through the:
medium.commonError: Confusing the three reasons aggregate demand slopes downward.
medium.feedback: A lower domestic price level can lower interest rates and the currency value, raising net exports.

medium.q: Assume SRAS is unchanged. Based on the AD shift shown, what happens to equilibrium real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Both real GDP and the price level increase
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: A rightward shift of AD raises spending pressure, so equilibrium output and the price level both rise in the short run.

medium.q: Which event is most consistent with the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: Higher planned spending by C, I, G, or NX
Higher input costs that reduce short-run aggregate supply
Lower productivity that reduces long-run aggregate supply
Higher wages that reduce short-run aggregate supply
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Aggregate demand shifts right when planned spending rises.

medium.q: Holding SRAS fixed, what short-run equilibrium pattern follows from the demand change in the second AD diagram?
options: Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: A leftward shift of AD lowers spending pressure, reducing equilibrium output and the price level in the short run.

medium.q: Which event best matches the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: A fall in input costs that raises short-run aggregate supply
A rise in productivity that raises long-run aggregate supply
A fall in planned consumption or investment spending
A rise in expected prices that shifts short-run aggregate supply
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Lower overall spending shifts aggregate demand left.

hard.q: Consumer confidence rises while firms become more pessimistic about future sales. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
options: The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the sizes of the consumption and investment changes.
The economy moves down along the same AD curve
hard.commonError: Letting one shifter determine the combined result.
hard.feedback: Confidence raises consumption, while pessimism lowers investment; magnitudes determine the net shift.

hard.q: The price level falls, but taxes rise at the same time. Which statement is most precise?
options: Both changes cause movement along AD.
The price-level change shifts AD right and the tax increase shifts AD left.
The price-level change causes movement along AD, while the tax increase shifts AD left.
hard.commonError: Confusing a change in the price level with a nonprice AD shifter.
hard.feedback: The price level is on the graph’s vertical axis; taxes are an external shifter.

hard.q: Foreign income falls sharply while domestic firms increase investment. The effect on domestic aggregate demand is:
options: Ambiguous because net exports fall while investment rises.
hard.commonError: Ignoring offsetting components of aggregate demand.
hard.feedback: Lower foreign income reduces exports, while higher investment raises AD.

hard.q: A higher price level increases money demand, which raises interest rates and reduces investment. This sequence explains:
options: A movement upward and leftward along the existing AD curve.
hard.commonError: Treating the interest-rate effect as a shift of AD.
hard.feedback: The interest-rate effect is one reason quantity of real GDP demanded falls as the price level rises.

hard.q: A depreciation of the domestic currency occurs for reasons unrelated to the domestic price level. Holding other factors constant, aggregate demand shifts:
options: Left because domestic goods become more expensive to foreigners.
Right because exports rise and imports fall.
Nowhere because exchange rates matter only along AD.
hard.commonError: Reversing the net-export effect of currency depreciation.
hard.feedback: A weaker domestic currency tends to raise net exports and aggregate demand.

hard.q: A rise in the price level reduces the real value of household money balances. The immediate AD implication is:
options: Higher net exports and a rightward AD shift.
Higher consumption and a rightward AD shift.
Lower consumption and a movement upward along AD.
Lower investment and a leftward SRAS shift.
hard.commonError: Confusing the wealth effect with an AD shifter.
hard.feedback: The wealth effect reduces quantity of output demanded as the price level rises.

hard.q: At a price level of 50, by how much does real GDP demanded differ between AD0 and AD1?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: At price level 50, the quantity of output demanded rises from 100 to 150, an increase of 50.

hard.q: Use the second AD graph at price level 45. What horizontal GDP gap separates AD0 and AD1?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: At price level 45, quantity demanded falls from 150 to 100, a decrease of 50.

elite.q: A country experiences higher consumer confidence, lower expected business profits, and a rise in foreign income. Which components of AD move first?
options: Consumption falls, investment rises, and net exports fall.
Consumption and net exports rise, while investment falls.
elite.commonError: Failing to trace each shifter to the correct AD component.
elite.feedback: Confidence affects consumption, expected profits affect investment, and foreign income affects exports.

elite.q: The price level rises at the same time that the government cuts taxes. Which graph description is correct?
options: There is movement downward along AD plus a leftward shift
There is movement upward along AD plus a rightward shift of the AD curve.
elite.commonError: Treating simultaneous movement and shift as mutually exclusive.
elite.feedback: The price-level change causes movement along AD; the tax cut shifts the curve.

elite.q: Domestic interest rates fall because the central bank expands money supply, while foreign income also falls. What can be said about AD?
options: Investment tends to rise and net exports tend to fall, so the net shift is ambiguous.
Only a movement along AD occurs
elite.commonError: Ignoring offsetting investment and net-export effects.
elite.feedback: The two shifters push different AD components in opposite directions.

elite.q: A student says, “Any fall in real GDP means AD shifted left.” What is the best correction?
options: Real GDP can fall from movement along AD or from shifts in AD or AS; the graph cause must be identified.
Real GDP changes only when AD shifts
A fall in real GDP always means SRAS shifted right
elite.commonError: Inferring a curve shift from an outcome without identifying the cause.
elite.feedback: Observed output changes do not by themselves reveal which curve moved.

elite.q: A student says AD1 must represent aggregate supply because real GDP is larger. What is the best correction?
options: Any curve farther right must be an aggregate-supply curve.
The graph is LRAS because real GDP is on the horizontal axis.
Both curves are AD; AD1 is the rightward demand shift.
A price-level axis means the curves cannot represent demand.
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: The label and downward slope identify the curves as AD. A larger quantity demanded at each price level is an increase in aggregate demand.

elite.q: If policymakers wanted to offset the AD shift shown, which short-run pattern are they responding to?
options: Lower output with downward pressure on the price level
Higher output with upward pressure on the price level
Higher output with downward pressure on the price level
Lower output with upward pressure on the price level
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: A decrease in AD lowers both real GDP and the price level in the short run.

legendary.q: The domestic price level rises, consumer confidence strengthens, and foreign income declines. Which analysis is complete?
options: AD shifts left with no offsetting force
There is movement upward along AD, a rightward pressure from consumption, and a leftward pressure from net exports.
AD shifts right with no movement along it
All changes move the economy along the same AD curve
legendary.commonError: Collapsing simultaneous movement and multiple shifts into one effect.
legendary.feedback: The price level changes quantity demanded; confidence and foreign income shift the curve in opposite directions.

legendary.q: A lower price level raises the real value of money balances, lowers interest rates, and makes domestic goods cheaper relative to foreign goods. What happens along AD?
options: Consumption, investment, and net exports all tend to rise.
All three channels shift AD rather than cause movement along it.
Consumption falls while investment and net exports rise.
legendary.commonError: Misclassifying the three slope mechanisms.
legendary.feedback: The wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects all raise quantity of real GDP demanded at a lower price level.

legendary.q: Businesses become optimistic, households become pessimistic, and the currency depreciates. Which AD components are initially affected?
options: Investment rises, consumption falls, and net exports rise.
Investment falls, consumption rises, and net exports fall.
legendary.commonError: Assigning shifters to the wrong spending components.
legendary.feedback: Expectations affect I and C, while depreciation affects NX.

legendary.q: A tax increase and higher government purchases occur together. Which statement is justified without numerical information?
options: The two policies push aggregate demand in opposite directions.
The policies cause only movement along AD
legendary.commonError: Assuming a combined policy has a predetermined net effect.
legendary.feedback: Higher G raises AD; higher taxes tend to reduce consumption and AD.

legendary.q: The price level is unchanged, but desired consumption, investment, and net exports all decline. The economy experiences:
options: A rightward shift of short-run aggregate supply.
A leftward shift of aggregate demand.
legendary.commonError: Using movement-along language when the price level is held fixed.
legendary.feedback: At a given price level, lower planned spending shifts AD left.

legendary.q: A country’s currency appreciates and foreign economies enter recession while domestic consumer confidence rises. The net AD effect is:
options: Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall for two reasons.
No change because the effects cancel exactly
legendary.commonError: Assuming offsetting forces are equal without evidence.
legendary.feedback: Confidence raises C, while appreciation and lower foreign income reduce NX.

legendary.q: Which statement correctly interprets the move from AD0 to AD1?
options: At each price level, AS1 shows more real GDP supplied.
At each output level, AD1 shows a lower price requirement.
AD0 and AD1 are two points on one aggregate-demand curve.
At each price level, AD1 shows more real GDP demanded.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: An AD increase means spending is higher at every price level. That is a shift of the entire demand curve, not a movement along it.

legendary.q: Which statement best captures the meaning of the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: At each price level, AS1 shows less real GDP supplied.
At each price level, AD1 shows less real GDP demanded.
At each output level, AD1 shows a higher price requirement.
AD0 and AD1 are two points on one aggregate-demand curve.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: The entire AD curve shifts left. That means spending is lower at each price level, not that the economy merely moved along AD0.

boss.q: Households become more confident about future income and increase planned consumption at every price level. What happens?
options: There is movement up along aggregate demand.
boss.commonError: Confusing movement along AD with a rightward shift.
boss.feedback: Higher planned consumption at each price level shifts aggregate demand right.

boss.q: The horizontal axis of an AD-AS graph measures:
boss.commonError: Reversing the graph axes.
boss.feedback: Real GDP or real output appears on the horizontal axis.

boss.q: A higher price level, by itself, causes:
options: Movement upward along the AD curve.
boss.commonError: Treating the price level as an AD shifter.
boss.feedback: The price level is on the vertical axis, so its change causes movement along AD.

boss.q: Firms expect stronger future sales. Aggregate demand shifts:
options: Nowhere because expectations affect only SRAS.
boss.commonError: Linking business expectations to the wrong component.
boss.feedback: More optimistic firms tend to increase investment spending.

boss.q: A higher price level reduces real money balances and consumption. This is the:
boss.commonError: Confusing the slope mechanisms.
boss.feedback: The wealth effect works through the purchasing power of money holdings.

boss.q: Foreign income falls. Domestic aggregate demand tends to:
options: Stay fixed because foreign income is not domestic.
boss.commonError: Ignoring export demand from foreign buyers.
boss.feedback: Lower foreign income reduces demand for domestic exports.

boss.q: The price level falls while firms cut investment. What occurs?
options: Movement downward along AD plus a leftward AD shift.
boss.commonError: Failing to separate price-level movement from a spending shift.
boss.feedback: The lower price level changes quantity demanded; lower investment shifts AD left.

boss.q: Consumer confidence rises and the currency appreciates. The net AD direction is:
options: No change because the effects are equal
Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall.
boss.commonError: Assuming offsetting shifters cancel exactly.
boss.feedback: The two components move in opposite directions, and magnitudes matter.

boss.q: Why does a higher price level reduce investment along AD?
options: Higher prices reduce expected input costs.
Higher money demand tends to raise interest rates.
Higher prices directly raise productive capacity.
boss.commonError: Confusing AD slope with supply-side changes.
boss.feedback: The interest-rate effect links a higher price level to less investment.

legendaryBoss.q: The price level rises, taxes fall, and foreign income falls. Which description is correct?
options: Movement upward along AD, a rightward tax-cut shift, and a leftward net-export shift.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Combining three distinct forces into one curve change.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The price level causes movement; taxes and foreign income shift AD in opposite directions.

legendaryBoss.q: Consumer confidence falls, investment expectations improve, and the currency depreciates. Which components move?
options: Consumption falls, investment rises, and net exports rise.
Consumption rises, investment falls, and net exports fall.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mapping shifters to the wrong components.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Confidence affects C, business expectations affect I, and depreciation affects NX.

legendaryBoss.q: A lower price level raises real balances, lowers interest rates, and weakens the currency. Which AD result follows?
options: SRAS shifts right because interest rates fell
Consumption, investment, and net exports tend to rise along the curve.
AD shifts right because the price level fell
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treating movement along AD as a curve shift.
legendaryBoss.feedback: All three classic channels raise quantity demanded at the lower price level.

repairQuestions.q: The AD curve slopes downward partly because a higher price level reduces:
repairQuestions.feedback: A higher price level reduces spending through wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects.

repairQuestions.q: Higher consumer confidence shifts AD:
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher confidence raises consumption and shifts AD right.

repairQuestions.q: A tax increase usually shifts AD:
repairQuestions.feedback: A tax increase lowers spending and shifts AD left.

repairQuestions.q: The vertical axis on a standard AD-AS graph measures:
repairQuestions.feedback: AD-AS graphs place the price level on the vertical axis and real output on the horizontal axis.

repairQuestions.q: A rightward shift of aggregate demand means:
options: Planned spending is higher at each price level
The price level has moved along AD
repairQuestions.feedback: A shift in AD changes total planned spending at every price level.

bridgeQuestions.q: A higher price level raises money demand, increases interest rates, and reduces investment. Which AD effect does this illustrate?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: This is the interest-rate effect behind the downward slope of AD.

bridgeQuestions.q: Business investment falls and shifts aggregate demand left. Which analysis determines the economy’s new short-run real output and price level?
options: Find the new intersection of aggregate demand and short-run aggregate supply.
Shift LRAS left by the same amount as investment falls.
Hold output fixed and change only the price level.
Calculate the money multiplier without using the AD–AS equilibrium.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: After identifying the AD shift, use its intersection with SRAS to determine the new short-run output and price level.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops after identifying an aggregate-demand shift and does not carry it into equilibrium analysis.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Aggregate demand and short-run aggregate supply graph with two AD curves, two AS curves, and labeled output-price combinations.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above/left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3, Y1, Y2 and P1, P2, P3. AD1 intersects AS2 at Y1/P1, AD1 intersects AS1 at Y3/P2, AD2 intersects AS2 at Y2/P2, and AD2 intersects AS1 at Y1/P3.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with LRAS at Y1, two aggregate-demand curves, two short-run aggregate-supply curves, and labeled gaps.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. LRAS is vertical at Y1. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above/left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3 left of LRAS, Y1 on LRAS, Y2 right of LRAS, and price levels P1, P2, P3. AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1; AD1-AS1 is Y3/P2; AD2-AS2 is Y2/P2; AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Aggregate demand graph with AD0 and a dashed AD1 curve to the right, showing an increase in aggregate demand.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP and the vertical axis is price level. AD0 slopes downward from price level 100 at real GDP 0 to price level 0 at real GDP 200. A dashed curve AD1 lies to the right of AD0, running from about 125 at real GDP 0 to 0 at real GDP 250. This indicates an increase in aggregate demand. At price level 50, AD0 corresponds to real GDP 100 and AD1 corresponds to real GDP 150.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Aggregate demand graph with AD0 and a dashed AD1 curve to the left, showing a decrease in aggregate demand.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP and the vertical axis is price level. AD0 slopes downward from price level 120 at real GDP 0 to price level 0 at real GDP 240. A dashed curve AD1 lies to the left of AD0, running from about 95 at real GDP 0 to 0 at real GDP 190. This indicates a decrease in aggregate demand. At price level 45, AD0 corresponds to real GDP 150 and AD1 corresponds to real GDP 100.

short-run-aggregate-supply.title: Short-Run Aggregate Supply
short-run-aggregate-supply.description: Analyze the SRAS slope, expected prices, input costs, productivity, and short-run aggregate-supply shifts.

easy.q: The short-run aggregate supply curve slopes upward mainly because:
options: Wages, prices, or perceptions do not adjust instantly
Money is neutral in every period
easy.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to the short run.
easy.feedback: SRAS slopes upward because sticky wages, sticky prices, and misperceptions allow price-level changes to affect output.

easy.q: A decrease in oil prices would most likely shift:
easy.commonError: Treating production cost changes as AD shifts.
easy.feedback: Lower production costs shift short-run aggregate supply to the right.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from AS2 to AS1 represents:
options: A decrease in short-run aggregate supply
An increase in short-run aggregate supply
easy.commonError: Reversing AS1 and AS2.
easy.feedback: AS1 is up and left of AS2, so moving from AS2 to AS1 is a decrease in SRAS.
