assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP and the vertical axis is price level. LRAS0 is vertical at real GDP 100. AD0 intersects SRAS0 at point C, where real GDP is 100 and price level is 125. AD1 intersects SRAS0 at point D, where real GDP is 125 and price level is 150. AD0 intersects SRAS1 at point A, where real GDP is 75 and price level is 150. AD1 intersects SRAS1 and LRAS0 at point B, where real GDP is 100 and price level is 175. The graph can be used to trace an AD increase from original long-run equilibrium C to short-run point D and then to long-run point B after SRAS shifts left.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: AD-AS-LRAS graph with AD0, SRAS0, SRAS1, LRAS0, LRAS1, and labeled points A and B.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP and the vertical axis is price level. AD0 slopes downward. Point A is the original long-run equilibrium where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 intersect at real GDP 100 and price level 125. A dashed SRAS1 curve lies below SRAS0, and a dashed LRAS1 line lies to the right of LRAS0 at real GDP 115. Point B is the new long-run equilibrium where AD0, SRAS1, and LRAS1 intersect at real GDP 115 and price level 110. The graph shows a positive supply-side change that raises long-run output and lowers the price level.

long-run-macroeconomic-self-adjustment.title: Long-Run Macroeconomic Self-Adjustment
long-run-macroeconomic-self-adjustment.description: Trace short-run-to-long-run self-correction and movement back toward potential output.

easy.q: In the long run, an economy returns to natural output because:
easy.commonError: Thinking short-run gaps last forever.
easy.feedback: Over time, wages, prices, and expectations adjust, moving output back toward natural output.

easy.q: Real GDP is below potential and labor-market slack is putting downward pressure on nominal wage growth. If aggregate demand does not change again, which adjustment helps the economy self-correct?
options: SRAS shifts right as wage and production-cost pressures ease.
AD shifts right automatically because unemployment is high.
LRAS shifts left until it reaches the depressed output level.
SRAS shifts left because firms are producing below potential.
easy.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
easy.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

medium.q: A boom in foreign economies raises net exports and pushes output above potential. In the long run, expected prices likely:
medium.commonError: Thinking output stays above potential forever.
medium.feedback: When output is above potential, pressures raise expected prices and shift SRAS left over time.

medium.q: A negative demand shock pushes output below potential. If policymakers do nothing, long-run adjustment likely involves:
options: Falling expected prices and SRAS shifting right
Rising expected prices and SRAS shifting left
medium.commonError: Missing self-correction through expectations.
medium.feedback: Below-potential output puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, shifting SRAS right.

medium.q: A temporary demand boom pushes production above potential. Policymakers do nothing, and wage contracts are gradually renegotiated as workers and firms revise price expectations upward. Which change is most consistent with self-correction?
options: Higher wages and input costs shift SRAS left while aggregate demand stays at its post-boom position.
Aggregate demand shifts left automatically as soon as wages rise.
LRAS shifts right because the economy briefly produced above potential.
SRAS shifts right because firms respond to the higher price level by cutting costs.
medium.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
medium.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

hard.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, long-run self-correction most likely shifts:
hard.commonError: Missing expected price adjustment after an expansionary gap.
hard.feedback: At Y2 output is above potential, so rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left.

hard.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, long-run self-correction most likely shifts:
hard.commonError: Missing expected price adjustment after a recessionary gap.
hard.feedback: At Y3 output is below potential, so wages and expected prices tend to fall, shifting SRAS right.

hard.q: A negative AD shock lowers output and prices. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
hard.commonError: Thinking recessionary gaps cannot self-correct.
hard.feedback: Lower wages and expected prices shift SRAS right and help output return to natural.

hard.q: A positive AD shock pushes output above potential. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
hard.commonError: Thinking booms above potential persist forever.
hard.feedback: Higher wages and expected prices shift SRAS left and return output to potential.

elite.q: Which statement best describes the macro outcome shown by the move from A to B?
options: Demand-pull inflation with no long-run growth.
Long-run growth with lower price pressure.
No change in either output or the price level.
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: Higher LRAS and SRAS support more output alongside a lower price level.

elite.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, which long-run adjustment is most consistent with self-correction?
options: SRAS shifts left until output returns to Y1
SRAS shifts right until output reaches Y3
AD shifts right until output reaches Y2
LRAS shifts right until it reaches Y2
elite.commonError: Moving LRAS instead of SRAS during short-run self-correction.
elite.feedback: At Y2, output is above natural output, so rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left toward long-run equilibrium.

elite.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, which long-run adjustment is most consistent with self-correction?
options: SRAS shifts right until output returns to Y1
SRAS shifts left until output returns to Y3
AD shifts left until output returns to Y3
LRAS shifts left until it reaches Y3
elite.commonError: Moving AD or LRAS instead of SRAS during self-correction.
elite.feedback: At Y3, output is below natural output, so falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right toward long-run equilibrium.

elite.q: An economy is above potential because of a demand boom. Which policy and long-run force push in the same direction?
options: Contractionary policy and rising expected prices
Expansionary policy and falling expected prices
Contractionary policy and falling expected prices
Expansionary policy and rising expected prices
elite.commonError: Pairing the wrong policy with the wrong output gap.
elite.feedback: Contractionary policy shifts AD left, while rising expected prices shift SRAS left; both reduce output toward potential.

elite.q: An economy is below potential because AD collapsed. Which policy and long-run force push in the same direction?
options: Expansionary policy and falling expected prices
Contractionary policy and rising expected prices
Expansionary policy and rising expected prices
Contractionary policy and falling expected prices
elite.commonError: Pairing recessionary gaps with contractionary policy.
elite.feedback: Expansionary policy shifts AD right, while falling expected prices shift SRAS right; both raise output toward potential.

elite.q: An economy begins at natural output. AD rises unexpectedly, then expected prices rise. Which sequence is most likely?
options: Output rises first, then SRAS shifts left
Output falls first, then SRAS shifts right
Prices fall first, then AD shifts left
LRAS shifts right, then output falls
elite.commonError: Skipping the short-run expansion before long-run adjustment.
elite.feedback: An unexpected AD increase raises output in the short run, but higher expected prices later shift SRAS left.

elite.q: An economy begins at natural output. AD falls unexpectedly, then expected prices fall. Which sequence is most likely?
options: Output falls first, then SRAS shifts right
Output rises first, then SRAS shifts left
Prices rise first, then LRAS shifts left
AD rises first, then unemployment rises
elite.commonError: Skipping the short-run recession before self-correction.
elite.feedback: An unexpected AD decrease lowers output first, then lower expected prices shift SRAS right over time.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, expected prices adjust upward with no policy response. Which movement fits the model?
options: SRAS shifts left toward AS1 and output returns toward Y1.
SRAS shifts right toward AS2 and output rises toward Y2.
AD shifts right toward AD2 and output remains above potential.
LRAS shifts right toward Y2 because actual output was high.
legendary.commonError: Confusing short-run output with long-run potential output.
legendary.feedback: When output is above potential, rising expected prices shift SRAS left and return output toward LRAS.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, expected prices adjust downward with no policy response. Which movement fits the model?
options: SRAS shifts right toward AS2 and output returns toward Y1.
SRAS shifts left toward AS1 and output falls toward Y3.
AD shifts left toward AD1 and prices rise toward P3.
LRAS shifts left toward Y3 because unemployment is high.
legendary.commonError: Moving LRAS instead of SRAS during self-correction.
legendary.feedback: When output is below potential, falling expected prices shift SRAS right and restore output toward natural output.

legendary.q: A temporary negative aggregate-demand shock lowers output below potential. With no policy response and flexible wages and expected prices over time, what is the long-run outcome?
options: SRAS shifts right and output returns to potential at a lower price level.
Output remains permanently below potential with the original price level.
LRAS shifts left until productive capacity matches the recession output.
Aggregate demand automatically shifts right because unemployment increased.
legendary.commonError: Treating a temporary demand shock as a permanent change in productive capacity.
legendary.feedback: Falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right, restoring natural output while leaving the price level lower.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. A demand increase has moved the economy to the intersection of AD2 and AS2 at Y2 and P2. If no policy reverses AD2 and long-run adjustment is completed, which comparison between the short-run and long-run effects is supported by the graph?
options: The temporary output gain disappears as output returns to Y1, while the price level rises further toward P3.
Output remains at Y2 because long-run adjustment changes only the price level, which falls all the way back toward P1.
Output falls to Y3 as SRAS shifts left past AS1, while the price level stays fixed at the short-run level P2.
Both real output and the price level return to their original Y1 and P1 values once wage contracts and expectations adjust.
legendary.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
legendary.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

legendary.q: Two economies have identical recessionary gaps. In Economy A, most wages can be reset monthly; in Economy B, most wages are fixed by three-year contracts. With no policy response, which prediction best follows from the long-run adjustment model?
options: Economy B should self-correct faster because longer wage contracts make SRAS respond more quickly to the recessionary gap.
Both economies must return to potential at exactly the same speed because a vertical LRAS fixes the timing as well as the destination.
Neither economy can self-correct without an aggregate-demand policy change because wage and cost adjustment cannot move SRAS.
Economy A should tend to self-correct faster because wages and production costs can adjust sooner.
legendary.commonError: Assumes self-correction is instantaneous even when wages and expectations are sticky.
legendary.feedback: Long-run adjustment can take time because wage contracts, input costs, and price expectations may change gradually.

legendary.q: After a negative aggregate-demand shock, real output begins recovering toward potential even though policymakers make no fiscal or monetary change. Nominal wage growth has slowed and firms report easing unit labor costs. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: The evidence requires LRAS to have shifted left until it met current output, converting the recessionary gap into long-run equilibrium.
The recovery shows wage adjustment is irrelevant because only changes in aggregate demand can move real output back toward potential.
The evidence is consistent with self-correction through a rightward SRAS shift, not necessarily an active stabilization policy.
The recovery proves aggregate demand was shifted right by discretionary policy even though no fiscal or monetary action is observed.
legendary.commonError: Attributes any recovery toward potential to active policy even when wages and expectations are adjusting with no policy change.
legendary.feedback: Self-correction is the endogenous SRAS response to an output gap; stabilization policy is a separate deliberate intervention.

boss.q: An economy has a recessionary gap and policymakers do nothing. Which self-correcting sequence is most consistent with the model?
options: Higher wages shift SRAS left and deepen the recessionary gap.
LRAS shifts left until potential output equals the depressed output level.
Lower wage and price expectations shift SRAS right toward potential.
Aggregate demand rises automatically because the current price level is fixed.
boss.commonError: Reversing the wage and SRAS adjustment in a recessionary gap.
boss.feedback: Below-potential output puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, allowing SRAS to shift right.

boss.q: Demand growth pushes output above potential. If no stabilization policy is used, which long-run adjustment is most likely?
options: Falling wages shift SRAS right and push output farther above potential.
LRAS shifts right solely because the current price level has increased.
Output stays permanently above potential without creating inflation pressure.
Rising costs shift SRAS left, returning output to potential at a higher price level.
boss.commonError: Using recessionary-gap adjustment for an inflationary gap.
boss.feedback: An overheated labor market raises costs and expected prices, shifting SRAS left and closing the inflationary gap.

boss.q: Output is below potential and unemployment is unusually high. If policymakers do nothing, which pressure is part of the opening self-correction mechanism?
options: Weak labor demand restrains wage and cost growth, creating pressure for SRAS to shift right.
High unemployment automatically shifts aggregate demand right.
Weak labor demand shifts LRAS left by definition.
High unemployment causes SRAS to shift left through higher wage growth.
boss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
boss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

boss.q: Refer to the graph. The economy begins at AD1-AS2 at Y1 and then a demand boom shifts AD to AD2, moving output to Y2. With no policy response, which pair of changes completes long-run adjustment?
options: AD shifts back to AD1 automatically; output returns to Y1 at P1.
LRAS shifts right to Y2; output remains above its original potential.
SRAS shifts right beyond AS2; output rises further while the price level falls.
SRAS shifts left toward AS1; output returns to Y1 while the price level rises toward P3.
boss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
boss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

boss.q: An economy is above potential because of a temporary surge in household spending. Which observation would be the strongest evidence that long-run self-correction has begun?
options: Aggregate demand is automatically shifting left with no change in spending.
Nominal wage growth is falling, pushing SRAS farther to the right.
Nominal wage and unit-cost growth are rising, putting leftward pressure on SRAS.
Potential output is falling simply because current output is high.
boss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
boss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

boss.q: Refer to the graph. At AD1 and AS1 the economy is at Y3, below Y1. If AD1 remains fixed, which change must occur for self-correction toward Y1?
options: SRAS shifts farther left from AS1, reducing output below Y3.
Falling wage and price expectations shift SRAS right from AS1 toward AS2.
Aggregate demand shifts from AD1 to AD2 while SRAS remains at AS1.
LRAS shifts left from Y1 to Y3 because output is currently low.
boss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
boss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

legendaryBoss.q: A negative demand shock leaves the economy below potential, and no policy response occurs. Which statement best identifies the long-run adjustment mechanism before tracing the details?
options: Slack puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, allowing SRAS to shift right.
Aggregate demand must automatically shift right enough to restore potential output without any change in wages or expectations.
LRAS must move left until it passes through current output, eliminating the gap without any cost adjustment.
High unemployment raises wage growth and shifts SRAS left, moving output even farther below potential.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
legendaryBoss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS1 at Y3, expected prices and nominal cost pressures fall gradually while AD1 stays fixed. Which sequence is consistent with the model?
options: SRAS moves farther left from AS1, pushing output below Y3 while the price level rises above its starting point.
AD shifts to AD2 and output jumps to Y2 even though the prompt holds aggregate demand fixed throughout the adjustment.
LRAS shifts left from Y1 to Y3, redefining the depressed output level as potential without any wage or expectation adjustment.
SRAS moves toward AS2, output rises toward Y1, and the price level falls toward P1.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
legendaryBoss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

repairQuestions.q: If output is below natural output, falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS:
repairQuestions.feedback: A recessionary gap tends to push wages and expected prices down, shifting SRAS right.

repairQuestions.q: If output is above natural output, rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS:
repairQuestions.feedback: An expansionary gap tends to push wages and expected prices up, shifting SRAS left.

bridgeQuestions.q: Output is above potential and self-correction through rising wages and costs is expected to be slow. Which stabilization-policy question becomes relevant?
options: Stabilization policy—whether and how to use an active policy response instead of waiting for self-correction.
Money measurement—whether currency should be counted in M1 or M2.
Growth accounting—how much of productivity comes from capital deepening.
CPI measurement—whether the market basket overstates cost-of-living changes.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Long-run adjustment describes self-correction; stabilization policy asks whether policymakers should actively shift aggregate demand rather than wait.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treats passive long-run adjustment and deliberate stabilization as the same mechanism.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with LRAS at Y1, two aggregate-demand curves, two short-run aggregate-supply curves, and labeled gaps.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. LRAS is vertical at Y1. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above/left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3 left of LRAS, Y1 on LRAS, Y2 right of LRAS, and price levels P1, P2, P3. AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1; AD1-AS1 is Y3/P2; AD2-AS2 is Y2/P2; AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: AD-AS-LRAS graph with AD0, SRAS0, SRAS1, LRAS0, LRAS1, and labeled points A and B.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP and the vertical axis is price level. AD0 slopes downward. Point A is the original long-run equilibrium where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 intersect at real GDP 100 and price level 125. A dashed SRAS1 curve lies below SRAS0, and a dashed LRAS1 line lies to the right of LRAS0 at real GDP 115. Point B is the new long-run equilibrium where AD0, SRAS1, and LRAS1 intersect at real GDP 115 and price level 110. The graph shows a positive supply-side change that raises long-run output and lowers the price level.

short-run-phillips-curve.title: Short-Run Phillips Curve
short-run-phillips-curve.description: Interpret movements along the short-run inflation–unemployment tradeoff.

easy.q: The Phillips curve shows a short-run trade-off between:
easy.commonError: Confusing the Phillips curve with the money market.
easy.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

easy.q: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the vertical axis measures:
easy.commonError: Reversing the Phillips curve axes.
easy.feedback: The vertical axis measures the inflation rate.

easy.q: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the horizontal axis measures:
easy.commonError: Reversing the Phillips curve axes.
easy.feedback: The horizontal axis measures the unemployment rate.

easy.q: In the short run, expansionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
easy.commonError: Missing the short-run tradeoff.
easy.feedback: Expansionary policy raises inflation pressure and lowers unemployment in the short run.

easy.q: In the short run, contractionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
easy.commonError: Reversing contractionary policy effects.
easy.feedback: Contractionary policy lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Point a has:
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation than point c
Higher unemployment and lower inflation than point c
The same unemployment and lower inflation than point c
easy.commonError: Reading the Phillips curve axes backward.
easy.feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, while point c is at U2 and I1.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from point c to point a shows:
easy.commonError: Reversing movement along SRPC.
easy.feedback: Moving from c to a raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run.

easy.q: In the long run, unemployment returns to:
easy.commonError: Thinking policymakers can permanently hold unemployment below natural.
easy.feedback: The natural-rate hypothesis says unemployment returns to its natural rate in the long run.

easy.q: At point A, what is the unemployment rate?
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point A lies directly above 5 on the unemployment axis.

easy.q: Relative to point A, what does point B show on SRPC0?
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point B is left of A on the unemployment axis and above A on the inflation axis.

easy.q: How does point B compare with the natural-rate point A in the displayed Phillips-curve graph?
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point B is to the right of A on the unemployment axis and below A on the inflation axis.

medium.q: The short-run Phillips curve slopes downward because higher AD tends to:
options: Raise output, lower unemployment, and raise inflation
Lower output, lower unemployment, and lower inflation
Raise unemployment while lowering inflation forever
medium.commonError: Missing the AD-to-unemployment channel.
medium.feedback: Higher AD raises output and prices, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation.

medium.q: Why is there no permanent Phillips-curve tradeoff?
options: Expectations adjust; unemployment returns to normal
AD stops affecting the short run
medium.commonError: Treating the short-run tradeoff as permanent.
medium.feedback: Once expectations adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point c, expansionary policy that raises inflation above expectations moves the economy to:
medium.commonError: Moving to the long-run point immediately.
medium.feedback: Expansionary policy moves the economy along SRPC1 from c to a: higher inflation and lower unemployment.

medium.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A move along SRPC1 from c toward b means:
medium.commonError: Reading movement along the curve backward.
medium.feedback: Moving up-left along SRPC1 raises inflation and lowers unemployment.

medium.q: At point A, what is the inflation rate?
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The horizontal guide through point A hits the inflation axis at 2.5 percent.

medium.q: How far below the natural rate is unemployment at point B?
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The natural rate is 5 percent at point A on the LRPC, while point B has 3 percent unemployment.

medium.q: What type of change is the move from A to B?
options: An upward shift from SRPC0 to another SRPC
A leftward shift of the LRPC
A movement along the same SRPC0
A movement along the vertical LRPC
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: Both A and B lie on the same SRPC0, so the graph shows a movement along the curve, not a curve shift.

medium.q: Point B is to the right of the LRPC. By how many percentage points does its unemployment rate exceed the natural rate?
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The natural rate is 5 percent at A, and point B is at 7 percent unemployment.

medium.q: Points A and B lie on the same short-run Phillips curve. How should the change from A to B be classified?
options: A movement along the same SRPC0
A downward shift from SRPC0 to another SRPC
A rightward shift of the LRPC
A movement along the vertical LRPC
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: A and B lie on the same SRPC0, so the graph shows a movement along the short-run curve.

medium.q: Aggregate demand rises unexpectedly while expected inflation is fixed. Which Phillips-curve change best represents the immediate effect?
options: A move up and left along the current SRPC
An upward shift of the SRPC at every unemployment rate
A rightward shift of the vertical LRPC
A move down and right along the current SRPC
medium.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
medium.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

medium.q: Inflation and unemployment both rise after a sharp increase in energy costs. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Aggregate demand causes movement up one unchanged SRPC
Lower expected inflation shifts the SRPC downward
The natural rate necessarily falls and shifts LRPC left
The adverse supply shock shifts the SRPC upward
medium.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
medium.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which point reflects unemployment below the natural rate with inflation above I1?
hard.commonError: Ignoring the LRPC natural rate.
hard.feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, so unemployment is below the natural rate U2 and inflation is above I1.

hard.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Moving from b to c along SRPC1 means:
hard.commonError: Reading movement along SRPC backward.
hard.feedback: Moving down-right along SRPC1 lowers inflation and raises unemployment.

hard.q: A policymaker claims higher inflation can permanently hold unemployment below natural. What is the flaw?
hard.commonError: Believing in a permanent Phillips curve menu.
hard.feedback: Once expected inflation adjusts, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

hard.q: Which event moves along SRPC rather than shifting SRPC?
hard.commonError: Confusing movement along SRPC with shifts of SRPC.
hard.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion moves the economy along the existing SRPC in the short run.

hard.q: Which answer best separates short-run and long-run Phillips curve logic?
options: Policy can move unemployment temporarily, but expectations restore the natural rate
Policy cannot affect unemployment even briefly, because money is neutral in every period
Policy permanently lowers unemployment whenever inflation rises above zero
Policy shifts LRPC whenever actual inflation changes
hard.commonError: Confusing short-run effects with long-run neutrality.
hard.feedback: Demand policy can move unemployment in the short run, but expectations adjust and unemployment returns to natural.

hard.q: Moving leftward along SRPC0 from point A implies which short-run relationship?
options: No change in unemployment as inflation changes
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: A downward-sloping SRPC shows an inverse short-run relationship: less unemployment comes with more inflation.

hard.q: At point B, how do unemployment and inflation compare with the natural-rate point A?
options: Unemployment is higher; inflation is lower
Unemployment is lower; inflation is lower
Unemployment is higher; inflation is higher
Unemployment is lower; inflation is higher
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: Point B combines a higher inflation rate with unemployment below the 5-percent natural rate.

hard.q: At the right-hand point B, which inflation-unemployment comparison with A is correct?
options: Unemployment is lower; inflation is higher
Unemployment is higher; inflation is lower
Unemployment is higher; inflation is higher
Unemployment is lower; inflation is lower
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: Point B has 1.5 percent inflation instead of 2.5 percent, and unemployment is above the 5-percent natural rate.

hard.q: Two years have the same unemployment rate, but inflation is higher in the second after wage setters revise expected inflation upward. What changed?
options: Aggregate demand alone fixed both outcomes
The economy is on a higher SRPC
The economy moved up one unchanged SRPC
hard.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
hard.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, which sequence best shows an attempted permanent unemployment reduction through expansionary policy?
elite.commonError: Thinking point a can be held permanently.
elite.feedback: Expansion lowers unemployment at a temporarily, but expectations adjust and unemployment returns to natural at b.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which policy mistake is shown by treating point a as permanent?
elite.commonError: Believing unemployment can stay below natural without expectations changing.
elite.feedback: Point a is temporary because expected inflation eventually rises and moves the economy toward point b.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. If policy moves the economy from c to b on SRPC1, what must be true?
options: Actual inflation rises while unemployment falls
Expected inflation rises while unemployment stays fixed
Natural unemployment rises while inflation falls
elite.commonError: Confusing movement along SRPC with a shift of SRPC.
elite.feedback: Movement up-left along the same SRPC means higher inflation and lower unemployment.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, policymakers try to keep unemployment at U1 through repeated demand expansion. What eventually breaks the plan?
options: Expected inflation rises and shifts the SRPC upward.
Actual inflation falls and shifts the SRPC downward.
The LRPC shifts left because inflation is higher.
The natural rate disappears because output rose once.
legendary.commonError: Believing policymakers can permanently buy lower unemployment with inflation.
legendary.feedback: Expansion can move unemployment below natural temporarily, but expected inflation adjusts and SRPC shifts upward.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. The economy moves from c to a, then policymakers mistake a as sustainable. What is the likely correction?
options: Expected inflation rises, SRPC shifts up, and the economy moves toward b.
Expected inflation falls, SRPC shifts down, and the economy moves toward d.
The natural rate falls, LRPC shifts left, and the economy stays at a.
The price level falls, AD shifts left, and unemployment stays at U1.
legendary.commonError: Treating a short-run Phillips curve point as permanent.
legendary.feedback: Point a is temporary. Expected inflation adjusts upward and the economy returns to the natural rate at higher inflation.

legendary.q: Two episodes produce the same increase in inflation. In one, unemployment falls after aggregate demand expands; in the other, unemployment rises after an adverse supply shock. What explains the difference?
options: Both episodes are movements along one SRPC, but they begin from different unemployment rates.
Both episodes shift the LRPC because inflation changes the natural rate in opposite directions.
The supply shock lowers expected inflation and moves the economy down an unchanged SRPC.
The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.
legendary.commonError: Assuming every inflation change is a movement along one fixed Phillips curve.
legendary.feedback: Demand changes can move the economy along a given SRPC; supply shocks alter the inflation-unemployment relationship and shift the SRPC.

legendary.q: Which pair of descriptions matches the two curves shown?
options: SRPC0: no short-run tradeoff; LRPC: permanent tradeoff
SRPC0: long-run neutrality; LRPC: short-run tradeoff
SRPC0: fixed unemployment; LRPC: fixed inflation
SRPC0: short-run tradeoff; LRPC: no long-run tradeoff
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: That is the whole point of showing both curves together: a short-run tradeoff and a vertical long-run benchmark.

legendary.q: A demand expansion moves the economy to lower unemployment and higher inflation. A year later unemployment returns to its original rate while inflation remains higher. Which sequence fits?
options: A supply improvement followed by movement down the SRPC
Movement along an SRPC followed by an upward SRPC shift
Two movements along one permanently fixed SRPC
An LRPC shift left followed by falling expectations
legendary.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendary.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation while output falls. How should the AD-AS result transfer to the Phillips model?
options: Higher inflation and unemployment indicate an upward SRPC shift
Higher inflation and lower unemployment indicate movement along SRPC
Lower inflation and unemployment indicate a downward SRPC shift
Unchanged inflation with lower unemployment indicates an LRPC shift
legendary.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
legendary.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

legendary.q: A policymaker cites the downward-sloping SRPC as proof that permanently higher inflation will secure permanently lower unemployment. What is the decisive flaw?
options: The SRPC actually slopes upward for every demand change
Inflation cannot respond to aggregate demand in the short run
The natural rate is always zero after an expansion
Expected inflation adjusts, so the short-run unemployment gain is not permanent
legendary.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
legendary.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

boss.commonError: Confusing the Phillips curve with the AD-AS model.
boss.q: What does the short-run Phillips curve show?
options: A short-run tradeoff between inflation and unemployment
A long-run tradeoff between inflation and output
A fixed relationship between money supply and GDP
A direct measure of government spending
boss.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation.

boss.commonError: Reversing the short-run inflation-unemployment tradeoff.
boss.q: Expansionary policy raises aggregate demand. In the short run, what Phillips curve movement should follow?
boss.feedback: Expansionary policy raises AD, which can lower unemployment but raises inflation in the short run.

boss.q: Aggregate demand contracts unexpectedly while expected inflation is initially fixed. What short-run Phillips-curve movement is most likely?
options: Toward lower inflation and higher unemployment.
Toward higher inflation and lower unemployment.
The entire SRPC shifts up-right immediately.
Unemployment stays fixed at the natural rate in the short run.
boss.commonError: Confusing a demand-driven movement along the SRPC with a shift of the curve.
boss.feedback: An unexpected demand contraction moves the economy down and right along the current SRPC.

boss.q: On a given SRPC, which combination lies farther up and left?
boss.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
boss.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

boss.q: Expected inflation is unchanged and aggregate demand falls. What happens first?

The economy moves down and right along its SRPC
The SRPC shifts upward at every unemployment rate
The LRPC shifts left of the natural rate

boss.q: Which event most directly shifts rather than moves along the SRPC?

A temporary change in real spending
A movement between two points on one curve

boss.q: A demand boom first lowers unemployment, then wage expectations catch up. Which complete Phillips sequence is most defensible?
options: Shift LRPC left, then move down the same SRPC as expectations rise
Shift SRPC downward, then keep unemployment permanently below natural
Move down-right along SRPC, then shift LRPC right after wages adjust
Move up-left along SRPC, then shift SRPC upward toward the natural rate

boss.q: A supply disruption raises inflation and unemployment together. Which interpretation survives both the graph and mechanism tests?
options: The LRPC shifts left because inflation increased
The SRPC shifts downward because output fell
The SRPC shifts upward because the tradeoff worsens
The economy moves up-left along a fixed SRPC
boss.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
boss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

boss.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands demand. Which claim correctly separates the short run from the long run?
options: Inflation falls temporarily and remains lower after all contracts adjust
Unemployment may fall temporarily, but expectations adjustment removes the permanent tradeoff
Unemployment falls permanently because the SRPC stays downward sloping after expectations adjust
The SRPC immediately becomes vertical before output or nominal wages can change
boss.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
boss.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

legendaryBoss.q: A demand expansion moves unemployment below natural. Wage contracts later incorporate the higher inflation. What is the next Phillips-curve development?
options: The SRPC shifts upward and unemployment moves back toward natural
The economy stays on the original SRPC at permanently lower unemployment
The LRPC shifts left because nominal wages increased
The SRPC shifts downward as expected inflation rises
legendaryBoss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: One episode has rising inflation with falling unemployment; another has rising inflation with rising unemployment. What distinguishes them?
options: Both are identical movements along one unchanged SRPC despite their opposite unemployment changes in the two episodes
The first shifts LRPC left while the second shifts aggregate demand right
Both establish a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff without expectations adjustment
The first can be demand movement along SRPC; the second can be an adverse supply shift
legendaryBoss.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
legendaryBoss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

legendaryBoss.q: A government tries repeated demand expansions to hold unemployment one point below natural. Which model-consistent end state is most likely?
options: LRPC shifts left solely because repeated nominal spending increased
Expected inflation falls until deflation permanently restores the initial unemployment rate
Unemployment returns toward natural at a higher inflation rate after expectations adjust
Unemployment remains below natural with unchanged inflation after wage contracts renew
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
legendaryBoss.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

repairQuestions.q: A demand increase raises inflation and lowers unemployment while expectations are unchanged. Is this a movement or a shift?
options: A movement along the current SRPC
An upward shift of the entire SRPC
A leftward shift of the LRPC
A downward shift of the entire SRPC
repairQuestions.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.
repairQuestions.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.

repairQuestions.q: Expected inflation rises while unemployment is held fixed. What happens to the SRPC?
options: The economy moves up the same SRPC
repairQuestions.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

options: An upward shift of the SRPC

A downward shift of the SRPC

bridgeQuestions.q: Aggregate demand expands unexpectedly, raising output and the price level. What linked Phillips result follows first?
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation along the current SRPC
Higher unemployment and higher inflation from an SRPC shift
Lower unemployment and lower inflation from an LRPC shift
Unchanged unemployment with a downward SRPC shift

bridgeQuestions.q: After a move to lower unemployment and higher inflation, wage setters revise inflation forecasts upward. What happens to the short-run Phillips curve?

Money demand shifts the SRPC downward
Expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward

A sacrifice ratio equal to unemployment
The vertical LRPC at the natural rate

GDP accounting identities for measuring current national output
Comparative advantage from differences in opportunity cost

long-run-phillips-curve.title: Long-Run Phillips Curve
long-run-phillips-curve.description: Apply the natural-rate hypothesis and vertical long-run Phillips curve.

easy.q: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at:
easy.commonError: Confusing SRPC with LRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Which unemployment rate is the natural rate?
easy.commonError: Ignoring the vertical LRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is drawn at U2, so U2 is the natural rate of unemployment.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At U3, SRPC2 has inflation rate:
easy.commonError: Reading the wrong curve at the same unemployment rate.
easy.feedback: At U3, the upper curve SRPC2 is at I4.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At U4 on SRPC1, inflation is:
easy.commonError: Reading the upper curve instead of SRPC1.
easy.feedback: The lower point at U4 on SRPC1 is at I1.

easy.q: Where is the long-run Phillips curve drawn?
options: Vertically at the natural rate of unemployment
Horizontally at the current inflation rate
Downward sloping through every short-run point
easy.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

easy.q: What does a vertical LRPC imply?
options: Inflation is fixed in the long run
The natural rate always equals zero
There is no permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff
easy.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which pair of points are long-run equilibria?
medium.commonError: Treating all SRPC points as long-run equilibria.
medium.feedback: Points b and c lie on the vertical LRPC at U2.

medium.q: Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent while unemployment remains at its natural rate. Which long-run outcome fits the vertical Phillips curve?
options: Inflation is higher, but unemployment is unchanged at the natural rate.
Inflation is higher and unemployment is permanently lower.
Inflation is unchanged and unemployment falls to zero.
Both inflation and unemployment are permanently higher.
medium.commonError: Treating a higher expected inflation rate as a permanent way to lower unemployment.
medium.feedback: Along the long-run Phillips curve, different inflation rates can coexist with the same natural rate of unemployment.

medium.q: What natural rate of unemployment is shown by the LRPC?
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The vertical LRPC is drawn at 5 percent unemployment, so that is the natural rate.

medium.q: If inflation rises while the economy remains on the LRPC, what happens to unemployment in this graph?
options: It becomes equal to the inflation rate
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: A vertical long-run Phillips curve means the long-run unemployment rate is pinned at the natural rate.

medium.q: Demand expansion temporarily pushes unemployment below natural. After expected inflation adjusts, where does unemployment tend to go?
options: To zero regardless of labor institutions
Above natural forever with no inflation change
Permanently farther below the natural rate
medium.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
medium.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

medium.q: Job-matching technology improves and lowers structural unemployment. What Phillips-curve change can follow?
options: The LRPC shifts left to a lower natural rate
The economy moves left along the same LRPC
The SRPC must shift upward at every point
medium.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
medium.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

medium.q: A rise in long-term mismatch raises the natural rate. What happens to the LRPC?
options: It stays fixed at the old natural rate
medium.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
medium.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

medium.q: Why can many inflation rates appear on the same vertical LRPC?
options: Inflation is unable to change nominal wages
Every point has zero expected inflation
Aggregate demand fixes the natural rate
Long-run unemployment equals natural after expectations adjust
medium.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
medium.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which point reflects high inflation with unemployment at the natural rate?
hard.commonError: Confusing short-run and long-run points.
hard.feedback: Point b lies on the LRPC at U2 and inflation I2.

hard.q: If actual inflation equals expected inflation, the Phillips curve equation implies unemployment is:
hard.commonError: Missing the role of inflation surprises.
hard.feedback: With no inflation surprise, unemployment equals the natural rate.

hard.q: Which event is most likely to shift the LRPC right?
hard.commonError: Confusing inflation changes with natural-rate changes.
hard.feedback: The LRPC shifts when the natural rate of unemployment changes.

hard.q: Which event is most likely to shift the LRPC left?
hard.commonError: Treating expected inflation as a natural-rate change.
hard.feedback: Better labor-market matching can lower the natural rate and shift the LRPC left.

hard.q: Inflation rises permanently after repeated demand expansion, but labor-market structure is unchanged. Which long-run statement is strongest?
options: Unemployment remains permanently below natural after expectations fully adjust
The LRPC shifts right because the price level rose over time
Unemployment returns toward the same natural rate on an unchanged LRPC
The LRPC shifts left because higher inflation permanently improves job matching
hard.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
hard.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

hard.q: The natural rate falls because job search becomes faster. How should SRPC and LRPC reasoning be separated?
options: LRPC stays fixed while unemployment permanently departs from its vertical location
LRPC shifts left; short-run curves may also reposition around the new natural rate
The economy merely moves upward along the old LRPC as inflation changes
Only inflation expectations can shift LRPC in the long-run model
hard.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
hard.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which comparison best captures the long-run result of higher expected inflation?
options: b and c have same unemployment but different inflation
a and b have same unemployment but different inflation
c and d have same inflation but different unemployment
a and d have same inflation but different unemployment
elite.commonError: Missing vertical long-run logic.
elite.feedback: Both b and c lie on the LRPC at U2, but b has higher inflation.

elite.q: Policymakers repeatedly expand aggregate demand to keep unemployment below its natural rate. Once workers and firms adjust expectations, what is required to keep unemployment below that rate?
options: A lower natural rate without any labor-market change.
A one-time reduction in expected inflation.
elite.commonError: Assuming one expansion can hold unemployment below the natural rate forever.
elite.feedback: After expectations catch up, only new inflation surprises can again push unemployment temporarily below its natural rate.

elite.q: Which feature of the graph shows that the natural rate is unchanged after the SRPC shift?
options: LRPC stays vertical at 5 percent unemployment
LRPC shifts left to 3 percent unemployment
SRPC1 becomes vertical at 6 percent unemployment
Point B moves to the right of point A
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: The LRPC staying fixed at 5 percent says the natural rate is unchanged, so inflation changes do not permanently buy lower unemployment.

elite.q: Which description of point A is correct?
options: A is only on SRPC0 and remains below the natural unemployment rate.
A is only on LRPC and remains above the natural unemployment rate.
A is on both SRPC0 and LRPC at the natural rate
A is the location where SRPC0 turns into a vertical Phillips curve.
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: Point A is where the short-run curve crosses the long-run curve, so unemployment equals the natural rate there.

elite.q: If point B persists and expectations adjust, what long-run change is predicted?
options: SRPC shifts upward; unemployment returns to 5 percent
LRPC shifts left; unemployment stays at 3 percent
SRPC shifts downward; unemployment stays at 3 percent
LRPC shifts right; unemployment rises above 5 percent
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: With unemployment below the natural rate, expectations eventually adjust, shifting the SRPC and bringing unemployment back to the natural rate.

elite.q: With unemployment above the natural rate at B, what long-run Phillips-curve adjustment should follow?
options: LRPC shifts right; unemployment stays at 7 percent
SRPC shifts up; unemployment stays at 7 percent
SRPC shifts down; unemployment returns to 5 percent
LRPC shifts left; unemployment falls below 5 percent
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: With unemployment above the natural rate, inflation expectations tend to fall, shifting the SRPC downward and returning unemployment to the natural rate.

legendary.q: Two economies have the same natural unemployment rate but very different average inflation rates over many years. Which observation is most consistent with a vertical long-run Phillips curve?
options: The higher-inflation economy must have permanently lower unemployment because inflation buys a lasting tradeoff.
The lower-inflation economy must have permanently higher unemployment because prices grow more slowly.
Both can remain at the same long-run unemployment rate despite different inflation rates.
Different inflation rates require different natural unemployment rates even when labor markets are otherwise alike.
legendary.commonError: Inferring a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff from cross-country inflation differences.
legendary.feedback: The vertical LRPC allows different steady inflation rates at the same natural unemployment rate.

legendary.q: A national job-matching system reduces the time workers spend searching for suitable positions. What happens to the long-run Phillips curve, other things equal?
options: It shifts right because expected inflation rises.
The economy moves upward along an unchanged LRPC.
It becomes horizontal at the new inflation rate.
It shifts left because the natural rate of unemployment falls.
legendary.commonError: Confusing a change in the natural rate with a movement caused by inflation.
legendary.feedback: A lasting improvement in labor-market matching can lower the natural rate and move the entire LRPC left.

legendary.q: An unexpected monetary expansion temporarily lowers unemployment. Inflation expectations then fully adjust while the higher inflation rate persists. What is the long-run result?
options: Unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate.
Unemployment remains permanently below the natural rate.
Unemployment rises permanently above the natural rate.
Inflation returns automatically to its original rate while unemployment stays low.
legendary.commonError: Stopping the analysis before expectations adjust.
legendary.feedback: The short-run unemployment effect disappears when expectations adjust, leaving higher inflation and natural-rate unemployment.

legendary.q: Policy holds unemployment below natural with successive demand expansions. Expected inflation rises each round. Which path is consistent with the natural-rate model?
options: A sequence of upward-shifting SRPCs ending back at natural unemployment with higher inflation
One unchanged SRPC delivering permanently lower unemployment after every contract renewal
A leftward LRPC shift caused solely by faster inflation with unchanged labor structure
A downward SRPC shift ending in deflation and a lower natural unemployment rate
legendary.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendary.q: Economy A lowers its natural rate through better job matching; Economy B only creates an unexpected demand boom. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both economies permanently shift LRPC left because unemployment initially declines
Only Economy B changes long-run unemployment by raising aggregate demand
Neither economy can affect unemployment at either a short or long horizon
A can shift LRPC left; B can only move unemployment below natural temporarily
legendary.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
legendary.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

legendary.q: Inflation expectations instantly match a fully anticipated monetary expansion in the model. What Phillips prediction is most consistent?
options: A rightward LRPC shift from higher money growth and unchanged labor institutions
A guaranteed fall in both inflation and unemployment after expectations adjust
Little or no temporary unemployment movement away from the natural rate
A permanent unemployment decline along the SRPC once nominal spending increases
legendary.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
legendary.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

boss.commonError: Confusing the short-run and long-run Phillips curves.
boss.q: What does the vertical long-run Phillips curve represent?
boss.feedback: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

boss.commonError: Reading the natural rate from the wrong point.
boss.q: On the graph, where does the LRPC identify the natural rate of unemployment?
boss.feedback: The LRPC is drawn at U2, so U2 is the natural rate of unemployment.

boss.q: A government insists on holding unemployment below the natural rate after inflation expectations have adjusted. What does the long-run Phillips-curve model predict?
options: A stable inflation rate will permanently sustain lower unemployment.
The policy requires continuously accelerating inflation.
Unemployment will fall to zero without further inflation.
The natural rate automatically falls whenever aggregate demand rises.
boss.commonError: Believing a stable higher inflation rate buys a permanent unemployment reduction.
boss.feedback: Once expected inflation catches up, maintaining below-natural unemployment requires repeated new inflation surprises.

boss.q: At what unemployment rate is the LRPC located?
boss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
boss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

boss.q: What makes the LRPC vertical?
options: Expected inflation adjusts in the long run
Aggregate demand never changes output even temporarily
Inflation must remain constant at every natural-rate point
Unemployment cannot change during a short-run demand surprise
boss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
boss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

boss.q: Which event can shift the LRPC?
options: A one-time surprise demand expansion with fixed expectations
A movement along the current SRPC after demand changes
A temporary inflation forecast error in wage contracts
A structural change in the natural rate
boss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
boss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

boss.q: A policy claim says 6% inflation can permanently hold unemployment below natural. Which model result rejects it?
options: The natural rate falls whenever inflation rises
Expectations adjustment returns unemployment toward the vertical LRPC
The SRPC is always vertical even in the short run
boss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
boss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

boss.q: Job-search reform lowers mismatch while inflation expectations are unchanged. Which graph change captures the durable labor effect?
options: The LRPC shifts left to the new natural rate
An upward SRPC shift from higher expected inflation
A permanent move left along one SRPC
boss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
boss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

boss.q: Unemployment is below natural and actual inflation exceeds expected inflation. What long-run adjustment follows?
options: Expected inflation falls and SRPC shifts downward
Natural unemployment disappears as inflation continues
Expected inflation rises and unemployment returns toward natural
LRPC shifts left and locks in the lower unemployment
boss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
boss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: A surprise expansion moves unemployment below natural; later contracts incorporate the higher inflation. What identifies the long-run endpoint?
options: A permanently lower natural rate caused by nominal demand after contracts renew
A horizontal LRPC at the new inflation rate with lower permanent unemployment
Lower inflation with unemployment still below natural after expectations fully adjust
The same natural unemployment rate with higher expected and actual inflation
legendaryBoss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: A labor-market reform lowers the natural rate while a demand expansion temporarily lowers unemployment even further. Which distinction is essential?
options: Demand shifts LRPC permanently while reform only changes the current inflation rate
Neither change can alter a Phillips curve once expectations are specified
The reform shifts LRPC; the demand expansion creates temporary movement relative to it
Both changes are movements along one unchanged SRPC despite different mechanisms
legendaryBoss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
legendaryBoss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: Two economies have different steady unemployment rates but the same long-run inflation. What can explain the difference without restoring a long-run tradeoff?
options: A common SRPC that never shifts
Different natural rates locate their vertical LRPCs differently
Different inflation rates along the same downward LRPC
Permanent forecast errors in both economies
legendaryBoss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
legendaryBoss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

repairQuestions.q: Why does higher inflation not permanently lower unemployment in the natural-rate model?
options: Expected inflation adjusts and unemployment returns toward natural
Aggregate demand has no short-run effect
The natural rate always falls with inflation
Nominal wages never respond to prices
repairQuestions.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
repairQuestions.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

repairQuestions.q: Structural unemployment falls because matching improves. Is that movement along or a shift of LRPC?
options: Movement left along a fixed LRPC
An upward shift of SRPC only
A leftward shift of the LRPC
repairQuestions.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.
repairQuestions.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation has fully adjusted after an expansion. Which prior family idea now leads to the LRPC conclusion?
options: The temporary SRPC movement ends at natural unemployment
The SRPC remains a permanent menu of choices
The sacrifice ratio becomes the natural rate
Deflation moves LRPC to zero unemployment
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.

bridgeQuestions.q: The LRPC places unemployment at its natural rate. Which labor-family concept supplies that location?
options: Natural-rate unemployment from frictional and structural forces
Cyclical unemployment at every inflation rate
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

bridgeQuestions.q: A central bank begins disinflation from the natural rate. Which next family concept measures the possible output cost of the temporary adjustment?

bridgeQuestions.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
