disinflation-and-policy.title: Disinflation and Policy
disinflation-and-policy.description: Trace monetary disinflation, unemployment costs, and expectations adjustment.

easy.q: If the Fed reduces money growth to fight inflation, unemployment usually:
easy.commonError: Ignoring the short-run cost of disinflation.
easy.feedback: Disinflation usually raises unemployment temporarily as the economy moves along the SRPC.

easy.q: Disinflation means that:
options: The overall price level is falling because average prices are declining.
Unemployment is falling even though output remains below potential.
Inflation is slowing, although the price level may still be rising.
Nominal wages are fixed while real wages rise automatically.
easy.commonError: Confusing disinflation with deflation.
easy.feedback: Disinflation is slower price growth; deflation is a falling price level.

easy.q: Why can a credible anti-inflation announcement reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
options: It permanently eliminates the natural rate of unemployment.
It guarantees that the price level falls immediately.
Expected inflation may adjust downward more quickly.
easy.commonError: Ignoring the role of expected inflation in the transition.
easy.feedback: When expectations fall sooner, wage and price setting can adjust with less output and unemployment loss.

easy.q: The sacrifice ratio measures the:
options: Cumulative output lost per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
The permanent unemployment rate created by a recession.
The price-level increase caused by one point of money growth.
The share of public spending financed by current taxes.
easy.commonError: Treating the sacrifice ratio as a permanent unemployment rate.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio summarizes the output cost of lowering inflation.

easy.q: Inflation slows from 6% to 3%, so the price level still rises more slowly. What is this?
options: A falling real interest rate by definition
easy.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
easy.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

easy.q: Which short-run effect commonly accompanies contractionary disinflation policy?
options: A permanently lower natural unemployment rate
An immediate rise in aggregate demand
easy.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
easy.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point b, contractionary policy that lowers inflation below expectations moves the economy in the short run to:
medium.commonError: Moving directly to lower expected inflation.
medium.feedback: Contractionary policy moves along SRPC2 from b to d: lower inflation and higher unemployment.

medium.q: If the Fed reduces money growth to lower inflation, the short-run Phillips curve predicts:
options: Lower inflation and temporarily higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment immediately
medium.commonError: Ignoring the short-run unemployment cost.
medium.feedback: Disinflation usually moves the economy toward lower inflation and higher unemployment in the short run.

medium.q: A central bank reduces aggregate demand to lower inflation. What Phillips movement is expected before expectations adjust?
options: An upward SRPC shift from lower expected inflation
Down and right along the current SRPC
Up and left along the current SRPC
medium.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
medium.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

medium.q: Why can a credible lower-inflation target reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
options: It causes aggregate demand to expand during contraction
It may lower expected inflation and shift the SRPC downward sooner
It permanently lowers the natural rate by announcement
It guarantees wages and prices adjust instantly
medium.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
medium.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

medium.q: Inflation falls from 4% to 1%, but prices continue rising. Which statement is correct?
options: The economy has disinflation, not deflation
The economy has deflation because inflation fell
The price level must be below its initial level
The natural rate must have declined
medium.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
medium.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

medium.q: Why might gradual disinflation be chosen instead of a rapid contraction?
options: It always produces zero cumulative output loss
It guarantees expected inflation never changes
It can spread adjustment and reduce a severe short-run output gap
medium.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
medium.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence matches disinflation and expectations adjustment?
hard.commonError: Skipping the temporary unemployment cost.
hard.feedback: Disinflation moves from b to d in the short run; expected inflation falls and the economy moves to c.

hard.q: If actual inflation is less than expected inflation, unemployment is likely:
hard.commonError: Reversing the effect of unexpectedly low inflation.
hard.feedback: When actual inflation is below expected inflation, unemployment tends to rise above the natural rate.

hard.q: A policymaker wants lower inflation but ignores unemployment during transition. What model warns about this cost?
hard.commonError: Ignoring short-run disinflation costs.
hard.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that reducing inflation can temporarily raise unemployment.

hard.q: A central bank announces a gradual disinflation, but households and firms doubt that the plan will continue. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The natural unemployment rate immediately falls to zero.
High expected inflation can prolong the output and job losses.
The price level must begin falling throughout the adjustment.
Unemployment cannot rise because the disinflation is gradual.
hard.commonError: Assuming gradualism automatically produces low transition costs.
hard.feedback: If the plan lacks credibility, expected inflation can adjust slowly and make the disinflation more costly.

hard.q: A disinflation announcement is not credible, and wage contracts embed 6% inflation. What makes immediate costless adjustment unlikely?
options: Deflation is required before unemployment changes
Expected inflation and nominal contracts may adjust slowly
The LRPC must shift left before policy begins
hard.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
hard.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

hard.q: Two paths reach 2% inflation. The rapid path has a deep one-year recession; the gradual path has smaller gaps for several years. What must be compared?
options: The price levels at the start, without output data
Their cumulative output losses and inflation reductions
Only the largest annual unemployment rate
Only the final year’s output level
hard.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
hard.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence best shows disinflation with temporary unemployment costs?
elite.commonError: Skipping the temporary move above natural unemployment.
elite.feedback: Disinflation lowers actual inflation first, moving to d, then expectations fall and the economy returns to c.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which policy lesson fits the move from b to d to c?
options: Expected inflation must rise after contraction
elite.commonError: Missing the temporary cost of disinflation.
elite.feedback: The move from b to d shows higher unemployment during disinflation; d to c shows expectations adjusting downward.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, the Fed credibly reduces money growth. Which path best shows disinflation with adjustment?
legendary.commonError: Skipping the short-run unemployment cost of disinflation.
legendary.feedback: Disinflation moves from b to d first, then expected inflation falls and the economy returns to c.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. The economy moves from b to d during disinflation. What must happen for it to reach c?
options: Expected inflation must fall enough to shift SRPC downward.
Expected inflation must rise enough to shift SRPC upward.
The natural rate must rise enough to shift LRPC right.
Actual inflation must rise above expected inflation again.
legendary.commonError: Missing the expectation adjustment needed after disinflation.
legendary.feedback: After contractionary policy, expected inflation must fall for the SRPC to shift downward and return unemployment to natural.

legendary.q: Country A has a sacrifice ratio of 2, while Country B has a sacrifice ratio of 5. If both reduce inflation by 3 percentage points, which comparison is correct?
options: A loses about 15% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 6%.
Both lose about 3% of annual GDP because the inflation reduction is equal.
A loses about 6% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 15%.
A has no output loss because its sacrifice ratio is below the inflation reduction.
legendary.commonError: Reversing the sacrifice ratios or treating equal inflation reductions as equal output costs.
legendary.feedback: Cumulative output loss equals the sacrifice ratio times the inflation reduction: 2 × 3 = 6 for A and 5 × 3 = 15 for B.

legendary.q: A credible central bank announces a lower inflation target, expected inflation falls partly, and policy still contracts demand. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: The downward SRPC shift may reduce but need not eliminate the short-run output cost
Credibility guarantees unemployment never rises during the contractionary adjustment
The LRPC shifts left because the announced target permanently lowers natural unemployment
Disinflation necessarily becomes deflation before expected inflation can decline
legendary.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
legendary.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendary.q: Inflation falls 3 points while cumulative output loss equals 6% of annual GDP. Unemployment later returns to natural. Which synthesis is correct?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 0.5, and unemployment stays permanently high
The ratio is 3, and LRPC shifts right permanently
The ratio is 6, and the price level must have fallen
The sacrifice ratio is 2, and the unemployment cost was temporary in the model
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendary.q: An adverse supply shock has raised inflation and unemployment. Why can disinflation policy face a harder near-term tradeoff than after a demand boom?
options: The LRPC becomes downward sloping during supply shocks
Contraction shifts the SRPC downward with no demand effect
Contraction can lower inflation pressure while worsening an already weak output position
Supply shocks automatically lower the sacrifice ratio to zero
legendary.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
legendary.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

boss.commonError: Ignoring the short-run unemployment cost of reducing inflation.
boss.q: What does contractionary monetary policy do on the short-run Phillips curve?
options: It lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run
It raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run
It lowers both inflation and unemployment immediately
It raises both inflation and unemployment immediately
boss.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy can reduce inflation, but it usually raises unemployment temporarily.

boss.commonError: Skipping the short-run move before expectations adjust.
boss.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at b, the Fed reduces inflation below expectations. Where does the economy move in the short run?
boss.feedback: Starting at b, lower actual inflation moves the economy to d: lower inflation and higher unemployment.

boss.q: Two central banks pursue the same reduction in inflation. One has strong credibility and expected inflation falls quickly. Compared with the less credible bank, what is the likely transition?
options: A permanently lower natural rate of unemployment.
A larger price-level increase caused by credibility.
A smaller temporary output and unemployment cost.
boss.commonError: Assuming credibility changes the long-run natural rate rather than the transition cost.
boss.feedback: Faster adjustment of expected inflation can reduce the sacrifice required to lower actual inflation.

boss.q: Inflation drops from 5% to 2% while prices still rise. What is occurring?
boss.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
boss.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

boss.q: Which policy direction normally lowers aggregate demand to pursue disinflation?
boss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
boss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

boss.q: What is the usual short-run Phillips cost of disinflation?
boss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
boss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

boss.q: A rapid plan loses 5% of annual GDP to cut inflation 2 points; a gradual plan loses 6% to cut it 3 points. Which has the lower sacrifice ratio?
options: The gradual plan has ratio 3 versus the rapid plan’s 2
The gradual plan has ratio 2 versus the rapid plan’s 2.5
The rapid plan has ratio 2 versus the gradual plan’s 3
Both plans have a sacrifice ratio of 2.5
boss.commonError: Compares total output losses without scaling each by its own inflation reduction.
boss.feedback: The rapid path ratio is 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5; the gradual path ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

boss.q: After contraction raises unemployment above natural, expected inflation falls. What long-run adjustment is expected?
options: SRPC shifts downward and unemployment returns toward natural
LRPC shifts right and locks in higher unemployment
SRPC shifts upward and inflation rises
boss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
boss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

boss.q: A trusted announcement lowers expected inflation. What is the relevant Phillips mechanism?
options: SRPC shifts upward because credibility raises the announced inflation target
Aggregate demand expands automatically without any change in policy instruments
SRPC can shift downward before all actual inflation adjustment occurs
LRPC shifts left and eliminates the natural rate before contracts reset
boss.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
boss.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendaryBoss.q: A central bank with mixed credibility begins rapid disinflation. Which full chain is most model-consistent?
options: Demand expands, unemployment falls, and inflation drops immediately without any wage, price, or expectations adjustment
LRPC shifts right permanently because lower inflation raises the natural unemployment rate
Expected inflation rises first and shifts SRPC upward before the contraction begins
Demand contracts, unemployment rises temporarily, expectations fall gradually, and output returns toward potential
legendaryBoss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

legendaryBoss.q: Policy A cuts inflation 4 points with 8% cumulative output loss. Policy B cuts 2.5 points with 4% loss. Which cost comparison is correct?
options: A has ratio 4; B has ratio 2.5, using final inflation as denominator
Both have ratio 2 because each lowers inflation from a positive starting rate
A has ratio 2; B has ratio 1.6, so B loses less output per point
A has ratio 0.5; B has ratio 0.625, so A has the lower cost
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: Inflation is down to 1% after disinflation, unemployment is back at natural, and the price level is higher than before. Which diagnosis is complete?
options: The price level should have returned to its starting value once unemployment normalized
Disinflation succeeded without requiring deflation; the short-run labor cost has unwound
Deflation occurred because the inflation rate fell even though prices remained higher
The natural rate must now be permanently lower because unemployment first increased
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

repairQuestions.q: Inflation falls from 5% to 2% but remains positive. Did the price level fall?
options: Yes; any inflation decline lowers prices
Yes; disinflation and deflation are identical
No; the price level stayed exactly fixed
repairQuestions.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.
repairQuestions.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.

repairQuestions.q: Contractionary disinflation raises unemployment in the short run. Is that necessarily permanent?
options: Yes; every contraction shifts LRPC right
Yes; the SRPC never shifts after policy
No; unemployment must fall below natural immediately
No; unemployment can return toward natural as expectations adjust
repairQuestions.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
repairQuestions.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Contractionary monetary policy reduces spending and inflation pressure. Which Phillips connection follows initially?
options: Movement toward higher unemployment and lower inflation along SRPC
A permanent LRPC shift to higher unemployment after expected inflation adjusts
Movement toward lower unemployment and lower inflation along the same curve
An upward SRPC shift caused by lower expected inflation during contraction
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation falls and the economy later returns to natural unemployment. Which family links explain the transition?
options: A permanent move along one SRPC only
An LRPC shift caused by the price level
A sacrifice-ratio shift of aggregate demand
A downward SRPC shift followed by long-run return to LRPC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.

bridgeQuestions.q: A policy team has computed cumulative output loss per inflation point. What applied question should that sacrifice ratio now inform?
options: How alternative disinflation paths trade speed against short-run cost
How to classify liquid assets between M1 and broader monetary aggregates
How to calculate nominal GDP from current prices and quantities
How to shift the production frontier through resource accumulation
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

sacrifice-ratio.title: Sacrifice Ratio
sacrifice-ratio.description: Calculate and interpret output losses associated with disinflation.

easy.q: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing:
easy.commonError: Confusing sacrifice ratio with unemployment rate.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures how much output is lost when inflation is reduced.

easy.q: Credible anti-inflation policy can reduce the sacrifice ratio by causing expected inflation to:
easy.commonError: Ignoring expectations in disinflation.
easy.feedback: If expected inflation falls faster, the short-run cost of disinflation can be smaller.

easy.q: What does a sacrifice ratio of 3 mean?
options: About 3% of one year’s output is lost per 1-percentage-point inflation reduction
The price level falls 3% during every disinflation
easy.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

easy.q: An analyst divides output loss by the final 4% inflation rate after inflation began at 7%. What denominator should replace 4%?
options: The initial 7% inflation rate before policy
The 11% sum of the two inflation rates
The final 4% inflation rate already used
easy.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
easy.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

easy.q: Which loss belongs in the usual sacrifice-ratio numerator?
options: The total fall in the price level
Cumulative output lost relative to potential during disinflation
The permanent increase in the unemployment rate
easy.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

easy.q: A disinflation has a lower sacrifice ratio than another. Under comparable measurement, what does that indicate?
options: A higher inflation target after policy ends
Less cumulative output loss per inflation point reduced
A larger fall in the price level
A permanently higher natural unemployment rate
easy.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

medium.q: If expected inflation falls quickly after a credible policy announcement, the sacrifice ratio is likely to be:
medium.commonError: Ignoring credibility and expectations.
medium.feedback: Faster adjustment of expected inflation reduces the output cost of disinflation.

medium.q: Cumulative output loss is 12% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls 3 percentage points. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 4% of one year’s output per inflation point
medium.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
medium.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

medium.q: A planned inflation reduction is 2.5 percentage points and the estimated sacrifice ratio is 3. What cumulative output loss is implied?
medium.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
medium.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

medium.q: The output gap is −1.5% in year one and −2.5% in year two while inflation falls 2 percentage points. Using the sum of annual gaps, what is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 2% of one year’s output per inflation point
medium.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
medium.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

medium.q: Inflation declines from 8% to 5%. Which calculation uses the correct denominator?
options: Final output divided by 13 percentage points
Cumulative output loss divided by 3 percentage points
Cumulative output loss divided by the final 5%
Cumulative output loss divided by the initial 8%
medium.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
medium.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

medium.q: Path A loses 6% of one year’s output to cut inflation 3 points. Path B loses 5% to cut inflation 2 points. Which has the lower sacrifice ratio?
options: Path A has a ratio of 2; Path B has a ratio of 2.5
Path B has a ratio of 2; Path A has a ratio of 2.5
Both paths have a sacrifice ratio of 2
Path A has a ratio of 3; Path B has a ratio of 2
medium.commonError: Compares total losses without dividing each by its own inflation-point reduction.
medium.feedback: Path A: 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Path B: 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5, so Path A has the lower sacrifice ratio.

hard.q: A credible disinflation lowers expected inflation before unemployment rises much. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
hard.commonError: Ignoring credibility in disinflation costs.
hard.feedback: Credibility lowers expected inflation faster and can reduce the output cost of disinflation.

hard.q: A student says disinflation has no cost if the Fed announces it. What is the correction?
options: Credibility can lower the cost, not guarantee zero cost
hard.commonError: Overstating credibility effects.
hard.feedback: Credibility can reduce the sacrifice ratio, but it does not automatically make disinflation costless.

hard.q: Potential GDP is $500 billion. Output is 2% below potential for one year and 1% below for two more years while inflation falls 4 points. What is the loss per inflation point?
hard.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
hard.feedback: The cumulative loss is $10 billion + $5 billion + $5 billion = $20 billion; $20 billion ÷ 4 = $5 billion per inflation point.

hard.q: A disinflation creates cumulative output loss equal to 9% of annual GDP. If the sacrifice ratio is 3, how far did inflation fall?
hard.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
hard.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

hard.q: Real GDP growth slows from 4% to 1%, but output remains above potential. Why can the 3-point growth slowdown not automatically be the sacrifice-ratio numerator?
options: Only the final inflation rate belongs in the numerator of this measure
The numerator measures an output-level loss relative to a benchmark, not merely slower growth
Any growth slowdown is exactly the cumulative output gap relative to potential
The numerator must be a permanent unemployment-rate change rather than output
hard.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
hard.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

hard.q: Cumulative output loss is 6.5% of one year’s GDP and inflation falls 3 percentage points. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.17% of one year’s output per inflation point
hard.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
hard.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

elite.q: The Fed announces disinflation, but workers doubt it and expected inflation stays high. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
elite.commonError: Assuming announcements alone make policy credible.
elite.feedback: If expected inflation does not fall quickly, reducing actual inflation tends to require more output loss.

elite.q: If inflation falls from 12 percent to 7 percent and the sacrifice ratio is 3.5, output loss equals:
elite.commonError: Adding the sacrifice ratio to the inflation reduction.
elite.feedback: Inflation falls by 5 points, so output loss is 3.5 x 5 = 17.5 percent of one year's output.

elite.q: If output loss is 14 percent and inflation falls by 4 percentage points, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 3.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
10% of one year’s output per inflation point
18% of one year’s output per inflation point
elite.commonError: Uses the inflation change or output loss alone rather than dividing cumulative loss by the percentage-point reduction.
elite.feedback: Divide the 14% cumulative output loss by the 4-percentage-point inflation reduction: 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5% of one year’s output per point.

elite.q: A disinflation plan is credible, wage contracts adjust quickly, and expected inflation falls fast. Which path is most likely?
options: Smaller unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
Larger unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
No change in expected inflation despite credibility
elite.commonError: Ignoring expectations in sacrifice-ratio logic.
elite.feedback: Credibility and fast expectation adjustment reduce the output and unemployment cost of lowering inflation.

elite.q: A disinflation plan lacks credibility, wage contracts are slow, and expected inflation remains high. Which path is most likely?
options: Larger output loss for the same inflation reduction
Smaller output loss for the same inflation reduction
elite.commonError: Assuming disinflation costs vanish without credibility.
elite.feedback: If expected inflation stays high, lowering actual inflation usually requires a larger output loss.

legendary.q: Inflation falls from 10 percent to 6 percent. Output loss is 18 percent of one year's GDP. What does the sacrifice ratio imply?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 4.5, showing a costly disinflation.
The sacrifice ratio is 2.5, showing a mild disinflation.
The sacrifice ratio is 16, showing no output cost.
The sacrifice ratio is 24, showing inflation rose.
legendary.commonError: Dividing by the wrong inflation change.
legendary.feedback: Inflation falls by 4 points, and 18/4 = 4.5.

legendary.q: A disinflation reduces inflation by 5 percentage points. The sacrifice ratio is 2.8. What output cost should be expected?
legendary.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
legendary.feedback: Output loss equals sacrifice ratio times inflation reduction, so 2.8 x 5 = 14 percent.

legendary.q: The Fed reduces inflation from 9 percent to 5 percent. Output loss equals 10 percent of one year's GDP. Which memo is strongest?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 2.5, so disinflation was costly but not extreme.
The sacrifice ratio is 4, so output loss was smaller than inflation reduction.
The sacrifice ratio is 14, so inflation increased during disinflation.
The sacrifice ratio is 0.4, so the policy had no output cost.
legendary.commonError: Using the ending inflation rate instead of the inflation reduction.
legendary.feedback: Inflation fell by 4 points, and 10/4 = 2.5.

legendary.q: The Federal Reserve reduces inflation by 6 percentage points. The sacrifice ratio is 1.75. What output loss should be expected?
legendary.commonError: Adding the inflation reduction and sacrifice ratio.
legendary.feedback: Output loss equals 1.75 x 6 = 10.5 percent of one year's output.

legendary.q: A three-year disinflation produces annual output gaps of −2%, −1%, and 0%, cutting inflation from 6.5% to 4.5%. A faster path produces one year at −4% and cuts inflation the same amount. Which comparison is correct?
options: The gradual path ratio is 3; the fast path ratio is 4
Both paths have a ratio of 2
The gradual path ratio is 2; the fast path ratio is 1.5
The gradual path ratio is 1.5; the fast path ratio is 2
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendary.q: Economy A loses 8% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls from 9% to 5%. Economy B loses 6% while inflation falls from 5% to 2%. What can be concluded?
options: A has a ratio of 0.5 and B has a ratio of 0.67
A has a lower ratio because its inflation drop is larger
A has a ratio of 2 and B also has a ratio of 2
A has a ratio of 4 and B has a ratio of 3
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

calculation.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 4 and inflation falls by 2 percentage points, the output cost is:
calculation.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
calculation.feedback: The output cost is 4 x 2 = 8 percent of one year's output.

calculation.q: Potential GDP is $400 billion. Cumulative output loss is $24 billion while inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 2% of one year’s output per inflation point
calculation.commonError: Divides the dollar loss directly by the inflation change without converting loss to a share of potential output.
calculation.feedback: The $24 billion loss is 6% of $400 billion. Inflation falls 3 percentage points, so the ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

calculation.q: If inflation falls by 3 points and the output loss is 12 percent of one year’s GDP, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 12% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
3% of one year’s output per inflation point
9% of one year’s output per inflation point
calculation.commonError: Uses the inflation reduction or cumulative output loss alone rather than dividing loss by points reduced.
calculation.feedback: Divide cumulative output loss by the inflation reduction: 12 ÷ 3 = 4% of one year’s output per inflation point.

calculation.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 3 and inflation falls from 8 percent to 5 percent, the output cost is:
calculation.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
calculation.feedback: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points, so output loss is 3 x 3 = 9 percent of one year's output.

boss.commonError: Confusing the sacrifice ratio with the inflation rate itself.
boss.q: What does the sacrifice ratio measure?
options: The output cost of reducing inflation
The unemployment rate at zero inflation
The tax increase needed to raise AD
boss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing inflation.

boss.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
boss.q: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points. If the sacrifice ratio is 4, what output loss should be expected?
boss.feedback: Output loss equals sacrifice ratio times inflation reduction, so 4 x 3 = 12 percent of one year's output.

boss.q: Which formula states the sacrifice ratio?
options: Price-level decline over the episode ÷ nominal GDP growth
Cumulative output loss ÷ inflation reduction in percentage points
Inflation reduction in points ÷ cumulative output loss relative to potential
Permanent unemployment increase ÷ the final positive inflation rate
boss.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
boss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

boss.q: Inflation falls from 6% to 4%. What is the denominator?
boss.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
boss.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

boss.q: A ratio of 2 is best read as what?
options: Inflation falls two percent for every percentage point of unemployment added
Unemployment stays two points above natural after expectations completely adjust
The price level declines two percent in each year of disinflation
Two percent of one year’s output lost per inflation point reduced
boss.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
boss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

boss.q: Annual output gaps are −1%, −2%, and −1%; inflation falls from 7% to 5%. What is the ratio?
options: 2% of one year’s output per inflation point
boss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
boss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

boss.q: A report divides cumulative output loss by the final inflation rate. What correction is required?
options: Divide by the percentage-point reduction in inflation
Divide by the initial inflation rate before the policy began
Multiply by the final inflation rate
boss.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
boss.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

boss.q: Path X loses 7.2% of annual GDP to reduce inflation 3 points. Path Y loses 5% to reduce inflation 2 points. Which is more output-efficient?
options: Path Y, with a ratio of 2 versus 2.4
Path X, with a ratio of 3 versus 2
They are equal because both lower inflation
Path X, with a ratio of 2.4 versus 2.5
boss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
boss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

boss.q: Loss is 10% of annual GDP and inflation falls 4 points. What is the ratio?
options: 2.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
boss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
boss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: A two-year policy creates output gaps of −2.4% and −1.8%, lowering inflation from 7.0% to 5.2%. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.33% of one year’s output per inflation point
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: A credible plan lowers expected inflation and produces a 3% cumulative output loss for a 2-point inflation reduction. A less credible plan loses 7.5% for a 3-point reduction. Which comparison is correct?
options: The plans are equal because both reduce inflation
The credible plan ratio is 1.5; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 2; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 0.67; the other is 0.4
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: Potential output is $800 billion. A policy creates gaps of 1.5% for two years and 0.5% for one year while inflation falls 2.8 points. What is cumulative loss per inflation point?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The cumulative loss is 3.5% of $800 billion = $28 billion. Dividing by 2.8 inflation points gives $10 billion per point.
legendaryBoss.roundingRule: Report the exact dollar amount per inflation point.

repairQuestions.q: Inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What number belongs in the sacrifice-ratio denominator?
repairQuestions.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.

repairQuestions.q: Should annual output gaps be added before calculating a multi-year sacrifice ratio?
options: No, only the worst year counts
No, only the final year counts
Yes, but add inflation rates too
Yes, to obtain cumulative output loss
repairQuestions.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
repairQuestions.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

repairQuestions.q: Does the sacrifice ratio normally measure an unemployment increase per inflation point?
options: Yes, but only when inflation stays positive
No, it measures the fall in the price level
No, it measures cumulative output loss per inflation point
Yes, unemployment is always the numerator
repairQuestions.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.

bridgeQuestions.q: The economy temporarily moves above natural unemployment during disinflation. How is this cost measured?
options: Sum the output losses and divide by the inflation-point reduction
Divide the unemployment increase by the final positive inflation rate
Treat the change in the price level as the cumulative output numerator
Shift LRPC right by the cumulative inflation reduction during policy
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation falls faster after a credible announcement. How can that connect to the sacrifice ratio?
options: A lower final inflation rate automatically raises the ratio even with unchanged loss
Credibility changes the denominator from inflation reduction to unemployment
The ratio must become zero in every credible disinflation plan
A smaller cumulative output loss can lower the measured ratio
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Two disinflation paths reach the same inflation target. Which family destination uses their sacrifice ratios to compare costs?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.

easy.q: Higher government spending usually shifts aggregate demand:
easy.commonError: Reversing expansionary fiscal policy.
easy.feedback: Higher government spending raises aggregate demand.

easy.q: A tax cut usually shifts aggregate demand:
easy.commonError: Confusing tax cuts and tax increases.
easy.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption, shifting AD right.

easy.q: Expansionary fiscal policy includes
options: higher government spending or lower taxes
lower government spending or higher taxes
a decrease in the money supply
easy.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy
easy.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy uses higher government spending or lower taxes to increase aggregate demand.

easy.q: Contractionary fiscal policy includes
options: lower government spending or higher taxes
higher government spending or lower taxes
a decrease in interest on reserves only
easy.commonError: confusing fiscal tightening with monetary tightening
easy.feedback: Contractionary fiscal policy means lower government spending or higher taxes, which reduces aggregate demand.

easy.q: An increase in government spending shifts aggregate demand
options: only downward along the same curve
not at all because G is not part of AD
easy.commonError: forgetting that G is a component of aggregate demand
easy.feedback: Government spending is part of aggregate demand, so an increase in G shifts AD right.

easy.q: A decrease in taxes usually shifts aggregate demand
options: nowhere because taxes are not related to spending
easy.commonError: thinking tax cuts reduce consumption
easy.feedback: Lower taxes raise disposable income, which can raise consumption and shift AD right.

easy.q: The multiplier effect means that government spending can shift AD by:
options: Less than the initial spending only
easy.commonError: Ignoring induced consumption.
easy.feedback: The multiplier effect occurs when initial spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

easy.q: Crowding out occurs when fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces:
easy.commonError: Missing the interest-rate channel.
easy.feedback: Crowding out reduces private investment when fiscal expansion raises interest rates.

easy.q: The multiplier effect occurs because an initial increase in spending
options: raises income and causes additional consumption spending
always raises interest rates enough to cancel itself completely
easy.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the first round of spending
easy.feedback: The multiplier effect happens because one person's spending becomes another person's income, causing additional consumption.

easy.q: The marginal propensity to consume is the fraction of extra income that households
easy.commonError: confusing MPC with the fraction saved
easy.feedback: MPC is the fraction of extra income that households consume rather than save.

easy.q: The simple spending multiplier is calculated as
easy.commonError: using MPC itself as the multiplier
easy.feedback: The simple spending multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

easy.q: Crowding out occurs when expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates and reduces
easy.commonError: thinking crowding out makes government spending disappear
easy.feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment spending.

easy.q: If the MPC is 0.75, the simple government purchases multiplier is:
easy.commonError: Using MPC as the multiplier.
easy.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so 1/(1-0.75)=4.

easy.q: If MPC = 0.8, then a $100 increase in income raises consumption by
easy.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
easy.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the income increase: 0.8 x $100 = $80.

easy.q: If MPC = 0.75, the simple spending multiplier equals
easy.commonError: dividing MPC by 1 instead of using 1 divided by 1 minus MPC
easy.feedback: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.

easy.q: A liquidity trap occurs when monetary policy has trouble stimulating AD because:
easy.commonError: Thinking monetary policy is always equally powerful.
easy.feedback: In a liquidity trap, nominal interest rates are near zero, making traditional monetary stimulus weaker.

easy.q: An automatic stabilizer is best described as:
options: A built-in response to the economy
easy.commonError: Confusing automatic stabilizers with discretionary policy.
easy.feedback: Automatic stabilizers, such as taxes and transfer payments, respond automatically as conditions change.

easy.q: Policy lags matter because stabilization policy may:
options: Arrive after conditions have already changed
Make money neutral in the short run
easy.commonError: Ignoring timing problems in stabilization policy.
easy.feedback: Policy can become destabilizing if it takes effect after the economy has already moved.

easy.q: A policy lag is a reason stabilization policy can be risky because policy actions may
options: take effect after conditions have already changed
remove the need for aggregate demand
make money supply impossible to change
easy.commonError: thinking stabilization policy works instantly
easy.feedback: Policy lags matter because by the time policy takes effect, the economy may have already changed.

easy.q: If a recession lowers aggregate demand, a stabilization policy response could be
options: lower government spending and lower money supply
higher taxes and higher interest rates
doing anything that shifts AD left
easy.commonError: choosing contractionary policy during weak demand
easy.feedback: If aggregate demand is too low, expansionary policy can help shift AD right.

easy.q: If aggregate demand is pushing output above its natural level and raising inflation pressure, policymakers might use
options: higher government spending and lower interest rates
only policies that shift AD right
easy.commonError: using expansionary policy when AD is already too strong
easy.feedback: When AD is too high and inflation pressure builds, contractionary policy can shift AD left.

easy.q: One argument in favor of stabilization policy is that it can help offset
easy.commonError: thinking stabilization policy is meant to eliminate scarcity
easy.feedback: Supporters argue stabilization policy can reduce the damage caused by short-run aggregate demand shocks.

easy.q: One argument against aggressive stabilization policy is that
options: policy lags can cause actions to hit the economy too late
monetary and fiscal policy always work instantly
easy.commonError: thinking policy timing is never a problem
easy.feedback: Critics warn that policy lags can make stabilization efforts arrive after the economy has already changed.

easy.q: If policymakers respond too late to a recession that has already recovered, expansionary policy may
easy.commonError: thinking late expansionary policy is harmless
easy.feedback: If expansionary policy arrives after recovery is underway, it can push aggregate demand too far and create inflation pressure.

easy.q: In the standard AD–AS convention, the vertical axis measures:
easy.commonError: Confusing output with the price level.
easy.feedback: The vertical axis in the AD-AS model measures the price level.

easy.q: In the standard AD–AS convention, the horizontal axis measures:
easy.commonError: Confusing the AD-AS axes.
easy.feedback: The horizontal axis in the AD-AS model measures real GDP or output.

easy.q: Which change shifts aggregate demand to the right?
easy.commonError: Confusing AD shifters with SRAS shifters.
easy.feedback: Higher consumer confidence increases consumption and shifts AD to the right.

easy.q: Which change shifts aggregate demand to the left?
easy.commonError: Thinking every policy shifts AD right.
easy.feedback: A tax increase reduces spending and shifts aggregate demand left.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from AD1 to AD2 represents:
easy.commonError: Reversing left and right shifts of AD.
easy.feedback: AD2 lies to the right of AD1, so the graph shows an increase in aggregate demand.

easy.q: A decrease in household wealth, holding other factors constant, shifts aggregate demand:
options: Not at all because wealth is not part of spending.
Up along the same AD curve.
easy.commonError: Confusing a spending shifter with a movement along AD.
easy.feedback: Lower wealth tends to reduce consumption, shifting aggregate demand left.

easy.q: What change from AD0 to AD1 is shown?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: A rightward shift of AD means aggregate demand has increased.

easy.q: How should AD1 be classified relative to AD0 in the second aggregate-demand diagram?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: A leftward shift of AD means aggregate demand has decreased.

easy.q: The short-run aggregate supply curve slopes upward mainly because:
options: Wages, prices, or perceptions do not adjust instantly
Money is neutral in every period
easy.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to the short run.
easy.feedback: SRAS slopes upward because sticky wages, sticky prices, and misperceptions allow price-level changes to affect output.

easy.q: A decrease in oil prices would most likely shift:
easy.commonError: Treating production cost changes as AD shifts.
easy.feedback: Lower production costs shift short-run aggregate supply to the right.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from AS2 to AS1 represents:
options: A decrease in short-run aggregate supply
An increase in short-run aggregate supply
easy.commonError: Reversing AS1 and AS2.
easy.feedback: AS1 is up and left of AS2, so moving from AS2 to AS1 is a decrease in SRAS.

easy.q: An increase in nominal wages, holding productivity and expected prices constant, shifts short-run aggregate supply:
options: Down along the same SRAS curve.
easy.commonError: Reversing the effect of higher production costs.
easy.feedback: Higher nominal wages raise firms’ costs and reduce output supplied at each price level.

easy.q: What change from AS0 to AS1 is shown?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: When the aggregate supply curve shifts left/up, less output is supplied at each price level, which is a decrease in aggregate supply.

easy.q: How should AS1 be classified relative to AS0 in the second aggregate-supply diagram?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: A downward/rightward shift of the AS curve means aggregate supply has increased.

easy.q: Which curve is vertical in the long run?
easy.commonError: Confusing SRAS and LRAS.
easy.feedback: LRAS is vertical because long-run output depends on resources, capital, technology, and institutions.

easy.q: A rise in economy-wide productivity shifts long-run aggregate supply:
options: Not at all because productivity affects only demand.
easy.commonError: Confusing productive capacity with aggregate demand.
easy.feedback: Higher productivity raises the economy’s sustainable level of output.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At AD1 and AS2, the economy is at:
easy.commonError: Reading the wrong intersection.
easy.feedback: AD1 and AS2 intersect at Y1 and P1.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At AD2 and AS2, the economy is at:
easy.commonError: Ignoring the curve labels.
easy.feedback: AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2 and P2.

easy.q: If the economy is below natural output, unemployment is usually:
easy.commonError: Missing the link between output and unemployment.
easy.feedback: When output is below potential, unemployment is usually above the natural rate.

easy.q: In the AD-AS-LRAS graph, which labeled point represents the original long-run equilibrium before aggregate demand increases?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: The original long-run equilibrium is where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 meet. That is point C.

easy.q: Which labeled point is the original long-run equilibrium in the graph with LRAS0 and LRAS1?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: Point A is where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 intersect.

easy.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Which output level is natural output?
easy.commonError: Confusing natural output with the highest output shown.
easy.feedback: Natural output is where LRAS is located, which is Y1.

easy.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Output level Y2 is:
easy.commonError: Ignoring LRAS when judging output gaps.
easy.feedback: Y2 is to the right of LRAS, so output is above natural output.

easy.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Output level Y3 is:
easy.commonError: Ignoring LRAS when judging output gaps.
easy.feedback: Y3 is to the left of LRAS, so output is below natural output.

easy.q: A recessionary gap means output is:
easy.commonError: Reversing recessionary and expansionary gaps.
easy.feedback: A recessionary gap occurs when output is below natural output.

easy.q: A sudden increase in oil prices is best treated as:
easy.commonError: Calling an oil shock a demand shock.
easy.feedback: Higher oil prices raise production costs and shift SRAS left.

easy.q: A negative demand shock usually causes which short-run outcome?
easy.commonError: Confusing demand shocks with supply shocks.
easy.feedback: A leftward AD shift lowers output and the price level in the short run.

easy.q: An adverse supply shock usually causes which short-run outcome?
easy.commonError: Thinking all recessions lower inflation.
easy.feedback: An adverse supply shock lowers output and raises the price level.

easy.q: Stagflation means:
easy.commonError: Treating stagflation as any recession.
easy.feedback: Stagflation is the combination of falling output and rising prices.

easy.q: In the AD-AS graph, which point shows the original equilibrium before aggregate demand rises?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: Point A is the intersection of AD0 and AS0.

easy.q: Which point marks the original equilibrium where AD0 and AS0 intersect?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: Point A is the initial intersection of AD0 and AS0.

easy.q: In the long run, an economy returns to natural output because:
easy.commonError: Thinking short-run gaps last forever.
easy.feedback: Over time, wages, prices, and expectations adjust, moving output back toward natural output.

easy.q: Real GDP is below potential and labor-market slack is putting downward pressure on nominal wage growth. If aggregate demand does not change again, which adjustment helps the economy self-correct?
options: SRAS shifts right as wage and production-cost pressures ease.
AD shifts right automatically because unemployment is high.
LRAS shifts left until it reaches the depressed output level.
SRAS shifts left because firms are producing below potential.
easy.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
easy.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

easy.q: The Phillips curve shows a short-run trade-off between:
easy.commonError: Confusing the Phillips curve with the money market.
easy.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

easy.q: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the vertical axis measures:
easy.commonError: Reversing the Phillips curve axes.
easy.feedback: The vertical axis measures the inflation rate.

easy.q: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the horizontal axis measures:
easy.commonError: Reversing the Phillips curve axes.
easy.feedback: The horizontal axis measures the unemployment rate.

easy.q: In the short run, expansionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
easy.commonError: Missing the short-run tradeoff.
easy.feedback: Expansionary policy raises inflation pressure and lowers unemployment in the short run.

easy.q: In the short run, contractionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
easy.commonError: Reversing contractionary policy effects.
easy.feedback: Contractionary policy lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Point a has:
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation than point c
Higher unemployment and lower inflation than point c
The same unemployment and lower inflation than point c
easy.commonError: Reading the Phillips curve axes backward.
easy.feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, while point c is at U2 and I1.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from point c to point a shows:
easy.commonError: Reversing movement along SRPC.
easy.feedback: Moving from c to a raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run.

easy.q: In the long run, unemployment returns to:
easy.commonError: Thinking policymakers can permanently hold unemployment below natural.
easy.feedback: The natural-rate hypothesis says unemployment returns to its natural rate in the long run.

easy.q: At point A, what is the unemployment rate?
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point A lies directly above 5 on the unemployment axis.

easy.q: Relative to point A, what does point B show on SRPC0?
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point B is left of A on the unemployment axis and above A on the inflation axis.

easy.q: How does point B compare with the natural-rate point A in the displayed Phillips-curve graph?
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point B is to the right of A on the unemployment axis and below A on the inflation axis.

easy.q: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at:
easy.commonError: Confusing SRPC with LRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Which unemployment rate is the natural rate?
easy.commonError: Ignoring the vertical LRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is drawn at U2, so U2 is the natural rate of unemployment.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At U3, SRPC2 has inflation rate:
easy.commonError: Reading the wrong curve at the same unemployment rate.
easy.feedback: At U3, the upper curve SRPC2 is at I4.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At U4 on SRPC1, inflation is:
easy.commonError: Reading the upper curve instead of SRPC1.
easy.feedback: The lower point at U4 on SRPC1 is at I1.

easy.q: Where is the long-run Phillips curve drawn?
options: Vertically at the natural rate of unemployment
Horizontally at the current inflation rate
Downward sloping through every short-run point
easy.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

easy.q: What does a vertical LRPC imply?
options: Inflation is fixed in the long run
The natural rate always equals zero
There is no permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff
easy.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
easy.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from point a to point b most likely shows:
easy.commonError: Thinking unemployment stays below natural permanently.
easy.feedback: After inflation expectations adjust upward, the SRPC shifts and unemployment returns to the natural rate at point b.

easy.q: If expected inflation rises, the short-run Phillips curve shifts:
easy.commonError: Reversing expected inflation shifts.
easy.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up and right.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. SRPC2 compared with SRPC1 represents:
options: A fall in money supply only
easy.commonError: Missing that the higher SRPC reflects worse inflation expectations.
easy.feedback: SRPC2 is above SRPC1, meaning higher expected inflation or a worse tradeoff.

easy.q: An adverse supply shock shifts the short-run Phillips curve:
easy.commonError: Treating supply shocks as movement along the same SRPC.
easy.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the tradeoff by shifting the SRPC up and right.

easy.q: A surge in oil prices can cause inflation and unemployment to:
easy.commonError: Thinking inflation and unemployment always move opposite ways.
easy.feedback: A negative supply shock can raise inflation and unemployment together.

easy.q: Compared with point A, what combination is shown at point B?
easy.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
easy.feedback: Point A is at 5 percent unemployment and 3 percent inflation, while point B is at 6 percent unemployment and 6 percent inflation.

easy.q: Workers and firms begin expecting higher inflation next year. Holding unemployment fixed, what happens to the short-run Phillips curve?
options: The economy moves down one unchanged curve
easy.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
easy.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

easy.q: If the Fed reduces money growth to fight inflation, unemployment usually:
easy.commonError: Ignoring the short-run cost of disinflation.
easy.feedback: Disinflation usually raises unemployment temporarily as the economy moves along the SRPC.

easy.q: Disinflation means that:
options: The overall price level is falling because average prices are declining.
Unemployment is falling even though output remains below potential.
Inflation is slowing, although the price level may still be rising.
Nominal wages are fixed while real wages rise automatically.
easy.commonError: Confusing disinflation with deflation.
easy.feedback: Disinflation is slower price growth; deflation is a falling price level.

easy.q: Why can a credible anti-inflation announcement reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
options: It permanently eliminates the natural rate of unemployment.
It guarantees that the price level falls immediately.
Expected inflation may adjust downward more quickly.
easy.commonError: Ignoring the role of expected inflation in the transition.
easy.feedback: When expectations fall sooner, wage and price setting can adjust with less output and unemployment loss.

easy.q: The sacrifice ratio measures the:
options: Cumulative output lost per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
The permanent unemployment rate created by a recession.
The price-level increase caused by one point of money growth.
The share of public spending financed by current taxes.
easy.commonError: Treating the sacrifice ratio as a permanent unemployment rate.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio summarizes the output cost of lowering inflation.

easy.q: Inflation slows from 6% to 3%, so the price level still rises more slowly. What is this?
options: A falling real interest rate by definition
easy.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
easy.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

easy.q: Which short-run effect commonly accompanies contractionary disinflation policy?
options: A permanently lower natural unemployment rate
An immediate rise in aggregate demand
easy.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
easy.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

easy.q: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing:
easy.commonError: Confusing sacrifice ratio with unemployment rate.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures how much output is lost when inflation is reduced.

easy.q: Credible anti-inflation policy can reduce the sacrifice ratio by causing expected inflation to:
easy.commonError: Ignoring expectations in disinflation.
easy.feedback: If expected inflation falls faster, the short-run cost of disinflation can be smaller.

easy.q: What does a sacrifice ratio of 3 mean?
options: About 3% of one year’s output is lost per 1-percentage-point inflation reduction
The price level falls 3% during every disinflation
easy.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

easy.q: An analyst divides output loss by the final 4% inflation rate after inflation began at 7%. What denominator should replace 4%?
options: The initial 7% inflation rate before policy
The 11% sum of the two inflation rates
The final 4% inflation rate already used
easy.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
easy.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

easy.q: Which loss belongs in the usual sacrifice-ratio numerator?
options: The total fall in the price level
Cumulative output lost relative to potential during disinflation
The permanent increase in the unemployment rate
easy.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

easy.q: A disinflation has a lower sacrifice ratio than another. Under comparable measurement, what does that indicate?
options: A higher inflation target after policy ends
Less cumulative output loss per inflation point reduced
A larger fall in the price level
A permanently higher natural unemployment rate
easy.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easy.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

easy.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 4 and inflation falls by 2 percentage points, the output cost is:
easy.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
easy.feedback: The output cost is 4 x 2 = 8 percent of one year's output.

medium.q: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Moving from AD1 to AD2 changes output from:
medium.commonError: Reading the graph backward.
medium.feedback: At the same price level, output rises from Y1 to Y2 when AD shifts from AD1 to AD2.

medium.q: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Which curve shows the largest aggregate demand level?
medium.commonError: Confusing curve position with label order.
medium.feedback: AD3 is farthest to the right, so it shows the largest AD at price level P.

medium.q: Which policy is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: Selling government bonds by the Fed
medium.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with Fed policy
medium.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy uses higher government spending or lower taxes to raise aggregate demand.

medium.q: Which policy is contractionary fiscal policy?
options: Buying government bonds by the Fed
medium.commonError: confusing fiscal and monetary policy tools
medium.feedback: Higher taxes are contractionary fiscal policy because they reduce disposable income and aggregate demand.

medium.q: A tax cut shifts aggregate demand right mainly because it
options: forces banks to hold more reserves
medium.commonError: thinking tax cuts work through bank reserves
medium.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.

medium.q: A cut in government purchases shifts aggregate demand left because
options: government spending is a component of aggregate demand
medium.commonError: forgetting that G is directly part of AD
medium.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD, so reducing G shifts AD left.

medium.q: If Congress increases infrastructure spending during a recession, the direct effect is to
medium.commonError: treating fiscal stimulus like contractionary policy
medium.feedback: Higher infrastructure spending raises G and shifts AD right.

medium.q: If the government raises taxes during an expansion, the likely AD effect is
medium.commonError: thinking tax increases raise consumption
medium.feedback: Higher taxes reduce disposable income and consumption, shifting AD left.

medium.q: If fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces investment, the final AD shift is likely:
options: Larger because crowding out amplifies it
Smaller because crowding out offsets it
Zero because fiscal policy cannot affect AD
medium.commonError: Thinking the multiplier is never offset.
medium.feedback: Crowding out weakens the final effect of fiscal expansion on AD.

medium.q: The multiplier effect exists because one person's spending becomes
options: a fall in money demand every time
medium.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the initial spending increase
medium.feedback: The multiplier works because spending becomes income, and some of that income gets spent again.

medium.q: The movement from the first AD shift to the larger final AD shift represents

medium.feedback: The multiplier effect is the extra AD shift caused by income leading to additional consumption spending.

medium.q: The initial shift in aggregate demand from higher government spending is followed by a larger shift because
options: higher income leads to additional consumption spending
interest rates always fall to zero
medium.commonError: thinking only the first round of government spending matters
medium.feedback: The first increase in spending raises income, which causes more consumption and a further AD shift.

medium.q: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion because higher government spending can raise interest rates and reduce
medium.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens fiscal stimulus
medium.feedback: Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise.

medium.q: Which situation would make the multiplier effect larger?
medium.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
medium.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, which makes the multiplier larger.

medium.q: Which situation would make fiscal stimulus less powerful?
options: A high MPC with no interest-rate effect
A large initial increase in government spending
A high willingness to consume extra income
medium.commonError: ignoring offsetting effects from interest rates

medium.q: If the government raises spending by $50 billion and the multiplier is 3, the first-pass AD increase before crowding out is:

medium.q: If MPC = 0.6 and income rises by $1,000, consumption rises by
medium.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
medium.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the change in income: 0.6 x $1,000 = $600.

medium.q: If MPC = 0.6, the simple spending multiplier is
medium.commonError: using MPC itself as the multiplier
medium.feedback: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.6) = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5.

medium.q: If MPC = 0.8 and government spending increases by $50 billion, the simple multiplier predicts a total AD increase of
medium.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
medium.feedback: With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5. Total increase is 5 x $50 billion = $250 billion.

medium.q: Which policy pair is expansionary for aggregate demand?
options: Higher taxes and lower money supply
Lower taxes and higher money supply
Higher reserve requirements and lower spending
medium.commonError: Mixing expansionary and contractionary tools.
medium.feedback: Lower taxes and higher money supply both tend to shift AD right.

medium.q: A recession begins, but Congress passes stimulus after the economy has already recovered. This illustrates:
medium.commonError: Ignoring timing problems.
medium.feedback: Policy lags can make stabilization arrive after conditions have changed.

medium.q: If the economy is in a liquidity trap, a traditional money-supply increase may fail because:
options: Interest rates cannot fall much further
medium.commonError: Thinking monetary policy works the same at zero rates.
medium.feedback: When rates are near zero, traditional monetary policy may not lower rates enough to boost spending.

medium.q: If a negative demand shock pushes output below its natural level, stabilization policy would most likely try to
medium.commonError: choosing contractionary policy during a demand slump
medium.feedback: A negative demand shock reduces output, so stabilization policy would typically try to shift AD right.

medium.q: If aggregate demand is too high and inflation pressure is building, stabilization policy would most likely try to
medium.commonError: stimulating AD when inflation pressure is already high
medium.feedback: If AD is too strong, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

medium.q: A key argument for active stabilization policy is that policymakers can
medium.commonError: thinking stabilization policy is meant to solve every economic problem
medium.feedback: Supporters argue that active policy can reduce the damage caused by short-run AD shocks.

medium.q: A key argument against aggressive stabilization policy is that
options: policy lags can cause poorly timed interventions
the Fed cannot affect interest rates
government spending is not part of aggregate demand
medium.commonError: thinking stabilization policy works instantly and perfectly
medium.feedback: Policy lags can cause interventions to arrive after conditions have already changed.

medium.q: If policymakers misread a temporary shock as a lasting recession, they risk
options: turning fiat money into commodity money
medium.commonError: thinking wrong policy timing has no cost
medium.feedback: If policymakers stimulate after the economy is already recovering, they may push AD too far.

medium.q: A pandemic reduces production and also weakens spending. Why is stabilization policy harder here than with a simple demand shock?
options: Because both supply and demand may be affected.
Because monetary policy cannot affect interest rates in any economy.
Because fiscal policy cannot affect aggregate demand.
Because money demand must be zero during pandemics.
medium.commonError: treating every downturn as only an aggregate demand problem
medium.feedback: A mixed shock is harder because policy may support demand, but it cannot instantly fix lost production capacity.

medium.q: A rise in the price level reduces consumption because money holdings buy less. This is the:
medium.commonError: Confusing the three reasons AD slopes downward.
medium.feedback: The wealth effect works through reduced real purchasing power of money holdings.

medium.q: A rise in the price level raises money demand and interest rates, reducing investment. This is the:
medium.commonError: Confusing AD slope effects with SRAS theories.
medium.feedback: The interest-rate effect explains how a higher price level reduces investment spending.

medium.q: If foreign incomes rise and foreigners buy more U.S. exports, U.S. aggregate demand should:
medium.commonError: Forgetting net exports are part of AD.
medium.feedback: Higher exports raise net exports and shift aggregate demand right.

medium.q: If firms become pessimistic and reduce investment spending, aggregate demand should:
medium.commonError: Treating investment changes as supply changes.
medium.feedback: Lower investment reduces total spending and shifts AD left.

medium.q: If a price-level increase raises money demand, the interest rate rises, and investment falls. This explains:
medium.commonError: Mixing the AD slope with policy shifts.
medium.feedback: This is the interest-rate effect behind the downward-sloping AD curve.
