medium.q: A lower domestic price level makes domestic goods relatively cheaper to foreign buyers. This supports the downward slope of AD through the:
medium.commonError: Confusing the three reasons aggregate demand slopes downward.
medium.feedback: A lower domestic price level can lower interest rates and the currency value, raising net exports.

medium.q: Assume SRAS is unchanged. Based on the AD shift shown, what happens to equilibrium real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Both real GDP and the price level increase
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: A rightward shift of AD raises spending pressure, so equilibrium output and the price level both rise in the short run.

medium.q: Which event is most consistent with the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: Higher planned spending by C, I, G, or NX
Higher input costs that reduce short-run aggregate supply
Lower productivity that reduces long-run aggregate supply
Higher wages that reduce short-run aggregate supply
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Aggregate demand shifts right when planned spending rises.

medium.q: Holding SRAS fixed, what short-run equilibrium pattern follows from the demand change in the second AD diagram?
options: Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: A leftward shift of AD lowers spending pressure, reducing equilibrium output and the price level in the short run.

medium.q: Which event best matches the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: A fall in input costs that raises short-run aggregate supply
A rise in productivity that raises long-run aggregate supply
A fall in planned consumption or investment spending
A rise in expected prices that shifts short-run aggregate supply
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Lower overall spending shifts aggregate demand left.

medium.q: Sticky-wage theory explains upward-sloping SRAS because unexpected price-level changes affect:
options: Real labor costs and firm production decisions
medium.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to short-run wages.
medium.feedback: When nominal wages are sticky, price-level changes alter real labor costs and production.

medium.q: If expected prices rise, short-run aggregate supply usually shifts:
medium.commonError: Reversing expected price effects on SRAS.
medium.feedback: Higher expected prices push wages and costs upward, shifting SRAS left.

medium.q: If workers and firms expect a higher price level before contracts are set, short-run aggregate supply tends to:
options: Remain fixed because expectations affect only AD.
medium.commonError: Reversing the expected-price effect.
medium.feedback: Higher expected prices tend to produce higher nominal wages and other input costs.

medium.q: A temporary payroll-tax reduction lowers firms’ labor costs. Holding other factors constant, SRAS shifts:
medium.commonError: Treating a production-cost change as an AD shifter.
medium.feedback: Lower per-worker cost raises short-run output supplied at each price level.

medium.q: Why can an unexpected rise in the price level increase output in the short run under sticky-wage theory?
options: Household wealth rises and shifts AD
Nominal wages immediately rise more than prices
Product prices rise before nominal wages fully adjust, lowering real labor cost.
medium.commonError: Confusing short-run wage rigidity with long-run capacity.
medium.feedback: With sticky wages, unexpected price increases can make production temporarily more profitable.

medium.q: Which event best matches the shift from AS0 to AS1?
options: Higher consumer confidence that boosts spending
A cut in income taxes that raises aggregate demand
A rise in input prices that makes production more costly
A fall in the overall price level causing a movement along AS0
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Higher production costs shift short-run aggregate supply left.

medium.q: If aggregate demand stays put, what equilibrium effect follows from the supply change in the second AS diagram?
options: Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: A rightward shift of AS increases output and lowers the price level.

medium.q: Which favorable production-side change could account for the shift displayed in the second AS diagram?
options: A fall in input costs or an improvement in productivity
An increase in government purchases that shifts AD right
A rise in inflation expectations that shifts SRAS left
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Lower costs or better productivity shift aggregate supply right.

medium.q: A hurricane destroys factories and transport infrastructure. Which long-run effect is most likely?
options: LRAS shifts left because productive capacity falls.
SRAS shifts right because inputs are scarcer.
LRAS shifts right because rebuilding spending rises.
medium.commonError: Focusing on reconstruction spending while ignoring lost capacity.
medium.feedback: Destroyed capital reduces the economy’s potential output.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD2-AS2, what happens?
options: Output rises and the price level rises
Output falls and the price level falls
Output rises and the price level falls
Output falls and the price level rises
medium.commonError: Reading only one axis after an AD shift.
medium.feedback: The economy moves from Y1-P1 to Y2-P2, so both output and the price level rise.

medium.q: After wages and expectations adjust, SRAS shifts from SRAS0 to SRAS1. Which point shows the new long-run equilibrium?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: The new long-run equilibrium occurs where AD1, SRAS1, and LRAS0 intersect: point B.

medium.q: Which labeled point is the new long-run equilibrium after the supply-side improvement?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Point B is where AD0, SRAS1, and LRAS1 intersect.

medium.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy is at Y2, the main short-run concern is:
options: The price level is below zero
medium.commonError: Ignoring LRAS when judging gaps.
medium.feedback: Y2 is to the right of LRAS, so output is above potential.

medium.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy is at Y3, unemployment is most likely:
medium.commonError: Missing the output-unemployment link.
medium.feedback: Y3 is below natural output, so unemployment is usually above the natural rate.

medium.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD2-AS2, the short-run result is:
medium.commonError: Treating any AD increase as long-run equilibrium.
medium.feedback: The move ends at Y2, which is above natural output, creating an expansionary gap.

medium.q: Assume aggregate demand is unchanged. Based on the AS shift shown, what happens to equilibrium real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: An inward/leftward AS shift reduces output and raises the price level.

medium.q: A recession caused by falling consumer confidence is most directly a:
medium.commonError: Calling lower spending a supply shock.
medium.feedback: Falling confidence reduces consumption and shifts AD left.

medium.q: An oil price spike causes output to fall and prices to rise. Which curve moved first?
medium.commonError: Treating stagflation as an AD shock.
medium.feedback: Higher oil prices raise production costs and shift SRAS left.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD1-AS1, what happens?
options: Output rises and price level falls
Output falls and price level rises
Output rises and price level rises
Output falls and price level falls
medium.commonError: Reading an SRAS left shift as lower prices.
medium.feedback: The economy moves from Y1-P1 to Y3-P2, so output falls and the price level rises.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. If AD rises from AD1 to AD2 while SRAS rises from AS1 to AS2, the final point is:
medium.commonError: Tracking only one curve shift.
medium.feedback: AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2 and P2.

medium.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD1-AS1, the short-run result is:
medium.commonError: Missing stagflation from an adverse supply shock.
medium.feedback: The move ends at Y3 and P2: lower output, higher prices, and unemployment pressure.

medium.q: Which policy would most directly offset a recessionary AD shock?
medium.commonError: Using contraction when AD is already weak.
medium.feedback: Expansionary policy can shift AD right to offset a recessionary demand shock.

medium.q: Which statement best describes an adverse supply shock policy problem?
options: Policy faces a tradeoff between inflation and output losses
Policy can lower inflation and unemployment immediately
Fiscal expansion shifts SRAS right automatically
Monetary contraction raises output and lowers inflation
medium.commonError: Thinking supply shocks have an easy policy fix.
medium.feedback: A negative supply shock raises prices and lowers output, creating a difficult stabilization tradeoff.

medium.q: If aggregate demand increases from AD0 to AD1 while SRAS0 is still fixed in the short run, which point shows the short-run equilibrium?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: With AD1 and SRAS0, the short-run equilibrium is point D.

medium.q: From point A to point B, what happens to real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP rises from 100 to 115 while the price level falls from 125 to 110
Real GDP falls from 115 to 100 while the price level rises from 110 to 125
Both real GDP and the price level rise
Both real GDP and the price level fall
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: The graph shows more long-run output and a lower price level at the new equilibrium.

medium.q: After aggregate demand shifts from AD0 to AD1 while AS0 is fixed, which point shows the new short-run equilibrium?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Point B is where AD1 intersects AS0.

medium.q: From point A to point B, by how much does real GDP increase?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Real GDP rises from 150 to 175, an increase of 25.

medium.q: If only aggregate demand increases from AD0 to AD1 while AS0 stays in place, which point shows the new equilibrium?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: With AD1 and AS0, the equilibrium is point B.

medium.q: If only aggregate supply decreases from AS0 to AS1 while AD0 stays in place, which point shows the new equilibrium?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: With AD0 and AS1, the equilibrium is point D.

medium.q: A boom in foreign economies raises net exports and pushes output above potential. In the long run, expected prices likely:
medium.commonError: Thinking output stays above potential forever.
medium.feedback: When output is above potential, pressures raise expected prices and shift SRAS left over time.

medium.q: A negative demand shock pushes output below potential. If policymakers do nothing, long-run adjustment likely involves:
options: Falling expected prices and SRAS shifting right
Rising expected prices and SRAS shifting left
medium.commonError: Missing self-correction through expectations.
medium.feedback: Below-potential output puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, shifting SRAS right.

medium.q: A temporary demand boom pushes production above potential. Policymakers do nothing, and wage contracts are gradually renegotiated as workers and firms revise price expectations upward. Which change is most consistent with self-correction?
options: Higher wages and input costs shift SRAS left while aggregate demand stays at its post-boom position.
Aggregate demand shifts left automatically as soon as wages rise.
LRAS shifts right because the economy briefly produced above potential.
SRAS shifts right because firms respond to the higher price level by cutting costs.
medium.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
medium.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

medium.q: The short-run Phillips curve slopes downward because higher AD tends to:
options: Raise output, lower unemployment, and raise inflation
Lower output, lower unemployment, and lower inflation
Raise unemployment while lowering inflation forever
medium.commonError: Missing the AD-to-unemployment channel.
medium.feedback: Higher AD raises output and prices, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation.

medium.q: Why is there no permanent Phillips-curve tradeoff?
options: Expectations adjust; unemployment returns to normal
AD stops affecting the short run
medium.commonError: Treating the short-run tradeoff as permanent.
medium.feedback: Once expectations adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point c, expansionary policy that raises inflation above expectations moves the economy to:
medium.commonError: Moving to the long-run point immediately.
medium.feedback: Expansionary policy moves the economy along SRPC1 from c to a: higher inflation and lower unemployment.

medium.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A move along SRPC1 from c toward b means:
medium.commonError: Reading movement along the curve backward.
medium.feedback: Moving up-left along SRPC1 raises inflation and lowers unemployment.

medium.q: At point A, what is the inflation rate?
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The horizontal guide through point A hits the inflation axis at 2.5 percent.

medium.q: How far below the natural rate is unemployment at point B?
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The natural rate is 5 percent at point A on the LRPC, while point B has 3 percent unemployment.

medium.q: What type of change is the move from A to B?
options: An upward shift from SRPC0 to another SRPC
A leftward shift of the LRPC
A movement along the same SRPC0
A movement along the vertical LRPC
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: Both A and B lie on the same SRPC0, so the graph shows a movement along the curve, not a curve shift.

medium.q: Point B is to the right of the LRPC. By how many percentage points does its unemployment rate exceed the natural rate?
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The natural rate is 5 percent at A, and point B is at 7 percent unemployment.

medium.q: Points A and B lie on the same short-run Phillips curve. How should the change from A to B be classified?
options: A movement along the same SRPC0
A downward shift from SRPC0 to another SRPC
A rightward shift of the LRPC
A movement along the vertical LRPC
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: A and B lie on the same SRPC0, so the graph shows a movement along the short-run curve.

medium.q: Aggregate demand rises unexpectedly while expected inflation is fixed. Which Phillips-curve change best represents the immediate effect?
options: A move up and left along the current SRPC
An upward shift of the SRPC at every unemployment rate
A rightward shift of the vertical LRPC
A move down and right along the current SRPC
medium.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
medium.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

medium.q: Inflation and unemployment both rise after a sharp increase in energy costs. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Aggregate demand causes movement up one unchanged SRPC
Lower expected inflation shifts the SRPC downward
The natural rate necessarily falls and shifts LRPC left
The adverse supply shock shifts the SRPC upward
medium.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
medium.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which pair of points are long-run equilibria?
medium.commonError: Treating all SRPC points as long-run equilibria.
medium.feedback: Points b and c lie on the vertical LRPC at U2.

medium.q: Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent while unemployment remains at its natural rate. Which long-run outcome fits the vertical Phillips curve?
options: Inflation is higher, but unemployment is unchanged at the natural rate.
Inflation is higher and unemployment is permanently lower.
Inflation is unchanged and unemployment falls to zero.
Both inflation and unemployment are permanently higher.
medium.commonError: Treating a higher expected inflation rate as a permanent way to lower unemployment.
medium.feedback: Along the long-run Phillips curve, different inflation rates can coexist with the same natural rate of unemployment.

medium.q: What natural rate of unemployment is shown by the LRPC?
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: The vertical LRPC is drawn at 5 percent unemployment, so that is the natural rate.

medium.q: If inflation rises while the economy remains on the LRPC, what happens to unemployment in this graph?
options: It becomes equal to the inflation rate
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: A vertical long-run Phillips curve means the long-run unemployment rate is pinned at the natural rate.

medium.q: Demand expansion temporarily pushes unemployment below natural. After expected inflation adjusts, where does unemployment tend to go?
options: To zero regardless of labor institutions
Above natural forever with no inflation change
Permanently farther below the natural rate
medium.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
medium.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

medium.q: Job-matching technology improves and lowers structural unemployment. What Phillips-curve change can follow?
options: The LRPC shifts left to a lower natural rate
The economy moves left along the same LRPC
The SRPC must shift upward at every point
medium.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
medium.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

medium.q: A rise in long-term mismatch raises the natural rate. What happens to the LRPC?
options: It stays fixed at the old natural rate
medium.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
medium.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

medium.q: Why can many inflation rates appear on the same vertical LRPC?
options: Inflation is unable to change nominal wages
Every point has zero expected inflation
Aggregate demand fixes the natural rate
Long-run unemployment equals natural after expectations adjust
medium.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
medium.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point a, expected inflation adjusts upward. The long-run movement is to:
medium.commonError: Keeping unemployment below natural forever.
medium.feedback: Expectations adjust upward, SRPC shifts up, and unemployment returns to U2 at point b.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Moving from d to c most likely reflects:
medium.commonError: Missing downward expectations adjustment.
medium.feedback: As expected inflation falls, the SRPC shifts downward and unemployment returns to U2 at point c.

medium.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Moving from SRPC1 to SRPC2 at the same unemployment rate means:
options: Inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate
Inflation is lower at the same unemployment rate
medium.commonError: Missing the upward SRPC shift.
medium.feedback: SRPC2 is above SRPC1, so inflation is higher for a given unemployment rate.

medium.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. If the economy moves from c on SRPC1 to the upper point at the same unemployment rate, the likely cause is:
options: A fall in actual inflation only
medium.commonError: Confusing a curve shift with movement along one curve.
medium.feedback: At the same unemployment rate, a higher SRPC reflects higher expected inflation or a worse tradeoff.

medium.q: An adverse supply shock affects the Phillips curve by:
options: Moving down along the same SRPC
medium.commonError: Treating supply shocks as normal AD movements.
medium.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

medium.q: If policymakers expand AD to reduce unemployment below the natural rate, what happens after expectations adjust?
options: Unemployment returns to natural and inflation stays higher
medium.commonError: Believing in a permanent policy tradeoff.
medium.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up, returning unemployment to natural at higher inflation.

medium.q: Suppose expected inflation rises while the natural rate is unchanged. Which curve change shown is consistent with that assumption?
options: SRPC0 shifts downward away from SRPC1
LRPC shifts left to a lower natural rate
The economy only moves along unchanged SRPC0
medium.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
medium.feedback: An upward shift of the short-run Phillips curve is the standard way to show higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock with the natural rate unchanged.

medium.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point b, contractionary policy that lowers inflation below expectations moves the economy in the short run to:
medium.commonError: Moving directly to lower expected inflation.
medium.feedback: Contractionary policy moves along SRPC2 from b to d: lower inflation and higher unemployment.

medium.q: If the Fed reduces money growth to lower inflation, the short-run Phillips curve predicts:
options: Lower inflation and temporarily higher unemployment
Lower inflation and lower unemployment immediately
medium.commonError: Ignoring the short-run unemployment cost.
medium.feedback: Disinflation usually moves the economy toward lower inflation and higher unemployment in the short run.

medium.q: A central bank reduces aggregate demand to lower inflation. What Phillips movement is expected before expectations adjust?
options: An upward SRPC shift from lower expected inflation
Down and right along the current SRPC
Up and left along the current SRPC
medium.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
medium.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

medium.q: Why can a credible lower-inflation target reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
options: It causes aggregate demand to expand during contraction
It may lower expected inflation and shift the SRPC downward sooner
It permanently lowers the natural rate by announcement
It guarantees wages and prices adjust instantly
medium.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
medium.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

medium.q: Inflation falls from 4% to 1%, but prices continue rising. Which statement is correct?
options: The economy has disinflation, not deflation
The economy has deflation because inflation fell
The price level must be below its initial level
The natural rate must have declined
medium.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
medium.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

medium.q: Why might gradual disinflation be chosen instead of a rapid contraction?
options: It always produces zero cumulative output loss
It guarantees expected inflation never changes
It can spread adjustment and reduce a severe short-run output gap
medium.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
medium.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

medium.q: If expected inflation falls quickly after a credible policy announcement, the sacrifice ratio is likely to be:
medium.commonError: Ignoring credibility and expectations.
medium.feedback: Faster adjustment of expected inflation reduces the output cost of disinflation.

medium.q: Cumulative output loss is 12% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls 3 percentage points. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 4% of one year’s output per inflation point
medium.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
medium.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

medium.q: A planned inflation reduction is 2.5 percentage points and the estimated sacrifice ratio is 3. What cumulative output loss is implied?
medium.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
medium.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

medium.q: The output gap is −1.5% in year one and −2.5% in year two while inflation falls 2 percentage points. Using the sum of annual gaps, what is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 2% of one year’s output per inflation point
medium.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
medium.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

medium.q: Inflation declines from 8% to 5%. Which calculation uses the correct denominator?
options: Final output divided by 13 percentage points
Cumulative output loss divided by 3 percentage points
Cumulative output loss divided by the final 5%
Cumulative output loss divided by the initial 8%
medium.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
medium.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

medium.q: Path A loses 6% of one year’s output to cut inflation 3 points. Path B loses 5% to cut inflation 2 points. Which has the lower sacrifice ratio?
options: Path A has a ratio of 2; Path B has a ratio of 2.5
Path B has a ratio of 2; Path A has a ratio of 2.5
Both paths have a sacrifice ratio of 2
Path A has a ratio of 3; Path B has a ratio of 2
medium.commonError: Compares total losses without dividing each by its own inflation-point reduction.
medium.feedback: Path A: 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Path B: 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5, so Path A has the lower sacrifice ratio.

medium.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 3 and inflation falls from 8 percent to 5 percent, the output cost is:
medium.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
medium.feedback: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points, so output loss is 3 x 3 = 9 percent of one year's output.

hard.q: Congress increases government purchases by $80 billion while households cut consumption by $50 billion for unrelated reasons. Before multiplier effects, the net direct change in aggregate demand is:
hard.commonError: Adding changes without respecting their directions.
hard.feedback: Government purchases add $80 billion while consumption subtracts $50 billion.

hard.q: A $120 billion tax rebate is issued and households spend 65 percent of the added disposable income initially. What is the first-round consumption increase?
hard.commonError: Using the MPS or the full tax cut as first-round consumption.
hard.feedback: First-round consumption is 0.65 × $120 billion = $78 billion.

hard.q: A government raises taxes and increases purchases by the same dollar amount. Which statement is most precise about the immediate AD effects?
options: The two actions must cancel exactly before behavior is considered.
Both actions shift AD right by the same amount.
Taxes enter AD directly as a negative component.
Purchases enter AD directly, while higher taxes reduce consumption indirectly.
hard.commonError: Treating taxes as a direct component of aggregate demand.
hard.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD; taxes work through disposable income and consumption.

hard.q: A temporary tax cut is mostly saved because households expect it to be reversed next year. Compared with a tax cut that is mostly spent, the AD shift is:
hard.commonError: Ignoring household spending behavior.
hard.feedback: A smaller consumption response weakens the tax cut’s effect on aggregate demand.

hard.q: The government cuts purchases during a recession but also cuts taxes. Which conclusion is valid without knowing the magnitudes and household response?
options: The two policies always cancel exactly.
The net direction of aggregate demand is ambiguous.
hard.commonError: Assuming one policy label determines the combined outcome.
hard.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left, while a tax cut tends to shift it right; magnitudes matter.

hard.q: A tax increase of $60 billion reduces consumption by $42 billion in the first round. The implied MPC is:
hard.commonError: Dividing in the wrong direction or using the MPS.
hard.feedback: MPC = $42 billion / $60 billion = 0.70.

hard.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
hard.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
hard.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is MPC times disposable income: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

hard.q: Refer to the AD multiplier graph. If government spending first shifts AD from AD1 to AD2, the multiplier effect is best shown by:
hard.commonError: Confusing the initial shift with the multiplied shift.
hard.feedback: The multiplier effect expands the initial AD shift farther right, from AD2 to AD3.

hard.q: Refer to the AD multiplier graph. If crowding out occurs after AD reaches AD3, the final AD position may move back toward:
hard.commonError: Thinking crowding out amplifies AD.
hard.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of fiscal expansion, pulling the final effect back from AD3 toward AD2.

hard.q: If the initial government spending increase shifts AD by $20 billion, why might the final shift be larger?
options: The spending raises income, which triggers additional consumption spending.
The spending lowers income, which reduces consumption.
The spending automatically reduces money supply.
The spending makes MPC equal zero.
hard.commonError: thinking only the first spending round matters
hard.feedback: The multiplier effect comes from income causing additional consumption, which pushes AD farther.

hard.q: If MPC is higher, the distance between the initial AD shift and the final AD shift should
hard.commonError: thinking a higher MPC weakens the multiplier
hard.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, so the final AD shift is larger.

hard.q: If expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates, which effect offsets part of the multiplier?
hard.commonError: confusing crowding out with the multiplier effect itself
hard.feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment, offsetting fiscal stimulus.

hard.q: Which fiscal policy has the strongest predicted multiplier effect before crowding out?
options: MPC = 0.9 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.5 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.25 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.1 and government spending rises by $50 billion
hard.commonError: thinking lower MPC creates a stronger multiplier
hard.feedback: Higher MPC means a larger multiplier. MPC = 0.9 gives the strongest multiplier here.

hard.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion, MPC is 0.75, and crowding out offsets $100 billion, final AD rises by:
hard.commonError: Ignoring crowding out after applying the multiplier.
hard.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so $80 billion x 4 = $320 billion; minus $100 billion gives $220 billion.

hard.q: If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, the government purchases multiplier changes from:
hard.commonError: Using MPC itself as the multiplier.
hard.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so it rises from 2 to 5.

hard.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the simple multiplier and total AD increase before crowding out?
hard.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
hard.feedback: Multiplier = 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4. Total AD increase = 4 x $80 billion = $320 billion.

hard.q: If MPC = 0.9 and government spending increases by $25 billion, what is the simple multiplier effect on AD before crowding out?
hard.commonError: using 0.9 as the multiplier instead of 10
hard.feedback: With MPC = 0.9, the multiplier is 10. AD increases by 10 x $25 billion = $250 billion.

hard.q: Suppose fiscal stimulus initially raises AD by $300 billion through the multiplier, but crowding out reduces investment by $80 billion. What is the net AD increase?
hard.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
hard.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the stimulus, so net AD rises by $300 billion - $80 billion = $220 billion.

hard.q: Congress cuts spending to reduce deficits during a recession. What policy concern is most direct?
options: AD may fall further before recovery
hard.commonError: Ignoring demand effects of spending cuts.
hard.feedback: Cutting spending during a recession can reduce AD further and deepen the downturn.

hard.q: If interest rates are near zero and output is below potential, why may monetary policy struggle?
options: Rates have little room to fall
hard.commonError: Treating monetary policy as equally strong at all rates.
hard.feedback: At near-zero nominal rates, standard rate-cut channels have little room to stimulate spending.

hard.q: A policy takes six months to pass and another year to affect spending. The main risk is:
options: The shock may reverse before policy hits
The money multiplier must equal zero
hard.commonError: Ignoring timing in stabilization policy.
hard.feedback: Inside and outside lags can make policy arrive after conditions have changed.

hard.q: Congress cuts government spending to reduce the deficit. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, what should it do?
options: Increase money supply to lower interest rates and support AD.
Decrease money supply to raise interest rates and reduce AD further.
Raise taxes to lower consumption further.
Do nothing because fiscal policy cannot affect AD.
hard.commonError: doubling down on contraction after AD falls
hard.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left. Expansionary monetary policy can partly offset that.

hard.q: A stock market boom increases household wealth and pushes output above its natural level. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, it should
options: reduce money supply and raise interest rates
increase money supply and lower interest rates
hard.commonError: using expansionary policy after a positive demand shock
hard.feedback: A positive AD shock can push output too high, so contractionary monetary policy can stabilize output.

hard.q: Which policy mix is most expansionary for aggregate demand?
options: Fed buys bonds and Congress increases government spending.
Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
Fed sells bonds and Congress cuts spending.
Fed raises interest rates and Congress raises taxes.
hard.commonError: mixing expansionary and contractionary tools
hard.feedback: Fed bond purchases are expansionary monetary policy, and higher government spending is expansionary fiscal policy.

hard.q: Which policy mix is most contractionary for aggregate demand?
options: Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
Fed buys bonds and Congress cuts taxes.
Fed buys bonds and Congress increases spending.
Fed lowers interest rates and Congress increases transfers.
hard.commonError: thinking bond sales are expansionary
hard.feedback: Fed bond sales reduce money supply, and tax increases reduce consumption. Both push AD left.

hard.q: Why can stabilization policy accidentally destabilize the economy?
options: Policy lags can make action arrive after conditions change.
Aggregate demand never responds to policy.
The Fed cannot change the money supply.
hard.commonError: thinking timing never matters
hard.feedback: Policy lags can make a policy hit after the original problem has faded, creating a new problem.

hard.q: A recession is already ending, but expansionary fiscal policy passed months earlier now takes effect. What is the risk?
options: AD may be pushed too far right, creating inflation pressure.
Interest rates must fall to zero forever.
hard.commonError: thinking late stimulus is always harmless
hard.feedback: Late stimulus can overstimulate demand after recovery is already underway.

hard.q: A supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why is the policy response harder than for a pure demand shock?
options: Stimulating AD may raise output somewhat but can worsen inflation.
Stimulating AD always lowers prices and raises output with no tradeoff.
Supply shocks only affect money demand.
hard.commonError: treating every downturn like a demand shock
hard.feedback: A supply shock creates a tradeoff: boosting aggregate demand may support output but can add inflation pressure.

hard.q: A negative AD shock reduces output and the price level. Which policy response best targets the shock without relying on supply-side repair?
options: Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy to shift AD right
Contractionary policy to shift AD left
Higher taxes and lower government spending
A policy that reduces investment spending
hard.commonError: using contractionary policy against weak demand
hard.feedback: A negative AD shock calls for policies that shift AD right if the goal is stabilizing output.

hard.q: An economy is above potential output because AD is too high. Which response best reduces the boom without increasing AD further?
options: Contractionary monetary policy or contractionary fiscal policy
Expansionary monetary policy and tax cuts
Higher government spending and lower interest rates
hard.commonError: stimulating an economy that is already overheating
hard.feedback: When AD is too high, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

hard.q: Consumer confidence rises while firms become more pessimistic about future sales. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
options: The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the sizes of the consumption and investment changes.
The economy moves down along the same AD curve
hard.commonError: Letting one shifter determine the combined result.
hard.feedback: Confidence raises consumption, while pessimism lowers investment; magnitudes determine the net shift.

hard.q: The price level falls, but taxes rise at the same time. Which statement is most precise?
options: Both changes cause movement along AD.
The price-level change shifts AD right and the tax increase shifts AD left.
The price-level change causes movement along AD, while the tax increase shifts AD left.
hard.commonError: Confusing a change in the price level with a nonprice AD shifter.
hard.feedback: The price level is on the graph’s vertical axis; taxes are an external shifter.

hard.q: Foreign income falls sharply while domestic firms increase investment. The effect on domestic aggregate demand is:
options: Ambiguous because net exports fall while investment rises.
hard.commonError: Ignoring offsetting components of aggregate demand.
hard.feedback: Lower foreign income reduces exports, while higher investment raises AD.

hard.q: A higher price level increases money demand, which raises interest rates and reduces investment. This sequence explains:
options: A movement upward and leftward along the existing AD curve.
hard.commonError: Treating the interest-rate effect as a shift of AD.
hard.feedback: The interest-rate effect is one reason quantity of real GDP demanded falls as the price level rises.

hard.q: A depreciation of the domestic currency occurs for reasons unrelated to the domestic price level. Holding other factors constant, aggregate demand shifts:
options: Left because domestic goods become more expensive to foreigners.
Right because exports rise and imports fall.
Nowhere because exchange rates matter only along AD.
hard.commonError: Reversing the net-export effect of currency depreciation.
hard.feedback: A weaker domestic currency tends to raise net exports and aggregate demand.

hard.q: A rise in the price level reduces the real value of household money balances. The immediate AD implication is:
options: Higher net exports and a rightward AD shift.
Higher consumption and a rightward AD shift.
Lower consumption and a movement upward along AD.
Lower investment and a leftward SRAS shift.
hard.commonError: Confusing the wealth effect with an AD shifter.
hard.feedback: The wealth effect reduces quantity of output demanded as the price level rises.

hard.q: At a price level of 50, by how much does real GDP demanded differ between AD0 and AD1?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: At price level 50, the quantity of output demanded rises from 100 to 150, an increase of 50.

hard.q: Use the second AD graph at price level 45. What horizontal GDP gap separates AD0 and AD1?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: At price level 45, quantity demanded falls from 150 to 100, a decrease of 50.

hard.q: Oil prices rise sharply, but firms also adopt a productivity-enhancing technology. What can be concluded about SRAS?
options: The net shift is ambiguous because costs rise while productivity improves.
hard.commonError: Allowing one supply shifter to dominate without magnitude information.
hard.feedback: Higher oil costs push SRAS left, while higher productivity pushes it right.

hard.q: Expected prices rise by 4 percent, but nominal wages are locked in long-term contracts. Compared with a setting where wages adjust immediately, the leftward SRAS shift is likely:
hard.commonError: Ignoring the mechanism through which expectations affect costs.
hard.feedback: If wages cannot yet adjust, expected-price changes have a weaker immediate cost effect.

hard.q: The price level rises unexpectedly while nominal wages are fixed. In the short run, firms tend to:
options: Increase production because output prices rise relative to wage costs.
Leave output unchanged because SRAS is vertical
Reduce production because real wages rise
hard.commonError: Reversing the real-wage effect.
hard.feedback: Unexpectedly higher output prices lower the real cost of contracted wages.

hard.q: A government permanently improves transportation infrastructure but finances it with a temporary business-energy surcharge. Which supply effects are possible?
options: LRAS may shift right while SRAS shifts left temporarily.
Both LRAS and SRAS must shift left permanently.
LRAS must remain fixed because taxes are involved.
hard.commonError: Treating all policy effects as demand-side or same-direction.
hard.feedback: Infrastructure can raise capacity while the temporary surcharge raises current production costs.

hard.q: Firms revise expected prices downward after a period of unexpectedly low inflation. Holding actual prices fixed, SRAS tends to:
options: Move upward along the same curve.
hard.commonError: Reversing how lower expected prices affect wage and cost setting.
hard.feedback: Lower expected prices tend to reduce nominal wage and input-cost growth.

hard.q: At real GDP of 150, what is the vertical price-level gap between AS0 and AS1?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: At the same output level, the price level increases from 150 to 190, a rise of 40.

hard.q: Use the second AS graph at real GDP 150. What vertical price-level distance separates AS0 and AS1?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: At the same output level, price level falls from 150 to 110, a decrease of 40.

hard.q: Which event best matches the joint shift from SRAS0/LRAS0 to SRAS1/LRAS1?
options: A confidence drop that lowers consumer and investment spending
A productivity gain that lowers costs and raises potential output
An energy-price increase that raises costs and lowers output
A government-spending increase that shifts aggregate demand right
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: A positive supply-side change can shift both SRAS right and LRAS right.

hard.q: A productivity improvement lowers production costs and raises potential output over time. Which curves are most likely affected?
hard.commonError: Treating productivity only as demand.
hard.feedback: Higher productivity can shift SRAS right and increase long-run aggregate supply.

hard.q: A permanent increase in the labor force raises potential output, while a temporary surge in energy prices raises costs. Which combination is most likely?
options: LRAS shifts right and SRAS shifts left.
LRAS shifts left and SRAS shifts right.
hard.commonError: Combining long-run capacity and short-run cost changes incorrectly.
hard.feedback: More labor raises capacity; higher energy prices reduce short-run supply.

hard.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy starts at AD1-AS2 and AD shifts to AD2, what gap appears?
hard.commonError: Ignoring LRAS after an AD shift.
hard.feedback: The economy moves to Y2, which is above natural output, so it creates an expansionary gap.

hard.q: A hurricane permanently destroys part of an economy's productive capital, and real GDP falls below its old potential level. Why would it be wrong to assume ordinary recessionary-gap self-correction must restore the old level of output?
options: The loss of productive capital can shift LRAS left, so the economy's new potential output may be lower.
Any fall in real GDP forces aggregate demand to shift permanently left.
Nominal wages cannot adjust after a supply-side disturbance.
SRAS always shifts right enough to restore the pre-shock LRAS position.
hard.commonError: Assumes every fall in real GDP is a temporary gap around an unchanged potential-output level.
hard.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy moves from AD1-AS1 to AD1-AS2, what happens?
hard.commonError: Reading a positive SRAS shift backward.
hard.feedback: Moving from AS1 to AS2 along AD1 raises output from Y3 to Y1 and lowers the price level from P2 to P1.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy starts at AD1-AS2 and both AD and SRAS increase, where does it end?
hard.commonError: Tracking only one curve shift.
hard.feedback: AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2 and P2.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS1, which change gets the economy to Y2 and P2?
hard.commonError: Forgetting both curves must change.
hard.feedback: Starting from AD1-AS1 at Y3-P2, moving to AD2-AS2 requires AD to rise and SRAS to rise.

hard.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, an adverse supply shock moves the economy to:
hard.commonError: Treating a supply shock as an AD shift.
hard.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts SRAS from AS2 to AS1, moving the economy to Y3 and P2.

hard.q: A tax hike reduces consumption and output falls below natural output. Which graph movement fits best?
options: AD shifts left, creating a recessionary gap
AD shifts right, creating an expansionary gap
hard.commonError: Confusing fiscal demand effects with supply shocks.
hard.feedback: A tax hike reduces aggregate demand and can create a recessionary gap.

hard.q: An economy faces higher oil prices and falling output. Why is aggressive AD stimulus risky?
options: It may restore output but add inflation pressure
It must lower prices and raise unemployment
It shifts SRAS right without cost
hard.commonError: Thinking supply-shock policy has no tradeoff.
hard.feedback: Stimulating AD can support output but may worsen inflation after an adverse supply shock.

hard.q: Which shock produces higher prices and lower output without first changing AD?
hard.commonError: Treating stagflation as a demand shock.
hard.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts SRAS left, raising prices and lowering output.

hard.q: Which sequence correctly traces the economy after an increase in aggregate demand starting from the original long-run equilibrium?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: The economy begins at C, moves to D in the short run when AD increases, and returns to long-run output at B after SRAS shifts left.

hard.q: From point A to point B, by how much does the price level increase?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: The price level rises from 125 to 137.5, an increase of 12.5.

hard.q: If aggregate demand increases from AD0 to AD1 at the same time aggregate supply decreases from AS0 to AS1, which point shows the resulting equilibrium?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: The simultaneous changes place the economy at the intersection of AD1 and AS1, which is point C.

hard.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, long-run self-correction most likely shifts:
hard.commonError: Missing expected price adjustment after an expansionary gap.
hard.feedback: At Y2 output is above potential, so rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left.

hard.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, long-run self-correction most likely shifts:
hard.commonError: Missing expected price adjustment after a recessionary gap.
hard.feedback: At Y3 output is below potential, so wages and expected prices tend to fall, shifting SRAS right.

hard.q: A negative AD shock lowers output and prices. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
hard.commonError: Thinking recessionary gaps cannot self-correct.
hard.feedback: Lower wages and expected prices shift SRAS right and help output return to natural.

hard.q: A positive AD shock pushes output above potential. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
hard.commonError: Thinking booms above potential persist forever.
hard.feedback: Higher wages and expected prices shift SRAS left and return output to potential.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which point reflects unemployment below the natural rate with inflation above I1?
hard.commonError: Ignoring the LRPC natural rate.
hard.feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, so unemployment is below the natural rate U2 and inflation is above I1.

hard.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Moving from b to c along SRPC1 means:
hard.commonError: Reading movement along SRPC backward.
hard.feedback: Moving down-right along SRPC1 lowers inflation and raises unemployment.

hard.q: A policymaker claims higher inflation can permanently hold unemployment below natural. What is the flaw?
hard.commonError: Believing in a permanent Phillips curve menu.
hard.feedback: Once expected inflation adjusts, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

hard.q: Which event moves along SRPC rather than shifting SRPC?
hard.commonError: Confusing movement along SRPC with shifts of SRPC.
hard.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion moves the economy along the existing SRPC in the short run.

hard.q: Which answer best separates short-run and long-run Phillips curve logic?
options: Policy can move unemployment temporarily, but expectations restore the natural rate
Policy cannot affect unemployment even briefly, because money is neutral in every period
Policy permanently lowers unemployment whenever inflation rises above zero
Policy shifts LRPC whenever actual inflation changes
hard.commonError: Confusing short-run effects with long-run neutrality.
hard.feedback: Demand policy can move unemployment in the short run, but expectations adjust and unemployment returns to natural.

hard.q: Moving leftward along SRPC0 from point A implies which short-run relationship?
options: No change in unemployment as inflation changes
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: A downward-sloping SRPC shows an inverse short-run relationship: less unemployment comes with more inflation.

hard.q: At point B, how do unemployment and inflation compare with the natural-rate point A?
options: Unemployment is higher; inflation is lower
Unemployment is lower; inflation is lower
Unemployment is higher; inflation is higher
Unemployment is lower; inflation is higher
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: Point B combines a higher inflation rate with unemployment below the 5-percent natural rate.

hard.q: At the right-hand point B, which inflation-unemployment comparison with A is correct?
options: Unemployment is lower; inflation is higher
Unemployment is higher; inflation is lower
Unemployment is higher; inflation is higher
Unemployment is lower; inflation is lower
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: Point B has 1.5 percent inflation instead of 2.5 percent, and unemployment is above the 5-percent natural rate.

hard.q: Two years have the same unemployment rate, but inflation is higher in the second after wage setters revise expected inflation upward. What changed?
options: Aggregate demand alone fixed both outcomes
The economy is on a higher SRPC
The economy moved up one unchanged SRPC
hard.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
hard.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which point reflects high inflation with unemployment at the natural rate?
hard.commonError: Confusing short-run and long-run points.
hard.feedback: Point b lies on the LRPC at U2 and inflation I2.

hard.q: If actual inflation equals expected inflation, the Phillips curve equation implies unemployment is:
hard.commonError: Missing the role of inflation surprises.
hard.feedback: With no inflation surprise, unemployment equals the natural rate.

hard.q: Which event is most likely to shift the LRPC right?
hard.commonError: Confusing inflation changes with natural-rate changes.
hard.feedback: The LRPC shifts when the natural rate of unemployment changes.

hard.q: Which event is most likely to shift the LRPC left?
hard.commonError: Treating expected inflation as a natural-rate change.
hard.feedback: Better labor-market matching can lower the natural rate and shift the LRPC left.

hard.q: Inflation rises permanently after repeated demand expansion, but labor-market structure is unchanged. Which long-run statement is strongest?
options: Unemployment remains permanently below natural after expectations fully adjust
The LRPC shifts right because the price level rose over time
Unemployment returns toward the same natural rate on an unchanged LRPC
The LRPC shifts left because higher inflation permanently improves job matching
hard.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
hard.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

hard.q: The natural rate falls because job search becomes faster. How should SRPC and LRPC reasoning be separated?
options: LRPC stays fixed while unemployment permanently departs from its vertical location
LRPC shifts left; short-run curves may also reposition around the new natural rate
The economy merely moves upward along the old LRPC as inflation changes
Only inflation expectations can shift LRPC in the long-run model
hard.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
hard.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, which sequence matches expansionary policy and expectations adjustment?
hard.commonError: Skipping the short-run movement along SRPC.
hard.feedback: Expansion moves from c to a in the short run; expected inflation rises and moves the economy to b.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which movement shows expectations falling after contractionary policy?
hard.commonError: Reversing expectation shifts.
hard.feedback: Moving from d to c reflects lower expected inflation and return to the natural unemployment rate.

hard.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At U3, moving from SRPC1 to SRPC2 changes inflation from:
hard.commonError: Reading the wrong inflation level at U3.
hard.feedback: At U3, the lower curve is at I2 and the upper curve is at I4.

hard.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, the move from SRPC1 to SRPC2 implies unemployment is:
hard.commonError: Missing worse tradeoff at the same inflation rate.
hard.feedback: At a given inflation rate, the higher SRPC implies a higher unemployment rate.

hard.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A shift from SRPC1 to SRPC2 is most consistent with:
options: Higher expected inflation or adverse supply shock
Lower expected inflation or favorable supply shock
Higher money supply with expectations fixed
Lower unemployment at every inflation rate
hard.commonError: Treating SRPC shifts as ordinary movement along a curve.
hard.feedback: The upward SRPC shift reflects higher expected inflation or a worsened supply-side tradeoff.

hard.q: If the Fed unexpectedly increases inflation while expected inflation is fixed, unemployment moves:
hard.commonError: Ignoring the gap between actual and expected inflation.
hard.feedback: When actual inflation exceeds expected inflation, unemployment can temporarily fall below the natural rate.

hard.q: Which event shifts both SRAS left and SRPC up-right?
hard.commonError: Confusing supply shocks with AD shocks.
hard.feedback: An oil price surge raises production costs and worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

hard.q: If expected inflation rises but actual inflation does not rise with it, unemployment tends to:
hard.commonError: Ignoring expected inflation in the Phillips curve equation.
hard.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts SRPC up, so unchanged actual inflation corresponds to higher unemployment.

hard.q: If expected inflation falls while actual inflation is held steady, unemployment tends to:
hard.commonError: Reversing the effect of lower expected inflation.
hard.feedback: Lower expected inflation shifts SRPC down, so the same actual inflation can mean lower unemployment.

hard.q: A student says an oil shock causes only movement along the SRPC. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC because costs and prices change directly
It shifts only AD because spending changes directly
It shifts only LRPC because inflation changes
It moves only along LRAS because output changes
hard.commonError: Treating supply shocks as AD movements.
hard.feedback: A supply shock shifts the SRPC because it directly changes firms' costs and inflation pressure.

hard.q: A student says higher expected inflation lowers unemployment permanently. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC upward and worsens the short-run tradeoff
It shifts LRPC left and improves the long-run tradeoff
It shifts AD right and lowers prices
It raises money demand and lowers rates
hard.commonError: Treating expected inflation as beneficial stimulus.
hard.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward, giving higher inflation at each unemployment rate.

hard.q: At a given unemployment rate, how does SRPC1 compare with SRPC0?
options: SRPC1 shows a lower inflation rate
SRPC1 shows the same inflation rate
SRPC1 shows a lower natural rate
SRPC1 shows a higher inflation rate
hard.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
hard.feedback: Point B lies on a different short-run Phillips curve, SRPC1, so the graph is showing a curve shift rather than a movement along SRPC0.

hard.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence matches disinflation and expectations adjustment?
hard.commonError: Skipping the temporary unemployment cost.
hard.feedback: Disinflation moves from b to d in the short run; expected inflation falls and the economy moves to c.

hard.q: If actual inflation is less than expected inflation, unemployment is likely:
hard.commonError: Reversing the effect of unexpectedly low inflation.
hard.feedback: When actual inflation is below expected inflation, unemployment tends to rise above the natural rate.

hard.q: A policymaker wants lower inflation but ignores unemployment during transition. What model warns about this cost?
hard.commonError: Ignoring short-run disinflation costs.
hard.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that reducing inflation can temporarily raise unemployment.

hard.q: A central bank announces a gradual disinflation, but households and firms doubt that the plan will continue. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The natural unemployment rate immediately falls to zero.
High expected inflation can prolong the output and job losses.
The price level must begin falling throughout the adjustment.
Unemployment cannot rise because the disinflation is gradual.
hard.commonError: Assuming gradualism automatically produces low transition costs.
hard.feedback: If the plan lacks credibility, expected inflation can adjust slowly and make the disinflation more costly.

hard.q: A disinflation announcement is not credible, and wage contracts embed 6% inflation. What makes immediate costless adjustment unlikely?
options: Deflation is required before unemployment changes
Expected inflation and nominal contracts may adjust slowly
The LRPC must shift left before policy begins
hard.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
hard.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

hard.q: Two paths reach 2% inflation. The rapid path has a deep one-year recession; the gradual path has smaller gaps for several years. What must be compared?
options: The price levels at the start, without output data
Their cumulative output losses and inflation reductions
Only the largest annual unemployment rate
Only the final year’s output level
hard.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
hard.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

hard.q: A credible disinflation lowers expected inflation before unemployment rises much. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
hard.commonError: Ignoring credibility in disinflation costs.
hard.feedback: Credibility lowers expected inflation faster and can reduce the output cost of disinflation.

hard.q: A student says disinflation has no cost if the Fed announces it. What is the correction?
options: Credibility can lower the cost, not guarantee zero cost
hard.commonError: Overstating credibility effects.
hard.feedback: Credibility can reduce the sacrifice ratio, but it does not automatically make disinflation costless.

hard.q: Potential GDP is $500 billion. Output is 2% below potential for one year and 1% below for two more years while inflation falls 4 points. What is the loss per inflation point?
hard.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
hard.feedback: The cumulative loss is $10 billion + $5 billion + $5 billion = $20 billion; $20 billion ÷ 4 = $5 billion per inflation point.

hard.q: A disinflation creates cumulative output loss equal to 9% of annual GDP. If the sacrifice ratio is 3, how far did inflation fall?
hard.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
hard.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

hard.q: Real GDP growth slows from 4% to 1%, but output remains above potential. Why can the 3-point growth slowdown not automatically be the sacrifice-ratio numerator?
options: Only the final inflation rate belongs in the numerator of this measure
The numerator measures an output-level loss relative to a benchmark, not merely slower growth
Any growth slowdown is exactly the cumulative output gap relative to potential
The numerator must be a permanent unemployment-rate change rather than output
hard.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
hard.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

hard.q: Cumulative output loss is 6.5% of one year’s GDP and inflation falls 3 percentage points. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.17% of one year’s output per inflation point
hard.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
hard.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

hard.q: Potential GDP is $400 billion. Cumulative output loss is $24 billion while inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 2% of one year’s output per inflation point
hard.commonError: Divides the dollar loss directly by the inflation change without converting loss to a share of potential output.
hard.feedback: The $24 billion loss is 6% of $400 billion. Inflation falls 3 percentage points, so the ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

hard.q: If inflation falls by 3 points and the output loss is 12 percent of one year’s GDP, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 12% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
3% of one year’s output per inflation point
9% of one year’s output per inflation point
hard.commonError: Uses the inflation reduction or cumulative output loss alone rather than dividing loss by points reduced.
hard.feedback: Divide cumulative output loss by the inflation reduction: 12 ÷ 3 = 4% of one year’s output per inflation point.

elite.q: A tax cut occurs while households expect future taxes to rise and save much of the extra income. What happens to the tax multiplier?
options: It is weaker than simple models predict
It shifts SRAS instead of AD
elite.commonError: Assuming every tax cut creates the same consumption response.
elite.feedback: If households save much of the tax cut, the increase in consumption and AD is weaker.

elite.q: An economy faces a positive AD shock of $240 billion. If policymakers use a tax increase that reduces disposable income by $100 billion and MPC is 0.8, what is the first-round consumption reduction?
elite.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
elite.feedback: The first-round consumption reduction is MPC times the disposable income change: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

elite.q: A fiscal package raises government purchases by $120 billion and taxes by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, the package’s first-round effect on AD is:
elite.commonError: Ignoring that the tax increase reduces consumption by MPC times the tax change.
elite.feedback: Purchases add $120 billion; the tax increase reduces consumption by $80 billion.

elite.q: A tax cut is announced, but credit-constrained households spend 90 percent while high-income households spend 30 percent. Which feature matters most for the AD effect?
options: The long-run natural rate of output
Whether government purchases are counted in GDP
Only the statutory size of the tax cut
How the tax cut is distributed across groups with different marginal propensities to consume.
elite.commonError: Assuming every dollar of tax reduction produces the same consumption response.
elite.feedback: The aggregate consumption response depends on who receives the tax cut and how much they spend.

elite.q: Fiscal expansion raises AD through the multiplier, but interest rates rise and investment falls. Which description best fits the final result?
options: Initial AD shift partly offset by crowding out
SRAS shift fully offset by lower taxes
LRPC shift partly offset by higher inflation
Money demand shift fully offset by M1
elite.commonError: Treating the multiplier as the final effect every time.
elite.feedback: Fiscal expansion can be amplified by the multiplier but weakened by crowding out.

elite.q: Refer to the multiplier graph. Government spending initially moves AD1 to AD2, the multiplier moves AD2 to AD3, and crowding out offsets part of it. The final effect is likely:
elite.commonError: Ignoring crowding out after multiplier expansion.
elite.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the multiplied AD increase, so the final shift may land between AD2 and AD3.

elite.q: If government spending rises, MPC is high, and interest rates do not rise, which effect dominates?
elite.commonError: Assuming crowding out always dominates fiscal policy.
elite.feedback: A high MPC strengthens the multiplier, and little interest-rate increase means crowding out is weak.

elite.q: If government spending rises, MPC is low, and interest rates rise sharply, which concern dominates?
options: Weak multiplier with strong crowding out
Strong multiplier with no crowding out
Money neutrality with no AD change
elite.commonError: Ignoring both MPC size and interest-rate effects.
elite.feedback: A low MPC weakens the multiplier, while higher rates crowd out private investment.

elite.q: If government spending initially shifts AD right by $40 billion and MPC is 0.75, what is the total shift before crowding out?
elite.commonError: using MPC as the multiplier instead of 1 divided by 1 minus MPC
elite.feedback: With MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is 4. A $40 billion initial shift becomes $160 billion before crowding out.

elite.q: If the initial AD shift is $30 billion and the final shift is $150 billion, what MPC is implied by the simple multiplier?
elite.commonError: using final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
elite.feedback: The multiplier is 150/30 = 5. If 1/(1-MPC)=5, then MPC = 0.8.

elite.q: If the initial shift is $50 billion and MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.5, what happens to the final AD shift before crowding out?
options: It falls from $250 billion to $100 billion.
It rises from $100 billion to $250 billion.
It falls from $250 billion to $50 billion.
elite.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
elite.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so $250 billion. MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so $100 billion.

elite.q: Suppose the multiplier would shift AD right by $200 billion, but crowding out reduces investment by $60 billion. What is the net shift?
elite.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
elite.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the multiplier effect. Net shift is $200 billion - $60 billion = $140 billion.

elite.q: If policymakers expect the multiplier shift to close a recessionary gap exactly, but crowding out is stronger than expected, what is the likely result?
options: AD does not shift far enough right to fully close the gap.
AD shifts too far right because crowding out magnifies fiscal policy.
AD shifts left because government spending is not part of AD.
elite.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens the fiscal multiplier
elite.feedback: Stronger crowding out reduces the net AD shift, so stimulus may fall short.

elite.q: If government spending rises by $60 billion, MPC is 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $50 billion, what is the net AD shift?
elite.commonError: forgetting to apply the multiplier before subtracting crowding out
elite.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so the gross shift is $240 billion. Subtract $50 billion crowding out for a net $190 billion.

elite.q: A government spending increase raises income, consumption, and AD, but also raises interest rates and lowers investment. Which answer correctly names both effects?
elite.commonError: treating all fiscal policy effects as multiplier effects only
elite.feedback: The multiplier amplifies the AD increase; crowding out offsets part of it by reducing investment.

elite.q: A recessionary demand shock hits, but the Fed is at the zero lower bound. Which option best describes the policy problem?
options: AD needs support, but rate cuts have limited room
AD is too high, and rate cuts work too strongly
SRAS needs support, but wages rise instantly
LRPC must shift, but M2 is too small
elite.commonError: Ignoring why zero rates weaken monetary stimulus.
elite.feedback: When rates are near zero, traditional monetary policy may struggle to shift AD right enough.

elite.q: A government passes stimulus after a recession has ended, and the economy is already above potential. What is the risk?
options: The stimulus may worsen inflation pressure
The stimulus must lower output below potential
The stimulus shifts SRAS right automatically
The stimulus lowers expected prices instantly
elite.commonError: Ignoring policy timing after recovery.
elite.feedback: Because of lags, stimulus can hit after recovery and add excess demand.

elite.q: Fiscal stimulus raises AD, but the central bank offsets it with tighter money. Which final outcome is most plausible?
options: AD rises less than fiscal policy alone suggests
AD rises more than fiscal policy alone suggests
SRAS shifts right because interest rates rise
LRPC shifts left because taxes fall
elite.commonError: Ignoring policy interactions.
elite.feedback: Tighter monetary policy can offset fiscal stimulus by raising interest rates and weakening AD.

elite.q: Suppose output is below its natural level because AD is weak. Which Fed action through the money market would move AD in the stabilizing direction?
options: Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
Shift money demand right to raise r and lower investment.
Keep money supply fixed and raise taxes.
elite.commonError: choosing tighter money during a demand slump
elite.feedback: When AD is weak, expansionary monetary policy shifts MS right, lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

elite.q: Suppose output is above its natural level because AD is too strong. Which Fed action through the money market would move AD in the stabilizing direction?
options: Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
Shift money demand left to lower r and raise investment.
elite.commonError: stimulating AD when output is already above natural level
elite.feedback: When AD is too strong, tighter money shifts MS left, raises rates, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

elite.q: If the economy is already near full employment and fiscal policy shifts AD right through the multiplier, what risk becomes more important?
options: A lower price level from higher government spending
A smaller price level because MPC is positive
elite.commonError: thinking all rightward AD shifts are good regardless of starting point
elite.feedback: If the economy is already near capacity, more AD can create inflation pressure instead of useful output gains.

elite.q: A recession lowers AD by $300 billion. The government increases spending by $100 billion and MPC is 0.5. Ignoring crowding out, what remains of the AD shortfall?
elite.commonError: not comparing stimulus size to the original AD shortfall
elite.feedback: MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2. A $100 billion spending increase shifts AD by $200 billion, leaving a $100 billion shortfall.

elite.q: Congress cuts spending during a recession while the Fed also sells bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
options: Both policies shift AD left or reduce support for AD, worsening the demand problem.
Both policies shift AD right, stabilizing output.
Fiscal policy shifts AD right while monetary policy shifts AD right.
elite.commonError: missing that Fed bond sales are contractionary
elite.feedback: Cutting spending reduces AD, and Fed bond sales raise rates and reduce investment. That is contraction on top of contraction.

elite.q: Congress raises spending during an inflationary boom while the Fed buys bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
options: Both policies shift AD right, risking more inflation pressure.
Both policies shift AD left, reducing inflation pressure.
Fiscal policy shifts AD left while monetary policy shifts AD left.
Neither affects AD because output is already high.
elite.commonError: thinking expansionary policy is always appropriate
elite.feedback: Spending increases and bond purchases both shift AD right. During an inflationary boom, that pours gasoline on the fire.

elite.q: A negative supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why can expansionary AD policy be a blunt tool here?
options: It may raise output somewhat but can worsen the price-level increase.
It directly restores lost productive capacity with no inflation risk.
It lowers prices and lowers output at the same time.
elite.commonError: treating supply shocks like pure demand shocks
elite.feedback: AD stimulus can support spending, but it does not fix the supply loss and may worsen inflation.

elite.q: A negative demand shock reduces output and prices. Why is expansionary monetary policy more directly suited to this case than to a pure supply shock?
options: It targets weak spending by lowering r and raising investment.
It directly increases labor, capital, and natural resources.
It shifts SRAS right by changing the reserve ratio.
It lowers AD to reduce output further.
elite.commonError: not distinguishing AD shocks from AS shocks
elite.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy works through spending, so it is more directly suited to weak AD than to lost productive capacity.

elite.q: A policy is passed to fight a recession, but because of recognition, implementation, and impact lags, it takes effect after output has already recovered. What is the likely stabilization problem?
options: The delayed policy can push AD too far right and create inflation pressure.
The delayed policy must shift AD left automatically.
The delayed policy cannot affect AD after recovery.
The delayed policy eliminates crowding out.
elite.commonError: thinking late stimulus is harmless because it was originally well-intended
elite.feedback: Good timing matters. Late expansion can overstimulate AD after the recession has already passed.

elite.q: A country experiences higher consumer confidence, lower expected business profits, and a rise in foreign income. Which components of AD move first?
options: Consumption falls, investment rises, and net exports fall.
Consumption and net exports rise, while investment falls.
elite.commonError: Failing to trace each shifter to the correct AD component.
elite.feedback: Confidence affects consumption, expected profits affect investment, and foreign income affects exports.

elite.q: The price level rises at the same time that the government cuts taxes. Which graph description is correct?
