options: There is movement downward along AD plus a leftward shift
There is movement upward along AD plus a rightward shift of the AD curve.
elite.commonError: Treating simultaneous movement and shift as mutually exclusive.
elite.feedback: The price-level change causes movement along AD; the tax cut shifts the curve.

elite.q: Domestic interest rates fall because the central bank expands money supply, while foreign income also falls. What can be said about AD?
options: Investment tends to rise and net exports tend to fall, so the net shift is ambiguous.
Only a movement along AD occurs
elite.commonError: Ignoring offsetting investment and net-export effects.
elite.feedback: The two shifters push different AD components in opposite directions.

elite.q: A student says, “Any fall in real GDP means AD shifted left.” What is the best correction?
options: Real GDP can fall from movement along AD or from shifts in AD or AS; the graph cause must be identified.
Real GDP changes only when AD shifts
A fall in real GDP always means SRAS shifted right
elite.commonError: Inferring a curve shift from an outcome without identifying the cause.
elite.feedback: Observed output changes do not by themselves reveal which curve moved.

elite.q: A student says AD1 must represent aggregate supply because real GDP is larger. What is the best correction?
options: Any curve farther right must be an aggregate-supply curve.
The graph is LRAS because real GDP is on the horizontal axis.
Both curves are AD; AD1 is the rightward demand shift.
A price-level axis means the curves cannot represent demand.
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: The label and downward slope identify the curves as AD. A larger quantity demanded at each price level is an increase in aggregate demand.

elite.q: If policymakers wanted to offset the AD shift shown, which short-run pattern are they responding to?
options: Lower output with downward pressure on the price level
Higher output with upward pressure on the price level
Higher output with downward pressure on the price level
Lower output with upward pressure on the price level
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: A decrease in AD lowers both real GDP and the price level in the short run.

elite.q: Workers expect 6 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 2 percent and wage contracts reflect the higher expectation. What happens to SRAS relative to contracts based on accurate expectations?
options: SRAS is farther left because nominal labor costs are higher than necessary.
SRAS is farther right because real wages are lower
elite.commonError: Ignoring how excessive expected inflation enters wage contracts.
elite.feedback: Higher expected prices can produce higher nominal wages and lower short-run supply.

elite.q: A severe storm destroys capital, while emergency deregulation lowers current compliance costs. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: LRAS shifts left, while the SRAS effect is ambiguous because cost relief offsets disruption.
LRAS shifts right because regulation falls
Both curves must shift left by the same amount
elite.commonError: Assuming all supply forces have the same horizon and direction.
elite.feedback: Capital destruction lowers capacity; lower compliance cost pushes SRAS right, while storm disruption may push it left.

elite.q: A student says, “Any rise in the price level shifts SRAS right.” What is the best correction?
options: Any price-level rise shifts aggregate demand left only
A change in the actual price level causes movement along SRAS; expected prices or costs shift the curve.
Actual prices shift LRAS, not SRAS
The statement is correct in every case
elite.commonError: Confusing movement along SRAS with a curve shift.
elite.feedback: The actual price level is an axis variable, not a supply shifter by itself.

elite.q: With aggregate demand unchanged, which macro outcome is consistent with the AS shift shown?
options: Lower output with a higher price level
Higher output with a lower price level
Higher output with a higher price level
Lower output with a lower price level
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: A leftward shift of AS reduces output and raises prices, the classic stagflation pattern.

elite.q: For the second AS diagram, what output-price pattern would follow if aggregate demand stayed fixed?
options: Lower output with a higher price level
Higher output with a higher price level
Higher output with a lower price level
Lower output with a lower price level
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: Demand-pull expansions raise both price level and output. This graph instead shows more output paired with a lower price level, which is an AS increase.

elite.q: A country receives a permanent productivity improvement and a temporary spike in imported input prices. Which graph change best fits?
options: LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
LRAS shifts right, while SRAS may shift left initially.
elite.commonError: Failing to separate permanent capacity from temporary production costs.
elite.feedback: Productivity raises potential output; costly imported inputs can reduce short-run supply.

elite.q: Comparing the original long-run equilibrium C with the new long-run equilibrium B, what is true?
options: GDP returns to 100; prices rise from 125 to 175.
GDP rises to 125; prices remain fixed at 125 throughout.
GDP falls to 75; prices remain fixed at 150 throughout.
GDP stays at 100; prices fall from 125 back to 100.
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: LRAS stays at 100, so long-run real GDP returns to 100. The long-run price level is higher at B than at C.

elite.q: Which description best matches the move from A to B?
options: AD rises; the economy moves upward along fixed AS0.
AS rises; the economy moves downward along fixed AD0.
AD falls; the economy moves downward along fixed AS0.
Both AD and AS shift; output returns to its starting level.
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: With AS0 unchanged, the AD increase causes a movement along the AS curve to a new short-run equilibrium.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS2, AD rises to AD2 while SRAS falls to AS1. What is the final point?
elite.commonError: Following only AD or only SRAS.
elite.feedback: AD2 and AS1 intersect at Y1 and P3, so output returns to Y1 while the price level rises.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD2-AS1, AD falls to AD1 while SRAS rises to AS2. What is the final point?
elite.commonError: Tracking the starting point but not both curve shifts.
elite.feedback: AD1 and AS2 intersect at Y1 and P1.

elite.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, an oil shock shifts AS2 to AS1, then policymakers shift AD1 to AD2. What happens?
options: Output returns to Y1 but prices rise to P3
Output rises to Y2 while prices stay P2
Output falls to Y3 while prices fall P1
Output returns to Y1 while prices fall P1
elite.commonError: Missing the inflation cost of accommodating a supply shock.
elite.feedback: Accommodation restores output from Y3 to Y1, but the price level rises to P3.

elite.q: A supply shock raises prices and lowers output. The central bank tightens policy to fight inflation. What is the likely short-run danger?
elite.commonError: Ignoring output costs of tightening after a supply shock.
elite.feedback: Tightening reduces AD and may lower inflation pressure, but it can worsen the output decline.

elite.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, which shock-policy combination moves the economy to Y1 and P3?
options: Adverse supply shock plus AD stimulus
Positive supply shock plus AD contraction
Negative AD shock plus SRAS expansion
elite.commonError: Missing the price cost of accommodation.
elite.feedback: A supply shock moves AS2 to AS1 and AD stimulus moves AD1 to AD2, ending at Y1 and P3.

elite.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, which shock creates stagflation before any policy response?
elite.commonError: Calling stagflation an AD movement.
elite.feedback: AS2 shifting left to AS1 lowers output to Y3 and raises the price level to P2.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD2-AS2, which movement could reduce output without lowering the price level?
elite.commonError: Assuming lower output always lowers prices.
elite.feedback: A leftward SRAS shift from AS2 to AS1 moves from Y2-P2 to Y1-P3: output falls while prices rise.

elite.q: Compare point A with point C. Which statement is correct?
options: Real GDP rises to 100; the price level stays at 100.
Real GDP falls to 50; the price level stays at 125.
Real GDP stays 75; the price level rises from 100 to 150.
Real GDP stays 75; the price level falls from 150 to 100.
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: The AD increase and AS decrease offset each other in output but reinforce each other on the price level.

elite.q: Which statement best describes the macro outcome shown by the move from A to B?
options: Demand-pull inflation with no long-run growth.
Long-run growth with lower price pressure.
No change in either output or the price level.
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: Higher LRAS and SRAS support more output alongside a lower price level.

elite.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, which long-run adjustment is most consistent with self-correction?
options: SRAS shifts left until output returns to Y1
SRAS shifts right until output reaches Y3
AD shifts right until output reaches Y2
LRAS shifts right until it reaches Y2
elite.commonError: Moving LRAS instead of SRAS during short-run self-correction.
elite.feedback: At Y2, output is above natural output, so rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left toward long-run equilibrium.

elite.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, which long-run adjustment is most consistent with self-correction?
options: SRAS shifts right until output returns to Y1
SRAS shifts left until output returns to Y3
AD shifts left until output returns to Y3
LRAS shifts left until it reaches Y3
elite.commonError: Moving AD or LRAS instead of SRAS during self-correction.
elite.feedback: At Y3, output is below natural output, so falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right toward long-run equilibrium.

elite.q: An economy is above potential because of a demand boom. Which policy and long-run force push in the same direction?
options: Contractionary policy and rising expected prices
Expansionary policy and falling expected prices
Contractionary policy and falling expected prices
Expansionary policy and rising expected prices
elite.commonError: Pairing the wrong policy with the wrong output gap.
elite.feedback: Contractionary policy shifts AD left, while rising expected prices shift SRAS left; both reduce output toward potential.

elite.q: An economy is below potential because AD collapsed. Which policy and long-run force push in the same direction?
options: Expansionary policy and falling expected prices
Contractionary policy and rising expected prices
Expansionary policy and rising expected prices
Contractionary policy and falling expected prices
elite.commonError: Pairing recessionary gaps with contractionary policy.
elite.feedback: Expansionary policy shifts AD right, while falling expected prices shift SRAS right; both raise output toward potential.

elite.q: An economy begins at natural output. AD rises unexpectedly, then expected prices rise. Which sequence is most likely?
options: Output rises first, then SRAS shifts left
Output falls first, then SRAS shifts right
Prices fall first, then AD shifts left
LRAS shifts right, then output falls
elite.commonError: Skipping the short-run expansion before long-run adjustment.
elite.feedback: An unexpected AD increase raises output in the short run, but higher expected prices later shift SRAS left.

elite.q: An economy begins at natural output. AD falls unexpectedly, then expected prices fall. Which sequence is most likely?
options: Output falls first, then SRAS shifts right
Output rises first, then SRAS shifts left
Prices rise first, then LRAS shifts left
AD rises first, then unemployment rises
elite.commonError: Skipping the short-run recession before self-correction.
elite.feedback: An unexpected AD decrease lowers output first, then lower expected prices shift SRAS right over time.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, which sequence best shows an attempted permanent unemployment reduction through expansionary policy?
elite.commonError: Thinking point a can be held permanently.
elite.feedback: Expansion lowers unemployment at a temporarily, but expectations adjust and unemployment returns to natural at b.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which policy mistake is shown by treating point a as permanent?
elite.commonError: Believing unemployment can stay below natural without expectations changing.
elite.feedback: Point a is temporary because expected inflation eventually rises and moves the economy toward point b.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. If policy moves the economy from c to b on SRPC1, what must be true?
options: Actual inflation rises while unemployment falls
Expected inflation rises while unemployment stays fixed
Natural unemployment rises while inflation falls
elite.commonError: Confusing movement along SRPC with a shift of SRPC.
elite.feedback: Movement up-left along the same SRPC means higher inflation and lower unemployment.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which comparison best captures the long-run result of higher expected inflation?
options: b and c have same unemployment but different inflation
a and b have same unemployment but different inflation
c and d have same inflation but different unemployment
a and d have same inflation but different unemployment
elite.commonError: Missing vertical long-run logic.
elite.feedback: Both b and c lie on the LRPC at U2, but b has higher inflation.

elite.q: Policymakers repeatedly expand aggregate demand to keep unemployment below its natural rate. Once workers and firms adjust expectations, what is required to keep unemployment below that rate?
options: A lower natural rate without any labor-market change.
A one-time reduction in expected inflation.
elite.commonError: Assuming one expansion can hold unemployment below the natural rate forever.
elite.feedback: After expectations catch up, only new inflation surprises can again push unemployment temporarily below its natural rate.

elite.q: Which feature of the graph shows that the natural rate is unchanged after the SRPC shift?
options: LRPC stays vertical at 5 percent unemployment
LRPC shifts left to 3 percent unemployment
SRPC1 becomes vertical at 6 percent unemployment
Point B moves to the right of point A
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: The LRPC staying fixed at 5 percent says the natural rate is unchanged, so inflation changes do not permanently buy lower unemployment.

elite.q: Which description of point A is correct?
options: A is only on SRPC0 and remains below the natural unemployment rate.
A is only on LRPC and remains above the natural unemployment rate.
A is on both SRPC0 and LRPC at the natural rate
A is the location where SRPC0 turns into a vertical Phillips curve.
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: Point A is where the short-run curve crosses the long-run curve, so unemployment equals the natural rate there.

elite.q: If point B persists and expectations adjust, what long-run change is predicted?
options: SRPC shifts upward; unemployment returns to 5 percent
LRPC shifts left; unemployment stays at 3 percent
SRPC shifts downward; unemployment stays at 3 percent
LRPC shifts right; unemployment rises above 5 percent
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: With unemployment below the natural rate, expectations eventually adjust, shifting the SRPC and bringing unemployment back to the natural rate.

elite.q: With unemployment above the natural rate at B, what long-run Phillips-curve adjustment should follow?
options: LRPC shifts right; unemployment stays at 7 percent
SRPC shifts up; unemployment stays at 7 percent
SRPC shifts down; unemployment returns to 5 percent
LRPC shifts left; unemployment falls below 5 percent
elite.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
elite.feedback: With unemployment above the natural rate, inflation expectations tend to fall, shifting the SRPC downward and returning unemployment to the natural rate.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A move from c on SRPC1 to the upper point at U3 on SRPC2 means:
elite.commonError: Reading the curve shift as movement along SRPC1.
elite.feedback: At U3, SRPC2 shows a higher inflation rate than SRPC1.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, comparing SRPC1 and SRPC2 shows:
elite.commonError: Missing the worse tradeoff after SRPC shifts upward.
elite.feedback: At the same inflation rate, the higher SRPC shows higher unemployment.

elite.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands AD. Later, workers build the higher inflation into wage demands. Which sequence is most accurate?
options: Move along SRPC, then SRPC shifts up
SRPC shifts down, then move along LRPC
LRPC shifts left, then AD falls
Move along LRAS, then M1 falls
elite.commonError: Confusing immediate inflation surprise with later expectation adjustment.
elite.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion first moves along the SRPC; later expected inflation rises and shifts SRPC upward.

elite.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Which labeled move isolates an upward SRPC shift at unemployment U3?
options: The move from point c to point f
The move from point a to point f
The move from point b to point e
The move from point c to point a
elite.commonError: Compares points with different unemployment rates, so movement and shift effects are mixed.
elite.feedback: Points c and f share unemployment U3; moving from c on SRPC1 to f on SRPC2 isolates higher inflation at the same unemployment rate.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence best shows disinflation with temporary unemployment costs?
elite.commonError: Skipping the temporary move above natural unemployment.
elite.feedback: Disinflation lowers actual inflation first, moving to d, then expectations fall and the economy returns to c.

elite.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which policy lesson fits the move from b to d to c?
options: Expected inflation must rise after contraction
elite.commonError: Missing the temporary cost of disinflation.
elite.feedback: The move from b to d shows higher unemployment during disinflation; d to c shows expectations adjusting downward.

elite.q: The Fed announces disinflation, but workers doubt it and expected inflation stays high. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
elite.commonError: Assuming announcements alone make policy credible.
elite.feedback: If expected inflation does not fall quickly, reducing actual inflation tends to require more output loss.

elite.q: If inflation falls from 12 percent to 7 percent and the sacrifice ratio is 3.5, output loss equals:
elite.commonError: Adding the sacrifice ratio to the inflation reduction.
elite.feedback: Inflation falls by 5 points, so output loss is 3.5 x 5 = 17.5 percent of one year's output.

elite.q: If output loss is 14 percent and inflation falls by 4 percentage points, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 3.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
10% of one year’s output per inflation point
18% of one year’s output per inflation point
elite.commonError: Uses the inflation change or output loss alone rather than dividing cumulative loss by the percentage-point reduction.
elite.feedback: Divide the 14% cumulative output loss by the 4-percentage-point inflation reduction: 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5% of one year’s output per point.

elite.q: A disinflation plan is credible, wage contracts adjust quickly, and expected inflation falls fast. Which path is most likely?
options: Smaller unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
Larger unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
No change in expected inflation despite credibility
elite.commonError: Ignoring expectations in sacrifice-ratio logic.
elite.feedback: Credibility and fast expectation adjustment reduce the output and unemployment cost of lowering inflation.

elite.q: A disinflation plan lacks credibility, wage contracts are slow, and expected inflation remains high. Which path is most likely?
options: Larger output loss for the same inflation reduction
Smaller output loss for the same inflation reduction
elite.commonError: Assuming disinflation costs vanish without credibility.
elite.feedback: If expected inflation stays high, lowering actual inflation usually requires a larger output loss.

legendary.q: A government increases purchases by $50 billion and raises taxes by $50 billion. MPC is 0.75. Before subsequent multiplier rounds, the net first-round AD change is:
legendary.commonError: Assuming equal spending and tax changes have equal direct AD effects.
legendary.feedback: Purchases add $50 billion; the tax increase cuts consumption by $37.5 billion.

legendary.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $160 billion. Households spend 60 percent of the increase initially. If later rounds follow a simple spending multiplier of 2.5, the total AD increase before other offsets is:
legendary.commonError: Applying the multiplier to the full tax cut instead of the first-round consumption change.
legendary.feedback: First-round consumption rises $96 billion; multiplying by 2.5 gives $240 billion.

legendary.q: The government increases infrastructure purchases, but imports rise sharply because much of the equipment is purchased abroad. Relative to a package using domestic inputs, the increase in domestic aggregate demand is likely:
options: Leftward because any import increase reduces government purchases.
Identical because all government spending counts equally.
Smaller because part of the spending leaks into imports.
Larger because imports are part of domestic production.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring import leakage from domestic demand.
legendary.feedback: Spending on imports does not directly purchase domestically produced output.

legendary.q: A tax cut and transfer increase have the same budget cost. The transfer is targeted to households with a higher MPC. Which package is likely to shift AD more in the short run?
options: The broad tax cut regardless of spending behavior.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring differences in marginal propensity to consume.
legendary.feedback: More of the targeted transfer is likely to be spent, producing a larger initial consumption increase.

legendary.q: A government plans contractionary fiscal policy. Which combination most clearly supports that goal?
options: Higher government purchases and lower taxes.
Lower government purchases and higher taxes.
legendary.commonError: Mixing expansionary and contractionary tools.
legendary.feedback: Lower purchases and higher taxes both push aggregate demand left.

legendary.q: A recessionary economy receives a temporary tax rebate. Households use half to repay debt, save one quarter, and spend one quarter. The immediate consumption channel equals:
legendary.commonError: Treating saving or debt repayment as immediate consumption.
legendary.feedback: Only the portion spent on current consumption directly raises the consumption component of AD.

legendary.q: A temporary $120 billion tax credit is split equally between two household groups. One group has MPC 0.90 and the other MPC 0.40. Before multiplier rounds or crowding out, what is the first-round change in aggregate demand from consumption?
legendary.commonError: Applies one MPC to the entire tax change even when recipient groups have different spending responses.
legendary.feedback: Compute each group’s first-round consumption response separately, then add them before considering later multiplier rounds.

legendary.q: Congress replaces $100 billion of government purchases with a $100 billion tax cut. Households have MPC 0.80. Holding other AD determinants fixed and looking only at the first round, what happens to aggregate demand?
options: AD is unchanged because the two fiscal changes are equal.
legendary.commonError: Treats equal-dollar spending and tax changes as having identical direct effects on aggregate demand.
legendary.feedback: Government purchases enter AD directly, while tax changes affect AD through the share of disposable income households spend.

legendary.q: A student says fiscal expansion raises AD and therefore can never crowd out investment. What is the best correction?
options: Fiscal expansion can raise AD while higher rates reduce private investment.
Fiscal expansion lowers rates because government borrowing reduces money demand.
Fiscal expansion shifts SRAS right because firms face lower costs.
Fiscal expansion eliminates the multiplier because taxes disappear.
legendary.commonError: Thinking multiplier effects rule out crowding out.
legendary.feedback: Fiscal expansion can increase AD, but rising interest rates can reduce investment and offset part of the effect.

legendary.q: Refer to the aggregate-demand multiplier graph. AD moves from AD1 to AD2, then from AD2 to AD3, followed by a partial move back. Which interpretation fits?
options: Initial fiscal shift, multiplier expansion, then crowding out offset.
Initial monetary contraction, SRAS expansion, then LRPC adjustment.
Initial supply shock, expected price decline, then AD collapse.
Initial inflation tax, M1 expansion, then velocity collapse.
legendary.commonError: Confusing multiplier and crowding-out stages.
legendary.feedback: Fiscal policy can shift AD right, the multiplier can push it farther, and crowding out can pull the final effect back.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $70 billion and MPC = 0.8. What is the correct order of AD shifts before crowding out?
options: AD first shifts right by $70 billion, then shifts farther right to a total of $350 billion.
AD first shifts right by $350 billion, then shifts back to $70 billion.
AD shifts left by $70 billion, then left by $350 billion.
AD does not shift because the multiplier only affects money demand.
legendary.commonError: confusing the initial AD shift with the final multiplier shift
legendary.feedback: The first AD shift is the direct $70 billion increase in G. With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so the final AD shift is $350 billion.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $60 billion and the final AD shift is $300 billion. What order of AD shifts and implied MPC fit these data?
options: AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts right first by $300 billion, then back to $60 billion; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts left first by $60 billion, then left by $300 billion; MPC = 0.2.
AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.6.
legendary.commonError: treating final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of the multiplier
legendary.feedback: The multiplier is $300/$60 = 5. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 5, then MPC = 0.8.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $40 billion. If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, how does the order of AD shifts change?
options: The initial AD shift stays $40 billion, but the final shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion.
The initial AD shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion, but the final shift stays $40 billion.
Both the initial and final AD shifts stay $40 billion.
The initial AD shift becomes $200 billion and the final shift becomes $80 billion.
legendary.commonError: thinking same initial government spending creates same final AD shift regardless of MPC
legendary.feedback: The initial shift is still $40 billion. With MPC = 0.5, multiplier is 2 and final shift is $80 billion. With MPC = 0.8, multiplier is 5 and final shift is $200 billion.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $100 billion and MPC = 0.6. Crowding out reduces investment by $75 billion. What is the correct order of AD effects?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $175 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out increases it to $325 billion.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $250 billion, then crowding out leaves $175 billion.
AD shifts right $100 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
legendary.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it from the gross multiplier shift
legendary.feedback: MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. The $100 billion initial shift becomes $250 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $175 billion.

legendary.q: Two governments each increase purchases by $60 billion. Economy A has MPC 0.80 and $100 billion of crowding out; Economy B has MPC 0.60 and $20 billion of crowding out. Using the simple multiplier and the stated offsets, which comparison is correct?
options: Economy A has a $200 billion net AD increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy B.
Economy A has a $300 billion net increase and Economy B has a $150 billion net increase because crowding out does not affect AD.
Economy B has a $200 billion net increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy A.
Both economies have the same $180 billion net AD increase because the initial spending changes are equal.
legendary.commonError: Compares gross multiplier effects without subtracting the private spending displaced by higher interest rates.
legendary.feedback: For the simplified model used here, compare each policy’s gross multiplier effect and then subtract its stated crowding-out offset.

legendary.q: Government purchases rise by $80 billion and MPC is 0.75. The observed net increase in aggregate demand is $230 billion after crowding out. Under the simple model used in this bank, how much of the gross multiplier effect was crowded out?
legendary.commonError: Uses the net AD shift as if it were the gross multiplier effect.
legendary.feedback: First compute the gross multiplier effect, then infer the crowding-out offset from the difference between gross and observed net AD.

legendary.q: If the economy initially needed AD to fall by $300 billion and the MS1 to MS2 movement reduces AD by $200 billion, what remains?
options: Output rises from Y2 to Y1.
legendary.commonError: not comparing the graph's AD shift with the size of the gap
legendary.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. If AD needed to fall $300 billion but falls $200 billion, $100 billion of excess AD remains.

legendary.q: A contractionary monetary-policy move must reduce AD by $240 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what investment decrease is needed to produce that AD movement?
legendary.commonError: not dividing the AD target by the multiplier
legendary.feedback: The graph shows a leftward AD movement. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so investment must fall by $240 billion / 4 = $60 billion.

legendary.q: The MS1 to MS2 movement causes AD to shift left by $180 billion. A separate fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $60 billion. What is the net AD change?
legendary.commonError: adding both policies in the same direction without checking graph direction
legendary.feedback: The graph's monetary policy lowers AD by $180 billion. Fiscal policy raises AD by $60 billion. Net AD falls by $120 billion.

legendary.q: The Fed pushes r high enough to reduce investment by $90 billion, but AD only needed to move left by $240 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what happens?
options: AD falls $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.
AD falls $240 billion, closing the gap exactly.
legendary.commonError: failing to compare the multiplied AD effect to the needed AD change
legendary.feedback: The graph shows AD moving left. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so a $90 billion investment fall lowers AD by $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.

legendary.q: A $50 billion government spending increase is intended to close a $250 billion AD gap. MPC = 0.75, but crowding out reduces investment by $40 billion. What is the correct sequence?
options: AD first shifts right $50 billion, then the multiplier pushes it to $200 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $160 billion shift and a $90 billion gap.
AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a $210 billion surplus.
AD first shifts left $50 billion, then the multiplier shifts it left $200 billion, leaving a $90 billion gap.
AD shifts right $50 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
legendary.commonError: calculating the multiplier but ignoring the order: initial shift, multiplied shift, crowding-out offset
legendary.feedback: MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4. The $50 billion initial shift becomes $200 billion, then crowding out lowers the net shift to $160 billion, leaving a $90 billion gap.

legendary.q: The economy is already above potential output by $180 billion. Congress raises spending by $30 billion and MPC = 0.8. What is the correct AD-shift interpretation?
options: AD first shifts right $30 billion, then the multiplier expands the shift to $150 billion, worsening the overheating gap to $330 billion.
AD first shifts left $30 billion, then left $150 billion, reducing the overheating gap to $30 billion.
AD shifts right $30 billion only, closing part of the overheating gap.
AD does not shift because the economy is already above potential.
legendary.commonError: thinking any rightward AD shift is good regardless of the starting gap
legendary.feedback: MPC = 0.8 gives multiplier 5. The $30 billion spending increase becomes a $150 billion AD increase, making the $180 billion overheating gap worse.

legendary.q: The monetary-policy movement shifts AD left by $160 billion. Fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $160 billion. What is the net AD effect?
legendary.commonError: not matching the leftward AD shift in the graph before adding the fiscal offset
legendary.feedback: The graph shows monetary policy shifting AD left. A fiscal expansion of the same size shifts AD right by the same amount, so the net AD effect is zero.

legendary.q: A recessionary gap is $400 billion. Government spending rises by $100 billion and MPC = 0.75. What is the order of AD shifts and the final gap, ignoring crowding out?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier expands the shift to $400 billion, closing the gap.
AD first shifts right $400 billion, then falls back to $100 billion, leaving a $300 billion gap.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then left $400 billion, worsening the gap.
AD shifts right $100 billion only, leaving a $300 billion gap.
legendary.commonError: confusing the first AD shift with the final multiplied AD shift
legendary.feedback: MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4. The $100 billion initial spending increase becomes a $400 billion final AD shift, closing the gap.

legendary.q: A recessionary gap begins closing without new policy as wage growth slows and SRAS shifts right. A large discretionary stimulus designed for the original gap is still scheduled to take effect several quarters later. What is the strongest stabilization concern?
options: The delayed stimulus may arrive after much of the gap has self-corrected, pushing AD too far right and creating overheating pressure.
The stimulus becomes contractionary once SRAS begins shifting right.
Self-correction guarantees the stimulus has no effect on aggregate demand.
The delayed stimulus automatically shifts LRAS right by the amount of the original gap.
legendary.commonError: Assumes a policy designed for an old output gap remains correctly sized after self-correction has already reduced the gap.
legendary.feedback: Policy lags matter because wages, costs, expectations, and private spending can change before discretionary policy takes effect, creating overshoot risk.

legendary.q: Policymakers initially estimate a $300 billion recessionary gap and enact a $75 billion spending increase with a simple multiplier of 4. By the time the policy takes effect, revised data show the gap is only $100 billion. Ignoring crowding out, what is the implication?
options: The policy closes the revised gap exactly because it was calibrated to the original estimate.
The $75 billion initial spending increase leaves a $25 billion gap because only the first round matters.
The policy raises AD by $100 billion because stabilization automatically adjusts to revised data.
The $300 billion AD increase overshoots the revised gap by $200 billion.
legendary.commonError: Uses the original output-gap estimate even after newer data show a much smaller gap.
legendary.feedback: Compare the policy’s expected AD shift with the output gap that exists when the policy actually takes effect, not only the initial estimate.

legendary.q: Inflation pressure is being driven by excessive aggregate demand. Policymakers use contractionary stabilization policy and the policy succeeds in lowering aggregate demand. Before inflation expectations fully adjust, which short-run combination is most consistent with the policy mechanism?
options: Higher inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
No change in unemployment because stabilization policy affects only the price level.
Lower inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
Lower inflation pressure together with stronger output and lower unemployment.
legendary.commonError: Treats lower inflation pressure from contractionary demand policy as costless in the short run.
legendary.feedback: A contractionary AD policy can reduce inflation pressure while also lowering output and raising unemployment before expectations fully adjust.

legendary.q: A short recession causes tax receipts to fall and unemployment-benefit payments to rise automatically. Congress also approves an infrastructure stimulus, but construction begins after the economy has already recovered. Which comparison is strongest?
options: The infrastructure program cannot affect aggregate demand once the recession has ended.
The automatic stabilizers cushion the downturn and recede with conditions, while the delayed discretionary program can add demand after the original gap has faded.
Both responses have the same implementation timing because each changes the government budget.
The automatic stabilizers become contractionary during the recession, while delayed infrastructure is always stabilizing.
legendary.commonError: Assumes automatic stabilizers and discretionary fiscal programs have the same activation and phase-out timing.
legendary.feedback: Automatic stabilizers respond as income and employment change without new legislation; discretionary programs can arrive later and may outlast the original gap.

legendary.q: The domestic price level rises, consumer confidence strengthens, and foreign income declines. Which analysis is complete?
options: AD shifts left with no offsetting force
There is movement upward along AD, a rightward pressure from consumption, and a leftward pressure from net exports.
AD shifts right with no movement along it
All changes move the economy along the same AD curve
legendary.commonError: Collapsing simultaneous movement and multiple shifts into one effect.
legendary.feedback: The price level changes quantity demanded; confidence and foreign income shift the curve in opposite directions.

legendary.q: A lower price level raises the real value of money balances, lowers interest rates, and makes domestic goods cheaper relative to foreign goods. What happens along AD?
options: Consumption, investment, and net exports all tend to rise.
All three channels shift AD rather than cause movement along it.
Consumption falls while investment and net exports rise.
legendary.commonError: Misclassifying the three slope mechanisms.
legendary.feedback: The wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects all raise quantity of real GDP demanded at a lower price level.

legendary.q: Businesses become optimistic, households become pessimistic, and the currency depreciates. Which AD components are initially affected?
options: Investment rises, consumption falls, and net exports rise.
Investment falls, consumption rises, and net exports fall.
legendary.commonError: Assigning shifters to the wrong spending components.
legendary.feedback: Expectations affect I and C, while depreciation affects NX.

legendary.q: A tax increase and higher government purchases occur together. Which statement is justified without numerical information?
options: The two policies push aggregate demand in opposite directions.
The policies cause only movement along AD
legendary.commonError: Assuming a combined policy has a predetermined net effect.
legendary.feedback: Higher G raises AD; higher taxes tend to reduce consumption and AD.

legendary.q: The price level is unchanged, but desired consumption, investment, and net exports all decline. The economy experiences:
options: A rightward shift of short-run aggregate supply.
A leftward shift of aggregate demand.
legendary.commonError: Using movement-along language when the price level is held fixed.
legendary.feedback: At a given price level, lower planned spending shifts AD left.

legendary.q: A country’s currency appreciates and foreign economies enter recession while domestic consumer confidence rises. The net AD effect is:
options: Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall for two reasons.
No change because the effects cancel exactly
legendary.commonError: Assuming offsetting forces are equal without evidence.
legendary.feedback: Confidence raises C, while appreciation and lower foreign income reduce NX.

legendary.q: Which statement correctly interprets the move from AD0 to AD1?
options: At each price level, AS1 shows more real GDP supplied.
At each output level, AD1 shows a lower price requirement.
AD0 and AD1 are two points on one aggregate-demand curve.
At each price level, AD1 shows more real GDP demanded.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: An AD increase means spending is higher at every price level. That is a shift of the entire demand curve, not a movement along it.

legendary.q: Which statement best captures the meaning of the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: At each price level, AS1 shows less real GDP supplied.
At each price level, AD1 shows less real GDP demanded.
At each output level, AD1 shows a higher price requirement.
AD0 and AD1 are two points on one aggregate-demand curve.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: The entire AD curve shifts left. That means spending is lower at each price level, not that the economy merely moved along AD0.

legendary.q: Expected inflation rises, productivity improves, and oil prices fall. What can be concluded about SRAS?
options: The direction is ambiguous because expectations push left while productivity and cheaper oil push right.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring offsetting supply shifters.
legendary.feedback: Multiple cost and productivity forces push SRAS in opposite directions.

legendary.q: Nominal wages are fixed for one year. The price level rises unexpectedly, then wage contracts reset to reflect the higher expected price level. What sequence is most likely?
options: A rightward SRAS shift followed by movement down
Movement up along SRAS at first, followed later by a leftward SRAS shift.
legendary.commonError: Failing to distinguish immediate movement from later expectation adjustment.
legendary.feedback: Unexpected prices initially raise output along SRAS; higher wage expectations later shift SRAS left.

legendary.q: An economy’s expected price level falls while actual price level and productive resources are unchanged. At each actual price level, firms are likely to supply:
options: More potential output, so LRAS shifts right.
Less output, so SRAS shifts left.
The same output because expectations never matter.
More output, so SRAS shifts right.
legendary.commonError: Confusing expected-price effects with long-run capacity.
legendary.feedback: Lower expected prices tend to lower nominal input costs and raise short-run supply.

legendary.q: Which statement best interprets the shift from AS0 to AS1 without confusing it for a movement along a curve?
options: AS1 shows more output demanded at each price level.
AS1 shows less output supplied at each price level.
AS0 and AS1 are two points on one supply curve.
AS1 shows higher potential output on a shifted LRAS.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: The entire AS curve shifted up/left. That means production is less forthcoming at each price level, not that the economy merely moved to another point on AS0.

legendary.q: Which statement best interprets the move from AS0 to AS1?
options: AS1 shows less output demanded at each price level.
AS0 and AS1 are two points on one supply curve.
AS1 shows lower potential output on a shifted LRAS.
AS1 shows more output supplied at each price level.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: A lower AS curve means firms will supply more at each price level, or the same output at a lower price level. That is an increase in aggregate supply.

legendary.q: A permanent tax credit raises capital investment, while a temporary wage subsidy lowers current labor costs. Which supply changes are most likely?
options: LRAS shifts right over time and SRAS shifts right immediately.
SRAS shifts left because subsidies raise wages
LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
legendary.commonError: Failing to distinguish capacity growth from current cost reduction.
legendary.feedback: More capital raises potential output, while the subsidy lowers short-run production cost.

legendary.q: A country loses 5 percent of its capital stock but gains a technology that raises remaining capital productivity by 8 percent. What is the LRAS implication?
options: The net LRAS effect is ambiguous without knowing the relative output effects.
LRAS must shift right because productivity rose more in percentage terms.
LRAS cannot change when two forces offset.
LRAS must shift left because capital fell.
legendary.commonError: Comparing raw percentages that apply to different economic quantities.
legendary.feedback: The effect on potential output depends on how each change affects productive capacity.

legendary.q: A permanent improvement in education raises worker productivity, but a new regulation raises current compliance costs. Which statement is most complete?
options: LRAS shifts right, while SRAS may shift left in the short run.
Education affects AD rather than supply
legendary.commonError: Treating permanent productivity and current cost changes as identical.
legendary.feedback: Education raises capacity; compliance costs can reduce short-run supply.

legendary.q: A student says point B can only be explained by higher aggregate demand because real GDP is larger there. Which correction best fits the graph?
options: AD shifts right while SRAS and LRAS both stay fixed.
SRAS shifts left while AD0 and LRAS both stay fixed.
LRAS shifts left while SRAS and AD0 both stay fixed.
SRAS and LRAS shift right while AD0 stays fixed.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: The graph holds AD constant and shows the supply side improving. That raises potential output and lowers the price level.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, AS shifts to AS1 and then AD shifts to AD2. Which interpretation survives?
options: The policy restores output to Y1 but raises the price level to P3.
The policy lowers prices to P1 while restoring output to Y1.
The policy moves output to Y2 and keeps prices fixed at P2.
The policy leaves output at Y3 because AD cannot offset SRAS shocks.
legendary.commonError: Missing the inflation cost of accommodating a supply shock.
legendary.feedback: Accommodation moves AD1 to AD2 after AS2 shifts to AS1, restoring Y1 but raising prices to P3.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS2, AD shifts to AD2 and SRAS shifts to AS1. Which statement is correct?
options: Output stays at Y1, but the price level rises from P1 to P3.
Output rises to Y2, and the price level stays fixed at P2.
Output falls to Y3, and the price level falls from P2 to P1.
Output stays at Y1, and the price level falls from P3 to P1.
legendary.commonError: Following only one curve shift.
legendary.feedback: AD2 and AS1 intersect at Y1 and P3, so output returns to Y1 while the price level rises.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD2-AS1, AD shifts to AD1 and SRAS shifts to AS2. Which statement is correct?
options: Output stays at Y1, but the price level falls from P3 to P1.
Output falls to Y3, while the price level stays at P2.
Output rises to Y2, while the price level rises to P3.
Output stays at Y1, and the price level rises from P1 to P3.
legendary.commonError: Missing offsetting output effects from two shifts.
legendary.feedback: AD1 and AS2 intersect at Y1 and P1, so output returns to Y1 and prices fall from P3 to P1.

legendary.q: Consumer confidence falls while a major productivity improvement lowers firms’ production costs. Without knowing the size of either shock, what is certain in the short run?
options: Real output falls, while the price-level effect remains uncertain.
The price level falls, while the change in real output remains uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise because both shocks are expansionary.
Both real output and the price level fall because both shocks are contractionary.
legendary.commonError: Treating a negative demand shock and positive supply shock as if they move both outcomes in the same direction.
legendary.feedback: Lower aggregate demand and higher short-run aggregate supply both reduce the price level, but they push output in opposite directions.

legendary.q: An economy experiences an adverse supply shock. Policymakers fully stabilize real output with expansionary demand policy. What tradeoff follows?
options: The price level returns to its original value once output is restored.
Inflation and unemployment both fall because the policy removes the supply shock.
Output is stabilized, but inflation pressure becomes stronger.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because aggregate demand rises.
legendary.commonError: Assuming demand policy can reverse a supply shock without an inflation cost.
legendary.feedback: Expansionary demand policy can offset the output loss from an adverse supply shock, but it intensifies inflation pressure.

legendary.q: Real output rises while the price level falls. Which pair of simultaneous shifts can produce that pattern?
options: Both curves shift left, with the demand shift dominating the output effect.
Demand shifts right while supply shifts left, with demand dominating output.
Demand shifts left while supply shifts right, with demand dominating output.
Both curves shift right, with the supply shift dominating the price effect.
legendary.commonError: Matching one observed outcome to one curve while ignoring the second observed outcome.
legendary.feedback: Higher output can come from either shift, but a falling price level requires the rightward supply shift to dominate the demand effect.

legendary.q: A student says an aggregate-demand increase permanently raises real GDP above potential in this graph. Which correction is best?
options: D is a permanent equilibrium because SRAS never adjusts afterward.
D is above potential only short run; adjustment returns output to B.
A is above potential in the short run and B stays below potential.
C is below potential permanently because LRAS determines the price level.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: The graph shows short-run output above LRAS at D, but long-run adjustment returns output to LRAS at B while price level stays higher.

legendary.q: A student sees higher output and a higher price level at point B and concludes the graph must show an aggregate-supply increase. What is the best correction?
options: An AS increase raises both output and the price level here.
An AD increase raises both output and the price level here.
An AD increase lowers output while the price level rises here.
The graph cannot distinguish a demand change from a supply change.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: In a standard AD-AS model, a rightward AD shift raises both output and prices in the short run, unlike a rightward AS shift.

legendary.q: A student says the graph proves output must rise whenever aggregate demand increases. Which graph-based rebuttal is strongest?
options: The AD increase dominates both output and the price-level effects.
The AS decrease dominates both output and the price-level effects.
The two shifts offset the price level but reinforce the output effect.
The AS decrease offsets the AD increase in output, not prices.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: Point B isolates the AD increase and point D isolates the AS decrease. Point C shows their combination, where the output effect is offset but inflation is amplified.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, expected prices adjust upward with no policy response. Which movement fits the model?
options: SRAS shifts left toward AS1 and output returns toward Y1.
SRAS shifts right toward AS2 and output rises toward Y2.
AD shifts right toward AD2 and output remains above potential.
LRAS shifts right toward Y2 because actual output was high.
legendary.commonError: Confusing short-run output with long-run potential output.
legendary.feedback: When output is above potential, rising expected prices shift SRAS left and return output toward LRAS.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, expected prices adjust downward with no policy response. Which movement fits the model?
options: SRAS shifts right toward AS2 and output returns toward Y1.
SRAS shifts left toward AS1 and output falls toward Y3.
AD shifts left toward AD1 and prices rise toward P3.
LRAS shifts left toward Y3 because unemployment is high.
legendary.commonError: Moving LRAS instead of SRAS during self-correction.
legendary.feedback: When output is below potential, falling expected prices shift SRAS right and restore output toward natural output.

legendary.q: A temporary negative aggregate-demand shock lowers output below potential. With no policy response and flexible wages and expected prices over time, what is the long-run outcome?
options: SRAS shifts right and output returns to potential at a lower price level.
Output remains permanently below potential with the original price level.
LRAS shifts left until productive capacity matches the recession output.
Aggregate demand automatically shifts right because unemployment increased.
legendary.commonError: Treating a temporary demand shock as a permanent change in productive capacity.
legendary.feedback: Falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right, restoring natural output while leaving the price level lower.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. A demand increase has moved the economy to the intersection of AD2 and AS2 at Y2 and P2. If no policy reverses AD2 and long-run adjustment is completed, which comparison between the short-run and long-run effects is supported by the graph?
options: The temporary output gain disappears as output returns to Y1, while the price level rises further toward P3.
Output remains at Y2 because long-run adjustment changes only the price level, which falls all the way back toward P1.
Output falls to Y3 as SRAS shifts left past AS1, while the price level stays fixed at the short-run level P2.
Both real output and the price level return to their original Y1 and P1 values once wage contracts and expectations adjust.
legendary.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
legendary.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

legendary.q: Two economies have identical recessionary gaps. In Economy A, most wages can be reset monthly; in Economy B, most wages are fixed by three-year contracts. With no policy response, which prediction best follows from the long-run adjustment model?
options: Economy B should self-correct faster because longer wage contracts make SRAS respond more quickly to the recessionary gap.
Both economies must return to potential at exactly the same speed because a vertical LRAS fixes the timing as well as the destination.
Neither economy can self-correct without an aggregate-demand policy change because wage and cost adjustment cannot move SRAS.
Economy A should tend to self-correct faster because wages and production costs can adjust sooner.
legendary.commonError: Assumes self-correction is instantaneous even when wages and expectations are sticky.
legendary.feedback: Long-run adjustment can take time because wage contracts, input costs, and price expectations may change gradually.

legendary.q: After a negative aggregate-demand shock, real output begins recovering toward potential even though policymakers make no fiscal or monetary change. Nominal wage growth has slowed and firms report easing unit labor costs. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: The evidence requires LRAS to have shifted left until it met current output, converting the recessionary gap into long-run equilibrium.
The recovery shows wage adjustment is irrelevant because only changes in aggregate demand can move real output back toward potential.
The evidence is consistent with self-correction through a rightward SRAS shift, not necessarily an active stabilization policy.
The recovery proves aggregate demand was shifted right by discretionary policy even though no fiscal or monetary action is observed.
legendary.commonError: Attributes any recovery toward potential to active policy even when wages and expectations are adjusting with no policy change.
legendary.feedback: Self-correction is the endogenous SRAS response to an output gap; stabilization policy is a separate deliberate intervention.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, policymakers try to keep unemployment at U1 through repeated demand expansion. What eventually breaks the plan?
options: Expected inflation rises and shifts the SRPC upward.
Actual inflation falls and shifts the SRPC downward.
The LRPC shifts left because inflation is higher.
The natural rate disappears because output rose once.
legendary.commonError: Believing policymakers can permanently buy lower unemployment with inflation.
legendary.feedback: Expansion can move unemployment below natural temporarily, but expected inflation adjusts and SRPC shifts upward.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. The economy moves from c to a, then policymakers mistake a as sustainable. What is the likely correction?
options: Expected inflation rises, SRPC shifts up, and the economy moves toward b.
Expected inflation falls, SRPC shifts down, and the economy moves toward d.
The natural rate falls, LRPC shifts left, and the economy stays at a.
The price level falls, AD shifts left, and unemployment stays at U1.
legendary.commonError: Treating a short-run Phillips curve point as permanent.
legendary.feedback: Point a is temporary. Expected inflation adjusts upward and the economy returns to the natural rate at higher inflation.

legendary.q: Two episodes produce the same increase in inflation. In one, unemployment falls after aggregate demand expands; in the other, unemployment rises after an adverse supply shock. What explains the difference?
options: Both episodes are movements along one SRPC, but they begin from different unemployment rates.
Both episodes shift the LRPC because inflation changes the natural rate in opposite directions.
The supply shock lowers expected inflation and moves the economy down an unchanged SRPC.
The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.
legendary.commonError: Assuming every inflation change is a movement along one fixed Phillips curve.
legendary.feedback: Demand changes can move the economy along a given SRPC; supply shocks alter the inflation-unemployment relationship and shift the SRPC.

legendary.q: Which pair of descriptions matches the two curves shown?
options: SRPC0: no short-run tradeoff; LRPC: permanent tradeoff
SRPC0: long-run neutrality; LRPC: short-run tradeoff
SRPC0: fixed unemployment; LRPC: fixed inflation
SRPC0: short-run tradeoff; LRPC: no long-run tradeoff
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: That is the whole point of showing both curves together: a short-run tradeoff and a vertical long-run benchmark.

legendary.q: A demand expansion moves the economy to lower unemployment and higher inflation. A year later unemployment returns to its original rate while inflation remains higher. Which sequence fits?
options: A supply improvement followed by movement down the SRPC
Movement along an SRPC followed by an upward SRPC shift
Two movements along one permanently fixed SRPC
An LRPC shift left followed by falling expectations
legendary.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendary.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation while output falls. How should the AD-AS result transfer to the Phillips model?
options: Higher inflation and unemployment indicate an upward SRPC shift
Higher inflation and lower unemployment indicate movement along SRPC
Lower inflation and unemployment indicate a downward SRPC shift
Unchanged inflation with lower unemployment indicates an LRPC shift
legendary.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
legendary.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

legendary.q: A policymaker cites the downward-sloping SRPC as proof that permanently higher inflation will secure permanently lower unemployment. What is the decisive flaw?
options: The SRPC actually slopes upward for every demand change
Inflation cannot respond to aggregate demand in the short run
The natural rate is always zero after an expansion
Expected inflation adjusts, so the short-run unemployment gain is not permanent
legendary.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
legendary.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

legendary.q: Two economies have the same natural unemployment rate but very different average inflation rates over many years. Which observation is most consistent with a vertical long-run Phillips curve?
options: The higher-inflation economy must have permanently lower unemployment because inflation buys a lasting tradeoff.
The lower-inflation economy must have permanently higher unemployment because prices grow more slowly.
Both can remain at the same long-run unemployment rate despite different inflation rates.
Different inflation rates require different natural unemployment rates even when labor markets are otherwise alike.
legendary.commonError: Inferring a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff from cross-country inflation differences.
legendary.feedback: The vertical LRPC allows different steady inflation rates at the same natural unemployment rate.

legendary.q: A national job-matching system reduces the time workers spend searching for suitable positions. What happens to the long-run Phillips curve, other things equal?
options: It shifts right because expected inflation rises.
The economy moves upward along an unchanged LRPC.
It becomes horizontal at the new inflation rate.
It shifts left because the natural rate of unemployment falls.
legendary.commonError: Confusing a change in the natural rate with a movement caused by inflation.
legendary.feedback: A lasting improvement in labor-market matching can lower the natural rate and move the entire LRPC left.

legendary.q: An unexpected monetary expansion temporarily lowers unemployment. Inflation expectations then fully adjust while the higher inflation rate persists. What is the long-run result?
options: Unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate.
Unemployment remains permanently below the natural rate.
Unemployment rises permanently above the natural rate.
Inflation returns automatically to its original rate while unemployment stays low.
legendary.commonError: Stopping the analysis before expectations adjust.
legendary.feedback: The short-run unemployment effect disappears when expectations adjust, leaving higher inflation and natural-rate unemployment.

legendary.q: Policy holds unemployment below natural with successive demand expansions. Expected inflation rises each round. Which path is consistent with the natural-rate model?
options: A sequence of upward-shifting SRPCs ending back at natural unemployment with higher inflation
One unchanged SRPC delivering permanently lower unemployment after every contract renewal
A leftward LRPC shift caused solely by faster inflation with unchanged labor structure
A downward SRPC shift ending in deflation and a lower natural unemployment rate
legendary.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendary.q: Economy A lowers its natural rate through better job matching; Economy B only creates an unexpected demand boom. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both economies permanently shift LRPC left because unemployment initially declines
Only Economy B changes long-run unemployment by raising aggregate demand
Neither economy can affect unemployment at either a short or long horizon
A can shift LRPC left; B can only move unemployment below natural temporarily
legendary.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
legendary.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

legendary.q: Inflation expectations instantly match a fully anticipated monetary expansion in the model. What Phillips prediction is most consistent?
options: A rightward LRPC shift from higher money growth and unchanged labor institutions
A guaranteed fall in both inflation and unemployment after expectations adjust
Little or no temporary unemployment movement away from the natural rate
A permanent unemployment decline along the SRPC once nominal spending increases
legendary.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
legendary.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

legendary.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy moves from SRPC1 to SRPC2. Which statement should be rejected?
options: The tradeoff improved because higher inflation now buys lower unemployment at every point.
The tradeoff worsened because inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate.
Expected inflation may have increased and shifted the curve upward.
An adverse supply shock may have raised both inflation pressure and unemployment risk.
legendary.commonError: Calling an upward SRPC shift an improvement.
legendary.feedback: An upward SRPC shift worsens the tradeoff because inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate.

legendary.q: A policymaker says, 'Inflation is high, so unemployment must be low.' What is the best correction?
options: That only fits demand pressure; supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment together.
That is always true because the Phillips curve never shifts.
That is false only when M1 is larger than M2.
That is true in the long run because LRPC slopes downward.
legendary.commonError: Treating the Phillips curve as fixed under every shock.
legendary.feedback: The short-run tradeoff can worsen when SRPC shifts up, so inflation and unemployment can rise together.

legendary.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy is on SRPC2 rather than SRPC1. Which conclusion is most careful?
options: The tradeoff worsened, but the cause could be expected inflation or a supply shock.
The tradeoff improved, and policymakers can now lower unemployment without cost.
The LRPC shifted left, so natural unemployment must have fallen.
AD must have shifted right, so SRPC cannot have moved.
legendary.commonError: Assuming every SRPC shift has only one cause.
legendary.feedback: An upward SRPC shift can come from higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock, and both worsen the tradeoff.

legendary.q: At the unemployment rate marked by the LRPC, how does inflation on SRPC1 compare with inflation at point A on SRPC0?
options: Inflation is lower on SRPC1 while unemployment stays at 5 percent
Inflation is higher on SRPC1 while unemployment stays at 5 percent
Inflation is unchanged because SRPC0 and SRPC1 overlap there
Unemployment falls below 5 percent while inflation stays unchanged
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: Because the SRPC shifts up while the LRPC stays fixed, maintaining unemployment at the natural rate would involve a higher inflation rate than at point A.

legendary.q: If policymakers keep unemployment at point B, what expectations adjustment tends to follow?
options: Expected inflation falls and SRPC shifts downward
Expected inflation rises and SRPC shifts upward
Expected inflation stays fixed and LRPC shifts left
Expected inflation rises and LRPC shifts right
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: Below-natural-rate unemployment tends to raise inflation expectations, shifting the SRPC upward and moving unemployment back toward the natural rate.

legendary.q: If unemployment remains at the right-hand point B, how should inflation expectations and the SRPC adjust over time?
options: Expected inflation rises and SRPC shifts upward
Expected inflation stays fixed and LRPC shifts right
Expected inflation falls and LRPC shifts left
Expected inflation falls and SRPC shifts downward
legendary.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
legendary.feedback: Above-natural-rate unemployment tends to reduce inflation expectations, shifting the SRPC downward and returning unemployment toward the natural rate.

legendary.q: A surprise demand expansion initially lowers unemployment. Contracts renew after actual inflation repeatedly exceeds prior forecasts. Which response is most likely?
options: Expected inflation falls and the SRPC shifts downward
The LRPC shifts left because contracts renew
Expected inflation rises and the SRPC shifts upward
legendary.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
legendary.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

legendary.q: Two central banks announce the same lower inflation target. One has a stronger record of meeting targets. Under otherwise similar conditions, what can differ?
options: Actual inflation must reach zero with no output cost
The less credible bank must cause immediate deflation
Expected inflation may fall faster where the announcement is more credible
The natural rate must immediately fall only in the credible economy
legendary.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
legendary.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendary.q: Actual inflation is 5% while wage setters expected 3%, temporarily pushing unemployment below natural. What erodes that effect?
options: The price level returns to its initial value automatically
Forecasts adjust upward, shifting the SRPC until unemployment returns toward natural
The LRPC shifts left because actual inflation is above expected
Forecasts adjust downward, moving unemployment farther below natural
legendary.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
legendary.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, the Fed credibly reduces money growth. Which path best shows disinflation with adjustment?
legendary.commonError: Skipping the short-run unemployment cost of disinflation.
legendary.feedback: Disinflation moves from b to d first, then expected inflation falls and the economy returns to c.

legendary.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. The economy moves from b to d during disinflation. What must happen for it to reach c?
options: Expected inflation must fall enough to shift SRPC downward.
Expected inflation must rise enough to shift SRPC upward.
The natural rate must rise enough to shift LRPC right.
Actual inflation must rise above expected inflation again.
legendary.commonError: Missing the expectation adjustment needed after disinflation.
legendary.feedback: After contractionary policy, expected inflation must fall for the SRPC to shift downward and return unemployment to natural.

legendary.q: Country A has a sacrifice ratio of 2, while Country B has a sacrifice ratio of 5. If both reduce inflation by 3 percentage points, which comparison is correct?
options: A loses about 15% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 6%.
Both lose about 3% of annual GDP because the inflation reduction is equal.
A loses about 6% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 15%.
A has no output loss because its sacrifice ratio is below the inflation reduction.
legendary.commonError: Reversing the sacrifice ratios or treating equal inflation reductions as equal output costs.
legendary.feedback: Cumulative output loss equals the sacrifice ratio times the inflation reduction: 2 × 3 = 6 for A and 5 × 3 = 15 for B.

legendary.q: A credible central bank announces a lower inflation target, expected inflation falls partly, and policy still contracts demand. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: The downward SRPC shift may reduce but need not eliminate the short-run output cost
Credibility guarantees unemployment never rises during the contractionary adjustment
The LRPC shifts left because the announced target permanently lowers natural unemployment
Disinflation necessarily becomes deflation before expected inflation can decline
legendary.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
legendary.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendary.q: Inflation falls 3 points while cumulative output loss equals 6% of annual GDP. Unemployment later returns to natural. Which synthesis is correct?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 0.5, and unemployment stays permanently high
The ratio is 3, and LRPC shifts right permanently
The ratio is 6, and the price level must have fallen
The sacrifice ratio is 2, and the unemployment cost was temporary in the model
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendary.q: An adverse supply shock has raised inflation and unemployment. Why can disinflation policy face a harder near-term tradeoff than after a demand boom?
options: The LRPC becomes downward sloping during supply shocks
Contraction shifts the SRPC downward with no demand effect
Contraction can lower inflation pressure while worsening an already weak output position
Supply shocks automatically lower the sacrifice ratio to zero
legendary.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
legendary.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

legendary.q: Inflation falls from 10 percent to 6 percent. Output loss is 18 percent of one year's GDP. What does the sacrifice ratio imply?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 4.5, showing a costly disinflation.
The sacrifice ratio is 2.5, showing a mild disinflation.
The sacrifice ratio is 16, showing no output cost.
The sacrifice ratio is 24, showing inflation rose.
legendary.commonError: Dividing by the wrong inflation change.
legendary.feedback: Inflation falls by 4 points, and 18/4 = 4.5.

legendary.q: A disinflation reduces inflation by 5 percentage points. The sacrifice ratio is 2.8. What output cost should be expected?
legendary.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
legendary.feedback: Output loss equals sacrifice ratio times inflation reduction, so 2.8 x 5 = 14 percent.

legendary.q: The Fed reduces inflation from 9 percent to 5 percent. Output loss equals 10 percent of one year's GDP. Which memo is strongest?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 2.5, so disinflation was costly but not extreme.
The sacrifice ratio is 4, so output loss was smaller than inflation reduction.
The sacrifice ratio is 14, so inflation increased during disinflation.
The sacrifice ratio is 0.4, so the policy had no output cost.
legendary.commonError: Using the ending inflation rate instead of the inflation reduction.
legendary.feedback: Inflation fell by 4 points, and 10/4 = 2.5.

legendary.q: The Federal Reserve reduces inflation by 6 percentage points. The sacrifice ratio is 1.75. What output loss should be expected?
legendary.commonError: Adding the inflation reduction and sacrifice ratio.
legendary.feedback: Output loss equals 1.75 x 6 = 10.5 percent of one year's output.

legendary.q: A three-year disinflation produces annual output gaps of −2%, −1%, and 0%, cutting inflation from 6.5% to 4.5%. A faster path produces one year at −4% and cuts inflation the same amount. Which comparison is correct?
options: The gradual path ratio is 3; the fast path ratio is 4
Both paths have a ratio of 2
The gradual path ratio is 2; the fast path ratio is 1.5
The gradual path ratio is 1.5; the fast path ratio is 2
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendary.q: Economy A loses 8% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls from 9% to 5%. Economy B loses 6% while inflation falls from 5% to 2%. What can be concluded?
options: A has a ratio of 0.5 and B has a ratio of 0.67
A has a lower ratio because its inflation drop is larger
A has a ratio of 2 and B also has a ratio of 2
A has a ratio of 4 and B has a ratio of 3
legendary.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendary.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

easyBoss.q: Expansionary fiscal policy most directly includes:
options: Higher government purchases or lower taxes.
Lower government purchases or higher taxes.
easyBoss.commonError: Confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy or private behavior.
easyBoss.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government demand or supports private spending.

easyBoss.q: Which fiscal action shifts aggregate demand left through lower disposable income?
easyBoss.commonError: Reversing the effect of taxes on disposable income and consumption.
