easyBoss.feedback: A tax increase reduces disposable income and tends to reduce consumption.

easyBoss.q: Government purchases are:
options: A direct component of aggregate demand.
A direct component of short-run aggregate supply.
easyBoss.commonError: Misplacing government purchases in the macro model.
easyBoss.feedback: Government purchases are included directly in C + I + G + NX.

easyBoss.q: Households spend 75 cents of each additional dollar of disposable income. What does that imply?
options: The marginal propensity to save is 0.75, so the multiplier equals one.
The MPC is 0.75, so repeated spending creates a multiplier greater than one.
Crowding out must eliminate every later spending round.
easyBoss.commonError: Confusing the marginal propensity to consume with the multiplier itself.
easyBoss.feedback: An MPC of 0.75 means each spending round passes along 75 percent of added income, generating further rounds of expenditure.

easyBoss.q: What is the central mechanism of crowding out?
options: Fiscal expansion lowers interest rates and increases private investment.
Higher government spending directly reduces the money supply.
A larger multiplier forces households to stop consuming.
Fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces some private investment spending.
easyBoss.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate and investment effects of fiscal expansion.
easyBoss.feedback: Government borrowing and stronger money demand can raise interest rates, discouraging private investment.

easyBoss.q: Holding other factors constant, which change makes the simple spending multiplier larger?
options: A lower marginal propensity to save.
A higher marginal propensity to save.
A larger amount of crowding out.
A smaller initial change in government purchases.
easyBoss.commonError: Treating more saving as a force that strengthens repeated spending rounds.
easyBoss.feedback: A lower marginal propensity to save means a larger MPC, so more income is respent in each round.

easyBoss.q: Which example is an automatic stabilizer during a recession?
options: The central bank announces a new bond-purchase program.
Congress passes a one-time infrastructure bill.
A state raises sales taxes to balance its budget.
Unemployment-benefit payments rise without a new legislative vote.
easyBoss.commonError: Confusing automatic fiscal responses with newly enacted discretionary policy.
easyBoss.feedback: Unemployment benefits expand automatically as more workers qualify, supporting income without new legislation.

easyBoss.q: Real output is below potential and inflation pressure is weak. Which demand-management direction is appropriate?
options: Expansionary policy that shifts aggregate demand to the right.
Contractionary policy that shifts aggregate demand left.
A policy that shifts short-run aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect output in the short run.
easyBoss.commonError: Applying contractionary policy to a recessionary gap.
easyBoss.feedback: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can raise aggregate demand and reduce a recessionary gap.

easyBoss.q: Why can a long implementation lag make discretionary stabilization policy harmful?
options: The policy always reduces aggregate demand before it begins.
It may arrive after conditions change and destabilize the economy.
The lag permanently prevents prices from adjusting.
The lag converts fiscal policy into monetary policy.
easyBoss.commonError: Treating delayed policy as harmless regardless of the business-cycle phase.
easyBoss.feedback: A delayed response can arrive after recovery or after inflation has eased, creating a procyclical rather than stabilizing effect.

easyBoss.q: Households become more confident about future income and increase planned consumption at every price level. What happens?
options: There is movement up along aggregate demand.
easyBoss.commonError: Confusing movement along AD with a rightward shift.
easyBoss.feedback: Higher planned consumption at each price level shifts aggregate demand right.

easyBoss.q: The horizontal axis of an AD-AS graph measures:
easyBoss.commonError: Reversing the graph axes.
easyBoss.feedback: Real GDP or real output appears on the horizontal axis.

easyBoss.q: A higher price level, by itself, causes:
options: Movement upward along the AD curve.
easyBoss.commonError: Treating the price level as an AD shifter.
easyBoss.feedback: The price level is on the vertical axis, so its change causes movement along AD.

easyBoss.q: Which change shifts SRAS right?
easyBoss.commonError: Reversing the effect of input costs.
easyBoss.feedback: Lower input prices reduce production costs.

easyBoss.q: An unexpected price-level increase with sticky wages causes movement:
easyBoss.commonError: Confusing movement along the curve with a shift.
easyBoss.feedback: The actual price level changes quantity supplied along the existing SRAS curve.

easyBoss.q: LRAS is vertical because long-run output depends primarily on:
easyBoss.commonError: Treating the price level as the source of long-run output.
easyBoss.feedback: Potential output is determined by productive capacity.

easyBoss.q: In the long-run AD–AS model, natural output is determined mainly by:
options: Labor, capital, natural resources, technology, and institutions.
The latest movement in aggregate demand alone.
The nominal money supply with no real-side conditions.
easyBoss.commonError: Treating natural output as a price-level or demand choice.
easyBoss.feedback: Natural output reflects the economy’s productive capacity and real institutions.

easyBoss.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy is operating at Y3 rather than the LRAS level Y1, which condition is consistent with the gap shown?
options: An inflationary gap with unemployment below its natural rate.
Long-run equilibrium with no pressure on wages or expected prices.
A permanent increase in potential output from Y1 to Y3.
A recessionary gap with unemployment above its natural rate.
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses the highest output shown with potential output or reverses recessionary and inflationary gaps.
easyBoss.feedback: Compare current real output with the LRAS/potential-output level: below potential is recessionary; above potential is inflationary.

easyBoss.q: A sharp fall in household spending is primarily what kind of macroeconomic disturbance?
easyBoss.commonError: Confusing a spending disturbance with a production-cost disturbance.
easyBoss.feedback: Household spending is a component of aggregate demand, so a sharp decline shifts aggregate demand left.

easyBoss.q: An unexpected increase in energy costs usually shifts which curve first?
options: Long-run aggregate supply shifts right immediately.
easyBoss.commonError: Treating a production-cost shock as a demand shock.
easyBoss.feedback: Higher energy costs raise firms’ costs and reduce output supplied at each price level, shifting short-run aggregate supply left.

easyBoss.q: A negative aggregate-demand shock normally causes what short-run combination?
options: Lower real output and a higher price level.
Higher real output and a lower price level.
Lower real output and a lower price level.
Higher real output and a higher price level.
easyBoss.commonError: Reversing the price-level effect of a demand contraction.
easyBoss.feedback: A leftward aggregate-demand shift reduces both equilibrium output and the price level in the short run.

easyBoss.q: Output is below potential and unemployment is unusually high. If policymakers do nothing, which pressure is part of the opening self-correction mechanism?
options: Weak labor demand restrains wage and cost growth, creating pressure for SRAS to shift right.
High unemployment automatically shifts aggregate demand right.
Weak labor demand shifts LRAS left by definition.
High unemployment causes SRAS to shift left through higher wage growth.
easyBoss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
easyBoss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

easyBoss.q: On a given SRPC, which combination lies farther up and left?
easyBoss.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
easyBoss.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

easyBoss.q: Expected inflation is unchanged and aggregate demand falls. What happens first?
options: The economy moves up and left along its SRPC
The economy moves down and right along its SRPC
The SRPC shifts upward at every unemployment rate
The LRPC shifts left of the natural rate
easyBoss.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
easyBoss.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

easyBoss.q: Which event most directly shifts rather than moves along the SRPC?
options: An unexpected change in aggregate demand
A temporary change in real spending
A movement between two points on one curve
easyBoss.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
easyBoss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

easyBoss.q: At what unemployment rate is the LRPC located?
easyBoss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
easyBoss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

easyBoss.q: What makes the LRPC vertical?
options: Expected inflation adjusts in the long run
Aggregate demand never changes output even temporarily
Inflation must remain constant at every natural-rate point
Unemployment cannot change during a short-run demand surprise
easyBoss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
easyBoss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

easyBoss.q: Which event can shift the LRPC?
options: A one-time surprise demand expansion with fixed expectations
A movement along the current SRPC after demand changes
A temporary inflation forecast error in wage contracts
A structural change in the natural rate
easyBoss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
easyBoss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

easyBoss.q: If expected inflation increases, which SRPC change follows?
options: Only movement down the same curve
easyBoss.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
easyBoss.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

easyBoss.q: If expected inflation decreases, which SRPC change follows?
options: Only movement up the same curve
easyBoss.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
easyBoss.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

easyBoss.q: Why can actual inflation above expected inflation temporarily reduce unemployment?
options: Higher inflation permanently raises labor productivity
Some wages and prices were set using the lower forecast
The natural rate immediately becomes lower
easyBoss.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
easyBoss.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

easyBoss.q: Inflation drops from 5% to 2% while prices still rise. What is occurring?
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
easyBoss.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

easyBoss.q: Which policy direction normally lowers aggregate demand to pursue disinflation?
easyBoss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
easyBoss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

easyBoss.q: What is the usual short-run Phillips cost of disinflation?
easyBoss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
easyBoss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

easyBoss.q: Which formula states the sacrifice ratio?
options: Price-level decline over the episode ÷ nominal GDP growth
Cumulative output loss ÷ inflation reduction in percentage points
Inflation reduction in points ÷ cumulative output loss relative to potential
Permanent unemployment increase ÷ the final positive inflation rate
easyBoss.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easyBoss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

easyBoss.q: Inflation falls from 6% to 4%. What is the denominator?
easyBoss.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
easyBoss.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

easyBoss.q: A ratio of 2 is best read as what?
options: Inflation falls two percent for every percentage point of unemployment added
Unemployment stays two points above natural after expectations completely adjust
The price level declines two percent in each year of disinflation
Two percent of one year’s output lost per inflation point reduced
easyBoss.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
easyBoss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

mediumBoss.q: A $100 billion tax cut with MPC 0.8 raises first-round consumption by:
mediumBoss.commonError: Using the MPS or multiplier too early.
mediumBoss.feedback: MPC times the tax cut gives the first-round consumption increase.

mediumBoss.q: A cut in government purchases shifts AD left because it directly reduces:
mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing an AD shift with an AS or banking change.
mediumBoss.feedback: Government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.

mediumBoss.q: A tax cut has a weak AD effect when households:
options: Save most of the increase in disposable income.
Face a high marginal propensity to consume.
Increase consumption by more than the tax cut.
mediumBoss.commonError: Ignoring the consumption response.
mediumBoss.feedback: More saving means less immediate consumption and a smaller rightward AD shift.

mediumBoss.q: Government purchases rise by $20 billion and the MPC is 0.50. Ignoring crowding out, what is the predicted total increase in aggregate demand?
mediumBoss.commonError: Using the MPC itself as the multiplier or ignoring the repeated-spending process.
mediumBoss.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1 - 0.50) = 2, so a $20 billion increase produces a $40 billion gross shift.

mediumBoss.q: A fiscal package creates a gross $120 billion increase in aggregate demand, but higher interest rates reduce investment by $25 billion. What is the net shift?
mediumBoss.commonError: Adding the crowded-out investment to the gross effect rather than subtracting it.
mediumBoss.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the expansion: $120 billion minus $25 billion equals a $95 billion net increase.

mediumBoss.q: Why can an equal-dollar tax cut create a smaller initial aggregate-demand shift than an equal increase in government purchases?
options: Tax cuts always raise interest rates before households receive them.
Government purchases do not pass through the multiplier process.
Tax cuts reduce disposable income before they affect consumption.
Tax cuts are partly saved; government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.
mediumBoss.commonError: Assuming every dollar of a tax cut is spent immediately.
mediumBoss.feedback: Only the consumed portion of a tax cut enters the first spending round, whereas government purchases are direct expenditure.

mediumBoss.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises inflation and lowers real output. Why is stabilization difficult?
options: Both inflation and output automatically improve with any expansionary policy.
The shock shifts aggregate demand, so only tax policy can respond.
Supporting output may worsen inflation; fighting inflation may deepen the output loss.
Monetary and fiscal policy have identical effects on short-run aggregate supply.
mediumBoss.commonError: Treating a negative supply shock like a pure demand recession.
mediumBoss.feedback: A negative supply shock creates stagflation, forcing policymakers to weigh competing inflation and output objectives.

mediumBoss.q: The economy is near potential output, yet fiscal and monetary policy both become strongly expansionary. What is the main risk?
options: Aggregate demand must fall because the policies cancel each other.
Long-run aggregate supply immediately shifts left.
Crowding out guarantees that output and prices do not change.
Aggregate demand may overshoot capacity and increase inflation.
mediumBoss.commonError: Assuming two expansionary policies cannot create excessive aggregate demand.
mediumBoss.feedback: When both policies push spending upward near capacity, the combined demand increase can create an inflationary gap.

mediumBoss.q: The central bank tightens monetary policy while the government enacts fiscal expansion. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
options: The net effect is uncertain because the policies work in opposite directions.
Aggregate demand must rise because fiscal policy always dominates.
Aggregate demand must fall because monetary policy always dominates.
Both policies shift aggregate demand to the right.
mediumBoss.commonError: Declaring a definite outcome without comparing the strength of opposing policy impulses.
mediumBoss.feedback: Fiscal expansion pushes aggregate demand right, while monetary contraction pushes it left; the net change depends on magnitudes.

mediumBoss.q: Firms expect stronger future sales. Aggregate demand shifts:
options: Nowhere because expectations affect only SRAS.
mediumBoss.commonError: Linking business expectations to the wrong component.
mediumBoss.feedback: More optimistic firms tend to increase investment spending.

mediumBoss.q: A higher price level reduces real money balances and consumption. This is the:
mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing the slope mechanisms.
mediumBoss.feedback: The wealth effect works through the purchasing power of money holdings.

mediumBoss.q: Foreign income falls. Domestic aggregate demand tends to:
options: Stay fixed because foreign income is not domestic.
mediumBoss.commonError: Ignoring export demand from foreign buyers.
mediumBoss.feedback: Lower foreign income reduces demand for domestic exports.

mediumBoss.q: Higher expected prices usually shift SRAS:
mediumBoss.commonError: Reversing the expectation effect.
mediumBoss.feedback: Higher expected prices tend to raise nominal wages and costs.

mediumBoss.q: A sharp fall in oil prices tends to shift SRAS:
mediumBoss.commonError: Reversing the input-cost effect.
mediumBoss.feedback: Cheaper energy lowers production costs.

mediumBoss.q: A permanent rise in productivity most directly shifts:
mediumBoss.commonError: Misclassifying a capacity improvement.
mediumBoss.feedback: Higher productivity raises potential output.

mediumBoss.q: A surge in business investment shifts aggregate demand right. In the short run, what happens other things equal?
options: Real output rises and the price level falls.
Real output falls and the price level rises.
Real output and the price level both fall.
Real output and the price level both rise.
mediumBoss.commonError: Using supply-shock outcomes for a demand expansion.
mediumBoss.feedback: A rightward aggregate-demand shift moves the economy to higher short-run output and a higher price level.

mediumBoss.q: A widespread crop failure raises food-production costs. Which short-run outcome is most likely?
options: Real output falls while the price level rises.
Real output rises while the price level falls.
Real output and the price level both rise.
Real output and the price level both fall.
mediumBoss.commonError: Forgetting that an adverse supply shock creates stagflation pressure.
mediumBoss.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts short-run aggregate supply left, lowering output and raising the price level.

mediumBoss.q: Aggregate demand falls while short-run aggregate supply is unchanged. Which policy direction would most directly offset the output loss?
options: A policy that shifts aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect aggregate demand.
mediumBoss.commonError: Choosing contractionary policy during a demand-driven recession.
mediumBoss.feedback: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can shift aggregate demand right and counter a negative demand shock.

mediumBoss.q: An economy has a recessionary gap and policymakers do nothing. Which self-correcting sequence is most consistent with the model?
options: Higher wages shift SRAS left and deepen the recessionary gap.
LRAS shifts left until potential output equals the depressed output level.
Lower wage and price expectations shift SRAS right toward potential.
Aggregate demand rises automatically because the current price level is fixed.
mediumBoss.commonError: Reversing the wage and SRAS adjustment in a recessionary gap.
mediumBoss.feedback: Below-potential output puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, allowing SRAS to shift right.

mediumBoss.q: An economy is above potential because of a temporary surge in household spending. Which observation would be the strongest evidence that long-run self-correction has begun?
options: Aggregate demand is automatically shifting left with no change in spending.
Nominal wage growth is falling, pushing SRAS farther to the right.
Nominal wage and unit-cost growth are rising, putting leftward pressure on SRAS.
Potential output is falling simply because current output is high.
mediumBoss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
mediumBoss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

mediumBoss.q: Refer to the graph. At AD1 and AS1 the economy is at Y3, below Y1. If AD1 remains fixed, which change must occur for self-correction toward Y1?
options: SRAS shifts farther left from AS1, reducing output below Y3.
Falling wage and price expectations shift SRAS right from AS1 toward AS2.
Aggregate demand shifts from AD1 to AD2 while SRAS remains at AS1.
LRAS shifts left from Y1 to Y3 because output is currently low.
mediumBoss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
mediumBoss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing the Phillips curve with the AD-AS model.
mediumBoss.q: What does the short-run Phillips curve show?
options: A short-run tradeoff between inflation and unemployment
A long-run tradeoff between inflation and output
A fixed relationship between money supply and GDP
A direct measure of government spending
mediumBoss.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation.

mediumBoss.commonError: Reversing the short-run inflation-unemployment tradeoff.
mediumBoss.q: Expansionary policy raises aggregate demand. In the short run, what Phillips curve movement should follow?
mediumBoss.feedback: Expansionary policy raises AD, which can lower unemployment but raises inflation in the short run.

mediumBoss.q: Aggregate demand contracts unexpectedly while expected inflation is initially fixed. What short-run Phillips-curve movement is most likely?
options: Toward lower inflation and higher unemployment.
Toward higher inflation and lower unemployment.
The entire SRPC shifts up-right immediately.
Unemployment stays fixed at the natural rate in the short run.
mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing a demand-driven movement along the SRPC with a shift of the curve.
mediumBoss.feedback: An unexpected demand contraction moves the economy down and right along the current SRPC.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing the short-run and long-run Phillips curves.
mediumBoss.q: What does the vertical long-run Phillips curve represent?
mediumBoss.feedback: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

mediumBoss.commonError: Reading the natural rate from the wrong point.
mediumBoss.q: On the graph, where does the LRPC identify the natural rate of unemployment?
mediumBoss.feedback: The LRPC is drawn at U2, so U2 is the natural rate of unemployment.

mediumBoss.q: Unemployment is below natural and actual inflation exceeds expected inflation. What long-run adjustment follows?
options: Expected inflation falls and SRPC shifts downward
Natural unemployment disappears as inflation continues
Expected inflation rises and unemployment returns toward natural
LRPC shifts left and locks in the lower unemployment
mediumBoss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
mediumBoss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

mediumBoss.commonError: Treating expected inflation as movement along the same SRPC.
mediumBoss.q: What happens to the short-run Phillips curve when expected inflation rises?
options: It becomes the money demand curve
mediumBoss.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the short-run Phillips curve upward.

mediumBoss.commonError: Keeping unemployment below natural forever after an inflation surprise.
mediumBoss.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at c, expansionary policy moves the economy to a. After expected inflation rises, where does the economy move?
mediumBoss.feedback: After expected inflation rises, the SRPC shifts up and the economy moves to b at the natural rate of unemployment.

mediumBoss.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises firms’ costs. What happens to the short-run Phillips curve, other things equal?
options: It shifts down and to the left.
The economy only moves along an unchanged curve.
It shifts up and to the right.
It becomes vertical at zero unemployment.
mediumBoss.commonError: Treating an adverse supply shock as a movement along a fixed SRPC.
mediumBoss.feedback: An adverse supply shock can raise both inflation and unemployment, shifting the SRPC up-right.

mediumBoss.commonError: Ignoring the short-run unemployment cost of reducing inflation.
mediumBoss.q: What does contractionary monetary policy do on the short-run Phillips curve?
options: It lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run
It raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run
It lowers both inflation and unemployment immediately
It raises both inflation and unemployment immediately
mediumBoss.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy can reduce inflation, but it usually raises unemployment temporarily.

mediumBoss.commonError: Skipping the short-run move before expectations adjust.
mediumBoss.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at b, the Fed reduces inflation below expectations. Where does the economy move in the short run?
mediumBoss.feedback: Starting at b, lower actual inflation moves the economy to d: lower inflation and higher unemployment.

mediumBoss.q: A trusted announcement lowers expected inflation. What is the relevant Phillips mechanism?
options: SRPC shifts upward because credibility raises the announced inflation target
Aggregate demand expands automatically without any change in policy instruments
SRPC can shift downward before all actual inflation adjustment occurs
LRPC shifts left and eliminates the natural rate before contracts reset
mediumBoss.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
mediumBoss.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing the sacrifice ratio with the inflation rate itself.
mediumBoss.q: What does the sacrifice ratio measure?
options: The output cost of reducing inflation
The unemployment rate at zero inflation
The tax increase needed to raise AD
mediumBoss.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing inflation.

mediumBoss.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
mediumBoss.q: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points. If the sacrifice ratio is 4, what output loss should be expected?
mediumBoss.feedback: Output loss equals sacrifice ratio times inflation reduction, so 4 x 3 = 12 percent of one year's output.

mediumBoss.q: Loss is 10% of annual GDP and inflation falls 4 points. What is the ratio?
options: 2.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
mediumBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
mediumBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

finalBoss.q: Which policy combination is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: higher government spending or lower taxes
lower government spending or higher taxes
finalBoss.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy
finalBoss.feedback: Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxes. Expansionary fiscal policy raises G or lowers T.

finalBoss.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $120 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
finalBoss.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
finalBoss.feedback: First-round consumption rises by MPC times the tax cut: 0.8 x $120 billion = $96 billion.

finalBoss.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $120 billion. MPC = 0.8. If the first-round consumption increase enters the multiplier process, what is the total AD increase before crowding out?
finalBoss.commonError: multiplying the full tax cut by the multiplier before applying MPC
finalBoss.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is $96 billion. With MPC 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so AD rises $480 billion.

finalBoss.q: Why can an initial increase in spending generate a larger total increase in aggregate demand?
options: raises income and causes additional consumption spending
finalBoss.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the first spending round
finalBoss.feedback: The multiplier happens because spending becomes income, and part of that income is spent again.

finalBoss.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the gross AD shift before crowding out?
finalBoss.commonError: using MPC instead of the multiplier
finalBoss.feedback: MPC 0.75 gives multiplier 4. Gross AD shift is $80 billion x 4 = $320 billion.

finalBoss.q: Government spending rises by $80 billion, MPC = 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $70 billion. What is the net AD shift?
finalBoss.commonError: forgetting to subtract crowding out after applying the multiplier
finalBoss.feedback: Gross AD shift is $320 billion. Subtract $70 billion of crowding out, leaving $250 billion.

finalBoss.q: If output is below its natural level because aggregate demand is weak, stabilization policy would usually try to
finalBoss.commonError: using contractionary policy during weak demand
finalBoss.feedback: If AD is too weak, expansionary policy can shift AD right.

finalBoss.q: The economy has a recessionary AD gap of $500 billion. Monetary policy raises investment by $50 billion and fiscal policy raises government spending by $60 billion. If MPC = 0.75 and there is no crowding out, what happens?
options: AD rises $440 billion, leaving a $60 billion gap.
AD rises $110 billion, leaving a $390 billion gap.
AD rises $500 billion, closing the gap exactly.
finalBoss.commonError: not applying the multiplier to the combined spending impulse
finalBoss.feedback: Initial impulse is $50 billion + $60 billion = $110 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $440 billion, leaving a $60 billion gap.

finalBoss.q: A recessionary AD gap is $500 billion. Monetary policy raises investment by $50 billion, fiscal policy raises government spending by $60 billion, MPC = 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $40 billion. What gap remains?
finalBoss.commonError: not subtracting crowding out after applying the multiplier
finalBoss.feedback: Initial impulse is $110 billion. Multiplier is 4, so gross AD rise is $440 billion. Subtract $40 billion crowding out, net AD rise is $400 billion. A $100 billion gap remains.

finalBoss.q: The price level falls while firms cut investment. What occurs?
options: Movement downward along AD plus a leftward AD shift.
finalBoss.commonError: Failing to separate price-level movement from a spending shift.
finalBoss.feedback: The lower price level changes quantity demanded; lower investment shifts AD left.

finalBoss.q: Consumer confidence rises and the currency appreciates. The net AD direction is:
options: No change because the effects are equal
Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall.
finalBoss.commonError: Assuming offsetting shifters cancel exactly.
finalBoss.feedback: The two components move in opposite directions, and magnitudes matter.

finalBoss.q: Why does a higher price level reduce investment along AD?
options: Higher prices reduce expected input costs.
Higher money demand tends to raise interest rates.
Higher prices directly raise productive capacity.
finalBoss.commonError: Confusing AD slope with supply-side changes.
finalBoss.feedback: The interest-rate effect links a higher price level to less investment.

finalBoss.q: Expected prices fall while actual prices are unchanged. SRAS shifts:
finalBoss.commonError: Reversing lower expected cost pressure.
finalBoss.feedback: Lower expected prices tend to lower nominal wages and costs.

finalBoss.q: A price-level rise by itself causes:
options: Movement up along SRAS, not a shift of SRAS.
finalBoss.commonError: Confusing an axis change with a curve shifter.
finalBoss.feedback: Actual price level changes quantity supplied along SRAS.

finalBoss.q: A permanent labor-force increase occurs with a temporary oil-price spike. Which curves move?
finalBoss.commonError: Combining capacity and cost changes incorrectly.
finalBoss.feedback: More labor raises capacity; expensive oil reduces short-run supply.

finalBoss.q: Real GDP is below its old potential level after a permanent decline in labor-force participation. Which diagnostic prevents a mistaken forecast that ordinary self-correction must restore the old output level?
options: Check whether LRAS itself shifted left; if potential output fell, the old level is no longer the long-run anchor.
Assume every output decline is caused by aggregate demand.
Hold LRAS fixed because productive capacity cannot change.
Assume falling wages always restore the pre-shock quantity of labor and output.
finalBoss.commonError: Assumes every fall in real GDP is a temporary gap around an unchanged potential-output level.
finalBoss.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

finalBoss.q: Aggregate demand rises while short-run aggregate supply falls. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Real output rises, while the price level is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output rises.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
Both the price level and real output fall.
finalBoss.commonError: Claiming certainty about output when the two shocks move output in opposite directions.
finalBoss.feedback: Both shifts raise the price level, but aggregate demand raises output while adverse supply lowers it.

finalBoss.q: Aggregate demand falls while short-run aggregate supply rises. Which outcome is certain?
options: Real output falls, while the price level is uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output is uncertain.
finalBoss.commonError: Missing the shared price-level direction of the two shifts.
finalBoss.feedback: A demand contraction and favorable supply shock both lower the price level, but they push output in opposite directions.

finalBoss.q: After an adverse supply shock, policymakers use expansionary demand policy to restore output. Which risk remains?
options: The price level may rise even more than it did from the original shock.
Unemployment must rise because aggregate demand increased.
Short-run aggregate supply automatically returns to its old position.
The economy must move below potential output.
finalBoss.commonError: Assuming output stabilization eliminates the inflation tradeoff.
finalBoss.feedback: Demand expansion can support output after a supply shock, but it adds inflation pressure rather than repairing supply.

finalBoss.q: Demand growth pushes output above potential. If no stabilization policy is used, which long-run adjustment is most likely?
options: Falling wages shift SRAS right and push output farther above potential.
LRAS shifts right solely because the current price level has increased.
Output stays permanently above potential without creating inflation pressure.
Rising costs shift SRAS left, returning output to potential at a higher price level.
finalBoss.commonError: Using recessionary-gap adjustment for an inflationary gap.
finalBoss.feedback: An overheated labor market raises costs and expected prices, shifting SRAS left and closing the inflationary gap.

finalBoss.q: Refer to the graph. The economy begins at AD1-AS2 at Y1 and then a demand boom shifts AD to AD2, moving output to Y2. With no policy response, which pair of changes completes long-run adjustment?
options: AD shifts back to AD1 automatically; output returns to Y1 at P1.
LRAS shifts right to Y2; output remains above its original potential.
SRAS shifts right beyond AS2; output rises further while the price level falls.
SRAS shifts left toward AS1; output returns to Y1 while the price level rises toward P3.
finalBoss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
finalBoss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

finalBoss.q: A demand boom first lowers unemployment, then wage expectations catch up. Which complete Phillips sequence is most defensible?
options: Shift LRPC left, then move down the same SRPC as expectations rise
Shift SRPC downward, then keep unemployment permanently below natural
Move down-right along SRPC, then shift LRPC right after wages adjust
Move up-left along SRPC, then shift SRPC upward toward the natural rate
finalBoss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
finalBoss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

finalBoss.q: A supply disruption raises inflation and unemployment together. Which interpretation survives both the graph and mechanism tests?
options: The LRPC shifts left because inflation increased
The SRPC shifts downward because output fell
The SRPC shifts upward because the tradeoff worsens
The economy moves up-left along a fixed SRPC
finalBoss.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
finalBoss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

finalBoss.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands demand. Which claim correctly separates the short run from the long run?
options: Inflation falls temporarily and remains lower after all contracts adjust
Unemployment may fall temporarily, but expectations adjustment removes the permanent tradeoff
Unemployment falls permanently because the SRPC stays downward sloping after expectations adjust
The SRPC immediately becomes vertical before output or nominal wages can change
finalBoss.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
finalBoss.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

finalBoss.q: A government insists on holding unemployment below the natural rate after inflation expectations have adjusted. What does the long-run Phillips-curve model predict?
options: A stable inflation rate will permanently sustain lower unemployment.
The policy requires continuously accelerating inflation.
Unemployment will fall to zero without further inflation.
The natural rate automatically falls whenever aggregate demand rises.
finalBoss.commonError: Believing a stable higher inflation rate buys a permanent unemployment reduction.
finalBoss.feedback: Once expected inflation catches up, maintaining below-natural unemployment requires repeated new inflation surprises.

finalBoss.q: A policy claim says 6% inflation can permanently hold unemployment below natural. Which model result rejects it?
options: The natural rate falls whenever inflation rises
Expectations adjustment returns unemployment toward the vertical LRPC
The SRPC is always vertical even in the short run
finalBoss.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
finalBoss.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

finalBoss.q: Job-search reform lowers mismatch while inflation expectations are unchanged. Which graph change captures the durable labor effect?
options: The LRPC shifts left to the new natural rate
An upward SRPC shift from higher expected inflation
A permanent move left along one SRPC
finalBoss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
finalBoss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

finalBoss.q: A credible disinflation announcement lowers expected inflation before much demand contraction occurs. Which graph change is most consistent?
options: The economy can only move up-left along the old SRPC
The SRPC shifts downward, potentially reducing the short-run cost
The LRPC shifts right and permanently raises unemployment
The SRPC shifts upward because actual inflation may fall
finalBoss.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
finalBoss.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

finalBoss.q: Actual inflation remains above expected inflation for several contract cycles. Which sequence best fits adaptive expectations?
options: Expected inflation rises, shifting SRPC upward and undoing the temporary unemployment gain
Expected inflation falls, shifting SRPC downward and preserving the unemployment gain indefinitely
LRPC shifts left, locking in unemployment below natural after contracts renew
SRPC stays fixed because only actual inflation matters for wage setting
finalBoss.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
finalBoss.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

finalBoss.q: A supply shock raises inflation without a demand boom. Why might a simple expectations-only diagnosis be incomplete?
options: Expected inflation is the only possible SRPC shifter in the introductory model
Every inflation increase is movement along a fixed SRPC regardless of its cause
Supply shocks shift only the vertical LRPC while leaving SRPC unchanged
The shock can shift the SRPC even before expectations adapt
finalBoss.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
finalBoss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

finalBoss.q: Two central banks pursue the same reduction in inflation. One has strong credibility and expected inflation falls quickly. Compared with the less credible bank, what is the likely transition?
options: A permanently lower natural rate of unemployment.
A larger price-level increase caused by credibility.
A smaller temporary output and unemployment cost.
finalBoss.commonError: Assuming credibility changes the long-run natural rate rather than the transition cost.
finalBoss.feedback: Faster adjustment of expected inflation can reduce the sacrifice required to lower actual inflation.

finalBoss.q: A rapid plan loses 5% of annual GDP to cut inflation 2 points; a gradual plan loses 6% to cut it 3 points. Which has the lower sacrifice ratio?
options: The gradual plan has ratio 3 versus the rapid plan’s 2
The gradual plan has ratio 2 versus the rapid plan’s 2.5
The rapid plan has ratio 2 versus the gradual plan’s 3
Both plans have a sacrifice ratio of 2.5
finalBoss.commonError: Compares total output losses without scaling each by its own inflation reduction.
finalBoss.feedback: The rapid path ratio is 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5; the gradual path ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

finalBoss.q: After contraction raises unemployment above natural, expected inflation falls. What long-run adjustment is expected?
options: SRPC shifts downward and unemployment returns toward natural
LRPC shifts right and locks in higher unemployment
SRPC shifts upward and inflation rises
finalBoss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
finalBoss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

finalBoss.q: Annual output gaps are −1%, −2%, and −1%; inflation falls from 7% to 5%. What is the ratio?
options: 2% of one year’s output per inflation point
finalBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
finalBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

finalBoss.q: A report divides cumulative output loss by the final inflation rate. What correction is required?
options: Divide by the percentage-point reduction in inflation
Divide by the initial inflation rate before the policy began
Multiply by the final inflation rate
finalBoss.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
finalBoss.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

finalBoss.q: Path X loses 7.2% of annual GDP to reduce inflation 3 points. Path Y loses 5% to reduce inflation 2 points. Which is more output-efficient?
options: Path Y, with a ratio of 2 versus 2.4
Path X, with a ratio of 3 versus 2
They are equal because both lower inflation
Path X, with a ratio of 2.4 versus 2.5
finalBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
finalBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the multiplier graph. A $60 billion tax cut raises disposable income, and MPC = 0.75. What is the correct order of AD effects before crowding out?
options: Consumption first rises $45 billion, then the multiplier expands the AD shift to $180 billion.
AD first rises $60 billion, then the multiplier expands it to $240 billion.
Consumption first rises $15 billion, then AD rises $60 billion.
AD falls $45 billion, then the multiplier reduces it by $180 billion.
legendaryBoss.commonError: multiplying the full tax cut by the spending multiplier without first applying MPC
legendaryBoss.feedback: First-round consumption rises 0.75 x $60 billion = $45 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $180 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: Government purchases rise $90 billion and taxes rise $60 billion. MPC is 0.75. What is the net first-round change in AD?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Failing to distinguish the direct spending effect from the tax-induced consumption effect.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Purchases add $90 billion; taxes reduce consumption by $45 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: A $200 billion tax cut reaches two equal groups. One group spends 80 percent and the other spends 40 percent. What is the combined first-round consumption increase?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Applying one group’s MPC to the entire tax cut.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Each group receives $100 billion; spending rises $80 billion plus $40 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: Government spending rises by $90 billion and MPC = 0.8. Crowding out reduces investment by $180 billion. What is the correct order of AD effects?
options: AD first shifts right $90 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $450 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $270 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $450 billion, then crowding out increases the shift to $630 billion.
AD first shifts left $90 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $450 billion, then crowding out leaves $270 billion.
AD shifts right only $90 billion because crowding out eliminates the multiplier.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not following initial shift, multiplier shift, then crowding-out offset
legendaryBoss.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5. The $90 billion initial shift becomes $450 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $270 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: The initial government-spending shift is $100 billion and the final AD shift is $400 billion. What MPC is implied, and what is the correct shift order?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then to $400 billion; MPC = 0.75.
AD first shifts right $400 billion, then back to $100 billion; MPC = 0.75.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then left $400 billion; MPC = 0.25.
AD first shifts right $100 billion, then to $400 billion; MPC = 0.8.
legendaryBoss.commonError: treating final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: The multiplier is 400/100 = 4. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 4, MPC = 0.75.

legendaryBoss.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. Expansionary fiscal policy also raises interest rates through crowding out. What happens to investment if both effects occur?
options: Investment falls from both interest-rate channels.
Investment rises from both interest-rate channels.
Investment rises from the money-demand channel but falls from crowding out.
Investment is unaffected because r is not connected to investment.
legendaryBoss.commonError: tracking only one interest-rate channel
legendaryBoss.feedback: Higher money demand raises r. Crowding out also raises r. Higher r reduces investment.

legendaryBoss.q: AD is weak by $500 billion. Government spending rises by $80 billion, investment rises by $40 billion, and MPC = 0.75. Ignoring crowding out, what happens to the gap?
options: AD rises $480 billion, leaving a $20 billion gap.
AD rises $120 billion, leaving a $380 billion gap.
AD rises $500 billion, closing the gap exactly.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not adding investment and government spending before applying the multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial spending impulse is $80 billion + $40 billion = $120 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $480 billion, leaving a $20 billion gap.

legendaryBoss.q: Output is above potential by $360 billion. The Fed uses contractionary monetary policy, and the investment response is $50 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what overheating gap remains?
options: No gap remains; policy overshoots by $110 billion.
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the investment decrease without applying the multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph shows contractionary policy. MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so AD falls $250 billion. The remaining overheating gap is $110 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: A recessionary AD gap is $600 billion. Government spending rises $100 billion, MPC = 0.8, and crowding out is $150 billion. What is the correct order and remaining gap?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then gross shift reaches $500 billion, then crowding out leaves $350 billion net and a $250 billion gap.
AD first shifts right $600 billion, then crowding out leaves $450 billion net and a $150 billion gap.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then gross shift reaches $500 billion, worsening the gap.
AD shifts right only $100 billion because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
legendaryBoss.commonError: forgetting that crowding out reduces the gross multiplier effect
legendaryBoss.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so gross shift is $500 billion. Net after $150 billion crowding out is $350 billion, leaving a $250 billion gap.

legendaryBoss.q: Contractionary monetary policy is used when the economy is already above potential output. What is the likely effect?
options: It may reduce inflation pressure because it shifts AD left when AD is too high.
It worsens inflation pressure because it shifts AD right.
It cannot affect AD because output is above potential.
It directly shifts SRAS right and fixes supply constraints.
legendaryBoss.commonError: reading the contractionary graph as expansionary policy
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. If AD is too high, that can reduce inflation pressure.

legendaryBoss.q: A contractionary monetary-policy move reduces investment by $60 billion. A separate fiscal expansion raises AD by $400 billion after the multiplier. If MPC = 0.75, what is the final net AD effect?
legendaryBoss.commonError: subtracting only the initial investment drop instead of its multiplied AD effect
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy. A $60 billion investment fall times multiplier 4 reduces AD by $240 billion. Net effect is $400 billion - $240 billion = +$160 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: If policymakers use contractionary monetary policy during a negative supply shock, what is the strongest critique?
options: It may reduce inflation pressure but can worsen the output loss because AD shifts left.
It directly restores lost supply while keeping output unchanged.
It shifts AD right and raises output without inflation risk.
It eliminates the need to consider SRAS.
legendaryBoss.commonError: treating every supply shock as if AD policy has no tradeoff
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. That can cool inflation pressure, but during a negative supply shock it may deepen the output loss.

legendaryBoss.q: The price level rises, taxes fall, and foreign income falls. Which description is correct?
options: Movement upward along AD, a rightward tax-cut shift, and a leftward net-export shift.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Combining three distinct forces into one curve change.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The price level causes movement; taxes and foreign income shift AD in opposite directions.

legendaryBoss.q: Consumer confidence falls, investment expectations improve, and the currency depreciates. Which components move?
options: Consumption falls, investment rises, and net exports rise.
Consumption rises, investment falls, and net exports fall.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mapping shifters to the wrong components.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Confidence affects C, business expectations affect I, and depreciation affects NX.

legendaryBoss.q: A lower price level raises real balances, lowers interest rates, and weakens the currency. Which AD result follows?
options: SRAS shifts right because interest rates fell
Consumption, investment, and net exports tend to rise along the curve.
AD shifts right because the price level fell
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treating movement along AD as a curve shift.
legendaryBoss.feedback: All three classic channels raise quantity demanded at the lower price level.

legendaryBoss.q: Productivity rises permanently, expected prices rise, and oil prices fall. What is the most accurate result?
options: LRAS is unchanged and SRAS shifts left.
LRAS shifts right; the SRAS direction is ambiguous.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Forcing offsetting SRAS shifters into one predetermined direction.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Productivity raises capacity; expected prices and oil prices push SRAS in opposite directions.

legendaryBoss.q: Nominal wages are fixed when the price level unexpectedly rises, then contracts reset with higher expected inflation. What sequence follows?
options: Movement up along SRAS, then a leftward SRAS shift.
A rightward SRAS shift, then movement down.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Failing to separate current movement from later expectation adjustment.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Unexpected prices first change quantity supplied; updated wage expectations later shift SRAS.

legendaryBoss.q: Capital is destroyed while a new technology raises productivity. Which LRAS conclusion is valid?
options: LRAS cannot shift because the forces differ
The net direction is ambiguous without the relative output effects.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Comparing opposing capacity changes without magnitudes.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Lost capital and better technology push potential output in opposite directions.

legendaryBoss.q: An economy has a recessionary gap after aggregate demand falls. While wages are adjusting downward, a permanent productivity improvement raises productive capacity. Which conclusion best separates the two long-run forces?
options: The productivity gain shifts aggregate demand right while wage adjustment shifts LRAS left, so both forces alter potential output in opposite directions.
The original demand shock permanently fixes real output below potential, so neither wage adjustment nor improved productivity can change the long-run outcome.
SRAS adjustment helps close the demand-created gap, while higher productivity can shift LRAS right and change the potential-output target.
Both changes should be treated as the same SRAS movement, because productive capacity does not affect the location of LRAS in this model.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes every fall in real GDP is a temporary gap around an unchanged potential-output level.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

legendaryBoss.q: Government purchases rise while a technology breakthrough lowers unit costs. If output rises but the price level is unchanged, what does the evidence imply?
options: Neither curve shifted because the price level did not change.
The opposing price effects approximately offset while both shifts raise output.
Aggregate demand fell while short-run aggregate supply rose.
Aggregate demand rose while short-run aggregate supply fell.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assuming an unchanged price level means no macroeconomic shifts occurred.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Higher government purchases shift aggregate demand right and better technology shifts short-run aggregate supply right. Both raise output, while their price effects can offset.

legendaryBoss.q: Oil prices rise sharply and the central bank expands aggregate demand enough to keep real output unchanged. Compared with the initial equilibrium, what is most likely?
options: The price level is unchanged because real output is unchanged.
The price level is lower because monetary expansion reduces costs.
The price level is higher because both the supply shock and policy raise it.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because interest rates fall.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Equating stable output with a stable price level.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The adverse supply shock raises the price level, and the demand expansion used to stabilize output adds additional price pressure.

legendaryBoss.q: Consumer spending collapses at the same time firms adopt a major cost-saving technology. Prices fall sharply, but output changes little. Which interpretation fits best?
options: A positive demand shock and adverse supply shock offset in the price level.
Only aggregate demand shifted because prices fell.
Only short-run aggregate supply shifted because output was stable.
A negative demand shock and positive supply shock had offsetting output effects.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Using one observed variable to infer only one curve shifted.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Both shocks lower the price level, while one lowers output and the other raises it. Similar magnitudes can leave output nearly unchanged.

legendaryBoss.q: A negative demand shock leaves the economy below potential, and no policy response occurs. Which statement best identifies the long-run adjustment mechanism before tracing the details?
options: Slack puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, allowing SRAS to shift right.
Aggregate demand must automatically shift right enough to restore potential output without any change in wages or expectations.
LRAS must move left until it passes through current output, eliminating the gap without any cost adjustment.
High unemployment raises wage growth and shifts SRAS left, moving output even farther below potential.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
legendaryBoss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS1 at Y3, expected prices and nominal cost pressures fall gradually while AD1 stays fixed. Which sequence is consistent with the model?
options: SRAS moves farther left from AS1, pushing output below Y3 while the price level rises above its starting point.
AD shifts to AD2 and output jumps to Y2 even though the prompt holds aggregate demand fixed throughout the adjustment.
LRAS shifts left from Y1 to Y3, redefining the depressed output level as potential without any wage or expectation adjustment.
SRAS moves toward AS2, output rises toward Y1, and the price level falls toward P1.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
legendaryBoss.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

legendaryBoss.q: A demand expansion moves unemployment below natural. Wage contracts later incorporate the higher inflation. What is the next Phillips-curve development?
options: The SRPC shifts upward and unemployment moves back toward natural
The economy stays on the original SRPC at permanently lower unemployment
The LRPC shifts left because nominal wages increased
The SRPC shifts downward as expected inflation rises
legendaryBoss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: One episode has rising inflation with falling unemployment; another has rising inflation with rising unemployment. What distinguishes them?
options: Both are identical movements along one unchanged SRPC despite their opposite unemployment changes in the two episodes
The first shifts LRPC left while the second shifts aggregate demand right
Both establish a permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff without expectations adjustment
The first can be demand movement along SRPC; the second can be an adverse supply shift
legendaryBoss.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
legendaryBoss.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

legendaryBoss.q: A government tries repeated demand expansions to hold unemployment one point below natural. Which model-consistent end state is most likely?
options: LRPC shifts left solely because repeated nominal spending increased
Expected inflation falls until deflation permanently restores the initial unemployment rate
Unemployment returns toward natural at a higher inflation rate after expectations adjust
Unemployment remains below natural with unchanged inflation after wage contracts renew
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
legendaryBoss.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

legendaryBoss.q: A surprise expansion moves unemployment below natural; later contracts incorporate the higher inflation. What identifies the long-run endpoint?
options: A permanently lower natural rate caused by nominal demand after contracts renew
A horizontal LRPC at the new inflation rate with lower permanent unemployment
Lower inflation with unemployment still below natural after expectations fully adjust
The same natural unemployment rate with higher expected and actual inflation
legendaryBoss.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: A labor-market reform lowers the natural rate while a demand expansion temporarily lowers unemployment even further. Which distinction is essential?
options: Demand shifts LRPC permanently while reform only changes the current inflation rate
Neither change can alter a Phillips curve once expectations are specified
The reform shifts LRPC; the demand expansion creates temporary movement relative to it
Both changes are movements along one unchanged SRPC despite different mechanisms
legendaryBoss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
legendaryBoss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: Two economies have different steady unemployment rates but the same long-run inflation. What can explain the difference without restoring a long-run tradeoff?
options: A common SRPC that never shifts
Different natural rates locate their vertical LRPCs differently
Different inflation rates along the same downward LRPC
Permanent forecast errors in both economies
legendaryBoss.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
legendaryBoss.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

legendaryBoss.q: A surprise expansion lifts inflation from 2% to 5% while expected inflation remains 2%. What makes the unemployment effect temporary?
options: Expected inflation falls below 2% and shifts SRPC downward after workers observe prices
The LRPC becomes flatter as actual inflation rises above expected inflation
Expected inflation eventually rises toward actual inflation and shifts the SRPC upward
The natural rate permanently falls three points once actual inflation exceeds its forecast
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
legendaryBoss.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

legendaryBoss.q: A disinflation announcement is only partly credible and wage contracts reset slowly. Which conclusion is appropriately bounded?
options: The announcement necessarily causes the price level to fall for several years
Expectations may fall gradually, so some short-run output cost can remain
Partial credibility must eliminate every unemployment cost as soon as policy is announced
Expected inflation cannot change until actual inflation reaches the announced target
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

legendaryBoss.q: An adverse supply shock raises actual inflation, then wage setters incorporate it into next year’s contracts. What are the two stages?
options: An initial SRPC shift followed by reinforcement through higher expected inflation
Two movements along one fixed SRPC with no change in the inflation-unemployment relation
An LRPC shift followed by lower expected inflation when contracts renew
A demand contraction followed by an SRPC shift downward at each unemployment rate
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
legendaryBoss.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

legendaryBoss.q: A central bank with mixed credibility begins rapid disinflation. Which full chain is most model-consistent?
options: Demand expands, unemployment falls, and inflation drops immediately without any wage, price, or expectations adjustment
LRPC shifts right permanently because lower inflation raises the natural unemployment rate
Expected inflation rises first and shifts SRPC upward before the contraction begins
Demand contracts, unemployment rises temporarily, expectations fall gradually, and output returns toward potential
legendaryBoss.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

legendaryBoss.q: Policy A cuts inflation 4 points with 8% cumulative output loss. Policy B cuts 2.5 points with 4% loss. Which cost comparison is correct?
options: A has ratio 4; B has ratio 2.5, using final inflation as denominator
Both have ratio 2 because each lowers inflation from a positive starting rate
A has ratio 2; B has ratio 1.6, so B loses less output per point
A has ratio 0.5; B has ratio 0.625, so A has the lower cost
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: Inflation is down to 1% after disinflation, unemployment is back at natural, and the price level is higher than before. Which diagnosis is complete?
options: The price level should have returned to its starting value once unemployment normalized
Disinflation succeeded without requiring deflation; the short-run labor cost has unwound
Deflation occurred because the inflation rate fell even though prices remained higher
The natural rate must now be permanently lower because unemployment first increased
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

legendaryBoss.q: A two-year policy creates output gaps of −2.4% and −1.8%, lowering inflation from 7.0% to 5.2%. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.33% of one year’s output per inflation point
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: A credible plan lowers expected inflation and produces a 3% cumulative output loss for a 2-point inflation reduction. A less credible plan loses 7.5% for a 3-point reduction. Which comparison is correct?
options: The plans are equal because both reduce inflation
The credible plan ratio is 1.5; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 2; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 0.67; the other is 0.4
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

legendaryBoss.q: Potential output is $800 billion. A policy creates gaps of 1.5% for two years and 0.5% for one year while inflation falls 2.8 points. What is cumulative loss per inflation point?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The cumulative loss is 3.5% of $800 billion = $28 billion. Dividing by 2.8 inflation points gives $10 billion per point.
legendaryBoss.roundingRule: Report the exact dollar amount per inflation point.

repairQuestions.q: Congress increases government purchases while taxes and other aggregate-demand determinants are unchanged. Which change should a student predict in the AD-AS model?
repairQuestions.feedback: Government purchases and tax-induced consumption changes work primarily through aggregate demand in this Principles model.
repairQuestions.commonError: Confuses a fiscal-policy change with an aggregate-supply shift.

repairQuestions.q: A $40 billion tax cut raises disposable income and MPC is 0.75. Before later multiplier rounds, how much does consumption increase?
repairQuestions.feedback: The first-round consumption effect equals the change in disposable income times MPC.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the full tax cut as immediate consumption.
Classifies fiscal policy from the state of the economy rather than from what government purchases and taxes actually do.
repairQuestions.q: Congress lowers government purchases and raises taxes in the same bill to reduce excessive aggregate demand. How should the package be classified?
repairQuestions.feedback: Classify the package from its fiscal actions: higher purchases/lower taxes are expansionary; lower purchases/higher taxes are contractionary.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking fiscal expansion shifts AD left.
repairQuestions.q: Higher government spending usually shifts AD:
repairQuestions.feedback: Government spending is part of AD, so higher G shifts AD right.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting taxes work through disposable income and consumption.
repairQuestions.q: A tax cut usually increases:
repairQuestions.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income.

repairQuestions.commonError: Jumps from a tax change directly to total output without identifying the first spending channel.
repairQuestions.q: Why can a tax cut shift aggregate demand to the right in the short run?
options: It raises disposable income, which can raise consumption spending.
It directly increases the money supply.
It directly lowers firms’ production costs and shifts SRAS right.
repairQuestions.feedback: A tax change first changes disposable income, then consumption according to MPC, which shifts aggregate demand.

repairQuestions.q: If MPC = 0.5, the government purchases multiplier is:
repairQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so 1/(1-0.5)=2.

repairQuestions.q: Crowding out happens when fiscal expansion raises rates and reduces:
repairQuestions.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion by reducing private investment.

repairQuestions.q: Why might a tax cut have a smaller immediate effect than an equal increase in government purchases?
options: Households may save part of the tax cut
Government purchases are not part of GDP
repairQuestions.feedback: Some of a tax cut is saved, so its initial spending effect can be smaller than direct government purchases.

repairQuestions.q: The multiplier effect means an initial spending increase can raise AD by:
options: Only less than the initial spending
repairQuestions.feedback: The multiplier occurs when spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

repairQuestions.q: The multiplier effect means an initial increase in government spending can:
options: Create a larger total increase in aggregate demand and output
Affect only the first recipient of spending
Reduce GDP by the same amount
repairQuestions.feedback: Initial spending becomes income for others, whose further spending magnifies the total effect.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using MPC as the multiplier.
repairQuestions.q: The simple spending multiplier equals:
repairQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using MPC directly as the multiplier.
repairQuestions.q: If MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is:

repairQuestions.commonError: Adding crowding out instead of subtracting it.
repairQuestions.q: Crowding out reduces the effect of fiscal expansion by reducing:
repairQuestions.feedback: Crowding out happens when higher interest rates reduce private investment.

repairQuestions.commonError: Adding the crowding-out amount to the multiplier effect.
repairQuestions.q: If gross AD rises $200 billion and crowding out is $50 billion, net AD rises:
repairQuestions.feedback: Crowding out subtracts from the gross effect: $200 - $50 = $150 billion.

repairQuestions.q: Which policy acts automatically to cushion a recession without a new vote by Congress?
options: Unemployment benefits that rise as workers lose jobs
repairQuestions.feedback: Automatic stabilizers change with economic conditions; unemployment benefits rise as unemployment rises.

repairQuestions.q: If output is below potential because AD is weak, policy that shifts AD right is:
repairQuestions.feedback: Expansionary policy shifts AD right and can help close a recessionary gap.

repairQuestions.q: In a liquidity trap, interest rates are often near:
repairQuestions.feedback: A liquidity trap occurs when interest rates are near zero and monetary policy has less room to work.

repairQuestions.q: Policy lags matter because policy may arrive:
repairQuestions.feedback: Policy can become poorly timed if it takes effect after the economy has changed.

repairQuestions.commonError: Assumes a delayed policy has the same stabilizing effect regardless of how the economy changes before implementation.
repairQuestions.q: A stimulus is approved during a recession but takes effect only after output has returned close to potential. What problem should the student diagnose?
options: The delayed stimulus can push aggregate demand too far right after the original gap has faded.
The delay automatically turns the stimulus into contractionary policy.
The policy can no longer affect aggregate demand once recovery begins.
The delay directly shifts LRAS left.
repairQuestions.feedback: A policy can destabilize the economy if it arrives after the original gap has already narrowed or reversed.

repairQuestions.commonError: Choosing tighter policy in a recessionary gap.
repairQuestions.q: A recessionary AD gap can be addressed with:
repairQuestions.feedback: Expansionary policy can shift AD right.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treats a negative supply shock as if policymakers can simultaneously eliminate its inflation and output effects by shifting AD.
repairQuestions.q: A negative supply shock lowers real output and raises the price level. If policymakers use expansionary demand policy to support output, what tradeoff should the student remember?
options: It can support output while worsening inflation pressure.
It lowers the price level and raises output with no tradeoff.
It directly shifts SRAS right and restores productive capacity.
It must reduce both output and the price level.
repairQuestions.feedback: Demand stabilization during a negative supply shock involves a tradeoff: supporting output can worsen price pressure, while reducing inflation can deepen the output loss.

repairQuestions.commonError: Choosing expansionary policy during overheating.
repairQuestions.q: During an inflationary boom caused by excessive AD, policymakers may use:
repairQuestions.feedback: Contractionary policy shifts AD left and reduces inflation pressure.

repairQuestions.q: The AD curve slopes downward partly because a higher price level reduces:
