repairQuestions.feedback: A higher price level reduces spending through wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects.

repairQuestions.q: Higher consumer confidence shifts AD:
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher confidence raises consumption and shifts AD right.

repairQuestions.q: A tax increase usually shifts AD:
repairQuestions.feedback: A tax increase lowers spending and shifts AD left.

repairQuestions.q: The vertical axis on a standard AD-AS graph measures:
repairQuestions.feedback: AD-AS graphs place the price level on the vertical axis and real output on the horizontal axis.

repairQuestions.q: A rightward shift of aggregate demand means:
options: Planned spending is higher at each price level
The price level has moved along AD
repairQuestions.feedback: A shift in AD changes total planned spending at every price level.

repairQuestions.q: Higher expected prices usually shift SRAS:
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher expected prices raise costs and shift SRAS left.

repairQuestions.q: SRAS slopes upward mainly because wages, prices, or perceptions:
repairQuestions.feedback: Sticky wages, sticky prices, and misperceptions help explain upward-sloping SRAS.

repairQuestions.q: Higher production costs shift SRAS:
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher production costs reduce SRAS and shift it left.

repairQuestions.q: Lower production costs shift SRAS:
repairQuestions.feedback: Lower production costs increase SRAS and shift it right.

repairQuestions.q: A leftward shift of SRAS means:
options: Firms supply less output at each price level
The money supply fell by definition
repairQuestions.feedback: A leftward SRAS shift reflects higher costs or lower productive capacity in the short run.

repairQuestions.q: LRAS is vertical because long-run output depends mainly on:
repairQuestions.feedback: LRAS reflects productive capacity, not the current price level.

repairQuestions.q: When real output is below natural output, unemployment is usually:
repairQuestions.feedback: A recessionary gap means firms need fewer workers, so unemployment tends to exceed the natural rate.

repairQuestions.q: In an AD-AS graph, short-run equilibrium occurs where:
options: Aggregate demand intersects short-run aggregate supply
repairQuestions.feedback: The intersection of AD and SRAS determines the short-run equilibrium price level and real output.

repairQuestions.q: If output is below natural output, the economy has:
repairQuestions.feedback: Output below natural output is a recessionary gap.

repairQuestions.q: If output is above natural output, the economy has:
repairQuestions.feedback: Output above natural output is an expansionary gap.

repairQuestions.q: On an AD-AS graph, natural output is the output level where:
repairQuestions.feedback: Natural output is potential output, the economy's sustainable long-run production level.

repairQuestions.q: A sharp fall in consumer confidence is primarily which kind of shock?
repairQuestions.feedback: Lower consumer confidence reduces consumption and shifts aggregate demand left.

repairQuestions.q: A sudden rise in oil prices is primarily which kind of shock?
options: A change in the money multiplier
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher input costs shift SRAS left, making this a negative supply shock.

repairQuestions.q: Stagflation combines:
options: Balanced budgets and low interest rates
repairQuestions.feedback: Stagflation is the difficult combination of rising prices and weak employment/output conditions.

repairQuestions.q: An adverse supply shock creates a policy problem because inflation and unemployment can:
repairQuestions.feedback: Adverse supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment together.

repairQuestions.q: If AD falls while SRAS also falls, what outcome is certain?
repairQuestions.feedback: Both a leftward AD shift and a leftward SRAS shift reduce equilibrium output; their price-level effects conflict.

repairQuestions.q: A negative AD shock usually causes output and the price level to:
repairQuestions.feedback: A negative AD shock lowers output and the price level.

repairQuestions.q: An adverse supply shock usually causes output to fall and prices to:
repairQuestions.feedback: An adverse supply shock lowers output and raises prices.

repairQuestions.q: If output is below natural output, falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS:
repairQuestions.feedback: A recessionary gap tends to push wages and expected prices down, shifting SRAS right.

repairQuestions.q: If output is above natural output, rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS:
repairQuestions.feedback: An expansionary gap tends to push wages and expected prices up, shifting SRAS left.

repairQuestions.q: A demand increase raises inflation and lowers unemployment while expectations are unchanged. Is this a movement or a shift?
options: A movement along the current SRPC
An upward shift of the entire SRPC
A leftward shift of the LRPC
A downward shift of the entire SRPC
repairQuestions.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.
repairQuestions.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.

repairQuestions.q: Expected inflation rises while unemployment is held fixed. What happens to the SRPC?
options: The economy moves up the same SRPC
repairQuestions.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.
repairQuestions.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.

repairQuestions.q: On a Phillips graph, moving upward and left along one SRPC means what?
repairQuestions.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.

repairQuestions.q: Can a downward-sloping SRPC guarantee permanently lower unemployment from higher inflation?
options: No, because demand never affects unemployment
Yes, because the same SRPC is permanent
Yes, because natural unemployment becomes zero
repairQuestions.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.

repairQuestions.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation and unemployment together. What curve change is indicated?
options: An upward shift of the SRPC
Movement up-left along the same SRPC
A downward shift of the SRPC
A vertical movement along the LRPC
repairQuestions.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.
repairQuestions.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.

repairQuestions.q: Why does higher inflation not permanently lower unemployment in the natural-rate model?
options: Expected inflation adjusts and unemployment returns toward natural
Aggregate demand has no short-run effect
The natural rate always falls with inflation
Nominal wages never respond to prices
repairQuestions.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
repairQuestions.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

repairQuestions.q: Structural unemployment falls because matching improves. Is that movement along or a shift of LRPC?
options: Movement left along a fixed LRPC
An upward shift of SRPC only
A leftward shift of the LRPC
repairQuestions.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.
repairQuestions.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.

repairQuestions.q: Expected inflation rises from 2% to 4%. At a given unemployment rate, how does the SRPC move?
options: The economy moves down the same SRPC
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.
repairQuestions.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.

repairQuestions.q: Actual inflation repeatedly exceeds the rate workers expected. Which forecast adjustment is likely?
repairQuestions.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
repairQuestions.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

repairQuestions.q: Does a credible announcement guarantee costless disinflation?
options: No; credibility can never affect expectations
No; it can reduce costs without always eliminating them
Yes; credibility removes all nominal rigidities
repairQuestions.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
repairQuestions.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

repairQuestions.q: Inflation falls from 5% to 2% but remains positive. Did the price level fall?
options: Yes; any inflation decline lowers prices
Yes; disinflation and deflation are identical
No; the price level stayed exactly fixed
repairQuestions.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.
repairQuestions.commonError: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.

repairQuestions.q: Contractionary disinflation raises unemployment in the short run. Is that necessarily permanent?
options: Yes; every contraction shifts LRPC right
Yes; the SRPC never shifts after policy
No; unemployment must fall below natural immediately
No; unemployment can return toward natural as expectations adjust
repairQuestions.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
repairQuestions.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

repairQuestions.q: Inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What number belongs in the sacrifice-ratio denominator?
repairQuestions.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.

repairQuestions.q: Should annual output gaps be added before calculating a multi-year sacrifice ratio?
options: No, only the worst year counts
No, only the final year counts
Yes, but add inflation rates too
Yes, to obtain cumulative output loss
repairQuestions.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
repairQuestions.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

repairQuestions.q: Does the sacrifice ratio normally measure an unemployment increase per inflation point?
options: Yes, but only when inflation stays positive
No, it measures the fall in the price level
No, it measures cumulative output loss per inflation point
Yes, unemployment is always the numerator
repairQuestions.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.

bridgeQuestions.q: The government cuts spending during a recession. What happens to AD?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Lower government spending reduces aggregate demand.

bridgeQuestions.q: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption. What happens to AD?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher consumption shifts aggregate demand right.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
bridgeQuestions.q: A tax cut produces an $80 billion first-round increase in consumption. Which next idea is needed to move from that first-round fiscal impulse to the larger total aggregate-demand effect?
options: The multiplier process traces additional income-and-spending rounds.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts by the same $80 billion.
The inflation tax converts the consumption increase into government revenue.
The natural rate of unemployment determines the tax cut directly.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

bridgeQuestions.q: If MPC = 0.8, the government purchases multiplier is:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-0.8)=5.

bridgeQuestions.q: Fiscal expansion raises interest rates. Which part of spending is most likely crowded out?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher interest rates reduce private investment.

bridgeQuestions.q: Government spending rises by $20 billion and the multiplier is 3. Before crowding out, AD rises by:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The multiplier effect is $20 billion x 3 = $60 billion.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
bridgeQuestions.q: Government purchases rise $50 billion and MPC is 0.75. Which statement correctly connects the fiscal action to the multiplier concept?
options: The $50 billion first-round AD impulse is magnified to $200 billion before any crowding-out offset.
The $50 billion first-round impulse remains $50 billion because later spending rounds do not affect AD.
The multiplier reduces the initial AD impulse to $37.5 billion.
The fiscal action shifts LRAS rather than aggregate demand.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Carries the gross fiscal impulse into stabilization analysis even after an offset has been specified.
bridgeQuestions.q: A fiscal package generates a $300 billion gross AD increase, but crowding out reduces private investment by $80 billion in the simplified model. What AD impulse should stabilization analysis carry forward?
options: $300 billion because stabilization uses only the gross multiplier effect.
$80 billion because crowding out replaces the fiscal impulse.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Stabilization analysis should use the net aggregate-demand impulse after the multiplier and stated crowding-out offset.

bridgeQuestions.q: After a negative AD shock, output is below potential, but wages and input costs are already adjusting downward and SRAS is shifting right. What additional question belongs to stabilization-policy analysis?
options: Whether policymakers should deliberately shift AD right rather than wait for the self-correcting SRAS adjustment.
Whether LRAS should be moved left to meet the current level of output.
Whether the multiplier should be redefined as zero during every recession.
Whether unemployment should be excluded from the labor force until recovery is complete.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Long-run adjustment describes endogenous SRAS movement; stabilization policy asks whether policymakers should deliberately change AD instead of waiting.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treats self-correction and active stabilization as the same mechanism.

bridgeQuestions.q: The Fed increases money supply, but rates are already near zero and investment barely responds. What is this problem?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A liquidity trap weakens the usual interest-rate channel of monetary policy.

bridgeQuestions.q: A stimulus bill takes effect after the recession has already ended. What problem is this?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Policy lags can cause stimulus to arrive after economic conditions have changed.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Not comparing stimulus size to the recessionary gap.
bridgeQuestions.q: A recessionary AD gap is $300 billion. Policy raises spending by $75 billion and the multiplier is 4. What happens?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: $75 billion x 4 = $300 billion, so the gap closes exactly.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops with an AD shift and does not connect the short-run output response to unemployment and inflation pressure.
bridgeQuestions.q: Contractionary stabilization policy shifts AD left to cool an overheating economy. Which short-run labor-market effect connects this policy choice to Phillips-curve analysis?
options: Unemployment tends to rise as output weakens while inflation pressure falls.
Unemployment must fall because lower AD always increases hiring.
Unemployment is unchanged because only the price level responds to AD.
The natural rate permanently falls by the size of the AD shift.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A contractionary stabilization policy that lowers AD can reduce inflation pressure while raising unemployment in the short run, creating the bridge to Phillips-curve analysis.

bridgeQuestions.q: A higher price level raises money demand, increases interest rates, and reduces investment. Which AD effect does this illustrate?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: This is the interest-rate effect behind the downward slope of AD.

bridgeQuestions.q: Business investment falls and shifts aggregate demand left. Which analysis determines the economy’s new short-run real output and price level?
options: Find the new intersection of aggregate demand and short-run aggregate supply.
Shift LRAS left by the same amount as investment falls.
Hold output fixed and change only the price level.
Calculate the money multiplier without using the AD–AS equilibrium.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: After identifying the AD shift, use its intersection with SRAS to determine the new short-run output and price level.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops after identifying an aggregate-demand shift and does not carry it into equilibrium analysis.

bridgeQuestions.q: Workers expect higher prices and negotiate higher nominal wages. What happens to SRAS?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher expected prices raise wage demands and production costs, shifting SRAS left.

bridgeQuestions.q: If nominal wages are sticky and the price level rises unexpectedly, firms' real labor costs:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Sticky nominal wages mean a higher price level lowers real labor costs and can raise output.

bridgeQuestions.q: Oil prices fall and shift SRAS to the right while aggregate demand is unchanged. What should be done next to determine the macroeconomic outcome?
options: Locate the new intersection of SRAS and aggregate demand to infer output and the price level.
Move along the old SRAS curve without finding a new equilibrium.
Shift LRAS right automatically because oil became cheaper.
Treat the change as an aggregate-demand shock and ignore SRAS.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A supply shift changes the short-run equilibrium where the new SRAS curve intersects aggregate demand.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Identifies a supply shift but does not translate it into an equilibrium outcome.

bridgeQuestions.q: Better technology and more productive capital most directly shift which long-run curve?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Better productive capacity shifts LRAS right.

bridgeQuestions.q: Output is $19 trillion while natural output is $20 trillion. The economy has:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Actual output below natural output is a recessionary gap.

bridgeQuestions.q: An oil shock raises inflation while unemployment rises. Why is policy difficult?
options: Stimulus risks more inflation, while tightening risks more unemployment
Stimulus always lowers inflation, while tightening always raises output
Both stimulus and tightening shift SRAS right
Neither inflation nor unemployment can respond
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A supply shock creates a tradeoff: supporting output can worsen inflation, while fighting inflation can worsen unemployment.

bridgeQuestions.q: Consumer confidence collapses, shifting AD left and leaving real output below potential. With no new policy response, which process becomes relevant next?
options: Weak wage and price pressures can shift SRAS right over time, moving output back toward potential.
Aggregate demand must automatically shift right to its original position.
LRAS must shift left until it reaches the depressed output level.
A permanent adverse supply shock must occur before output can recover.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A negative AD shock can create a recessionary gap; with no policy response, wage and expectation adjustment can shift SRAS right over time.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops at the short-run demand-shock outcome and does not connect the recessionary gap to long-run self-correction.

bridgeQuestions.q: A major oil-price spike hits the economy. In the short run, output and the price level likely:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts SRAS left, lowering output and raising prices.

bridgeQuestions.q: Output is above potential and self-correction through rising wages and costs is expected to be slow. Which stabilization-policy question becomes relevant?
options: Stabilization policy—whether and how to use an active policy response instead of waiting for self-correction.
Money measurement—whether currency should be counted in M1 or M2.
Growth accounting—how much of productivity comes from capital deepening.
CPI measurement—whether the market basket overstates cost-of-living changes.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Long-run adjustment describes self-correction; stabilization policy asks whether policymakers should actively shift aggregate demand rather than wait.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treats passive long-run adjustment and deliberate stabilization as the same mechanism.

bridgeQuestions.q: Aggregate demand expands unexpectedly, raising output and the price level. What linked Phillips result follows first?
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation along the current SRPC
Higher unemployment and higher inflation from an SRPC shift
Lower unemployment and lower inflation from an LRPC shift
Unchanged unemployment with a downward SRPC shift
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.

bridgeQuestions.q: After a move to lower unemployment and higher inflation, wage setters revise inflation forecasts upward. What happens to the short-run Phillips curve?
options: Aggregate demand shifts the LRPC left
Money demand shifts the SRPC downward
Expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward
bridgeQuestions.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

bridgeQuestions.q: A short-run unemployment gain disappears as expectations adjust. Which family destination explains the long-run endpoint?
options: A horizontal LRPC at zero inflation
A sacrifice ratio equal to unemployment
The vertical LRPC at the natural rate
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

bridgeQuestions.q: A contraction moves the economy down the SRPC toward lower inflation and higher unemployment. Which applied destination studies that policy path?
options: Bank reserve creation through repeated lending and redepositing
GDP accounting identities for measuring current national output
Comparative advantage from differences in opportunity cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation has fully adjusted after an expansion. Which prior family idea now leads to the LRPC conclusion?
options: The temporary SRPC movement ends at natural unemployment
The SRPC remains a permanent menu of choices
The sacrifice ratio becomes the natural rate
Deflation moves LRPC to zero unemployment
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.

bridgeQuestions.q: The LRPC places unemployment at its natural rate. Which labor-family concept supplies that location?
options: Natural-rate unemployment from frictional and structural forces
Cyclical unemployment at every inflation rate
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

bridgeQuestions.q: A central bank begins disinflation from the natural rate. Which next family concept measures the possible output cost of the temporary adjustment?
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

bridgeQuestions.q: The economy moves up-left along SRPC after a demand surprise. Wage setters then revise forecasts upward. What connection is required?
options: A movement along SRPC becomes an upward shift as expectations adjust
The LRPC shifts left as aggregate demand rises and nominal wages renew
The same fixed SRPC supports permanently lower unemployment after forecasts update
A downward expectations shift reinforces the initial unemployment gain
bridgeQuestions.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation falls during a credible disinflation. Which applied family slice uses that change to assess policy costs?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expectations fully catch up after repeated inflation surprises. Which curve summarizes the long-run unemployment result?
options: The LRPC at the natural rate
The SRPC as a permanent menu
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

bridgeQuestions.q: Contractionary monetary policy reduces spending and inflation pressure. Which Phillips connection follows initially?
options: Movement toward higher unemployment and lower inflation along SRPC
A permanent LRPC shift to higher unemployment after expected inflation adjusts
Movement toward lower unemployment and lower inflation along the same curve
An upward SRPC shift caused by lower expected inflation during contraction
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation falls and the economy later returns to natural unemployment. Which family links explain the transition?
options: A permanent move along one SRPC only
An LRPC shift caused by the price level
A sacrifice-ratio shift of aggregate demand
A downward SRPC shift followed by long-run return to LRPC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.

bridgeQuestions.q: A policy team has computed cumulative output loss per inflation point. What applied question should that sacrifice ratio now inform?
options: How alternative disinflation paths trade speed against short-run cost
How to classify liquid assets between M1 and broader monetary aggregates
How to calculate nominal GDP from current prices and quantities
How to shift the production frontier through resource accumulation
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

bridgeQuestions.q: The economy temporarily moves above natural unemployment during disinflation. How is this cost measured?
options: Sum the output losses and divide by the inflation-point reduction
Divide the unemployment increase by the final positive inflation rate
Treat the change in the price level as the cumulative output numerator
Shift LRPC right by the cumulative inflation reduction during policy
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

bridgeQuestions.q: Expected inflation falls faster after a credible announcement. How can that connect to the sacrifice ratio?
options: A lower final inflation rate automatically raises the ratio even with unchanged loss
Credibility changes the denominator from inflation reduction to unemployment
The ratio must become zero in every credible disinflation plan
A smaller cumulative output loss can lower the measured ratio
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Two disinflation paths reach the same inflation target. Which family destination uses their sacrifice ratios to compare costs?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.

tax_cut_ad_direction.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
tax_cut_ad_direction.q: A tax cut produces an $80 billion first-round increase in consumption. Which next idea is needed to move from that first-round fiscal impulse to the larger total aggregate-demand effect?

tax_cut_ad.q: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption. What happens to AD?
tax_cut_ad.feedback: Higher consumption shifts aggregate demand right.

fiscal_policy_ad_shift.q: The government cuts spending during a recession. What happens to AD?
fiscal_policy_ad_shift.feedback: Lower government spending reduces aggregate demand.

multiplier_effect.q: Government spending rises by $20 billion and the multiplier is 3. Before crowding out, AD rises by:

$80 billion because crowding out replaces the fiscal impulse.
crowding_out_net_effect.feedback: Stabilization analysis should use the net aggregate-demand impulse after the multiplier and stated crowding-out offset.

spending_multiplier_formula.q: Government purchases rise $50 billion and MPC is 0.75. Which statement correctly connects the fiscal action to the multiplier concept?

spending_multiplier_formula.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

crowding_out_effect.q: Fiscal expansion raises interest rates. Which part of spending is most likely crowded out?

stabilization_response_recession.q: A recessionary AD gap is $300 billion. Policy raises spending by $75 billion and the multiplier is 4. What happens?

policy_lags.q: A stimulus bill takes effect after the recession has already ended. What problem is this?
policy_lags.feedback: Policy lags can cause stimulus to arrive after economic conditions have changed.

stabilization_response_overheating.commonError: Stops with an AD shift and does not connect the short-run output response to unemployment and inflation pressure.
stabilization_response_overheating.q: Contractionary stabilization policy shifts AD left to cool an overheating economy. Which short-run labor-market effect connects this policy choice to Phillips-curve analysis?

liquidity_trap.q: The Fed increases money supply, but rates are already near zero and investment barely responds. What is this problem?
liquidity_trap.feedback: A liquidity trap weakens the usual interest-rate channel of monetary policy.

choose_stabilization_response.q: After a negative AD shock, output is below potential, but wages and input costs are already adjusting downward and SRAS is shifting right. What additional question belongs to stabilization-policy analysis?

Whether the multiplier should be redefined as zero during every recession.
Whether unemployment should be excluded from the labor force until recovery is complete.

choose_stabilization_response.commonError: Treats self-correction and active stabilization as the same mechanism.

identify_ad_shifters.q: Business investment falls and shifts aggregate demand left. Which analysis determines the economy’s new short-run real output and price level?

identify_ad_shifters.commonError: Stops after identifying an aggregate-demand shift and does not carry it into equilibrium analysis.

explain_ad_slope.q: A higher price level raises money demand, increases interest rates, and reduces investment. Which AD effect does this illustrate?
explain_ad_slope.feedback: This is the interest-rate effect behind the downward slope of AD.

explain_sras_upward.q: If nominal wages are sticky and the price level rises unexpectedly, firms' real labor costs:

On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

assets.graphDescription: The left panel has interest rate r on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. The right panel has price level P on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

fiscal-policy-and-aggregate-demand.title: Fiscal Policy and Aggregate Demand
fiscal-policy-and-aggregate-demand.description: Trace government purchases and taxes into aggregate demand.

easy.q: Higher government spending usually shifts aggregate demand:
easy.commonError: Reversing expansionary fiscal policy.
easy.feedback: Higher government spending raises aggregate demand.

easy.q: A tax cut usually shifts aggregate demand:
easy.commonError: Confusing tax cuts and tax increases.
easy.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption, shifting AD right.

easy.q: Expansionary fiscal policy includes
options: higher government spending or lower taxes
lower government spending or higher taxes
a decrease in the money supply
easy.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy
easy.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy uses higher government spending or lower taxes to increase aggregate demand.

easy.q: Contractionary fiscal policy includes
options: lower government spending or higher taxes
higher government spending or lower taxes
a decrease in interest on reserves only
easy.commonError: confusing fiscal tightening with monetary tightening
easy.feedback: Contractionary fiscal policy means lower government spending or higher taxes, which reduces aggregate demand.

easy.q: An increase in government spending shifts aggregate demand
options: only downward along the same curve
not at all because G is not part of AD
easy.commonError: forgetting that G is a component of aggregate demand
easy.feedback: Government spending is part of aggregate demand, so an increase in G shifts AD right.

easy.q: A decrease in taxes usually shifts aggregate demand
options: nowhere because taxes are not related to spending
easy.commonError: thinking tax cuts reduce consumption
easy.feedback: Lower taxes raise disposable income, which can raise consumption and shift AD right.

medium.q: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Moving from AD1 to AD2 changes output from:
medium.commonError: Reading the graph backward.
medium.feedback: At the same price level, output rises from Y1 to Y2 when AD shifts from AD1 to AD2.

medium.q: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Which curve shows the largest aggregate demand level?
medium.commonError: Confusing curve position with label order.
medium.feedback: AD3 is farthest to the right, so it shows the largest AD at price level P.

medium.q: Which policy is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: Selling government bonds by the Fed
medium.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with Fed policy
medium.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy uses higher government spending or lower taxes to raise aggregate demand.

medium.q: Which policy is contractionary fiscal policy?
options: Buying government bonds by the Fed
medium.commonError: confusing fiscal and monetary policy tools
medium.feedback: Higher taxes are contractionary fiscal policy because they reduce disposable income and aggregate demand.

medium.q: A tax cut shifts aggregate demand right mainly because it
options: forces banks to hold more reserves
medium.commonError: thinking tax cuts work through bank reserves
medium.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.

medium.q: A cut in government purchases shifts aggregate demand left because
options: government spending is a component of aggregate demand
medium.commonError: forgetting that G is directly part of AD
medium.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD, so reducing G shifts AD left.

medium.q: If Congress increases infrastructure spending during a recession, the direct effect is to
medium.commonError: treating fiscal stimulus like contractionary policy
medium.feedback: Higher infrastructure spending raises G and shifts AD right.

medium.q: If the government raises taxes during an expansion, the likely AD effect is
medium.commonError: thinking tax increases raise consumption
medium.feedback: Higher taxes reduce disposable income and consumption, shifting AD left.

hard.q: Congress increases government purchases by $80 billion while households cut consumption by $50 billion for unrelated reasons. Before multiplier effects, the net direct change in aggregate demand is:
hard.commonError: Adding changes without respecting their directions.
hard.feedback: Government purchases add $80 billion while consumption subtracts $50 billion.

hard.q: A $120 billion tax rebate is issued and households spend 65 percent of the added disposable income initially. What is the first-round consumption increase?
hard.commonError: Using the MPS or the full tax cut as first-round consumption.
hard.feedback: First-round consumption is 0.65 × $120 billion = $78 billion.

hard.q: A government raises taxes and increases purchases by the same dollar amount. Which statement is most precise about the immediate AD effects?
options: The two actions must cancel exactly before behavior is considered.
Both actions shift AD right by the same amount.
Taxes enter AD directly as a negative component.
Purchases enter AD directly, while higher taxes reduce consumption indirectly.
hard.commonError: Treating taxes as a direct component of aggregate demand.
hard.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD; taxes work through disposable income and consumption.

hard.q: A temporary tax cut is mostly saved because households expect it to be reversed next year. Compared with a tax cut that is mostly spent, the AD shift is:
hard.commonError: Ignoring household spending behavior.
hard.feedback: A smaller consumption response weakens the tax cut’s effect on aggregate demand.

hard.q: The government cuts purchases during a recession but also cuts taxes. Which conclusion is valid without knowing the magnitudes and household response?
options: The two policies always cancel exactly.
The net direction of aggregate demand is ambiguous.
hard.commonError: Assuming one policy label determines the combined outcome.
hard.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left, while a tax cut tends to shift it right; magnitudes matter.

hard.q: A tax increase of $60 billion reduces consumption by $42 billion in the first round. The implied MPC is:
hard.commonError: Dividing in the wrong direction or using the MPS.
hard.feedback: MPC = $42 billion / $60 billion = 0.70.

elite.q: A tax cut occurs while households expect future taxes to rise and save much of the extra income. What happens to the tax multiplier?
options: It is weaker than simple models predict
It shifts SRAS instead of AD
elite.commonError: Assuming every tax cut creates the same consumption response.
elite.feedback: If households save much of the tax cut, the increase in consumption and AD is weaker.

elite.q: An economy faces a positive AD shock of $240 billion. If policymakers use a tax increase that reduces disposable income by $100 billion and MPC is 0.8, what is the first-round consumption reduction?
elite.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
elite.feedback: The first-round consumption reduction is MPC times the disposable income change: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

elite.q: A fiscal package raises government purchases by $120 billion and taxes by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, the package’s first-round effect on AD is:
elite.commonError: Ignoring that the tax increase reduces consumption by MPC times the tax change.
elite.feedback: Purchases add $120 billion; the tax increase reduces consumption by $80 billion.

elite.q: A tax cut is announced, but credit-constrained households spend 90 percent while high-income households spend 30 percent. Which feature matters most for the AD effect?
options: The long-run natural rate of output
Whether government purchases are counted in GDP
Only the statutory size of the tax cut
How the tax cut is distributed across groups with different marginal propensities to consume.
elite.commonError: Assuming every dollar of tax reduction produces the same consumption response.
elite.feedback: The aggregate consumption response depends on who receives the tax cut and how much they spend.

legendary.q: A government increases purchases by $50 billion and raises taxes by $50 billion. MPC is 0.75. Before subsequent multiplier rounds, the net first-round AD change is:
legendary.commonError: Assuming equal spending and tax changes have equal direct AD effects.
legendary.feedback: Purchases add $50 billion; the tax increase cuts consumption by $37.5 billion.

legendary.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $160 billion. Households spend 60 percent of the increase initially. If later rounds follow a simple spending multiplier of 2.5, the total AD increase before other offsets is:
legendary.commonError: Applying the multiplier to the full tax cut instead of the first-round consumption change.
legendary.feedback: First-round consumption rises $96 billion; multiplying by 2.5 gives $240 billion.

legendary.q: The government increases infrastructure purchases, but imports rise sharply because much of the equipment is purchased abroad. Relative to a package using domestic inputs, the increase in domestic aggregate demand is likely:
options: Leftward because any import increase reduces government purchases.
Identical because all government spending counts equally.
Smaller because part of the spending leaks into imports.
Larger because imports are part of domestic production.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring import leakage from domestic demand.
legendary.feedback: Spending on imports does not directly purchase domestically produced output.

legendary.q: A tax cut and transfer increase have the same budget cost. The transfer is targeted to households with a higher MPC. Which package is likely to shift AD more in the short run?
options: The broad tax cut regardless of spending behavior.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring differences in marginal propensity to consume.
legendary.feedback: More of the targeted transfer is likely to be spent, producing a larger initial consumption increase.

legendary.q: A government plans contractionary fiscal policy. Which combination most clearly supports that goal?
options: Higher government purchases and lower taxes.
Lower government purchases and higher taxes.
legendary.commonError: Mixing expansionary and contractionary tools.
legendary.feedback: Lower purchases and higher taxes both push aggregate demand left.

legendary.q: A recessionary economy receives a temporary tax rebate. Households use half to repay debt, save one quarter, and spend one quarter. The immediate consumption channel equals:
legendary.commonError: Treating saving or debt repayment as immediate consumption.
legendary.feedback: Only the portion spent on current consumption directly raises the consumption component of AD.

legendary.q: A temporary $120 billion tax credit is split equally between two household groups. One group has MPC 0.90 and the other MPC 0.40. Before multiplier rounds or crowding out, what is the first-round change in aggregate demand from consumption?
legendary.commonError: Applies one MPC to the entire tax change even when recipient groups have different spending responses.
legendary.feedback: Compute each group’s first-round consumption response separately, then add them before considering later multiplier rounds.

legendary.q: Congress replaces $100 billion of government purchases with a $100 billion tax cut. Households have MPC 0.80. Holding other AD determinants fixed and looking only at the first round, what happens to aggregate demand?
options: AD is unchanged because the two fiscal changes are equal.
legendary.commonError: Treats equal-dollar spending and tax changes as having identical direct effects on aggregate demand.
legendary.feedback: Government purchases enter AD directly, while tax changes affect AD through the share of disposable income households spend.

calculation.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
calculation.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
calculation.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is MPC times disposable income: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

calculation.q: Congress increases government purchases by $80 billion while households cut consumption by $50 billion for unrelated reasons. Before multiplier effects, the net direct change in aggregate demand is:
calculation.commonError: Adding changes without respecting their directions.
calculation.feedback: Government purchases add $80 billion while consumption subtracts $50 billion.

calculation.q: A $120 billion tax rebate is issued and households spend 65 percent of the added disposable income initially. What is the first-round consumption increase?
calculation.commonError: Using the MPS or the full tax cut as first-round consumption.
calculation.feedback: First-round consumption is 0.65 × $120 billion = $78 billion.

calculation.q: A tax increase of $60 billion reduces consumption by $42 billion in the first round. The implied MPC is:
calculation.commonError: Dividing in the wrong direction or using the MPS.
calculation.feedback: MPC = $42 billion / $60 billion = 0.70.

boss.q: Which policy combination is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: higher government spending or lower taxes
lower government spending or higher taxes
boss.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy
boss.feedback: Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxes. Expansionary fiscal policy raises G or lowers T.

boss.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $120 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
boss.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
boss.feedback: First-round consumption rises by MPC times the tax cut: 0.8 x $120 billion = $96 billion.

boss.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $120 billion. MPC = 0.8. If the first-round consumption increase enters the multiplier process, what is the total AD increase before crowding out?
boss.commonError: multiplying the full tax cut by the multiplier before applying MPC
boss.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is $96 billion. With MPC 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so AD rises $480 billion.

boss.q: Expansionary fiscal policy most directly includes:
options: Higher government purchases or lower taxes.
Lower government purchases or higher taxes.
boss.commonError: Confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy or private behavior.
boss.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government demand or supports private spending.

boss.q: Which fiscal action shifts aggregate demand left through lower disposable income?
boss.commonError: Reversing the effect of taxes on disposable income and consumption.
boss.feedback: A tax increase reduces disposable income and tends to reduce consumption.

boss.q: Government purchases are:
options: A direct component of aggregate demand.
A direct component of short-run aggregate supply.
boss.commonError: Misplacing government purchases in the macro model.
boss.feedback: Government purchases are included directly in C + I + G + NX.

boss.q: A $100 billion tax cut with MPC 0.8 raises first-round consumption by:
boss.commonError: Using the MPS or multiplier too early.
boss.feedback: MPC times the tax cut gives the first-round consumption increase.

boss.q: A cut in government purchases shifts AD left because it directly reduces:
boss.commonError: Confusing an AD shift with an AS or banking change.
boss.feedback: Government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.

boss.q: A tax cut has a weak AD effect when households:
options: Save most of the increase in disposable income.
Face a high marginal propensity to consume.
Increase consumption by more than the tax cut.
boss.commonError: Ignoring the consumption response.
boss.feedback: More saving means less immediate consumption and a smaller rightward AD shift.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the multiplier graph. A $60 billion tax cut raises disposable income, and MPC = 0.75. What is the correct order of AD effects before crowding out?
options: Consumption first rises $45 billion, then the multiplier expands the AD shift to $180 billion.
AD first rises $60 billion, then the multiplier expands it to $240 billion.
Consumption first rises $15 billion, then AD rises $60 billion.
AD falls $45 billion, then the multiplier reduces it by $180 billion.
legendaryBoss.commonError: multiplying the full tax cut by the spending multiplier without first applying MPC
legendaryBoss.feedback: First-round consumption rises 0.75 x $60 billion = $45 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $180 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: Government purchases rise $90 billion and taxes rise $60 billion. MPC is 0.75. What is the net first-round change in AD?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Failing to distinguish the direct spending effect from the tax-induced consumption effect.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Purchases add $90 billion; taxes reduce consumption by $45 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: A $200 billion tax cut reaches two equal groups. One group spends 80 percent and the other spends 40 percent. What is the combined first-round consumption increase?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Applying one group’s MPC to the entire tax cut.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Each group receives $100 billion; spending rises $80 billion plus $40 billion.

repairQuestions.q: Congress increases government purchases while taxes and other aggregate-demand determinants are unchanged. Which change should a student predict in the AD-AS model?
repairQuestions.feedback: Government purchases and tax-induced consumption changes work primarily through aggregate demand in this Principles model.
repairQuestions.commonError: Confuses a fiscal-policy change with an aggregate-supply shift.

repairQuestions.q: A $40 billion tax cut raises disposable income and MPC is 0.75. Before later multiplier rounds, how much does consumption increase?
repairQuestions.feedback: The first-round consumption effect equals the change in disposable income times MPC.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the full tax cut as immediate consumption.
Classifies fiscal policy from the state of the economy rather than from what government purchases and taxes actually do.
repairQuestions.q: Congress lowers government purchases and raises taxes in the same bill to reduce excessive aggregate demand. How should the package be classified?
repairQuestions.feedback: Classify the package from its fiscal actions: higher purchases/lower taxes are expansionary; lower purchases/higher taxes are contractionary.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking fiscal expansion shifts AD left.
repairQuestions.q: Higher government spending usually shifts AD:
repairQuestions.feedback: Government spending is part of AD, so higher G shifts AD right.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting taxes work through disposable income and consumption.
repairQuestions.q: A tax cut usually increases:
repairQuestions.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income.

repairQuestions.commonError: Jumps from a tax change directly to total output without identifying the first spending channel.
repairQuestions.q: Why can a tax cut shift aggregate demand to the right in the short run?
options: It raises disposable income, which can raise consumption spending.
It directly increases the money supply.
It directly lowers firms’ production costs and shifts SRAS right.
repairQuestions.feedback: A tax change first changes disposable income, then consumption according to MPC, which shifts aggregate demand.

bridgeQuestions.q: The government cuts spending during a recession. What happens to AD?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Lower government spending reduces aggregate demand.

bridgeQuestions.q: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption. What happens to AD?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher consumption shifts aggregate demand right.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
bridgeQuestions.q: A tax cut produces an $80 billion first-round increase in consumption. Which next idea is needed to move from that first-round fiscal impulse to the larger total aggregate-demand effect?
options: The multiplier process traces additional income-and-spending rounds.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts by the same $80 billion.
The inflation tax converts the consumption increase into government revenue.
The natural rate of unemployment determines the tax cut directly.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.
