fiscal-multipliers-and-crowding-out.title: Fiscal Multipliers and Crowding Out
fiscal-multipliers-and-crowding-out.description: Calculate multiplier effects and evaluate crowding out.

easy.q: The multiplier effect means that government spending can shift AD by:
options: Less than the initial spending only
easy.commonError: Ignoring induced consumption.
easy.feedback: The multiplier effect occurs when initial spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

easy.q: Crowding out occurs when fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces:
easy.commonError: Missing the interest-rate channel.
easy.feedback: Crowding out reduces private investment when fiscal expansion raises interest rates.

easy.q: The multiplier effect occurs because an initial increase in spending
options: raises income and causes additional consumption spending
always raises interest rates enough to cancel itself completely
easy.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the first round of spending
easy.feedback: The multiplier effect happens because one person's spending becomes another person's income, causing additional consumption.

easy.q: The marginal propensity to consume is the fraction of extra income that households
easy.commonError: confusing MPC with the fraction saved
easy.feedback: MPC is the fraction of extra income that households consume rather than save.

easy.q: The simple spending multiplier is calculated as
easy.commonError: using MPC itself as the multiplier
easy.feedback: The simple spending multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

easy.q: Crowding out occurs when expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates and reduces
easy.commonError: thinking crowding out makes government spending disappear
easy.feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment spending.

medium.q: If fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces investment, the final AD shift is likely:
options: Larger because crowding out amplifies it
Smaller because crowding out offsets it
Zero because fiscal policy cannot affect AD
medium.commonError: Thinking the multiplier is never offset.
medium.feedback: Crowding out weakens the final effect of fiscal expansion on AD.

medium.q: The multiplier effect exists because one person's spending becomes
options: a fall in money demand every time
medium.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the initial spending increase
medium.feedback: The multiplier works because spending becomes income, and some of that income gets spent again.

medium.q: The movement from the first AD shift to the larger final AD shift represents
medium.commonError: confusing the multiplier effect with monetary policy
medium.feedback: The multiplier effect is the extra AD shift caused by income leading to additional consumption spending.

medium.q: The initial shift in aggregate demand from higher government spending is followed by a larger shift because
options: higher income leads to additional consumption spending
interest rates always fall to zero
medium.commonError: thinking only the first round of government spending matters
medium.feedback: The first increase in spending raises income, which causes more consumption and a further AD shift.

medium.q: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion because higher government spending can raise interest rates and reduce
medium.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens fiscal stimulus
medium.feedback: Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise.

medium.q: Which situation would make the multiplier effect larger?
medium.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
medium.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, which makes the multiplier larger.

medium.q: Which situation would make fiscal stimulus less powerful?
options: A high MPC with no interest-rate effect
A large initial increase in government spending
A high willingness to consume extra income
medium.commonError: ignoring offsetting effects from interest rates
medium.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal stimulus by reducing private investment.

hard.q: Refer to the AD multiplier graph. If government spending first shifts AD from AD1 to AD2, the multiplier effect is best shown by:
hard.commonError: Confusing the initial shift with the multiplied shift.
hard.feedback: The multiplier effect expands the initial AD shift farther right, from AD2 to AD3.

hard.q: Refer to the AD multiplier graph. If crowding out occurs after AD reaches AD3, the final AD position may move back toward:
hard.commonError: Thinking crowding out amplifies AD.
hard.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of fiscal expansion, pulling the final effect back from AD3 toward AD2.

hard.q: If the initial government spending increase shifts AD by $20 billion, why might the final shift be larger?
options: The spending raises income, which triggers additional consumption spending.
The spending lowers income, which reduces consumption.
The spending automatically reduces money supply.
The spending makes MPC equal zero.
hard.commonError: thinking only the first spending round matters
hard.feedback: The multiplier effect comes from income causing additional consumption, which pushes AD farther.

hard.q: If MPC is higher, the distance between the initial AD shift and the final AD shift should
hard.commonError: thinking a higher MPC weakens the multiplier
hard.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, so the final AD shift is larger.

hard.q: If expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates, which effect offsets part of the multiplier?
hard.commonError: confusing crowding out with the multiplier effect itself
hard.feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment, offsetting fiscal stimulus.

hard.q: Which fiscal policy has the strongest predicted multiplier effect before crowding out?
options: MPC = 0.9 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.5 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.25 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.1 and government spending rises by $50 billion
hard.commonError: thinking lower MPC creates a stronger multiplier
hard.feedback: Higher MPC means a larger multiplier. MPC = 0.9 gives the strongest multiplier here.

elite.q: Fiscal expansion raises AD through the multiplier, but interest rates rise and investment falls. Which description best fits the final result?
options: Initial AD shift partly offset by crowding out
SRAS shift fully offset by lower taxes
LRPC shift partly offset by higher inflation
Money demand shift fully offset by M1
elite.commonError: Treating the multiplier as the final effect every time.
elite.feedback: Fiscal expansion can be amplified by the multiplier but weakened by crowding out.

elite.q: Refer to the multiplier graph. Government spending initially moves AD1 to AD2, the multiplier moves AD2 to AD3, and crowding out offsets part of it. The final effect is likely:
elite.commonError: Ignoring crowding out after multiplier expansion.
elite.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the multiplied AD increase, so the final shift may land between AD2 and AD3.

elite.q: If government spending rises, MPC is high, and interest rates do not rise, which effect dominates?
elite.commonError: Assuming crowding out always dominates fiscal policy.
elite.feedback: A high MPC strengthens the multiplier, and little interest-rate increase means crowding out is weak.

elite.q: If government spending rises, MPC is low, and interest rates rise sharply, which concern dominates?
options: Weak multiplier with strong crowding out
Strong multiplier with no crowding out
Money neutrality with no AD change
elite.commonError: Ignoring both MPC size and interest-rate effects.
elite.feedback: A low MPC weakens the multiplier, while higher rates crowd out private investment.

elite.q: If government spending initially shifts AD right by $40 billion and MPC is 0.75, what is the total shift before crowding out?
elite.commonError: using MPC as the multiplier instead of 1 divided by 1 minus MPC
elite.feedback: With MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is 4. A $40 billion initial shift becomes $160 billion before crowding out.

elite.q: If the initial AD shift is $30 billion and the final shift is $150 billion, what MPC is implied by the simple multiplier?
elite.commonError: using final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
elite.feedback: The multiplier is 150/30 = 5. If 1/(1-MPC)=5, then MPC = 0.8.

elite.q: If the initial shift is $50 billion and MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.5, what happens to the final AD shift before crowding out?
options: It falls from $250 billion to $100 billion.
It rises from $100 billion to $250 billion.
It falls from $250 billion to $50 billion.
elite.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
elite.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so $250 billion. MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so $100 billion.

elite.q: Suppose the multiplier would shift AD right by $200 billion, but crowding out reduces investment by $60 billion. What is the net shift?
elite.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
elite.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the multiplier effect. Net shift is $200 billion - $60 billion = $140 billion.

elite.q: If policymakers expect the multiplier shift to close a recessionary gap exactly, but crowding out is stronger than expected, what is the likely result?
options: AD does not shift far enough right to fully close the gap.
AD shifts too far right because crowding out magnifies fiscal policy.
AD shifts left because government spending is not part of AD.
elite.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens the fiscal multiplier
elite.feedback: Stronger crowding out reduces the net AD shift, so stimulus may fall short.

elite.q: If government spending rises by $60 billion, MPC is 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $50 billion, what is the net AD shift?
elite.commonError: forgetting to apply the multiplier before subtracting crowding out
elite.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so the gross shift is $240 billion. Subtract $50 billion crowding out for a net $190 billion.

elite.q: A government spending increase raises income, consumption, and AD, but also raises interest rates and lowers investment. Which answer correctly names both effects?
elite.commonError: treating all fiscal policy effects as multiplier effects only
elite.feedback: The multiplier amplifies the AD increase; crowding out offsets part of it by reducing investment.

legendary.q: A student says fiscal expansion raises AD and therefore can never crowd out investment. What is the best correction?
options: Fiscal expansion can raise AD while higher rates reduce private investment.
Fiscal expansion lowers rates because government borrowing reduces money demand.
Fiscal expansion shifts SRAS right because firms face lower costs.
Fiscal expansion eliminates the multiplier because taxes disappear.
legendary.commonError: Thinking multiplier effects rule out crowding out.
legendary.feedback: Fiscal expansion can increase AD, but rising interest rates can reduce investment and offset part of the effect.

legendary.q: Refer to the aggregate-demand multiplier graph. AD moves from AD1 to AD2, then from AD2 to AD3, followed by a partial move back. Which interpretation fits?
options: Initial fiscal shift, multiplier expansion, then crowding out offset.
Initial monetary contraction, SRAS expansion, then LRPC adjustment.
Initial supply shock, expected price decline, then AD collapse.
Initial inflation tax, M1 expansion, then velocity collapse.
legendary.commonError: Confusing multiplier and crowding-out stages.
legendary.feedback: Fiscal policy can shift AD right, the multiplier can push it farther, and crowding out can pull the final effect back.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $70 billion and MPC = 0.8. What is the correct order of AD shifts before crowding out?
options: AD first shifts right by $70 billion, then shifts farther right to a total of $350 billion.
AD first shifts right by $350 billion, then shifts back to $70 billion.
AD shifts left by $70 billion, then left by $350 billion.
AD does not shift because the multiplier only affects money demand.
legendary.commonError: confusing the initial AD shift with the final multiplier shift
legendary.feedback: The first AD shift is the direct $70 billion increase in G. With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so the final AD shift is $350 billion.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $60 billion and the final AD shift is $300 billion. What order of AD shifts and implied MPC fit these data?
options: AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts right first by $300 billion, then back to $60 billion; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts left first by $60 billion, then left by $300 billion; MPC = 0.2.
AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.6.
legendary.commonError: treating final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of the multiplier
legendary.feedback: The multiplier is $300/$60 = 5. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 5, then MPC = 0.8.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $40 billion. If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, how does the order of AD shifts change?
options: The initial AD shift stays $40 billion, but the final shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion.
The initial AD shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion, but the final shift stays $40 billion.
Both the initial and final AD shifts stay $40 billion.
The initial AD shift becomes $200 billion and the final shift becomes $80 billion.
legendary.commonError: thinking same initial government spending creates same final AD shift regardless of MPC
legendary.feedback: The initial shift is still $40 billion. With MPC = 0.5, multiplier is 2 and final shift is $80 billion. With MPC = 0.8, multiplier is 5 and final shift is $200 billion.

legendary.q: Government spending rises by $100 billion and MPC = 0.6. Crowding out reduces investment by $75 billion. What is the correct order of AD effects?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $175 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out increases it to $325 billion.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $250 billion, then crowding out leaves $175 billion.
AD shifts right $100 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
legendary.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it from the gross multiplier shift
legendary.feedback: MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. The $100 billion initial shift becomes $250 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $175 billion.

legendary.q: Two governments each increase purchases by $60 billion. Economy A has MPC 0.80 and $100 billion of crowding out; Economy B has MPC 0.60 and $20 billion of crowding out. Using the simple multiplier and the stated offsets, which comparison is correct?
options: Economy A has a $200 billion net AD increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy B.
Economy A has a $300 billion net increase and Economy B has a $150 billion net increase because crowding out does not affect AD.
Economy B has a $200 billion net increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy A.
Both economies have the same $180 billion net AD increase because the initial spending changes are equal.
legendary.commonError: Compares gross multiplier effects without subtracting the private spending displaced by higher interest rates.
legendary.feedback: For the simplified model used here, compare each policy’s gross multiplier effect and then subtract its stated crowding-out offset.

legendary.q: Government purchases rise by $80 billion and MPC is 0.75. The observed net increase in aggregate demand is $230 billion after crowding out. Under the simple model used in this bank, how much of the gross multiplier effect was crowded out?
legendary.commonError: Uses the net AD shift as if it were the gross multiplier effect.
legendary.feedback: First compute the gross multiplier effect, then infer the crowding-out offset from the difference between gross and observed net AD.

calculation.q: If the MPC is 0.75, the simple government purchases multiplier is:
calculation.commonError: Using MPC as the multiplier.
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so 1/(1-0.75)=4.

calculation.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion, MPC is 0.75, and crowding out offsets $100 billion, final AD rises by:
calculation.commonError: Ignoring crowding out after applying the multiplier.
calculation.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so $80 billion x 4 = $320 billion; minus $100 billion gives $220 billion.

calculation.q: If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, the government purchases multiplier changes from:
calculation.commonError: Using MPC itself as the multiplier.
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so it rises from 2 to 5.

calculation.q: If the government raises spending by $50 billion and the multiplier is 3, the first-pass AD increase before crowding out is:
calculation.commonError: Using the spending change instead of multiplying it.
calculation.feedback: The initial multiplier effect is $50 billion x 3 = $150 billion.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.6 and income rises by $1,000, consumption rises by
calculation.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
calculation.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the change in income: 0.6 x $1,000 = $600.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.6, the simple spending multiplier is
calculation.commonError: using MPC itself as the multiplier
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.6) = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.8 and government spending increases by $50 billion, the simple multiplier predicts a total AD increase of
calculation.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
calculation.feedback: With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5. Total increase is 5 x $50 billion = $250 billion.

calculation.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the simple multiplier and total AD increase before crowding out?
calculation.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
calculation.feedback: Multiplier = 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4. Total AD increase = 4 x $80 billion = $320 billion.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.9 and government spending increases by $25 billion, what is the simple multiplier effect on AD before crowding out?
calculation.commonError: using 0.9 as the multiplier instead of 10
calculation.feedback: With MPC = 0.9, the multiplier is 10. AD increases by 10 x $25 billion = $250 billion.

calculation.q: Suppose fiscal stimulus initially raises AD by $300 billion through the multiplier, but crowding out reduces investment by $80 billion. What is the net AD increase?
calculation.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
calculation.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the stimulus, so net AD rises by $300 billion - $80 billion = $220 billion.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.8, then a $100 increase in income raises consumption by
calculation.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
calculation.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the income increase: 0.8 x $100 = $80.

calculation.q: If MPC = 0.75, the simple spending multiplier equals
calculation.commonError: dividing MPC by 1 instead of using 1 divided by 1 minus MPC
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.

boss.q: Why can an initial increase in spending generate a larger total increase in aggregate demand?
options: raises income and causes additional consumption spending
boss.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the first spending round
boss.feedback: The multiplier happens because spending becomes income, and part of that income is spent again.

boss.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the gross AD shift before crowding out?
boss.commonError: using MPC instead of the multiplier
boss.feedback: MPC 0.75 gives multiplier 4. Gross AD shift is $80 billion x 4 = $320 billion.

boss.q: Government spending rises by $80 billion, MPC = 0.75, and crowding out reduces investment by $70 billion. What is the net AD shift?
boss.commonError: forgetting to subtract crowding out after applying the multiplier
boss.feedback: Gross AD shift is $320 billion. Subtract $70 billion of crowding out, leaving $250 billion.

boss.q: Households spend 75 cents of each additional dollar of disposable income. What does that imply?
options: The marginal propensity to save is 0.75, so the multiplier equals one.
The MPC is 0.75, so repeated spending creates a multiplier greater than one.
Crowding out must eliminate every later spending round.
boss.commonError: Confusing the marginal propensity to consume with the multiplier itself.
boss.feedback: An MPC of 0.75 means each spending round passes along 75 percent of added income, generating further rounds of expenditure.

boss.q: What is the central mechanism of crowding out?
options: Fiscal expansion lowers interest rates and increases private investment.
Higher government spending directly reduces the money supply.
A larger multiplier forces households to stop consuming.
Fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces some private investment spending.
boss.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate and investment effects of fiscal expansion.
boss.feedback: Government borrowing and stronger money demand can raise interest rates, discouraging private investment.

boss.q: Holding other factors constant, which change makes the simple spending multiplier larger?
options: A lower marginal propensity to save.
A higher marginal propensity to save.
A larger amount of crowding out.
A smaller initial change in government purchases.
boss.commonError: Treating more saving as a force that strengthens repeated spending rounds.
boss.feedback: A lower marginal propensity to save means a larger MPC, so more income is respent in each round.

boss.q: Government purchases rise by $20 billion and the MPC is 0.50. Ignoring crowding out, what is the predicted total increase in aggregate demand?
boss.commonError: Using the MPC itself as the multiplier or ignoring the repeated-spending process.
boss.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1 - 0.50) = 2, so a $20 billion increase produces a $40 billion gross shift.

boss.q: A fiscal package creates a gross $120 billion increase in aggregate demand, but higher interest rates reduce investment by $25 billion. What is the net shift?
boss.commonError: Adding the crowded-out investment to the gross effect rather than subtracting it.
boss.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of the expansion: $120 billion minus $25 billion equals a $95 billion net increase.

boss.q: Why can an equal-dollar tax cut create a smaller initial aggregate-demand shift than an equal increase in government purchases?
options: Tax cuts always raise interest rates before households receive them.
Government purchases do not pass through the multiplier process.
Tax cuts reduce disposable income before they affect consumption.
Tax cuts are partly saved; government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.
boss.commonError: Assuming every dollar of a tax cut is spent immediately.
boss.feedback: Only the consumed portion of a tax cut enters the first spending round, whereas government purchases are direct expenditure.

legendaryBoss.q: Government spending rises by $90 billion and MPC = 0.8. Crowding out reduces investment by $180 billion. What is the correct order of AD effects?
options: AD first shifts right $90 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $450 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $270 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $450 billion, then crowding out increases the shift to $630 billion.
AD first shifts left $90 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $450 billion, then crowding out leaves $270 billion.
AD shifts right only $90 billion because crowding out eliminates the multiplier.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not following initial shift, multiplier shift, then crowding-out offset
legendaryBoss.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5. The $90 billion initial shift becomes $450 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $270 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: The initial government-spending shift is $100 billion and the final AD shift is $400 billion. What MPC is implied, and what is the correct shift order?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then to $400 billion; MPC = 0.75.
AD first shifts right $400 billion, then back to $100 billion; MPC = 0.75.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then left $400 billion; MPC = 0.25.
AD first shifts right $100 billion, then to $400 billion; MPC = 0.8.
legendaryBoss.commonError: treating final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: The multiplier is 400/100 = 4. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 4, MPC = 0.75.

legendaryBoss.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. Expansionary fiscal policy also raises interest rates through crowding out. What happens to investment if both effects occur?
options: Investment falls from both interest-rate channels.
Investment rises from both interest-rate channels.
Investment rises from the money-demand channel but falls from crowding out.
Investment is unaffected because r is not connected to investment.
legendaryBoss.commonError: tracking only one interest-rate channel
legendaryBoss.feedback: Higher money demand raises r. Crowding out also raises r. Higher r reduces investment.

repairQuestions.q: If MPC = 0.5, the government purchases multiplier is:
repairQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so 1/(1-0.5)=2.

repairQuestions.q: Crowding out happens when fiscal expansion raises rates and reduces:
repairQuestions.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion by reducing private investment.

repairQuestions.q: Why might a tax cut have a smaller immediate effect than an equal increase in government purchases?
options: Households may save part of the tax cut
Government purchases are not part of GDP
repairQuestions.feedback: Some of a tax cut is saved, so its initial spending effect can be smaller than direct government purchases.

repairQuestions.q: The multiplier effect means an initial spending increase can raise AD by:
options: Only less than the initial spending
repairQuestions.feedback: The multiplier occurs when spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

repairQuestions.q: The multiplier effect means an initial increase in government spending can:
options: Create a larger total increase in aggregate demand and output
Affect only the first recipient of spending
Reduce GDP by the same amount
repairQuestions.feedback: Initial spending becomes income for others, whose further spending magnifies the total effect.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using MPC as the multiplier.
repairQuestions.q: The simple spending multiplier equals:
repairQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using MPC directly as the multiplier.
repairQuestions.q: If MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is:

repairQuestions.commonError: Adding crowding out instead of subtracting it.
repairQuestions.q: Crowding out reduces the effect of fiscal expansion by reducing:
repairQuestions.feedback: Crowding out happens when higher interest rates reduce private investment.

repairQuestions.commonError: Adding the crowding-out amount to the multiplier effect.
repairQuestions.q: If gross AD rises $200 billion and crowding out is $50 billion, net AD rises:
repairQuestions.feedback: Crowding out subtracts from the gross effect: $200 - $50 = $150 billion.

bridgeQuestions.q: If MPC = 0.8, the government purchases multiplier is:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-0.8)=5.

bridgeQuestions.q: Fiscal expansion raises interest rates. Which part of spending is most likely crowded out?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher interest rates reduce private investment.

bridgeQuestions.q: Government spending rises by $20 billion and the multiplier is 3. Before crowding out, AD rises by:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The multiplier effect is $20 billion x 3 = $60 billion.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
bridgeQuestions.q: Government purchases rise $50 billion and MPC is 0.75. Which statement correctly connects the fiscal action to the multiplier concept?
options: The $50 billion first-round AD impulse is magnified to $200 billion before any crowding-out offset.
The $50 billion first-round impulse remains $50 billion because later spending rounds do not affect AD.
The multiplier reduces the initial AD impulse to $37.5 billion.
The fiscal action shifts LRAS rather than aggregate demand.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Carries the gross fiscal impulse into stabilization analysis even after an offset has been specified.
bridgeQuestions.q: A fiscal package generates a $300 billion gross AD increase, but crowding out reduces private investment by $80 billion in the simplified model. What AD impulse should stabilization analysis carry forward?
options: $300 billion because stabilization uses only the gross multiplier effect.
$80 billion because crowding out replaces the fiscal impulse.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Stabilization analysis should use the net aggregate-demand impulse after the multiplier and stated crowding-out offset.

AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above and left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3 left of LRAS, Y1 on LRAS, Y2 right of LRAS, and price levels P1, P2, and P3. AD1-AS2 is at Y1/P1; AD1-AS1 is at Y3/P2; AD2-AS2 is at Y2/P2; AD2-AS1 is at Y1/P3.

MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right and upward and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

A horizontal line at price level P crosses three downward-sloping aggregate-demand curves.
