short-run-aggregate-supply.title: Short-Run Aggregate Supply
short-run-aggregate-supply.description: Analyze the SRAS slope, expected prices, input costs, productivity, and short-run aggregate-supply shifts.

easy.q: The short-run aggregate supply curve slopes upward mainly because:
options: Wages, prices, or perceptions do not adjust instantly
Money is neutral in every period
easy.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to the short run.
easy.feedback: SRAS slopes upward because sticky wages, sticky prices, and misperceptions allow price-level changes to affect output.

easy.q: A decrease in oil prices would most likely shift:
easy.commonError: Treating production cost changes as AD shifts.
easy.feedback: Lower production costs shift short-run aggregate supply to the right.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from AS2 to AS1 represents:
options: A decrease in short-run aggregate supply
An increase in short-run aggregate supply
easy.commonError: Reversing AS1 and AS2.
easy.feedback: AS1 is up and left of AS2, so moving from AS2 to AS1 is a decrease in SRAS.

easy.q: An increase in nominal wages, holding productivity and expected prices constant, shifts short-run aggregate supply:
options: Down along the same SRAS curve.
easy.commonError: Reversing the effect of higher production costs.
easy.feedback: Higher nominal wages raise firms’ costs and reduce output supplied at each price level.

easy.q: What change from AS0 to AS1 is shown?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: When the aggregate supply curve shifts left/up, less output is supplied at each price level, which is a decrease in aggregate supply.

easy.q: How should AS1 be classified relative to AS0 in the second aggregate-supply diagram?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: A downward/rightward shift of the AS curve means aggregate supply has increased.

medium.q: Sticky-wage theory explains upward-sloping SRAS because unexpected price-level changes affect:
options: Real labor costs and firm production decisions
medium.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to short-run wages.
medium.feedback: When nominal wages are sticky, price-level changes alter real labor costs and production.

medium.q: If expected prices rise, short-run aggregate supply usually shifts:
medium.commonError: Reversing expected price effects on SRAS.
medium.feedback: Higher expected prices push wages and costs upward, shifting SRAS left.

medium.q: If workers and firms expect a higher price level before contracts are set, short-run aggregate supply tends to:
options: Remain fixed because expectations affect only AD.
medium.commonError: Reversing the expected-price effect.
medium.feedback: Higher expected prices tend to produce higher nominal wages and other input costs.

medium.q: A temporary payroll-tax reduction lowers firms’ labor costs. Holding other factors constant, SRAS shifts:
medium.commonError: Treating a production-cost change as an AD shifter.
medium.feedback: Lower per-worker cost raises short-run output supplied at each price level.

medium.q: Why can an unexpected rise in the price level increase output in the short run under sticky-wage theory?
options: Household wealth rises and shifts AD
Nominal wages immediately rise more than prices
Product prices rise before nominal wages fully adjust, lowering real labor cost.
medium.commonError: Confusing short-run wage rigidity with long-run capacity.
medium.feedback: With sticky wages, unexpected price increases can make production temporarily more profitable.

medium.q: Which event best matches the shift from AS0 to AS1?
options: Higher consumer confidence that boosts spending
A cut in income taxes that raises aggregate demand
A rise in input prices that makes production more costly
A fall in the overall price level causing a movement along AS0
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Higher production costs shift short-run aggregate supply left.

medium.q: If aggregate demand stays put, what equilibrium effect follows from the supply change in the second AS diagram?
options: Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: A rightward shift of AS increases output and lowers the price level.

medium.q: Which favorable production-side change could account for the shift displayed in the second AS diagram?
options: A fall in input costs or an improvement in productivity
An increase in government purchases that shifts AD right
A rise in inflation expectations that shifts SRAS left
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Lower costs or better productivity shift aggregate supply right.

hard.q: Oil prices rise sharply, but firms also adopt a productivity-enhancing technology. What can be concluded about SRAS?
options: The net shift is ambiguous because costs rise while productivity improves.
hard.commonError: Allowing one supply shifter to dominate without magnitude information.
hard.feedback: Higher oil costs push SRAS left, while higher productivity pushes it right.

hard.q: Expected prices rise by 4 percent, but nominal wages are locked in long-term contracts. Compared with a setting where wages adjust immediately, the leftward SRAS shift is likely:
hard.commonError: Ignoring the mechanism through which expectations affect costs.
hard.feedback: If wages cannot yet adjust, expected-price changes have a weaker immediate cost effect.

hard.q: The price level rises unexpectedly while nominal wages are fixed. In the short run, firms tend to:
options: Increase production because output prices rise relative to wage costs.
Leave output unchanged because SRAS is vertical
Reduce production because real wages rise
hard.commonError: Reversing the real-wage effect.
hard.feedback: Unexpectedly higher output prices lower the real cost of contracted wages.

hard.q: A government permanently improves transportation infrastructure but finances it with a temporary business-energy surcharge. Which supply effects are possible?
options: LRAS may shift right while SRAS shifts left temporarily.
Both LRAS and SRAS must shift left permanently.
LRAS must remain fixed because taxes are involved.
hard.commonError: Treating all policy effects as demand-side or same-direction.
hard.feedback: Infrastructure can raise capacity while the temporary surcharge raises current production costs.

hard.q: Firms revise expected prices downward after a period of unexpectedly low inflation. Holding actual prices fixed, SRAS tends to:
options: Move upward along the same curve.
hard.commonError: Reversing how lower expected prices affect wage and cost setting.
hard.feedback: Lower expected prices tend to reduce nominal wage and input-cost growth.

hard.q: At real GDP of 150, what is the vertical price-level gap between AS0 and AS1?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: At the same output level, the price level increases from 150 to 190, a rise of 40.

hard.q: Use the second AS graph at real GDP 150. What vertical price-level distance separates AS0 and AS1?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: At the same output level, price level falls from 150 to 110, a decrease of 40.

hard.q: Which event best matches the joint shift from SRAS0/LRAS0 to SRAS1/LRAS1?
options: A confidence drop that lowers consumer and investment spending
A productivity gain that lowers costs and raises potential output
An energy-price increase that raises costs and lowers output
A government-spending increase that shifts aggregate demand right
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: A positive supply-side change can shift both SRAS right and LRAS right.

elite.q: Workers expect 6 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 2 percent and wage contracts reflect the higher expectation. What happens to SRAS relative to contracts based on accurate expectations?
options: SRAS is farther left because nominal labor costs are higher than necessary.
SRAS is farther right because real wages are lower
elite.commonError: Ignoring how excessive expected inflation enters wage contracts.
elite.feedback: Higher expected prices can produce higher nominal wages and lower short-run supply.

elite.q: A severe storm destroys capital, while emergency deregulation lowers current compliance costs. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: LRAS shifts left, while the SRAS effect is ambiguous because cost relief offsets disruption.
LRAS shifts right because regulation falls
Both curves must shift left by the same amount
elite.commonError: Assuming all supply forces have the same horizon and direction.
elite.feedback: Capital destruction lowers capacity; lower compliance cost pushes SRAS right, while storm disruption may push it left.

elite.q: A student says, “Any rise in the price level shifts SRAS right.” What is the best correction?
options: Any price-level rise shifts aggregate demand left only
A change in the actual price level causes movement along SRAS; expected prices or costs shift the curve.
Actual prices shift LRAS, not SRAS
The statement is correct in every case
elite.commonError: Confusing movement along SRAS with a curve shift.
elite.feedback: The actual price level is an axis variable, not a supply shifter by itself.

elite.q: With aggregate demand unchanged, which macro outcome is consistent with the AS shift shown?
options: Lower output with a higher price level
Higher output with a lower price level
Higher output with a higher price level
Lower output with a lower price level
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: A leftward shift of AS reduces output and raises prices, the classic stagflation pattern.

elite.q: For the second AS diagram, what output-price pattern would follow if aggregate demand stayed fixed?
options: Lower output with a higher price level
Higher output with a higher price level
Higher output with a lower price level
Lower output with a lower price level
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: Demand-pull expansions raise both price level and output. This graph instead shows more output paired with a lower price level, which is an AS increase.

legendary.q: Expected inflation rises, productivity improves, and oil prices fall. What can be concluded about SRAS?
options: The direction is ambiguous because expectations push left while productivity and cheaper oil push right.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring offsetting supply shifters.
legendary.feedback: Multiple cost and productivity forces push SRAS in opposite directions.

legendary.q: Nominal wages are fixed for one year. The price level rises unexpectedly, then wage contracts reset to reflect the higher expected price level. What sequence is most likely?
options: A rightward SRAS shift followed by movement down
Movement up along SRAS at first, followed later by a leftward SRAS shift.
legendary.commonError: Failing to distinguish immediate movement from later expectation adjustment.
legendary.feedback: Unexpected prices initially raise output along SRAS; higher wage expectations later shift SRAS left.

legendary.q: An economy’s expected price level falls while actual price level and productive resources are unchanged. At each actual price level, firms are likely to supply:
options: More potential output, so LRAS shifts right.
Less output, so SRAS shifts left.
The same output because expectations never matter.
More output, so SRAS shifts right.
legendary.commonError: Confusing expected-price effects with long-run capacity.
legendary.feedback: Lower expected prices tend to lower nominal input costs and raise short-run supply.

legendary.q: Which statement best interprets the shift from AS0 to AS1 without confusing it for a movement along a curve?
options: AS1 shows more output demanded at each price level.
AS1 shows less output supplied at each price level.
AS0 and AS1 are two points on one supply curve.
AS1 shows higher potential output on a shifted LRAS.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: The entire AS curve shifted up/left. That means production is less forthcoming at each price level, not that the economy merely moved to another point on AS0.

legendary.q: Which statement best interprets the move from AS0 to AS1?
options: AS1 shows less output demanded at each price level.
AS0 and AS1 are two points on one supply curve.
AS1 shows lower potential output on a shifted LRAS.
AS1 shows more output supplied at each price level.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: A lower AS curve means firms will supply more at each price level, or the same output at a lower price level. That is an increase in aggregate supply.

boss.q: Which change shifts SRAS right?
boss.commonError: Reversing the effect of input costs.
boss.feedback: Lower input prices reduce production costs.

boss.q: An unexpected price-level increase with sticky wages causes movement:
boss.commonError: Confusing movement along the curve with a shift.
boss.feedback: The actual price level changes quantity supplied along the existing SRAS curve.

boss.q: Higher expected prices usually shift SRAS:
boss.commonError: Reversing the expectation effect.
boss.feedback: Higher expected prices tend to raise nominal wages and costs.

boss.q: A sharp fall in oil prices tends to shift SRAS:
boss.commonError: Reversing the input-cost effect.
boss.feedback: Cheaper energy lowers production costs.

boss.q: Expected prices fall while actual prices are unchanged. SRAS shifts:
boss.commonError: Reversing lower expected cost pressure.
boss.feedback: Lower expected prices tend to lower nominal wages and costs.

boss.q: A price-level rise by itself causes:
options: Movement up along SRAS, not a shift of SRAS.
boss.commonError: Confusing an axis change with a curve shifter.
boss.feedback: Actual price level changes quantity supplied along SRAS.

legendaryBoss.q: Productivity rises permanently, expected prices rise, and oil prices fall. What is the most accurate result?
options: LRAS is unchanged and SRAS shifts left.
LRAS shifts right; the SRAS direction is ambiguous.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Forcing offsetting SRAS shifters into one predetermined direction.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Productivity raises capacity; expected prices and oil prices push SRAS in opposite directions.

legendaryBoss.q: Nominal wages are fixed when the price level unexpectedly rises, then contracts reset with higher expected inflation. What sequence follows?
options: Movement up along SRAS, then a leftward SRAS shift.
A rightward SRAS shift, then movement down.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Failing to separate current movement from later expectation adjustment.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Unexpected prices first change quantity supplied; updated wage expectations later shift SRAS.

repairQuestions.q: Higher expected prices usually shift SRAS:
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher expected prices raise costs and shift SRAS left.

repairQuestions.q: SRAS slopes upward mainly because wages, prices, or perceptions:
repairQuestions.feedback: Sticky wages, sticky prices, and misperceptions help explain upward-sloping SRAS.

repairQuestions.q: Higher production costs shift SRAS:
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher production costs reduce SRAS and shift it left.

repairQuestions.q: Lower production costs shift SRAS:
repairQuestions.feedback: Lower production costs increase SRAS and shift it right.

repairQuestions.q: A leftward shift of SRAS means:
options: Firms supply less output at each price level
The money supply fell by definition
repairQuestions.feedback: A leftward SRAS shift reflects higher costs or lower productive capacity in the short run.

bridgeQuestions.q: Workers expect higher prices and negotiate higher nominal wages. What happens to SRAS?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher expected prices raise wage demands and production costs, shifting SRAS left.

bridgeQuestions.q: If nominal wages are sticky and the price level rises unexpectedly, firms' real labor costs:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Sticky nominal wages mean a higher price level lowers real labor costs and can raise output.

bridgeQuestions.q: Oil prices fall and shift SRAS to the right while aggregate demand is unchanged. What should be done next to determine the macroeconomic outcome?
options: Locate the new intersection of SRAS and aggregate demand to infer output and the price level.
Move along the old SRAS curve without finding a new equilibrium.
Shift LRAS right automatically because oil became cheaper.
Treat the change as an aggregate-demand shock and ignore SRAS.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A supply shift changes the short-run equilibrium where the new SRAS curve intersects aggregate demand.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Identifies a supply shift but does not translate it into an equilibrium outcome.

long-run-aggregate-supply-and-potential-.title: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output
long-run-aggregate-supply-and-potential-.description: Analyze LRAS, natural or potential output, productive capacity, and long-run aggregate-supply shifts.

objectiveLabels.long-run-aggregate-supply-and-potential-: Long-Run Aggregate Supply and Potential Output

easy.q: Which curve is vertical in the long run?
easy.commonError: Confusing SRAS and LRAS.
easy.feedback: LRAS is vertical because long-run output depends on resources, capital, technology, and institutions.

easy.q: A rise in economy-wide productivity shifts long-run aggregate supply:
options: Not at all because productivity affects only demand.
easy.commonError: Confusing productive capacity with aggregate demand.
easy.feedback: Higher productivity raises the economy’s sustainable level of output.

medium.q: A hurricane destroys factories and transport infrastructure. Which long-run effect is most likely?
options: LRAS shifts left because productive capacity falls.
SRAS shifts right because inputs are scarcer.
LRAS shifts right because rebuilding spending rises.
medium.commonError: Focusing on reconstruction spending while ignoring lost capacity.
medium.feedback: Destroyed capital reduces the economy’s potential output.

hard.q: A productivity improvement lowers production costs and raises potential output over time. Which curves are most likely affected?
hard.commonError: Treating productivity only as demand.
hard.feedback: Higher productivity can shift SRAS right and increase long-run aggregate supply.

hard.q: A permanent increase in the labor force raises potential output, while a temporary surge in energy prices raises costs. Which combination is most likely?
options: LRAS shifts right and SRAS shifts left.
LRAS shifts left and SRAS shifts right.
hard.commonError: Combining long-run capacity and short-run cost changes incorrectly.
hard.feedback: More labor raises capacity; higher energy prices reduce short-run supply.

elite.q: A country receives a permanent productivity improvement and a temporary spike in imported input prices. Which graph change best fits?
options: LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
LRAS shifts right, while SRAS may shift left initially.
elite.commonError: Failing to separate permanent capacity from temporary production costs.
elite.feedback: Productivity raises potential output; costly imported inputs can reduce short-run supply.

legendary.q: A permanent tax credit raises capital investment, while a temporary wage subsidy lowers current labor costs. Which supply changes are most likely?
options: LRAS shifts right over time and SRAS shifts right immediately.
SRAS shifts left because subsidies raise wages
LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
legendary.commonError: Failing to distinguish capacity growth from current cost reduction.
legendary.feedback: More capital raises potential output, while the subsidy lowers short-run production cost.

legendary.q: A country loses 5 percent of its capital stock but gains a technology that raises remaining capital productivity by 8 percent. What is the LRAS implication?
options: The net LRAS effect is ambiguous without knowing the relative output effects.
LRAS must shift right because productivity rose more in percentage terms.
LRAS cannot change when two forces offset.
LRAS must shift left because capital fell.
legendary.commonError: Comparing raw percentages that apply to different economic quantities.
legendary.feedback: The effect on potential output depends on how each change affects productive capacity.

legendary.q: A permanent improvement in education raises worker productivity, but a new regulation raises current compliance costs. Which statement is most complete?
options: LRAS shifts right, while SRAS may shift left in the short run.
Education affects AD rather than supply
legendary.commonError: Treating permanent productivity and current cost changes as identical.
legendary.feedback: Education raises capacity; compliance costs can reduce short-run supply.

boss.q: LRAS is vertical because long-run output depends primarily on:
boss.commonError: Treating the price level as the source of long-run output.
boss.feedback: Potential output is determined by productive capacity.

boss.q: A permanent rise in productivity most directly shifts:
boss.commonError: Misclassifying a capacity improvement.
boss.feedback: Higher productivity raises potential output.

boss.q: A permanent labor-force increase occurs with a temporary oil-price spike. Which curves move?
boss.commonError: Combining capacity and cost changes incorrectly.
boss.feedback: More labor raises capacity; expensive oil reduces short-run supply.

legendaryBoss.q: Capital is destroyed while a new technology raises productivity. Which LRAS conclusion is valid?
options: LRAS cannot shift because the forces differ
The net direction is ambiguous without the relative output effects.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Comparing opposing capacity changes without magnitudes.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Lost capital and better technology push potential output in opposite directions.

repairQuestions.q: LRAS is vertical because long-run output depends mainly on:
repairQuestions.feedback: LRAS reflects productive capacity, not the current price level.

bridgeQuestions.q: Better technology and more productive capital most directly shift which long-run curve?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Better productive capacity shifts LRAS right.

ad-as-equilibrium-and-output-gaps.title: AD-AS Equilibrium and Output Gaps
ad-as-equilibrium-and-output-gaps.description: Read static AD-AS equilibrium and distinguish recessionary and inflationary gaps relative to potential output.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At AD1 and AS2, the economy is at:
easy.commonError: Reading the wrong intersection.
easy.feedback: AD1 and AS2 intersect at Y1 and P1.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At AD2 and AS2, the economy is at:
easy.commonError: Ignoring the curve labels.
easy.feedback: AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2 and P2.

easy.q: If the economy is below natural output, unemployment is usually:
easy.commonError: Missing the link between output and unemployment.
easy.feedback: When output is below potential, unemployment is usually above the natural rate.

easy.q: In the AD-AS-LRAS graph, which labeled point represents the original long-run equilibrium before aggregate demand increases?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: The original long-run equilibrium is where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 meet. That is point C.

easy.q: Which labeled point is the original long-run equilibrium in the graph with LRAS0 and LRAS1?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: Point A is where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 intersect.

easy.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Which output level is natural output?
easy.commonError: Confusing natural output with the highest output shown.
easy.feedback: Natural output is where LRAS is located, which is Y1.

easy.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Output level Y2 is:
easy.commonError: Ignoring LRAS when judging output gaps.
easy.feedback: Y2 is to the right of LRAS, so output is above natural output.

easy.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Output level Y3 is:
easy.commonError: Ignoring LRAS when judging output gaps.
easy.feedback: Y3 is to the left of LRAS, so output is below natural output.

easy.q: A recessionary gap means output is:
easy.commonError: Reversing recessionary and expansionary gaps.
easy.feedback: A recessionary gap occurs when output is below natural output.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD2-AS2, what happens?
options: Output rises and the price level rises
Output falls and the price level falls
Output rises and the price level falls
Output falls and the price level rises
medium.commonError: Reading only one axis after an AD shift.
medium.feedback: The economy moves from Y1-P1 to Y2-P2, so both output and the price level rise.

medium.q: After wages and expectations adjust, SRAS shifts from SRAS0 to SRAS1. Which point shows the new long-run equilibrium?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: The new long-run equilibrium occurs where AD1, SRAS1, and LRAS0 intersect: point B.

medium.q: Which labeled point is the new long-run equilibrium after the supply-side improvement?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Point B is where AD0, SRAS1, and LRAS1 intersect.

medium.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy is at Y2, the main short-run concern is:
options: The price level is below zero
medium.commonError: Ignoring LRAS when judging gaps.
medium.feedback: Y2 is to the right of LRAS, so output is above potential.

medium.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy is at Y3, unemployment is most likely:
medium.commonError: Missing the output-unemployment link.
medium.feedback: Y3 is below natural output, so unemployment is usually above the natural rate.

medium.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD2-AS2, the short-run result is:
medium.commonError: Treating any AD increase as long-run equilibrium.
medium.feedback: The move ends at Y2, which is above natural output, creating an expansionary gap.

hard.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy starts at AD1-AS2 and AD shifts to AD2, what gap appears?
hard.commonError: Ignoring LRAS after an AD shift.
hard.feedback: The economy moves to Y2, which is above natural output, so it creates an expansionary gap.

hard.q: A hurricane permanently destroys part of an economy's productive capital, and real GDP falls below its old potential level. Why would it be wrong to assume ordinary recessionary-gap self-correction must restore the old level of output?
options: The loss of productive capital can shift LRAS left, so the economy's new potential output may be lower.
Any fall in real GDP forces aggregate demand to shift permanently left.
Nominal wages cannot adjust after a supply-side disturbance.
SRAS always shifts right enough to restore the pre-shock LRAS position.
hard.commonError: Assumes every fall in real GDP is a temporary gap around an unchanged potential-output level.
hard.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

elite.q: Comparing the original long-run equilibrium C with the new long-run equilibrium B, what is true?
options: GDP returns to 100; prices rise from 125 to 175.
GDP rises to 125; prices remain fixed at 125 throughout.
GDP falls to 75; prices remain fixed at 150 throughout.
GDP stays at 100; prices fall from 125 back to 100.
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: LRAS stays at 100, so long-run real GDP returns to 100. The long-run price level is higher at B than at C.

elite.q: Which description best matches the move from A to B?
options: AD rises; the economy moves upward along fixed AS0.
AS rises; the economy moves downward along fixed AD0.
AD falls; the economy moves downward along fixed AS0.
Both AD and AS shift; output returns to its starting level.
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: With AS0 unchanged, the AD increase causes a movement along the AS curve to a new short-run equilibrium.

legendary.q: A student says point B can only be explained by higher aggregate demand because real GDP is larger there. Which correction best fits the graph?
options: AD shifts right while SRAS and LRAS both stay fixed.
SRAS shifts left while AD0 and LRAS both stay fixed.
LRAS shifts left while SRAS and AD0 both stay fixed.
SRAS and LRAS shift right while AD0 stays fixed.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: The graph holds AD constant and shows the supply side improving. That raises potential output and lowers the price level.

boss.q: In the long-run AD–AS model, natural output is determined mainly by:
options: Labor, capital, natural resources, technology, and institutions.
The latest movement in aggregate demand alone.
The nominal money supply with no real-side conditions.
boss.commonError: Treating natural output as a price-level or demand choice.
boss.feedback: Natural output reflects the economy’s productive capacity and real institutions.

boss.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy is operating at Y3 rather than the LRAS level Y1, which condition is consistent with the gap shown?
options: An inflationary gap with unemployment below its natural rate.
Long-run equilibrium with no pressure on wages or expected prices.
A permanent increase in potential output from Y1 to Y3.
A recessionary gap with unemployment above its natural rate.
boss.commonError: Confuses the highest output shown with potential output or reverses recessionary and inflationary gaps.
boss.feedback: Compare current real output with the LRAS/potential-output level: below potential is recessionary; above potential is inflationary.

boss.q: Real GDP is below its old potential level after a permanent decline in labor-force participation. Which diagnostic prevents a mistaken forecast that ordinary self-correction must restore the old output level?
options: Check whether LRAS itself shifted left; if potential output fell, the old level is no longer the long-run anchor.
Assume every output decline is caused by aggregate demand.
Hold LRAS fixed because productive capacity cannot change.
Assume falling wages always restore the pre-shock quantity of labor and output.
boss.commonError: Assumes every fall in real GDP is a temporary gap around an unchanged potential-output level.
boss.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

legendaryBoss.q: An economy has a recessionary gap after aggregate demand falls. While wages are adjusting downward, a permanent productivity improvement raises productive capacity. Which conclusion best separates the two long-run forces?
options: The productivity gain shifts aggregate demand right while wage adjustment shifts LRAS left, so both forces alter potential output in opposite directions.
The original demand shock permanently fixes real output below potential, so neither wage adjustment nor improved productivity can change the long-run outcome.
SRAS adjustment helps close the demand-created gap, while higher productivity can shift LRAS right and change the potential-output target.
Both changes should be treated as the same SRAS movement, because productive capacity does not affect the location of LRAS in this model.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes every fall in real GDP is a temporary gap around an unchanged potential-output level.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

repairQuestions.q: When real output is below natural output, unemployment is usually:
repairQuestions.feedback: A recessionary gap means firms need fewer workers, so unemployment tends to exceed the natural rate.

repairQuestions.q: In an AD-AS graph, short-run equilibrium occurs where:
options: Aggregate demand intersects short-run aggregate supply
repairQuestions.feedback: The intersection of AD and SRAS determines the short-run equilibrium price level and real output.

repairQuestions.q: If output is below natural output, the economy has:
repairQuestions.feedback: Output below natural output is a recessionary gap.

repairQuestions.q: If output is above natural output, the economy has:
repairQuestions.feedback: Output above natural output is an expansionary gap.

repairQuestions.q: On an AD-AS graph, natural output is the output level where:
repairQuestions.feedback: Natural output is potential output, the economy's sustainable long-run production level.

bridgeQuestions.q: Output is $19 trillion while natural output is $20 trillion. The economy has:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Actual output below natural output is a recessionary gap.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Aggregate demand and short-run aggregate supply graph with two AD curves, two AS curves, and labeled output-price combinations.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above/left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3, Y1, Y2 and P1, P2, P3. AD1 intersects AS2 at Y1/P1, AD1 intersects AS1 at Y3/P2, AD2 intersects AS2 at Y2/P2, and AD2 intersects AS1 at Y1/P3.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: AD-AS-LRAS graph with AD0, AD1, SRAS0, SRAS1, LRAS0, and labeled points A, B, C, and D.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP and the vertical axis is price level. LRAS0 is vertical at real GDP 100. AD0 intersects SRAS0 at point C, where real GDP is 100 and price level is 125. AD1 intersects SRAS0 at point D, where real GDP is 125 and price level is 150. AD0 intersects SRAS1 at point A, where real GDP is 75 and price level is 150. AD1 intersects SRAS1 and LRAS0 at point B, where real GDP is 100 and price level is 175. The graph can be used to trace an AD increase from original long-run equilibrium C to short-run point D and then to long-run point B after SRAS shifts left.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: AD-AS-LRAS graph with AD0, SRAS0, SRAS1, LRAS0, LRAS1, and labeled points A and B.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP and the vertical axis is price level. AD0 slopes downward. Point A is the original long-run equilibrium where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 intersect at real GDP 100 and price level 125. A dashed SRAS1 curve lies below SRAS0, and a dashed LRAS1 line lies to the right of LRAS0 at real GDP 115. Point B is the new long-run equilibrium where AD0, SRAS1, and LRAS1 intersect at real GDP 115 and price level 110. The graph shows a positive supply-side change that raises long-run output and lowers the price level.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with LRAS at Y1, two aggregate-demand curves, two short-run aggregate-supply curves, and labeled gaps.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. LRAS is vertical at Y1. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above/left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3 left of LRAS, Y1 on LRAS, Y2 right of LRAS, and price levels P1, P2, P3. AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1; AD1-AS1 is Y3/P2; AD2-AS2 is Y2/P2; AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3.

assetMetadata.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with AD0, AD1, AS0, and labeled points A and B.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP and the vertical axis is price level. AD0 intersects AS0 at point A, where real GDP is 150 and the price level is 125. A dashed AD1 curve lies to the right of AD0 and intersects AS0 at point B, where real GDP is 175 and the price level is 137.5. This graph shows an increase in aggregate demand moving the economy along a fixed short-run aggregate supply curve.

demand-and-supply-shocks.title: Demand and Supply Shocks
demand-and-supply-shocks.description: Classify and trace demand shocks, supply shocks, stagflation, and simultaneous short-run shocks.

easy.q: A sudden increase in oil prices is best treated as:
easy.commonError: Calling an oil shock a demand shock.
easy.feedback: Higher oil prices raise production costs and shift SRAS left.

easy.q: A negative demand shock usually causes which short-run outcome?
easy.commonError: Confusing demand shocks with supply shocks.
easy.feedback: A leftward AD shift lowers output and the price level in the short run.

easy.q: An adverse supply shock usually causes which short-run outcome?
easy.commonError: Thinking all recessions lower inflation.
easy.feedback: An adverse supply shock lowers output and raises the price level.

easy.q: Stagflation means:
easy.commonError: Treating stagflation as any recession.
easy.feedback: Stagflation is the combination of falling output and rising prices.

easy.q: In the AD-AS graph, which point shows the original equilibrium before aggregate demand rises?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: Point A is the intersection of AD0 and AS0.

easy.q: Which point marks the original equilibrium where AD0 and AS0 intersect?
easy.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
easy.feedback: Point A is the initial intersection of AD0 and AS0.

medium.q: Assume aggregate demand is unchanged. Based on the AS shift shown, what happens to equilibrium real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: An inward/leftward AS shift reduces output and raises the price level.

medium.q: A recession caused by falling consumer confidence is most directly a:
medium.commonError: Calling lower spending a supply shock.
medium.feedback: Falling confidence reduces consumption and shifts AD left.

medium.q: An oil price spike causes output to fall and prices to rise. Which curve moved first?
medium.commonError: Treating stagflation as an AD shock.
medium.feedback: Higher oil prices raise production costs and shift SRAS left.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD1-AS1, what happens?
options: Output rises and price level falls
Output falls and price level rises
Output rises and price level rises
Output falls and price level falls
medium.commonError: Reading an SRAS left shift as lower prices.
medium.feedback: The economy moves from Y1-P1 to Y3-P2, so output falls and the price level rises.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. If AD rises from AD1 to AD2 while SRAS rises from AS1 to AS2, the final point is:
medium.commonError: Tracking only one curve shift.
medium.feedback: AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2 and P2.

medium.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD1-AS1, the short-run result is:
medium.commonError: Missing stagflation from an adverse supply shock.
medium.feedback: The move ends at Y3 and P2: lower output, higher prices, and unemployment pressure.

medium.q: Which policy would most directly offset a recessionary AD shock?
medium.commonError: Using contraction when AD is already weak.
medium.feedback: Expansionary policy can shift AD right to offset a recessionary demand shock.

medium.q: Which statement best describes an adverse supply shock policy problem?
options: Policy faces a tradeoff between inflation and output losses
Policy can lower inflation and unemployment immediately
Fiscal expansion shifts SRAS right automatically
Monetary contraction raises output and lowers inflation
medium.commonError: Thinking supply shocks have an easy policy fix.
medium.feedback: A negative supply shock raises prices and lowers output, creating a difficult stabilization tradeoff.

medium.q: If aggregate demand increases from AD0 to AD1 while SRAS0 is still fixed in the short run, which point shows the short-run equilibrium?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: With AD1 and SRAS0, the short-run equilibrium is point D.

medium.q: From point A to point B, what happens to real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP rises from 100 to 115 while the price level falls from 125 to 110
Real GDP falls from 115 to 100 while the price level rises from 110 to 125
Both real GDP and the price level rise
Both real GDP and the price level fall
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: The graph shows more long-run output and a lower price level at the new equilibrium.

medium.q: After aggregate demand shifts from AD0 to AD1 while AS0 is fixed, which point shows the new short-run equilibrium?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Point B is where AD1 intersects AS0.

medium.q: From point A to point B, by how much does real GDP increase?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: Real GDP rises from 150 to 175, an increase of 25.

medium.q: If only aggregate demand increases from AD0 to AD1 while AS0 stays in place, which point shows the new equilibrium?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: With AD1 and AS0, the equilibrium is point B.

medium.q: If only aggregate supply decreases from AS0 to AS1 while AD0 stays in place, which point shows the new equilibrium?
medium.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
medium.feedback: With AD0 and AS1, the equilibrium is point D.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy moves from AD1-AS1 to AD1-AS2, what happens?
hard.commonError: Reading a positive SRAS shift backward.
hard.feedback: Moving from AS1 to AS2 along AD1 raises output from Y3 to Y1 and lowers the price level from P2 to P1.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy starts at AD1-AS2 and both AD and SRAS increase, where does it end?
hard.commonError: Tracking only one curve shift.
hard.feedback: AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2 and P2.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS1, which change gets the economy to Y2 and P2?
hard.commonError: Forgetting both curves must change.
hard.feedback: Starting from AD1-AS1 at Y3-P2, moving to AD2-AS2 requires AD to rise and SRAS to rise.

hard.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, an adverse supply shock moves the economy to:
hard.commonError: Treating a supply shock as an AD shift.
hard.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts SRAS from AS2 to AS1, moving the economy to Y3 and P2.

hard.q: A tax hike reduces consumption and output falls below natural output. Which graph movement fits best?
options: AD shifts left, creating a recessionary gap
AD shifts right, creating an expansionary gap
hard.commonError: Confusing fiscal demand effects with supply shocks.
hard.feedback: A tax hike reduces aggregate demand and can create a recessionary gap.

hard.q: An economy faces higher oil prices and falling output. Why is aggressive AD stimulus risky?
options: It may restore output but add inflation pressure
It must lower prices and raise unemployment
It shifts SRAS right without cost
hard.commonError: Thinking supply-shock policy has no tradeoff.
hard.feedback: Stimulating AD can support output but may worsen inflation after an adverse supply shock.

hard.q: Which shock produces higher prices and lower output without first changing AD?
hard.commonError: Treating stagflation as a demand shock.
hard.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts SRAS left, raising prices and lowering output.

hard.q: Which sequence correctly traces the economy after an increase in aggregate demand starting from the original long-run equilibrium?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: The economy begins at C, moves to D in the short run when AD increases, and returns to long-run output at B after SRAS shifts left.

hard.q: From point A to point B, by how much does the price level increase?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: The price level rises from 125 to 137.5, an increase of 12.5.

hard.q: If aggregate demand increases from AD0 to AD1 at the same time aggregate supply decreases from AS0 to AS1, which point shows the resulting equilibrium?
hard.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
hard.feedback: The simultaneous changes place the economy at the intersection of AD1 and AS1, which is point C.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS2, AD rises to AD2 while SRAS falls to AS1. What is the final point?
elite.commonError: Following only AD or only SRAS.
elite.feedback: AD2 and AS1 intersect at Y1 and P3, so output returns to Y1 while the price level rises.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD2-AS1, AD falls to AD1 while SRAS rises to AS2. What is the final point?
elite.commonError: Tracking the starting point but not both curve shifts.
elite.feedback: AD1 and AS2 intersect at Y1 and P1.

elite.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, an oil shock shifts AS2 to AS1, then policymakers shift AD1 to AD2. What happens?
options: Output returns to Y1 but prices rise to P3
Output rises to Y2 while prices stay P2
Output falls to Y3 while prices fall P1
Output returns to Y1 while prices fall P1
elite.commonError: Missing the inflation cost of accommodating a supply shock.
elite.feedback: Accommodation restores output from Y3 to Y1, but the price level rises to P3.

elite.q: A supply shock raises prices and lowers output. The central bank tightens policy to fight inflation. What is the likely short-run danger?
elite.commonError: Ignoring output costs of tightening after a supply shock.
elite.feedback: Tightening reduces AD and may lower inflation pressure, but it can worsen the output decline.

elite.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, which shock-policy combination moves the economy to Y1 and P3?
options: Adverse supply shock plus AD stimulus
Positive supply shock plus AD contraction
Negative AD shock plus SRAS expansion
elite.commonError: Missing the price cost of accommodation.
elite.feedback: A supply shock moves AS2 to AS1 and AD stimulus moves AD1 to AD2, ending at Y1 and P3.

elite.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, which shock creates stagflation before any policy response?
elite.commonError: Calling stagflation an AD movement.
elite.feedback: AS2 shifting left to AS1 lowers output to Y3 and raises the price level to P2.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD2-AS2, which movement could reduce output without lowering the price level?
elite.commonError: Assuming lower output always lowers prices.
elite.feedback: A leftward SRAS shift from AS2 to AS1 moves from Y2-P2 to Y1-P3: output falls while prices rise.

elite.q: Compare point A with point C. Which statement is correct?
options: Real GDP rises to 100; the price level stays at 100.
Real GDP falls to 50; the price level stays at 125.
Real GDP stays 75; the price level rises from 100 to 150.
Real GDP stays 75; the price level falls from 150 to 100.
elite.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
elite.feedback: The AD increase and AS decrease offset each other in output but reinforce each other on the price level.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, AS shifts to AS1 and then AD shifts to AD2. Which interpretation survives?
options: The policy restores output to Y1 but raises the price level to P3.
The policy lowers prices to P1 while restoring output to Y1.
The policy moves output to Y2 and keeps prices fixed at P2.
The policy leaves output at Y3 because AD cannot offset SRAS shocks.
legendary.commonError: Missing the inflation cost of accommodating a supply shock.
legendary.feedback: Accommodation moves AD1 to AD2 after AS2 shifts to AS1, restoring Y1 but raising prices to P3.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS2, AD shifts to AD2 and SRAS shifts to AS1. Which statement is correct?
options: Output stays at Y1, but the price level rises from P1 to P3.
Output rises to Y2, and the price level stays fixed at P2.
Output falls to Y3, and the price level falls from P2 to P1.
Output stays at Y1, and the price level falls from P3 to P1.
legendary.commonError: Following only one curve shift.
legendary.feedback: AD2 and AS1 intersect at Y1 and P3, so output returns to Y1 while the price level rises.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD2-AS1, AD shifts to AD1 and SRAS shifts to AS2. Which statement is correct?
options: Output stays at Y1, but the price level falls from P3 to P1.
Output falls to Y3, while the price level stays at P2.
Output rises to Y2, while the price level rises to P3.
Output stays at Y1, and the price level rises from P1 to P3.
legendary.commonError: Missing offsetting output effects from two shifts.
legendary.feedback: AD1 and AS2 intersect at Y1 and P1, so output returns to Y1 and prices fall from P3 to P1.

legendary.q: Consumer confidence falls while a major productivity improvement lowers firms’ production costs. Without knowing the size of either shock, what is certain in the short run?
options: Real output falls, while the price-level effect remains uncertain.
The price level falls, while the change in real output remains uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise because both shocks are expansionary.
Both real output and the price level fall because both shocks are contractionary.
legendary.commonError: Treating a negative demand shock and positive supply shock as if they move both outcomes in the same direction.
legendary.feedback: Lower aggregate demand and higher short-run aggregate supply both reduce the price level, but they push output in opposite directions.

legendary.q: An economy experiences an adverse supply shock. Policymakers fully stabilize real output with expansionary demand policy. What tradeoff follows?
options: The price level returns to its original value once output is restored.
Inflation and unemployment both fall because the policy removes the supply shock.
Output is stabilized, but inflation pressure becomes stronger.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because aggregate demand rises.
legendary.commonError: Assuming demand policy can reverse a supply shock without an inflation cost.
legendary.feedback: Expansionary demand policy can offset the output loss from an adverse supply shock, but it intensifies inflation pressure.

legendary.q: Real output rises while the price level falls. Which pair of simultaneous shifts can produce that pattern?
options: Both curves shift left, with the demand shift dominating the output effect.
Demand shifts right while supply shifts left, with demand dominating output.
Demand shifts left while supply shifts right, with demand dominating output.
Both curves shift right, with the supply shift dominating the price effect.
legendary.commonError: Matching one observed outcome to one curve while ignoring the second observed outcome.
legendary.feedback: Higher output can come from either shift, but a falling price level requires the rightward supply shift to dominate the demand effect.

legendary.q: A student says an aggregate-demand increase permanently raises real GDP above potential in this graph. Which correction is best?
options: D is a permanent equilibrium because SRAS never adjusts afterward.
D is above potential only short run; adjustment returns output to B.
A is above potential in the short run and B stays below potential.
C is below potential permanently because LRAS determines the price level.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: The graph shows short-run output above LRAS at D, but long-run adjustment returns output to LRAS at B while price level stays higher.

legendary.q: A student sees higher output and a higher price level at point B and concludes the graph must show an aggregate-supply increase. What is the best correction?
options: An AS increase raises both output and the price level here.
An AD increase raises both output and the price level here.
An AD increase lowers output while the price level rises here.
The graph cannot distinguish a demand change from a supply change.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: In a standard AD-AS model, a rightward AD shift raises both output and prices in the short run, unlike a rightward AS shift.

legendary.q: A student says the graph proves output must rise whenever aggregate demand increases. Which graph-based rebuttal is strongest?
options: The AD increase dominates both output and the price-level effects.
The AS decrease dominates both output and the price-level effects.
The two shifts offset the price level but reinforce the output effect.
The AS decrease offsets the AD increase in output, not prices.
legendary.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
legendary.feedback: Point B isolates the AD increase and point D isolates the AS decrease. Point C shows their combination, where the output effect is offset but inflation is amplified.

boss.q: A sharp fall in household spending is primarily what kind of macroeconomic disturbance?
boss.commonError: Confusing a spending disturbance with a production-cost disturbance.
boss.feedback: Household spending is a component of aggregate demand, so a sharp decline shifts aggregate demand left.

boss.q: An unexpected increase in energy costs usually shifts which curve first?
options: Long-run aggregate supply shifts right immediately.
boss.commonError: Treating a production-cost shock as a demand shock.
boss.feedback: Higher energy costs raise firms’ costs and reduce output supplied at each price level, shifting short-run aggregate supply left.

boss.q: A negative aggregate-demand shock normally causes what short-run combination?
options: Lower real output and a higher price level.
Higher real output and a lower price level.
Lower real output and a lower price level.
Higher real output and a higher price level.
boss.commonError: Reversing the price-level effect of a demand contraction.
boss.feedback: A leftward aggregate-demand shift reduces both equilibrium output and the price level in the short run.

boss.q: A surge in business investment shifts aggregate demand right. In the short run, what happens other things equal?
options: Real output rises and the price level falls.
Real output falls and the price level rises.
Real output and the price level both fall.
Real output and the price level both rise.
boss.commonError: Using supply-shock outcomes for a demand expansion.
boss.feedback: A rightward aggregate-demand shift moves the economy to higher short-run output and a higher price level.

boss.q: A widespread crop failure raises food-production costs. Which short-run outcome is most likely?
options: Real output falls while the price level rises.
Real output rises while the price level falls.
Real output and the price level both rise.
Real output and the price level both fall.
boss.commonError: Forgetting that an adverse supply shock creates stagflation pressure.
boss.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts short-run aggregate supply left, lowering output and raising the price level.

boss.q: Aggregate demand falls while short-run aggregate supply is unchanged. Which policy direction would most directly offset the output loss?
options: A policy that shifts aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect aggregate demand.
boss.commonError: Choosing contractionary policy during a demand-driven recession.
boss.feedback: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can shift aggregate demand right and counter a negative demand shock.

boss.q: Aggregate demand rises while short-run aggregate supply falls. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Real output rises, while the price level is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output rises.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
Both the price level and real output fall.
boss.commonError: Claiming certainty about output when the two shocks move output in opposite directions.
boss.feedback: Both shifts raise the price level, but aggregate demand raises output while adverse supply lowers it.

boss.q: Aggregate demand falls while short-run aggregate supply rises. Which outcome is certain?
options: Real output falls, while the price level is uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output is uncertain.
boss.commonError: Missing the shared price-level direction of the two shifts.
boss.feedback: A demand contraction and favorable supply shock both lower the price level, but they push output in opposite directions.

boss.q: After an adverse supply shock, policymakers use expansionary demand policy to restore output. Which risk remains?
options: The price level may rise even more than it did from the original shock.
Unemployment must rise because aggregate demand increased.
Short-run aggregate supply automatically returns to its old position.
The economy must move below potential output.
boss.commonError: Assuming output stabilization eliminates the inflation tradeoff.
boss.feedback: Demand expansion can support output after a supply shock, but it adds inflation pressure rather than repairing supply.

legendaryBoss.q: Government purchases rise while a technology breakthrough lowers unit costs. If output rises but the price level is unchanged, what does the evidence imply?
options: Neither curve shifted because the price level did not change.
The opposing price effects approximately offset while both shifts raise output.
Aggregate demand fell while short-run aggregate supply rose.
Aggregate demand rose while short-run aggregate supply fell.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assuming an unchanged price level means no macroeconomic shifts occurred.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Higher government purchases shift aggregate demand right and better technology shifts short-run aggregate supply right. Both raise output, while their price effects can offset.

legendaryBoss.q: Oil prices rise sharply and the central bank expands aggregate demand enough to keep real output unchanged. Compared with the initial equilibrium, what is most likely?
options: The price level is unchanged because real output is unchanged.
The price level is lower because monetary expansion reduces costs.
The price level is higher because both the supply shock and policy raise it.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because interest rates fall.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Equating stable output with a stable price level.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The adverse supply shock raises the price level, and the demand expansion used to stabilize output adds additional price pressure.

legendaryBoss.q: Consumer spending collapses at the same time firms adopt a major cost-saving technology. Prices fall sharply, but output changes little. Which interpretation fits best?
options: A positive demand shock and adverse supply shock offset in the price level.
Only aggregate demand shifted because prices fell.
Only short-run aggregate supply shifted because output was stable.
A negative demand shock and positive supply shock had offsetting output effects.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Using one observed variable to infer only one curve shifted.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Both shocks lower the price level, while one lowers output and the other raises it. Similar magnitudes can leave output nearly unchanged.

repairQuestions.q: A sharp fall in consumer confidence is primarily which kind of shock?
repairQuestions.feedback: Lower consumer confidence reduces consumption and shifts aggregate demand left.

repairQuestions.q: A sudden rise in oil prices is primarily which kind of shock?
options: A change in the money multiplier
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher input costs shift SRAS left, making this a negative supply shock.

repairQuestions.q: Stagflation combines:
options: Balanced budgets and low interest rates
repairQuestions.feedback: Stagflation is the difficult combination of rising prices and weak employment/output conditions.

repairQuestions.q: An adverse supply shock creates a policy problem because inflation and unemployment can:
repairQuestions.feedback: Adverse supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment together.

repairQuestions.q: If AD falls while SRAS also falls, what outcome is certain?
repairQuestions.feedback: Both a leftward AD shift and a leftward SRAS shift reduce equilibrium output; their price-level effects conflict.

repairQuestions.q: A negative AD shock usually causes output and the price level to:
repairQuestions.feedback: A negative AD shock lowers output and the price level.

repairQuestions.q: An adverse supply shock usually causes output to fall and prices to:
repairQuestions.feedback: An adverse supply shock lowers output and raises prices.

bridgeQuestions.q: An oil shock raises inflation while unemployment rises. Why is policy difficult?
options: Stimulus risks more inflation, while tightening risks more unemployment
Stimulus always lowers inflation, while tightening always raises output
Both stimulus and tightening shift SRAS right
Neither inflation nor unemployment can respond
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A supply shock creates a tradeoff: supporting output can worsen inflation, while fighting inflation can worsen unemployment.

bridgeQuestions.q: Consumer confidence collapses, shifting AD left and leaving real output below potential. With no new policy response, which process becomes relevant next?
options: Weak wage and price pressures can shift SRAS right over time, moving output back toward potential.
Aggregate demand must automatically shift right to its original position.
LRAS must shift left until it reaches the depressed output level.
A permanent adverse supply shock must occur before output can recover.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A negative AD shock can create a recessionary gap; with no policy response, wage and expectation adjustment can shift SRAS right over time.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops at the short-run demand-shock outcome and does not connect the recessionary gap to long-run self-correction.

bridgeQuestions.q: A major oil-price spike hits the economy. In the short run, output and the price level likely:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts SRAS left, lowering output and raising prices.
